## Chapter 1: Carrion

### Notes

### Text

When Zuko was nine, he saw a lion vulture eating a carcass on the beach. At first, he didn’t realize what was happening. But then the bird ripped a limb off of…whatever it was that had been brought in with the tide, and Azula had made a noise like she had never seen anything quite so disgustingly fascinating, and Zuko had realized that he was watching a dead thing that used to be an animal get torn apart.

It had made him queasy and uncomfortable which had made him mad because he hated being uncomfortable, even then. Especially then. Azula had noticed, of course, because she noticed everything, and had teased him incessantly about it, and had started describing in gleeful detail the things lion vultures would do to his body if he were to drop dead on the spot.

“They don’t even have to wait for you to be *dead*,” she had smirked, sharp and toothy. “They just need you to be still. Imagine not being able to move while one of those does *that* to you.”

Now, watching sea vultures circling on thermals above their cobbled-together, miraculously still afloat after who-knows-how-many-days raft, Zuko distantly wonders if seven years later he’s about going to find out. Maybe he was supposed to find out four years ago. Maybe if he had just let it happen then, he wouldn’t be awake for it now. Punishment, he supposes, for never being able to do anything right. Not even die.

&#45;-

He is salt-parched, drier than he ever thought he could be, hot in a way that makes bile sit in the back of his throat. His skin feels fragile and tender and burned because if Zuko knows anything, he knows what it feels like to burn. He wants to try to bend the heat away from himself, but he can’t seem to get a grasp on his own inner flame and the effort to do so seems…monumental. Which is probably a bad thing, if Zuko had enough energy to care about that anymore. At least it means that Zuko doesn’t have to try to do anything right now.

The sun is incessant, leeching away what little water he has left, buzzing through his bloodstream so that he can’t even escape into sleep, can only sprawl on his back and feel his limbs too heavy to move and his thoughts too sluggish to be of any use.

Uncle isn’t awake. That isn’t good, for a firebender as strong as he is, at the height of Agni’s arc across the sky.

&#45;-

Zuko isn’t sure how far Agni has moved across the sky when he vaguely remembers that he’s supposed to care about that.

&#45;-

Zuko watches the sea vultures circling and is reminded of Gao and the thought barely hurts at all, which is how Zuko knows he’s really in trouble. He tries thinking of Sokka just to see if he can still feel anything except burned and it hurts deep in his bones, which is awful, but at least Zuko knows he’s still alive.

Agni’s flaming cock, it better not hurt this fucking much to be dead.

&#45;-

Bad as the sun is, it’s worse under the moon. There’s relief from the baking heat, but under her cold glow the wide ocean is too easy to see as tinged electric-blue, the normal swell of waves too easily twisting into reaching hands, rising heads, the Great Spirit of the Ocean finally come for his vengeance, for the last firebenders to escape the North.

Zuko saw the others who escaped, floating face down and bloated. He wonders if they made it far enough toward the Earth Kingdom for the sea vultures to get them, too, or if the creatures of the ocean claimed them first.

&#45;-

It’s hard for Zuko to remember when he is in time. Slowly being seared by Agni’s light, floating on the waves in a motion so unfamiliar to anything he is used to, barely conscious, barely alive, Zuko can’t quite remember if he is sixteen or thirteen. This sticky feeling is terrifyingly familiar, if he had the energy for terror anymore, being burned and confused and hazy and dizzy with no idea what’s in front of him or quite how he got here.

&#45;-

He can’t sleep under the harsh eyes of the new moon. Not without reliving over and over the gut-wrenching terror of the Ocean unleashing its rage, of Zhao being swept away. Not without feeling over and over the desperate fear that they weren’t going to make it out of Agna Qel’a, choking in its intensity until Zuko is gasping and jerking and screaming back into wakefulness.

It takes Zuko days to realize that he should have been more afraid that they *would* make it out of the city, days to realize the creeping horror of being alone on the wide ocean with only the tides and what they could salvage and aphorisms and rambling parables and no idea if they will ever make it to land again.

Zuko’s already stopped being able to fully track the passage of time when it occurs to him that what he should really have feared is the way Uncle goes quieter and quieter until he stops saying anything altogether.

&#45;-

People talk about death like it’s a kind thing when they can bring themselves to talk about it at all. Gentle euphemisms about slipping quietly into the long night, about the end coming like an old friend, about the relief of escape to those who desperately need it. Zuko remembers those words, those cloying phrases, the way they pierced black, pain-lit unconsciousness when no one thought he would ever wake up at all, let alone be awake enough to hear.

Zuko knew then—knows now—that all those sweet turns of phrase are a load of shit. He has felt what it’s like to stand at the edge of that long night and feel his inner flame gutter and gasp and fade. He has felt the creeping cold hook into his lungs, the needles of ice creeping down his nerves one by one. There is no peace, no calm, no relief in those last moments. Only the primal panic of a wild thing willing to tear itself apart before giving in.

Back then Zuko had shielded himself from the cold using the one thing he had that made sense, the directive to never give up without a fight, simple and straightforward and easy because if Zuko knew anything it was how to refuse to stay down. Everything else had become anger, because rage was the only thing that put a spark back into his inner flame enough to melt the ice away.

Now…Zuko doesn’t know what to anchor himself on, now. He doesn’t want to give up, but —is it giving up, when he's already fought so hard and failed so completely?

&#45;-

Uncle is important, he remembers, as the moon begins to stretch talons of white across the empty ocean. Uncle surviving is important. If he concentrates, Zuko can still hear Uncle breathing over the rasp of his own breath, which is good. But Zuko hasn’t heard Uncle speak for…he can’t remember when, actually. Which is bad. They ran out of food…a long time ago. And a mostly intact teacup isn’t much use surrounded by saltwater, not when there’s no rain in the sky. Dry tea leaves are somehow even more disgusting than hot leaf juice, as it turns out. Even Uncle couldn’t pretend they weren’t.

They ran out of those a long time ago, too.

&#45;-

Agni prods Zuko out of a muddled, tense, thoroughly unrestful state that couldn’t really be referred to as sleep. He keeps seeing the ships being torn apart like paper, the bodies of men and women tossed around like toys, shredded, plunged into water so deep and dark and absolute that afterward you could think nothing living had ever been there at all. And for what? To rile a neutral party that didn’t particularly like the Fire Nation and wasn’t in any way inclined to do a single thing about it? For a fucking fish?

Making sure a travesty like that never happens again is also important, Zuko decides. Not that he’ll ever be in a position again to have anything to say about it. Not that he ever did.

&#45;-

At first Zuko thinks he's crying, which is so thoroughly unhelpful when you’re already surrounded by all the saltwater you could ever need that it takes him a long moment to realize through his self-disgust that actually, it’s not tears, it’s rain. Light, just a drizzle if it could even be called that, but fresh and cool and an aching relief on his burned skin and against his painfully dried-out scar. Zuko drags his tongue over cracked lips and tastes water and blood, and it’s the sweetest thing he can ever remember having.

Somehow, he musters the presence of mind to flail out an arm, to scrabble with leaden fingers through their meager supplies without turning his face away from the sky. He flips the teacup upright, cradling it carefully against the raft until the all-too-brief drizzle burns away into mist and unrelenting sun.

Zuko wants to scream, at that, but he doesn’t let himself because there’s no fucking point and he can’t afford to waste the energy on it even if there was. He just drags himself upright, carefully cradling the little half-teacup of water in his hand, staring hazily down at the way the blue glaze is refracted by the rippling water. It reminds him of Sokka’s eyes and it’s the stupidest, most useless thought he’s ever fucking had. Zuko shoves it viciously aside because he cannot afford to cry right now, not when he would probably lose every bit of water he has left. Zuko can’t do anything about Sokka. It’s far too late for that, no matter what it had felt like to lean into his warmth and pretend for one bare stretch of time that Zuko could let him beat back the cold.

Zuko shuffles to Uncle’s side instead, panting with the effort, legs trembling to find stability as his weight throws off the balance of their precarious raft. He grits his teeth and keeps crawling and carefully tips the water past Uncle’s chapped lips until there isn’t any left, until that’s the only loss Zuko wants to cry over.

&#45;-

The drizzle doesn’t stop the sea vultures from circling, lower now, in greater numbers now, getting ready now. Zuko didn’t expect it to, not really. He wonders if Azula will be disappointed that she wasn’t there in the end to see what they do to him and find out if her words were true. She had stayed on that beach long after Zuko had left, had brought it up again and again, drawn and painted it over and over, acted it out and talked about it in horrifying detail until Mother finally begged her to stop, please stop, they were trying to eat dinner. Father had laughed.

Zuko’s brain goes quiet at that, blank quiet, safe quiet. He thinks about opening his eyes, but he can feel Agni right above him and isn’t particularly interested in losing what sight he has left. Even firebenders can’t stare directly into the sun, not for long. So Zuko just stays still, so still, reaching up with his fire sense, ignoring the way his own inner flame is behaving in a way he doesn’t want to think about right now, ignoring the heat of Uncle beside him except to be relieved that it’s still there.

He reaches toward the sun as if he could take it in his hands and extinguish it, finally feeling the shape of black-bodied birds, hot and lazily circling after degrees and degrees of soaking in Agni’s rays. At one point one of them breaks off from the others, a hot shape spiraling down toward him.

Zuko’s breath is thin and uneven as he opens his palm, calling a ragged flame to life, such a wavering thing that most toddlers could do better. Then he wrenches his wrist, fist clenched, feeling the fire snap into a jagged dagger.

Zuko’s smile is sharp and toothy and bleeding as he slits open his good eye, tracking with sight and fire. Sea vultures hunt near the coast. Azula had loved to remind him of that.

If they try to eat him, Zuko is going to eat them back.

&#45;-

“Prince Zuko.” Zuko glances up at Uncle’s rasping voice, dry and harsh and amazing. Uncle is still lying prone, but his eyes are sharp as always as his gaze slowly tracks down Zuko’s body. He relaxes when he realizes the blood isn’t Zuko’s, closing his eyes again, a familiar neutral-but-laughing tone to his words that has Zuko’s shoulders unwinding, just a bit. “I see you have taken to sea life with new vigor.”

Zuko looks down at his hands crusted in blood, his bare chest spattered with more and who knows what else, then to the third bird he managed to shoot down with his fire. His hair is still dripping saltwater down his chest from his plunge into the ocean to retrieve the body, red-tinged rivulets seeping into his waistband. His cheek itches where he forgot his hands were filthy and rubbed at his face, leaving a crust of he doesn’t even want to know what behind.

“Something like that,” he finally mutters, bending back to trying to clean his kill with a jagged edge of sea vulture bone, keeping his good ear tilted to track Uncle’s even breathing and his good eye on the horizon in the direction the birds keep coming from.

&#45;-

The seaside resort is jarring, more dissonant for Zuko than any battle or screaming match or gleeful, pointed half-truth. Maybe because Zuko can’t seem to find it in himself to trust that any of it is real. He is pretty sure that Uncle is relaxing in a mud bath right now means that Zuko messed up somewhere along the way, he just can’t figure out where.

Zuko had managed to keep them going on the water, had hauled them to the beach and dragged them into town. But the moment they hit the resort Uncle had worked some kind of benevolent flirtatious old man magic with the front desk clerk and now here they are, with fine robes and clean rooms and baths and food and water and servants. As if none of it had ever happened, except for the dark rust of blood still beneath Zuko’s fingernails because he refuses to get a manicure and risk his calluses being worn off no matter how great Uncle says it will make him feel, and he can’t seem to scrub well enough on his own.

Uncle is relaxing as if there’s nothing to worry about, as if there’s never been anything to worry about, and it somehow sets Zuko even more on edge. Maybe because if Uncle is going to close his eyes and put fucking cucumber melon slices on them then Zuko is going to be the one to stay fucking alert. Maybe because Zuko still can’t stop flinching at every burst of laughter as if it were ice shattering beneath flaming stones. Every quiet, gentle attendant is a warrior coming up on his blind side. The calming wading pool throws him back to clawing his way up beneath falling chunks of metal, frantically kicking off his boots and layers, desperately clinging to Uncle’s hand because if he lets go then they’re never going to find each other again, not in this wreckage of wasted lives and twisted metal that used to be a fleet.

“Prince Zuko.” Uncle’s gentle voice jolts him out of his reverie and Zuko whips his head around, ignoring the fact that he doesn’t know how long he was staring into space or how many times Uncle tried to get his attention. The cucumber melon slices are gone. “Perhaps some calming tea would—”

“I don’t want *tea*.”

“Then perhaps a soothing massage. It is so relaxing, and would promote healing and recov —”

“No.”

“Then perhaps—”

“Shut up,” Zuko orders, repressing a shudder at the idea of some stranger’s hands on his skin, at being face down and prone and vulnerable in front of someone else by *choice*.

“Nephew.” Zuko glowers and finally meets Uncle’s gaze. “You are safe here.” Zuko snorts at that foolishness. “*We* are safe here. You can relax.”

“I’m fine,” Zuko snaps, and hides his hands when Uncle’s eyes flick to the blood still under his nails. “I’m *fine*.”

“Very well,” Uncle finally agrees. “Then it should be no problem to take a break and let your body rest. A nice sauna, perhaps? The steam would feel wonderful—”

“I don’t want to do that,” Zuko growls.

“Perhaps a game of pai sho, then.”

“*No,”* Zuko grits out. When has he ever wanted to play pai sho?

“Well then—”

“Why do you want me to *do* something so bad?” Zuko snarls, because he might be a twitchy fucking mess in the corner but that doesn’t mean he has to do something, even if he *hates* sitting here and pretending that everything is *fine*.

Uncle hesitates. “I am just concerned about your—”

“Stop it.” Zuko knows what a deflection sounds like when Uncle makes one. “Why.” Zuko narrows his eyes. It’s hard to read Uncle beneath the mud bath, and Zuko isn’t particularly good at reading people to begin with, but he’s fairly certain that Uncle is regretting something he has said.

“There is nothing for you to—”

“*Why?”*

Uncle sighs, sitting upright in his mud bath as if that lends the conversation any additional gravity. “I think that if you cannot find a way to relax and meditate, then it would be good to have something to occupy yourself with.” His tone is heavy and gentle in a particular way that makes Zuko want to crawl out of his skin. He hates when Uncle gets like this, always feels like he’s being slowly choked by it. Thank Agni that it only ever happens when he’s trying to make Zuko talk about—

Zuko snaps his head toward the window where the mid-summer sun is starting to set, then back toward Uncle who is looking at him steadily and kindly and a little bit sad. His inner flame wrenches back on itself. Zuko had lost track of how many days they spent at sea between escaping the North and finally making shore. He didn’t think it had been that many. He thought he still had time.

Zuko can taste smoke on the back of his tongue as he stalks out without another word, resisting the urge to slam the door behind him only because the door is fucking rice paper and he already snapped one and almost lit another on fire and who was Agni-damned stupid enough anyway to build a resort for Fire Nation citizens out of wood and paper. Zuko doesn’t know where he’s going, just that he needs to get out of here, away from Uncle, away from the attendants who won’t look at his face and the patrons who won’t stop staring at it. Zuko always loses what little tolerance he has to begin with for anything that remotely resembles *spectating* on the anniversary of his Agni Kai.

It must show on his face—Zuko learned early, how to warn people off with his new face— because no one tries to interact with him as he storms through the spa and out onto the grounds. Zuko finally stops when he reaches the cliffs overlooking the ocean and physically runs out of room. He glares at the fence blocking his path, briefly considers lighting it on fire, and then hops over it with an annoyed grumble instead. He settles with his back to a post, arms wrapped around his knees, toes inching into open air and waves crashing against rock below.

It sounds too much like his dreams. But Zuko doesn’t know where else to go, can’t face the idea of walking back through the resort to reach the forest instead.

Zuko can maybe forgive himself for not realizing the date all things considered, but forgiveness isn’t going to change the fact that he is still absolutely fucked. He isn’t *ready.* Zuko would hate this day to begin with, but Azula always makes it worse. She sent him to his banishment with a letter—Zuko burned it, not that it did anything to help him forget what it said—and commemorates it every year with more sharp words and brutal reminders, her letter always timed to arrive at the worst possible time, always throwing him right off his feet again just when he’s starting to feel a little more steady. Zuko isn’t ready for it, hasn’t had time to prepare and brace himself for whatever daggers she’s going to unsheathe this time.

Maybe Azula won’t be able to find him off the *Wani*. Maybe she'll think he died in the North...

But no. They both know Zuko is far too stubborn for that. And Uncle hasn’t exactly been inconspicuous the past few days here. Besides, Gao always seemed to be able to find Zuko no matter where he was in the world. He would expect any messenger hawk of Azula’s to be just as good.

Zuko heaves out a hard sigh and tips his head back, the fencepost salt-worn and rough against the back of his shaved head. No sea vultures in the sky this time, just the normal lizard gulls that seem to dot every coastline. He can’t stop reflexively searching the sky for the familiar shape of a messenger hawk even though the idea of hawks in general right now fills him with dread. And what would Zuko even do if Gao were here? Write to Sokka? Ask him to resend the last letter that Zuko lost to the waves before he ever got to read it? Try to find him? Try to put his thoughts into words and hope that somehow, after the North, Sokka would still be willing to read them?

Sokka didn’t leave Zuko to die on the tundra, so he can’t hate Zuko completely, but Zuko knows there are worlds of difference between not completely hating someone and wanting to hear from them. He is painfully aware that he has no right to hope for anything anymore when it comes to Sokka. That he never did. That he never should have in the first place.

He tries to content himself with the fact that Sokka is safe. Or at least he was, when Zuko last saw him, stumbling toward the Oasis as Zuko chased after Zhao , leaving Uncle to stay and try to do what he could for the Moon Spirit. And Uncle had said that Sokka wasn’t physically harmed. Which Zuko knows is careful wording, because Uncle had also said the girl had died and that Sokka had been distressed, in that particular understatement way that Zuko knows actually meant utterly and completely devastated. The idea of Sokka in physical pain makes Zuko’s inner flame feel wild like it’s going to burst, but the thought of Sokka in emotional pain hollows him out inside.

Zuko shudders, breathing around the emptiness of it, trying to pace his breaths like Uncle taught him to years ago. He tries to meditate to the sound of crashing waves but he keeps needing to remind himself that these waves are crashing against rock and not metal, so he switches to trying not to light the grass on fire in his fury that even this thing that he didn’t know he had, this learned comfort in the sound of the ocean after years on the *Wani*, has been taken and turned to violence and fear and pain.

Eventually Zuko gives up and just stares, watching the sun slowly setting on the waves and trying to think of nothing at all, wondering when Azula’s hawk will find him and how much more he can possibly hurt when it does. He knows that Azula can always find a way to do the thing that's hardest for everyone else. Zuko has learned by now to expect it.

&#45;-

He still never expected her to come in person, though.

&#45;-

Zuko tracks Uncle down later in the morning, the half-load of bread he snagged from the kitchen long since gone. Uncle is walking the beach, slow and contemplative, a basket in hand. Every few steps he pauses, bends down to consider something in the sand, and every once in a while places it in the basket. Zuko isn’t quite sure what he’s collecting and doesn’t much care to find out. All he can hear is the pounding surf ringing in his good ear, all he can see on the sand are bits of armor and metal and things that used to be people washed up by the waves.

“What are you doing?” Zuko finally rasps, biting off his words as he tries to force away the tension in his shoulders because he isn’t there anymore, they made it out. They made it.

“What does it look like I’m doing, Nephew?”

“Wasting time.”

Uncle raises an eyebrow. “Do we have somewhere to be, then?”

“Did you see the ship?”

“Hm. Yes.” As if anyone could miss the towering monstrosity currently crowding out every other boat in the harbor.

“Then you know we do.”

Uncle sighs, resettling his basket on his arm and looking out over the ocean, away from Azula’s transport. “I suppose we do, then. Do you know, this beach has quite the diverse set of shells on its shores…”

Uncle won’t stop talking about seashells the whole walk back to their room, as if Zuko cared at all about the difference between a cockle and a scallop beyond his ability to eat them.

“Why do you keep gathering all these useless things,” Zuko mutters, glaring at the basket and the way the woven straw is sagging under the weight of shells.

“They aren’t useless, Nephew!” Uncle protests as he steps into their room. “They are living art! The result of a lifetime of effort for a small creature!”

“A lifetime of effort that we have to carry now,” Zuko snaps, nearly running into Uncle’s back as the older man pulls up short. “*Move*, why in Agni’s—”

“Hello, Uncle Iroh. Brother.”

Zuko’s head jerks up at the lazy, amused voice he hasn’t heard in nearly four years outside of nightmares. The first thought that hits him is that Azula has grown up. It’s a totally useless thing to think, Zuko obviously knows she’s not still eleven—he could practically hear her crowing in sharp delight when she wrote about being fitted for her first set of armor as if she knew precisely the moment Zuko was scrounging for coins to replace his. But it’s different to see it. The Azula looking back at him is no longer a little girl. She doesn’t have to reach up to slouch insolently against tables anymore. Her face is sharper, eyebrows narrower, lips painted red with a brightness that is jarring, that doesn’t quite go with the paleness of her face and traps the eye on every smirk and moue and twist of displeasure, which is maybe the point.

The confidence is exactly the same, though. And her tawny eyes haven’t changed as they take him in return, narrowing in familiar judgment at whatever she sees.

Zuko’s second thought is that trailing Uncle into the room was a mistake. It was deferential, inferior, subordinate, not commanding, not the actions of a Crown Prince. Zuko can feel his shoulders tensing, can see Azula noticing which only makes him tense more, and he barely holds back the urge to openly snarl that he’s starting whatever this is just as wrong-footed as he knows she intended him to be.

“What are you doing here,” he snaps, crossing his arms and immediately regretting it because Agni’s flaming dick, could he look any more defensive.

“Tsk,” her nose wrinkles. “Is that any way to greet your sister after so long? So rude. I know you’ve been away from civilization but really, I wouldn’t have expected all your…polish, to rub off so easily, Zuzu.”

Zuko does snarl at that, his step forward cut short as Uncle opens his arms in an expansive gesture. “Princess Azula,” Iroh says, tone hospitable and neutral in a way that has her lips twitching in annoyance. “What a surprise, to find you here. To what do we owe the honor?”

“So *direct*. I’m not used to that from you, Uncle.” She raises an eyebrow like she’s inviting Zuko into some shared joke and flicks a speck of imaginary dust off her cuff. “I come with a message from home. After the…regrettable incident in the North—”

Zuko almost screams, and he’s sure she sees it.

“—Our Father has done some thinking. The Fire Lord has decided that family is too valuable to be so far-flung. You just can’t find good help these days.” She rolls her eyes, as if everything in the North could have been avoided if there were just competent support staff on hand. Agni’s tits, Zuko might actually light something on fire.

“What are you saying,” Zuko grinds out when she doesn’t continue. He hates these games, has never been good at them. He needs far more clues than she usually offers, and he knows that she knows that which just leads to a spiraling of knowing that she knows that he knows that she knows that—

“I’m saying, Zuzu, that family are the only ones you can really trust.” A heavy, expectant silence, eyes on his face. “Father regrets your banishment. He wants you home.”

Zuko can’t breathe. His mind is frantic, trying to parse her words, trying to fit them into a shape that makes sense. Zuko knows that Azula always lies, knows that more than anything, but the words she is saying—they’re everything he has ever wanted to hear, and the way she’s saying them…

“You should be *happy*, Zuzu,” Azula chides, finally sitting upright in her chair. “Excited. Grateful. I just gave you great news.”

“I am sure he just needs time to process,” Iroh murmurs when Zuko can only stare, dumbstruck. “We both do. Your news is so…unexpected.”

Azula waves Iroh away with a flick of her hand, lips tensing at the interruption. “I’m not talking to you, old man,” she huffs before pining Zuko with a tawny stare again. “Did you hear me, Brother? Our Father wants you to come home.”

Zuko barely even hears the awful nickname, the one she insists on using. “Father… regrets…?” It’s not a concept he finds he can wrap his mind around.

“Yes,” Azula rolls her eyes. “It *does* happen every once in a while, I assure you.”

Especially after you lose an entire Navy, but Zuko has still never heard anything more ridiculous in his life. Except Azula keeps *saying* it, and the way she is weaving lies in with truths—And she came here, in person, herself, instead of sending the news by hawk, or messenger. Which makes it so…personal. And she isn’t taunting, much, really, which is… nice. Unexpected.

For a moment Zuko lets himself imagine home. Let’s himself breathe the hot air, smell the spices redolent on the breeze, feel the weight of silk robes instead of armor, hear the quiet rustling of turtle ducks in the reeds.

“I see you need more time,” Azula murmurs, rising smoothly to her feet and gently pulling him to the present. “You can have the night. We leave tomorrow morning on the tide. I hope to see you there.” She pauses at his shoulder, her next words quiet, just for him. “The turtle duck pond is exactly the same, Brother.”

Zuko sucks in a hard breath staring blindly at her empty seat as she slips out the door. He feels like he is drowning in the idea of that garden, so quiet and serene, with nothing of the ocean or war or violence. Agni, he is drowning in the idea of being wanted, his craving for it deep and intense and numbing until it makes his hands tremble and his lungs feel tight.

She never even stared at his scar.

&#45;-

Zuko is too anxious to sit still, wild thoughts making his limbs buzz with nervous energy until he feels like he might break out of his own skin. He wants to train, to move, to run, but he can’t leave the room because it would be just like Azula to decide to take a spa day now that she’s casually upended Zuko’s place in the world. He paces under Uncle’s careful eye instead, which just itches along his skin in a different way. Zuko hates when people watch him without speaking, hates having to try to guess at their thoughts, hates trying to figure out if he’s the one who is supposed to speak first. He’s never right.

“You are restless, Nephew,” Uncle finally observes, cradling a cup of tea in his hands, a slight frown on his brow as Zuko shoots him an annoyed glance. What a useless comment.

“I have a lot to think about,” Zuko mutters.

“You are thinking of your sister’s words?”

“It’s unbelievable,” Zuko says, shaking his head. “We could go *home*.” Home, with its still waters and soft grass and gentle breezes and friendly, hungry animals nibbling at your cuffs looking for bread. Home, just the way he left it.

“Yes. It is rather unbelievable.”

Zuko scowls at the naked skepticism in Uncle’s tone. “You heard what she said. She said Father wants his family close.”

“I did hear that, yes.”

Zuko scowls harder. “She said that what happened up there—that it changed things.”

“Hmm.”

Zuko’s scowl is a glare now. “Why is it so hard to believe that?” Because Zuko can’t imagine *not* being changed by the North. He can’t fathom that any corner of the world could be unchanged.

“My brother is not known for changing his mind,” Uncle says quietly, gravely, gratingly.

“Because you know him so well?” Zuko challenges, inner fire sharp and restless.

“I think that in our family, things are often not the way they seem, Nephew.”

Zuko feels his fingertips spark, at that. Does Uncle really think that Zuko doesn’t *know*? Zuko wants to rage, that Uncle can sit there and say that and act like he sees so much when he sees *nothing*. That he can act like Zuko doesn’t know that lesson far more than Iroh ever will.

Instead of screaming or lighting this fucking tinderbox of a resort on fire Zuko just glares and throws himself back into pacing. Every step shifts his thoughts between the North and the waters and long fire-lit council rooms and the image Azula had painted for him. Between what it would feel like to regain his honor, to have his Father’s regard, to finally be able to walk the halls of the palace unafraid, and all that it took to reach this point.

&#45;-

“You act like you don’t even want to go home,” Zuko spits out in the middle of the afternoon as Uncle heats up yet another pot of tea. “Do you even *care* about the Fire Nation?”

“I care *deeply* about the Fire Nation, Prince Zuko,” Uncle says, pausing to meet his eyes. “I have always cared.”

“Then why don’t you care about going back!”

“Nephew,” Uncle sighs, setting aside the pot. “Why do *you* want to go back?”

“What?” Zuko spins around to turn his good ear toward Uncle, feeling the pull on his scar as his face twists in confusion.

“Why are you so eager to return home with your sister,” Uncle says gently, as if the question makes any more sense with repetition.

“…Why wouldn’t I be,” Zuko finally says, uncertainty knocking him off the edge of his anger.

“You would give up your quest?” Uncle probes, the question for once truly neutral with nothing else beneath which is weird and unsettling and makes Zuko feel like he’s being dangled over a sudden drop.

“The mission is to regain my honor so that I can go home,” Zuko says, speaking slowly. “Home is the whole point.” And he doesn’t have forever. And Azula is *here*.

“You think your father can give it back to you?”

Zuko isn’t sure if Uncle means his honor or his home, but either way it makes him grit his teeth. “It’s my birthright.” And it makes his inner flame tangle and snarl to need to justify this. It feels far too close to the questions Sokka asked him, the ones that used to scrape him raw, that still do when Zuko forgets that it’s dangerous to think about them.

“Will your birthright truly make you happy, Nephew?” Uncle frowns, concern in his eyes as Zuko pulls himself tighter and tighter in front of him.

“Happiness has nothing to do with it,” Zuko snaps. It never has. Responsibility and duty are what matter, have always been what mattered. His inner flame is shoving against his skin that Uncle can stand there as someone who used to be a Crown Prince and act as if he doesn’t know that. “But I wouldn’t expect someone who walked away from his responsibilities to understand.”

Zuko hurls himself back into pacing, ending the conversation and fixing his eyes on the floor and refusing to feel anything at all over the sadness on Uncle’s face.

&#45;-

The sun has barely finished cresting the horizon when Zuko sets out for Azula’s ship, dressed in the sturdiest loungewear he could find in the resort, which really isn’t saying much but is better than showing up in a robe like everyone else seems to wear. What little remains of his possessions are on his back. Zuko wishes he had indulged Uncle’s insistence in manicures and hair treatments and facials now that he’s going to be standing at Azula’s perfectly coiffed side looking like some kind of low-budget player in a decades-used costume. There’s nothing to do about it, though, so he just calls the tightness in his chest annoyance, which is easy enough to slide into rage, and uses the anger to bury the way his knees are still weak with relief over the fact that Uncle is walking at his side.

Zuko also uses it to bury a stab of pure envy as he approaches Azula’s ship. It's fucking gigantic compared to the *Wani*, polished to a high shine. It clearly never needed hasty repairs with whatever materials were on hand or had to scrounge cobbled together parts and pieces from the cast-off scraps left in the shipyard. The long walk up the gangplank feels endless, unfamiliar. But it’s still a Fire Nation ship, and it still feels a little bit like coming home to step onto its deck and hear the echo of metal beneath his boots again.

“Brother! Uncle!” Azula’s voice is delighted as she calls across the deck. “I’m so glad that you decided to join us! And just in time for the tide.”

“Azula,” Zuko says stiffly as she strides toward them. Her head comes up to his chin now. He didn’t notice yesterday. “You look well.”

“You look well also, Zuzu. It seems resort life suits you.” Her words are light, her smile easy, inviting Zuko in on the joke, and it's dissonant and weird and Zuko hates it. He isn’t used to seeing Azula baring so few teeth and her statement is so absurd that he can’t stop his involuntarily glance at Uncle in confusion. Zuko has seen himself in the mirror. By no definition of the word does he look ‘well.’

“And Uncle, thank you for joining us as well.” Her usual terseness with Uncle is nowhere to be seen and Zuko has to fight to keep from shifting uncomfortably at its absence. “You both must be ready to settle in after so long without proper accommodation as suits your rank. I must oversee our departure as acting commander on board, of course.” She sounds genuinely regretful about it which makes Zuko even more uncomfortable. Azula has never regretted a single thing in her entire life. “But I can have these officers show you to your rooms, if that suits, Brother, Uncle?”

“Of course, Princess Azula,” Uncle murmurs, casting his eyes over the bustle of a tightly run ship ready to depart, so different than the snarling and haranguing that would usually accompany the activity on the *Wani*. “We would be honored.”

“You two.” Azula waves a lazy hand that has two soldiers snapping to attention. “You will show our most honored guests to their rooms.”

“Of course, Princess!”

Zuko is jealous of the immediate obedience and the crips deference and precise adherence to regulation with none of Jee’s neutral-but-fuck-you attitude, so much that for a moment Zuko forgets to be wary. Not that Jee will ever give that attitude again. He probably died like the rest of them, terrified and drowning and alone, choking on the ocean he had lived his life on.

“Prince Zuko?” Uncle’s careful inquiry has Zuko jolting out of his reverie and he scowls to realize that he must have missed some question or request because everyone is staring at him. He grunts, jerking his head to show his readiness and carefully controlling his relieved breath when their guides usher them forward. That was the right response, apparently.

“This is a new tiger shark class ship, is it not?” Uncle asks their escort, looking with interest around the deck.

“Yes, Sir, it is.”

“Hm, wonderful! They’ve made so many updates since my day, you know. Back when I started our biggest ships could only hold two hundred soldiers!”

“This is just a bit bigger than that, Sir,” the other escort grins. “We have five hundred on board, and we’re not even at full capacity.”

“Wonderful, wonderful, so tell me…” Zuko sighs and hurries a half-step forward, trying to get distance from Uncle’s curious chatter as he asks about where the mess halls have been placed relative to the sleeping quarters, and what type of supplies the kitchen puts out, and do they still have the boiler room backing onto the kitchen or did they solve that particular design oversight? He doesn’t care about how the piping can distribute hot water throughout the ship for cold climates, or that the command and officer’s accommodations have been placed in the forward tower, or that the brig has replaced the barracks below the waterline where it’s always—

Zuko freezes at the top of the stairs leading below deck, slowly turning to look back over the deck toward the command tower at the front of the ship, back where they first walked onto the ship, back where Azula originally came from.

“Is something wrong, Sir?”

Zuko drags his eyes from the tower to their escort, taking in and actually registering the full armor, including helmets. Who wears helmets during routine operation? Even *Zuko* doesn’t do that. He flicks his gaze over their shoulders, counting the number of soldiers who seem quite busy with nothing much at all. Zuko knows enough about ships to know whatever they’re doing over there that it is *not* part of preparing to sail.

“Actually,” Zuko says slowly, inner flame creeping up to slide under his skin. “I think I would love to join my sister.”

“A wonderful idea, Nephew,” Uncle agrees immediately, smile magnificent in its enthusiasm.

“Sir, the Princess asked us to take you to your rooms.”

“And your *Prince*,” Zuko growls, “Is ordering you to take us to the command tower.”

“Sir, the *Princess* is in command of this capture, and—”

Zuko goes rigid, and Iroh reacts like he has been expecting the words, expecting this whole thing as he whips his basket of seashells into the face of the closest guard—Agni’s balls, Zuko had been wondering why Uncle picked those of all things to bring—and roughly shoves Zuko down to punch a controlled arc of fire across the deck.

Zuko surges upright with a roar, fury giving him heat and force as he punches his own gout of flame, kicking a whip of fire out as the soldiers stumble back before his attack. He lunges into the gap, Iroh at his back, flames stabbing and raging around them as the deck full of enemies closes in.

Iroh is solid, rooted, relentless as he grinds his way through the weight of soldiers arrayed against them. Zuko whips around him, lunging low and kicking high, wishing he had his dao, everything about trading fire with Fire Nation soldiers just making his anger burn hotter and hotter and hotter.

Zuko almost stumbles when he whirls to block an attack that doesn’t materialize, the soldiers in front of them scrambling back. For a moment, his inner flame flares in triumph, their escape right in front of—

“You never could let things be easy, could you, Brother?” Azula’s voice is amused and cold, smile full of just as many teeth as he remembers as her fire spills blue over her hands. “You will never learn, Zuzu.”

“Don’t *call* me that,” Zuko snarls, fists wreathed in flame.

Azula laughs like she’s never heard a better joke in her life, ostentatious wiping an imaginary tear from her eye and attacking. Zuko quickly loses track of Iroh, can only hope that he is holding his own against the soldiers because Zuko can only concentrate on what is in front of him as Azula dances and spins and flips, light-footed and sure and deadly as always. Her flames are spears, daggers, whips, crackling and warping the air with their heat. Every block sends Zuko’s feet skidding a few inches backward and every strike he throws in return is dodged with an air of casual disregard.

“Come now, Zuzu!” Azula chides as she flicks away a punch. “After four years with nothing to do but train, I really expected more than this.”

He growls and throws himself into a spinning kick, tired legs stumbling on the landing as Azula slides smoothly around his arc of flame.

“Is that really the best you can do?”

Her familiar taunting goads like always, feeding his desperate need to prove himself and shut. Her. Up. He lunges into another attack, shouting with effort as Azula just flips lightly into the air, laughing as she lands.

“So much *effort*, Zuzu. How are you still not any good?”

“Don’t *call* *me that*,” Zuko rages, throwing punch after punch after punch that Azula doesn’t even bother to block, just slipping and sliding back as he gasps for breath, fighting for control as his flames grow more and more ragged.

“Really, Zuzu.” Her voice goes hard, amusement suddenly gone. “It’s like you’re trying to embarrass yourself.”

Azula lunges forward so fast his tired eyes can barely see it, arrowing toward his left side. Zuko trips over his own feet as he tries to stop his momentum from carrying him forward, as he tries to keep her in his field of vision, overbalanced and overreaching. Her face is cold and angry as her booted foot hurtles into his chest, sending him flying backward, not into the edge of the railing but into open space.

*Fuck.*

Zuko’s shoulder crunches against metal, his body torqueing over to slam down hip-first, spinning and crashing down the steep gangplank. He crumples to a stop on the dock, skidding on salt-worn wood as the last of his breath is knocked from his lungs. For a moment he can only stare up at the sky, paralyzed. Then with a desperate heave, his chest unlocks and he sucks in a harsh breath, then another. Zuko forces himself up onto his knees, unsteady, ignoring bruises and splinters and sluggishly bleeding scratches to look up to see Azula at the top of the gangplank.

Her stance is rooted, hands raised, and like she was waiting for his eyes she starts slowly moving in fluid, unfamiliar motions. Zuko tracks her hands, wide-eyed, inner flame stuttering as lightning begins to dance around her fingertips, skittering up her arms. Azula’s tawny eyes are fixed on his, face serene, and Zuko can’t breathe. He’s never seen her look so at peace as her arm arcs slowly, deliberately, almost like she is putting on a demonstration before beginning its descent toward him, unavoidable, unstoppable.

Azula’s calm shatters as Iroh bursts into sight, trailing flames and grabbing Azula’s extended fingers to launch her lightning into the air in a deafening peal of thunder. Zuko can only gape, mind tripping over the fact that he has not, in fact, been attacked as Iroh uses Azula’s moment of uncharacteristic surprise to pull her into his grip, pivoting hard to turn her over his hip and launch her overboard. Zuko follows her descent, motionless, barely registering as Iroh grabs at his shoulder, trying to haul him upright.

Zuko can’t stop staring at the place where Azula plunged into the water in armor, in full armor, swallowed up by the waves. The acrid scent of blasting jelly burns his nose, and he doesn’t understand why Agni is shining down, why the light of the moon isn’t stretching its claws over dark water.

Azula’s hand knifes out of the water, shoving Zuko abruptly back into the present. She grabs onto a dangling rope, hauling herself half out of the water and glaring balefully at him, hair clinging to her face, watching as Zuko finally lets Uncle pull him up and haul him away.

&#45;-

When they finally stop running the summer sun has dried them and out left them drenched again, thoroughly soaked with sweat. Zuko and Uncle both collapse, panting, by the river, scooping up water with trembling hands. Zuko is reasonably sure that Azula isn’t following them, not yet. He knows her, and her penchant for symbolism. His little sister would never set out in pursuit looking like a half-drowned rat. The image sends a wave of dark amusement through him as he sits back, finally concentrating on getting his breathing under control for the first time since Azula kicked him off her ship.

Zuko stares down at his reflection, wavering and blurry in the gently flowing water. The figure staring back at him is pale, bald, scarred, ugly, hollow-eyed, still sunburned and wind-chapped from the raft. There is nothing of a Fire Nation Prince about him except for his one golden eye. Even his phoenix tail is an aberration, a mockery of the topknot he could wear if he were truly a man of the Fire Nation. Agni, what did Sokka ever see in all of this?

Zuko doesn’t give himself time to think. He is good at that. He just grabs the rope of his hair in one hand and the knife he swiped from a startled dockside guard with the other and holds his own gaze as he saws it off. His scalp feels weirdly light as the taut braid comes free and Zuko stares for a moment, thrown by how light it is in his hand before he drops the thick rope of hair into the river. He doesn’t watch it float away.

Uncle silently holds out a hand and Zuko passes the knife, distantly noting Uncle’s precise, solemn movements as he slices his own topknot free. Zuko doesn’t watch though, just continues to stare at his reflection, at this alien version of himself. Hair shouldn’t change so much, but Zuko feels like something in him is icing over, some door he always thought would be open shutting in his face.

Agni, is Zuko truly leaving behind his honor? His nation and his family? And if so—who is he now without it? Zuko feels overwhelmed trying to imagine what he could be without the weight of it all to hold him in place. By the stab of realization that if it was all going to end here no matter how hard he tried, then Zuko really did have a choice with Sokka, didn’t he. In the alley and on the ice and so many times before. And it’s just one more thing to sit like acid in his throat, one more thing lost through his own stupidity just like everything else.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

Who wants to hang out with Zuko for a while?

## Chapter 2: The Hand that Feeds

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warning for Zuko having some lingering PTSD / flashbacks to the North

### Text

Zuko is sure that things are supposed to be easier in the Earth Kingdom, in the forest, than they were floating on a makeshift raft in the vastness of the ocean. They’re on land, they’re following the river, they theoretically know where civilization is. But Agni, at least on the raft Zuko had the excuse of circumstance to account for their sorry, ragged state. At least on the raft Zuko didn’t have to think about what came next when everything else has been ripped away.

Azula’s message was obvious enough even for Zuko to read—the Fire Nation doesn’t want him. And Uncle is here and safe and annoyingly talkative, and Sokka—

Zuko can’t think about Sokka. Sokka was alive. That is the most Zuko can allow himself.

For the first time since he can remember, Zuko doesn’t have a higher purpose to point his driving need to survive toward, has no ability to say ‘this’ when the tired, persistent voice at the back of his mind asks ‘why.’ Now, he and Uncle trudge every day under the summer sun, traveling south because Zuko has no idea what to do other than not stand still.

And Zuko is terrible at everything he sets out to do, so of course he is terrible at this, too, fumbling again and again instead of adapting to a new way of surviving. He would try his hand at fishing, except the only thing he knows about it is that river fish are too fucking fast to catch by hand. His attempts to set snares would be laughable if he had any string to set them with in the first place, and what is he left to do, throw rocks at a pig deer? Zuko’s best bet is to lash out with his fire, which even he knows is not the subtle approach they need to escape Azula’s attention.

Besides, he already tried in a fit of sullen annoyance. Forest birds are a lot smaller and faster than the sea vultures were.

Zuko wishes he had asked Sokka about hunting and fishing instead of about maps and everything else, as useless a thing to dwell on right now as every other thing he thinks where Sokka is concerned.

Zuko didn’t think that he and Uncle would *thrive* on the run, exactly, but he at least thought they would do *okay*. Zuko hasn’t been around silk robes and servants in years, hasn’t been pampered in even longer. And Uncle used to lead *military campaigns*. But somehow neither one of them are used to being constantly *dirty*, or to the way their clothes get more and more ragged by the day, or to the constant ache from spending a whole day walking that does nothing but lead to such bone-deep exhaustion that Zuko can’t sleep at night. Zuko thought he was physically fit from training, but that’s apparently a different fitness than what is needed to be…fugitives. Traitors. Refugees.

The thought is a bitter one, as bitter as the realization that Uncle’s particular brand of wisdom is not particularly suited for roughing it.

“Uncle,” Zuko grits out, silently asking anything that will listen for patience. “Why would you drink that tea. Why.”

“I thought it was the rare white dragon bush! Its leaves make a tea—”

“So delicious it's heartbreaking,” Zuko choruses along. “Yes, I heard you before. Which is why I heard you *also* say that it could be white jade. Which is *poisonous!”*

“It’s not so bad as all that, Nephew,” Uncle smiles through swollen eyes. “I have time before the rash spreads to my throat and stops my breathing!” Zuko is going to scream. “And I found these berries! They are known to cure the poison of the white jade. Or they might be the kind that cause blindness.” Zuko is also going to set something on fire.

“Agni’s tits, why do you keep taking chances with these stupid *plants*,” Zuko snarls, slapping the berries out of Uncle’s hand and ignoring his disapproving look. If Uncle didn’t want Zuko to curse them he should have had an entirely different crew on the *Wani.*

“They are not stupid, Nephew, they are nature’s bounty! They are—”

“Going to *kill you* if you don’t stop putting random leaves in your mouth like a *toddler*,” Zuko shouts, pivoting away to gather up their meager supplies, pointedly not seeing Uncle’s dejected itching. “Can you walk?”

“Yes. Prince Zuko—”

“Don’t call me that.”

“—and where are we going?”

“Into town,” Zuko growls, folding his arms and watching critically as Uncle hauls himself to his feet. “I saw one over the ridge before. I’m done with this foraging shit. We’re buying you medicine.”

&#45;-

The town is bigger than Zuko expected it to be, which is a relief since that means it’s more likely to have a market where they can get real supplies. But it also makes him nervous, makes him twitchy, because bigger towns this far from any trade route means more people to see their faces and remember and answer questions when Azula inevitably blazes through behind him.

And Zuko is sure they will be remembered, even though their hair is looking less distinctive now that it’s had time to grow in, even though travel has made them as grubby as everything else in the Earth Kingdom. They’re going to be remembered because Zuko has no idea how to act in this town. He knows the rules of every Earth Kingdom port there is, knows how to conduct himself as a banished Crown Prince, the etiquette of being a Fire Nation noble in the Colonies, the precise regulation of military-adjacent Captain to enlisted officer.

He has no idea how he is supposed to conduct himself in this purely Earth Kingdom town, with its dust and browns and greens and them still wearing fucking Fire Nation spa *loungewear.* He doesn’t know the rules for being an honorless fugitive yet.

Zuko at least *does* know the value of money, from penny-pinching the *Wani’s* ridiculous budget for nearly four years, and he’s getting more and more furious at this *absurd* price gouging.

“You’re trying to tell me that a handful of these bacui berries cost the same as a sack of rice?” Zuko growls, glaring down at the little purple fruits.

“They’re very rare. Highly sought after, *Sir*,” the merchant puts a little extra emphasis on that, eyes making a sweep of Zuko’s ragged appearance.

“They aren’t rare at all!” Zuko snaps, inner fire tight and restless. “I saw some in the woods on the way here!”

“Then you can go back into the woods and pick them yourself,” the man sniffs, with a pointed look at Uncle who is leaning heavier and heavier onto Zuko’s shoulder.

“Maybe I will, and I’ll come back and sell them for half as much!” Zuko recognizes that he doesn’t have a great negotiating position here, but he’s going to wear this merchant down with his steadily rising volume if it’s the last fucking thing he does. He knows the look of someone who will eventually give in to make him stop screaming.

“Maybe you should take your scrawny little—”

“Maybe we should all calm down,” a chirpy voice calls out from his left. Zuko instinctively turns his flinch into a sharp turn toward the newcomer, only slightly hampered by Uncle’s weight on his shoulder. The voice in question belongs to a girl, probably only a bit older than Zuko, brown-haired and smooth-faced and big-eyed and giving the merchant a chiding smile.

“Song,” the man mutters, crossing his arms and staring down at her feet.

“Jian,” the girl—Song—replies. “You know we’ve talked about this.”

The man sighs. “I know.”

“You can’t try to take money from people who should be going to the hospital,” Song presses anyway, the softness of her expression taking the edge off her words.

“They came to me!” Jian protests.

“They’re *refugees*,” Song rolls her eyes, half-laughing as she looks at Zuko as if to invite him in on some joke. “You can’t rip off refugees!”

Zuko can feel himself flushing, stiffening, glaring, barely managing to bite back whatever words are going to burst forth over ‘refugee’ and thinking she needed to come in and *save* him, because she said hospital, and she said it like there‘s one here, and like she knows where it is, and like it would be cheaper than this, and Uncle’s breaths are starting to sound harsh even in Zuko’s bad ear. Song doesn’t seem phased by his hostility which…is good, probably. She just gives the merchant one last eye roll and beckons for Zuko and Uncle to follow.

“Have you been traveling long?” Song asks as she ducks easily under Uncle’s other arm, helping to move them along a bit faster, ignoring Zuko’s glower of warning.

“Long enough.”

“You must have just come into town then!”

Zuko grunts.

“What do you think of it so far?”

Zuko briefly closes his eyes, trying to muster what little patience he ever seems to have. Why did Uncle have to drink that fucking poison tea? Why couldn’t he be the one having this damn conversation? Zuko *hates* chitchat.

&#45;-

The hospital is bright and clean, small but orderly. Uncle is the only patient right now, which Zuko is deeply grateful for because he’s barely grunting his way through Song’s gentle, insistent questions and can’t imagine dealing with anyone else. He doesn’t want to answer but she’s treating Uncle, so Zuko grits his teeth through it and slouches determinedly against the wall, arms crossed, eyes tracking everything her hands do, the door in his periphery in case they need to move fast to get out of here.

“It’s a common error, really,” Song comments as she presses a tincture into Uncle’s hands and begins mixing up something to soothe the itching. “But we’re lucky that bacui berries are just as common!”

“Fucking knew it,” Zuko mutters, ignoring her questioning look to scowl in response to the behave-yourself expression on Uncle’s face.

“Why didn’t you both come here first? The hospital will never turn anyone away. That’s our whole mission here.”

Zuko just shrugs. He doesn’t want to admit that he didn’t know it was here, and even if he had that he would have assumed they would have to pay, and that doctors were always so pricey he hadn’t even considered trying to find one even if he actually thought he could get one to see them looking like the dirty, shabby messes they are.

“We aren’t from around here,” Uncle offers and Song hums in understanding, watching Uncle carefully and seeming pleased by whatever she’s seeing.

“Where are you from?”

“We’re travelers,” Zuko cuts in before Uncle can helpfully offer up all the around they’ve come from, adding an extra glare as Uncle starts absently scratching at the welts over his skin.

“Travelers, huh?” Her eyes flick over their ragged spa clothes, their lack of supplies. “Do you have names?”

“Um.” Zuko stares. “Yes.”

“…And they are?”

“My nephew’s name is Lee,” Uncle jumps in, smiling benevolently as Zuko glares.

“And my uncle’s name is Mushi,” Zuko bites out, pushing down his little flicker of satisfaction as Uncle’s eyes narrow and his itching hands momentarily still.

“But my nephew has an old family name,” Uncle adds, smirking. “So, we just call him Junior.”

“Mushi and Junior, huh?” Song’s voice is laughing in a way that Zuko’s pretty sure means she can tell their names are fake. “Well Mushi and Junior, travelers from nowhere, who are new to town, you look like you could use a good meal. My mom would be happy to have you share our table tonight.”

“We have to move on by—”

“We would love to,” Uncle enthuses, trying to wave Zuko to silence as if *that* has ever worked.

“We really don’t have time for—”

“*We would love to.”*

“Wonderful,” Song grins, her eyes laughing as she glances back at Zuko. “My mother always makes too much roast duck.”

Zuko folds his arms tighter and scowls as Uncle perks up and finally stops his itching to ask more about the menu, about where the house is, about Song’s mother. Zuko wants to storm out in a huff, but he has nowhere to storm *to*, no door to slam or room to hide in, no boots to stomp. So he just stays where he is and tries to stop the muscle ticking in his jaw. He doesn’t want this girl’s pity or her charity, and now he’s going to be fucking stuck with both for the night.

&#45;-

Zuko is borderline mad that the food is good. Excellent, even. Almost worth Uncle’s blatant flirting with Song’s mother. Alternately, Zuko has been subsisting on whatever they can scrounge up that Uncle is absolutely positive is not poisonous—which Zuko is really questioning now in hindsight—and anything that’s a step up from that is divine. He barely even bothers to scowl when Song pointedly refills his plate, just snatches it back with a belated muttered thanks and bends his head to eating, dodging her inquisitive eyes.

“So Mushi, Lee, my daughter tells me you’re both refugees?”

“Yes,” Uncle agrees with an ease that makes Zuko feel like his skin is too tight. “The war…”

“We understand.” Song’s mother sighs. “We were refugees ourselves before settling here. It’s a hard life. The traveling, and the uncertainty. Never knowing how long you can stay where you find yourself…”

“We left because of the war, too,” Song adds, eyes big and sad when Zuko makes the mistake of glancing up. “The Fire Nation raided when I was little.” Her eyes linger on his scar and Zuko bends his head back to his plate, jaw set so hard he is momentarily unable to take a bite. “They came when the men were coming back from farming…everyone was tired.” Strategically sound, to attack when the enemy is at their weakest. “All the men were taken. We never knew why, never found out. None of us ever saw any of them ever again. Not my father. Not even the boys…” Strategically ridiculous, to take children.

Zuko can feel his shoulders creeping toward his ears as she speaks, as her voice loses some of its cheer and bounce. He’s probably supposed to sympathize with her, or feel sorry for her, or find himself in her story or some shit like that. But this is war, and that’s what happens during war. It’s not *unique.* Territory is taken and resources are conscripted, and lives are sacrificed in the exchange.

Even if there’s no strategic importance to much of anything this far inland and this far north. Even if raiding around here would take more resources than would ever be replenished by the effort, given how poor the towns around here are off the coast, how little strategic importance they hold.

Zuko thinks of Sokka’s village, and the North, and takes a deep, controlled breath.

“What about you?”

Zuko glances up when the silence draws out, inner fire stilling with wariness as he realizes that the question was directed at him. “What?”

“You’re traveling with your Uncle…” Song trails off as if that were a question.

“Yes?” Zuko says cautiously, itching at the center of everyone’s attention.

“Is your dad fighting in the war?”

Zuko’s bark of laughter takes them all by surprise, himself included, overly loud and overly bitter. “Yes,” he bites out, shoving away from the table and any further questions. “My Father is fighting the war.”

He stalks toward the porch, ignoring the murmurs from the table and the sound of Uncle apologizing behind him, barely restraining the familiar urge to slam the door behind him, because he doesn’t want their pity or their charity or their guilt. He isn’t fucking sorry, not at all. Not for any of it. He isn’t.

&#45;-

Zuko stares into the night, trying to match his breathing to the still strangely unfamiliar sound of leaves rustling in the wind, trying to just think of absolutely nothing, which he’s usually great at according to everyone around him, which he’s not succeeding in at the moment because when does he ever succeed at anything he tries to do. The sound of the door opening has what little tension Zuko has been able to shed winding back up his spine in anticipation of one of Uncle’s gentle, cutting rebukes.

The steps are too light, too quick, though, and Zuko barely has time to register that before Song is settling down next to him on his left, startling a flinch out of him that he manages to suppress into a full-body twitch and a warning glare. Fuck. Zuko had wanted to climb up onto the roof to sit where Uncle couldn’t follow, but he had been pretty sure that they would hear him inside and didn’t want to deal with the questions that would inevitably follow. Restraining the impulse was obviously a mistake.

“I was upset a lot at first, too,” Song finally says, hugging her knees and resting her cheek on folded arms. Her steady gaze on the side of his face feels like insects crawling over his skin.

She hesitates, giving him space to reply, but Zuko just clenches his jaw and looks into the darkness, fantasizing about fleeing from whatever this is into the night, onto the roof, toward some tight quiet space no one knows about but him.

“It’s hard to be displaced, especially when it's fresh and new.”

Her tone is kind and Zuko wants to laugh. He might be newly a refugee—even in his head, he spits the word—but he’s not new to being displaced. Hasn’t been for a long time.

“It’s okay to be mad,” she offers, gentle, like she’s letting him in on some secret, giving him some permission. “It’s nothing to be ashamed of.” Like Zuko doesn’t live his whole life in nothing but rage and shame. “I found that it helped to talk about,” Song murmurs, resettling herself and somehow coming an inch or two closer. He can feel the expectation in her gaze. “A burden shared is a burden lightened.”

Zuko grunts. Amateur. She’s not nearly as good at opaque aphorism as Uncle.

“So..?”

Zuko cuts his eyes to her, using the shift of his head as an excuse to slide away, putting back the space between them she had stolen. “…What.”

“So, do you want to talk about it?” Her smiles like he just told some kind of joke, her expression infectious if Zuko did things like that. “I know what it’s like.”

Zuko’s snort of disbelief is involuntary, and she scrunches up her face, losing some of her smile but eyes somehow going even more gentle.

“I *do*,” she insists, unwinding herself and turning to face him more fully. “I know you don’t believe me, I get it. It’s so hard to imagine that anyone else could understand what it’s like. I remember. But just because my experience isn’t exactly the same doesn’t mean I don’t know how you feel, at least a little bit.”

Zuko closes his eyes against her words, against the way they echo those first letters from Sokka and his stubborn refusal to let Zuko shove him away. Agni’s tits, Sokka wrapped himself around Zuko so early, far before either of them ever had the wherewithal to notice. It feels like a knife to the center of his chest to feel the echo of that again and Zuko can’t hold back the noise that slips free, pained and small.

His eyes snap open as he realizes he vocalized the sound outside his own head, just in time to see Song reaching out for him, hand extended as if to brush her fingers over the left side of his face. Zuko recoils on instinct, using the flinch to skitter back and away and reclaim the space of the porch between them. His heart is beating rabaroo fast, inner fire shuddering beneath his skin as he stares at her, wide-eyed and immobile, waiting for her to chase so that he can escape.

“I understand that too.” Her voice is low, grave, and Zuko doesn’t know whether to be relieved or frustrated that she doesn’t try to follow his retreat and open up a path off the porch for him. “I know what it’s like to be hurt by the Fire Nation,” she continues, holding his eyes as she reaches down, hiking up the hem of her dress and what the fuck, what the *fuck*, what did Zuko do to make her think that he wanted—

His thoughts fizzle to nothing when she extends her calf, putting her bare skin and twisting rope of scar tissue into the light. Zuko follows the angry, livid marks with his eyes, tracing the path the fire must have taken. Zuko knows burns. This one was bad. The kind that doesn’t seem too terrible at first because there’s nothing left to feel the pain, not until it seeps down into your marrow, sliding into your veins, a persistent fire that you can never put out, never escape.

“I understand,” Song insists. “I do.” Zuko just stares at her leg, ignoring whatever plea is in her gaze and wondering what he’s supposed to feel here other than tired and numb. “The Fire Nation has hurt many people. It is okay to be mad and upset about that. Everyone will understand.”

Zuko shifts, uncomfortable down to his bones. He doesn’t know what to do with this, with any of whatever it is she’s trying to do, whatever it is she’s seeking from him. The idea that the Fire Nation has…hurt him—it’s not something Zuko lets himself consciously grapple with. There’s no point. Not when the only place it leads is to the kinds of things that are too dangerous to acknowledge out loud. Not when it’s something that no one would dare say to him except for Sokka, maybe, not even Uncle.

But then, Zuko isn’t that person anymore, whose reactions others need to care about and walk warily around. He’s a traitor. A fugitive. A refugee. Song can say whatever she wants. Zuko has no power to stop her.

&#45;-

Zuko doesn’t sleep in more than snatches that night, which is…fairly typical, really. But instead of being kept awake by his churning, twisting thoughts, now he’s trying to flee what he sees when he closes his eyes: dark water and glowing claws and reaching hands that can’t stretch far enough, can’t hold tight enough, that fail and fail and fail as Uncle falls away, swallowed into darkness.

&#45;-

Zuko is irritable and snappy and exhausted the next morning—so perfectly normal, for him— as Uncle putters around the kitchen as if they fucking *live* here, as if they didn’t stay the night on nothing but charity, offering nothing in return.

And now they’re dressed in more charity, sturdy clothes in Earth Nation colors that Song had pressed quietly but firmly into his hands. Zuko wants to throw them back at her, drop them onto the ground, but if he did then they would still only have fucking loungewear, so he grits his teeth and stalks behind the privacy screen to change. His skin looks alien next to olive green and dingy tan, sallow and wrong. He clenches his jaw and crosses his arm and glares from the corner of the room at everything around him so he doesn’t have to look at it.

Zuko can tell that Song wants to say something to him. She won’t stop glancing over, biting her lip, fluttering like she wants to approach but keeps talking herself out of it. Zuko hopes she keeps deciding not to. He doesn’t need another replay of last night, of feeling like he’s drowning in expectations he doesn’t understand and doesn’t want.

Uncle finally starts making noises about getting on the road and needing to be going and Zuko practically dives out the door into the morning sun. His relief is short-lived, though, because it’s not Uncle’s familiar steps that follow.

“Fuck,” Zuko mutters, folding his arms and clenching his fists and staring resolutely at the horizon as Song comes up beside him—on his right side, this time, at least.

“I’m sure that things seem hard right now,” Song starts, and Zuko blows out a sharp breath, refusing to turn his head. “But things will get better. It might be difficult to believe but I promise they will.” She sighs when Zuko doesn’t respond. “What you feel is valid, Lee. It is. And things are changing. They *will* get better, I know it. The Avatar is here now.”

Zuko nearly cringes, his heart shuddering as he scans the horizon for the source of the sudden acrid scent of blasting jelly beneath the bright smell of green earthen things. There is nothing to see, of course there isn’t, and they still need to get out of here as fast as possible. Just because he can’t see anything doesn’t mean it’s not there. His inner fire is climbing up into his chest and Zuko is going to light something on fire if she doesn’t stop *looking* at him. He clenches his fists and ruthlessly controls his breathing, shutting everything down hard and cold until he can stand there with eyes wide and dry and feel nothing but familiar rolling anger over the sick, numb memory of fear.

“Nephew.” Uncle’s voice breaks through Zuko’s reverie. Zuko’s borderline-eruption, more like. “These people have shown us great kindness.” Zuko just looks at him sidelong, distantly wondering when Song left his side, his inner fire winding back toward his core at the realization even as his fingers try to tremble over his lack of awareness. “Say thank you.”

“…Thanks,” Zuko grinds out, unable to turn back around. The word comes out hard and bitter, grating. Like a curse.

Uncle huffs but doesn’t force the issue, just shoulders his small bag of supplies—more charity, more pity—and trails Zuko up the winding path back toward the main road. The day is growing hot despite the early hour and Zuko can already feel dust beginning to cling to his skin and make his tongue gritty and thick. Uncle trudges next to him, face fixed in a mask of serenity and steps heavy. One night of food and rest isn’t enough to replenish after days of harsh living, not when you’re Uncle’s age.

Zuko sets his gaze in the mid-distance, trying to find a headspace where he can set his breaths to the rhythm of their steps and think about nothing while still staying alert for danger. Sometimes he can find a certain place where there’s nothing but the next step, where he can take in what’s around him without really registering it unless he has to, just more trees and hedges and ostrich horses and fences.

Zuko’s steady pace hitches, slows. Uncle’s contented humming continues forward without him as Zuko drifts to a stop, staring at hedges and ostrich horses and fences. The humming breaks off.

“…Nephew,” Uncle says quietly. “You need not do this.”

“Do what,” Zuko asks, as if they both don’t know exactly what he’s thinking as his hand drifts across the sun-worn wood of the fence, testing.

“These people have shown us great kindness,” Uncle presses, sighing when Zuko doesn’t reply. “Prince Zuko—”

“Don’t call me that.”

“—this is not needed.”

“Do you want to keep fleeing Azula on foot?” Zuko snaps, words hard but low as the ostrich horses come over to investigate his reaching hand. They’re already fucking *saddled.* “She’ll have mongoose lizards. How long do you think we’ll last?”

“There are other ways. There are other choices before you.”

“What choices,” Zuko hisses, soothing away the startled jerk of the friendliest ostrich horse’s head at his tone. “What other choices are there, other than walking and this? Tell me.” He glares when Uncle just silently frowns. “*Tell me*.”

“Just because the path is winding and confused, Nephew, does not mean that the path is not there.”

Zuko snorts, turning his back on Uncle’s useless, meaningless advice. “Don’t tell me that I have *choices* when I don’t,” he snarls, hands gentle as he catches the ostrich horse’s lead and guides it toward the gate. “Don’t act like this situation is some fucking fable.”

“The world remembers kindnesses done and not done,” Uncle says sadly as Zuko leads the ostrich horse willingly outside its enclosure. It cocks its head, giving itself an eager shake, beak warm and gentle as it tries to investigate Zuko’s bristly head of hair.

“The world remembers who lives and who wins,” Zuko grunts, vaulting onto the ostrich horse’s back. It shifts underneath him but sits quiet, alert, waiting for his signal. Good. If this isn’t a fucking sign from the Spirits or whatever Uncle is always on about then Zuko doesn’t know what is. He turns to Uncle, extending a hand. “Are you coming or not?”

For a moment Zuko’s heart can’t beat, his extended hand all he can see. But then Uncle reaches back and takes it, palm worn and warm and real as Zuko helps pull him into the saddle. The ostrich horse sets out at an even, steady pace when Zuko clicks his tongue and nudges with his heels, and Zuko lets himself have a sigh of relief as they begin to put real distance between themselves and Azula for the first time since they started running.

Uncle is a solid, judgmental presence at his back, but Zuko is used to that. He doesn’t need it, anyway. He’s perfectly fine at self-flagellation without Uncle weighing in on the matter. Zuko has stolen plenty before, but always from people who clearly deserved it, in his eyes at least. The kind of people who make a point of displaying relics from the graves of cultures lost to the war, or whose servants scurry in fear. The kind of people who specifically seek to invite a pain-addled, freshly burned, socially isolated teenager into their homes.

Fuck. For all of Song’s staring and attempts to touch, Zuko can’t try to cast her in the same boat as those others. He isn’t good at lying like that, not even to himself.

But in the balance of Song and Uncle. In the balance of an Earth Kingdom refugee displaced by his Father’s war and Uncle’s increasingly heavy step and their need to *move* to stay ahead of what is behind them…

Zuko mentally flinches away from what has become of his honor before remembering that he isn’t Fire Nation anymore, so he doesn’t have any honor to worry about to begin with. The thought isn't a freeing one like it probably should be. It’s just a new set of chains, being nationless and without honor. A new set of assumptions to try to fit himself into, just now without the weight of expectations and rules to hold him into place.

## Chapter 3: Untethered

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

No warnings for this one beyond Zuko continuing to be all up in his feels

### Text

The ostrich horse makes it better. Zuko names her Jasmine when Uncle won’t stop pestering him about a name—“If we’re going to take the animal then we need to treat her right and care for her properly!”—and hadn’t *that* name sent Uncle into flustered silence for a precious few moments. But they’re still struggling. They have more energy now to forage, can get by on fewer calories since they aren’t working as hard during the day, but they’re by no means doing anything other than scraping by.

Being refugees would have been hard on its own, but to be fugitives on top of that? A pair that the Earth Kingdom and Fire Nation alike would be equally enthusiastic to capture? Other refugees are searching for new roots, but Zuko knows even if Uncle dances around saying it out loud that there can be no true end for them to hiding and fleeing and constant vigilance.

Zuko accepts it with grim resignation, because nothing in his life has ever been easy and he knows that hard things can always get harder, and he tries to just be grateful to Agni that at least it isn’t worst.

But it’s hard to avoid being noticed drifting in and out of towns. It’s hard to have to constantly pull their bending in tight lest they reveal themselves, because *that* would certainly be memorable. Or rather, it’s hard for Zuko. Something about traveling over land instead of sea makes him feel more volatile than usual, like without the constant motion of the waves something in him doesn’t know how to be still. Smoke is constantly in the back of his throat, his inner flame restless to the point that he consciously needing to keep sparks off his fingertips when he guides Jasmine.
