Zuko takes to walking a few steps back into Uncle’s periphery when it’s his turn to be on foot so Uncle has to deliberately look to see Zuko bleeding off the restless heat inside himself when it gets to be too much, the already-hot air warping and shimmering around him.

It doesn’t help that the more they travel, the more Zuko grits his teeth and forces himself to accept that all that he knows—regional trade goods, important families, ceremonies, archaic languages, the nuances of cultures long dead—is good only for war, or hunting the Avatar, or both. All the things he used to focus on when everything else got to be too much are worthless now, and it's like swallowing glass to know that if Zuko is done with both Avatar hunting and war than he really doesn’t have anything left going for himself beyond a glare that is just as likely to start trouble as to warn it off. Fuck, Zuko can’t even offer a shoddy knowledge of the types of plants that probably won’t kill them, maybe, if they can just remember how to cook them right. All he has is common sense and instinct, and no one has ever said Zuko was particularly blessed in either department.

Zuko supposes he should be grateful that, between the two of them, he and Uncle had the collective foresight to start taking breaks during the height of the midday heat to give themselves and Jasmine a rest. The enforced stillness makes him itchy, though, even when he knows it’s necessary. Zuko will never be able to just doze off under Agni’s light no matter how tired he is—it’s just Zuko’s kind of luck, to be a strong enough firebender to have his sleeping hours dictated by the sun but not strong enough to be any good at anything. At most he can drift in a semi-conscious haze, mind as blank and empty as he can make it, sitting as far apart from Uncle as he can manage. A reprieve from their constant *togetherness*, as Sokka would have called it.

An image of Sokka rises behind his closed eyelids as if summoned by the thought, white wrist wraps and fingerless gloves and tan skin for miles, familiar blue clothes that are a relief to eyes exhausted by nothing but shades of drab and tan. Zuko’s awareness of the tree he’s sprawled against and the hard ground beneath him fades away as he turns his attention toward this picture, clearer than any memory. Agni, it feels like Zuko is on the edge of dreaming as blue eyes catch his own, except there’s nothing terrible about this dream. It feels almost real, like maybe his tired mind is desperately trying to serve up this one thing in a bid for relief from Zuko’s constant tension.

Zuko isn’t expecting anything other than an image of what he can’t have—he isn’t sure if he’s going to be upset later or embarrassingly gratified that this imaginary Sokka’s clothes are damp and clinging, like he recently waded through water and Agni’s balls is it ever a *look.* So his mind serving up the sound of Sokka *speaking* is nearly enough to jolt Zuko out of whatever this half-waking dream.

“Does this mean you’re dead, too?” Sokka’s voice sounds both close and far away, tone like the deceptive calm of the sea over a riptide.

“Um.” Certainly not what Zuko would have *consciously* chosen to hear Sokka say, but then, if his conscious mind were in control none of this would be happening in the first place. “Or are you real?” Sokka’s face is pinched, tense, as his eyes flit over Zuko’s body, taking in the nondescript Earth Kingdom clothes, the wide-brimmed hat hanging down his back, all of it dusty because even in his imagination Zuko can’t escape the feeling of being fucking coated in dirt

“…What?”

“I guess it doesn’t matter,” Sokka sighs, scrubbing at his face, expression exhausted when his hands drop. “Fucking Spirit mumbo jumbo.”

Zuko blinks. “It doesn’t matter if I’m dead?” That might very well be true, but it still…hurts. A lot.

Sokka waves Zuko’s question away with an annoyed flick. “Of course it matters if you’re dead,” he huffs, exasperated and reluctantly fond in a way that has Zuko’s shoulders dropping. “It just doesn’t matter what you say now.”

“Why not?” Zuko asks, utterly confused but relaxing nonetheless into the sound of Sokka’s voice, oddly willing to just see where this imaginary-Sokka takes the conversation. This strangeness is certainly preferable to Zuko’s usual dreams.

“Because this is some swamp gas hallucination,” Sokka says matter-of-factly, frowning around as if he is looking at something other than the gray mist Zuko can see. “So anything you say is just a product of my subconscious. The ultimate projection,” he adds with a rueful twist to his lips.

“Okay…” Zuko says slowly. That is…a highly specific thing for Zuko’s own probable-heat-stroke-hallucination to say, but whatever. “…It’s still good to see you.”

“I—yes.” Sokka blinks, coming out of his thoughts at Zuko’s words, meeting Zuko’s eyes again and looking for real this time and Zuko wants to drown in it. “It’s always good to see you. Even if it’s just my subconscious telling me things I want to hear.”

Zuko doesn’t hold back his smile at Sokka’s words, pleased to have pleased him, because this is a dream and so none of this matters. He can still feel a flush creeping up over his skin at the way Sokka stares at him doing it, though.

“You should do that more often,” Sokka says softly, drifting closer, his own mouth curling into a little grin. “It’s nice.”

“I would if you were around,” Zuko says, self-conscious even within his own mind under Sokka’s attention.

“Zuko…” Zuko shivers at the way Sokka says his name, like it’s something soft and precious that makes Sokka a little bit sad. “It’s hard when you say things like that.” He keeps coming closer, reaching across the last distance between them with a boldness he never had in real life to card his fingers through the close-cropped hair now covering Zuko’s head. “This is new,” he murmurs, and his expression is fascinated, wondering.

Zuko shudders beneath Sokka’s touch, nakedly leaning into it, letting himself have this thing even if it’s going to hurt when he wakes up. It feels so *real.* He wants to close his eyes so he can feel it even more intensely, but he doesn’t want to give up any second of being able to drink in the dark blue of Sokka’s gaze and catalog the expressions chasing across his face. “I’m sorry,” Zuko finally whispers, biting his lip against something that is definitely not regret when Sokka’s fingers curl, nails dragging along Zuko’s scalp.

“What for?”

“For saying things that are hard.” The idea of making things harder for Sokka…Agni, Zuko’s chest feels heavy with it, his inner fire low.

“Don’t be,” Sokka sighs, his hand falling away, and Zuko sways forward trying to chase after it before he catches himself. “I don’t want you to hold back for me.” His lips quirk and Zuko wants to bite them. “Especially not if I’m just making it all up anyway.” His smile falls away as he examines Zuko’s face though, a scowl beginning to tighten his features again. “You *could* be around, you know.”

Zuko winces, eyes dropping to the hollow of Sokka’s throat, tracking the beat of his pulse there. “I know,” he admits. He should have expected that his subconscious would drag him here given how thoroughly Zuko is refusing to entertain these thoughts when he is fully awake.

“I wish you hadn’t left,” Sokka frowns, folding his arms. Zuko wants to reach out and grab his wrists, to tug his arms back down and keep him from closing Zuko out, even just this little bit. “Things could have—why did you—I could have…” Sokka grits his teeth, shaking the thought away, visibly shaken in a way that makes Zuko’s body ache.

“I couldn’t stay,” Zuko says, tentatively reaching out to pull Sokka into something that’s too loose and far apart to quite qualify as a hug, his hands resting a little heavier on Sokka’s skin when his touch isn’t shoved off even as Sokka glares in response to his words.

“Don’t give me that shit, Zuko.”

“Sorry,” Zuko mutters, forcing himself to look into Sokka’s eyes, so close and open that it makes it hard to breathe. “You’re right. I could have. But Zhao…” Seeing the Admiral escaping in triumph as the world went dark, as Uncle cried out in horror and Sokka stumbled to his knees... “I couldn’t let him get away.”

Sokka is silent for too many beats of Zuko’s heart to count, chewing on Zuko’s words, face slowly shifting from angry and unhappy to just unhappy which…is an improvement, maybe. “Did you get him?”

“The Ocean did,” Zuko says, low and tight, looking at the way his hands fist into Sokka’s tunic. He gives the smallest of tugs to reassure himself that here, at least, Zuko is strong enough to hold on.

“…Good,” Sokka rasps, raw, and Zuko can’t help a tiny flinch at the new hardness in Sokka’s eyes, the new sadness weighing down his words beneath the anger.

Sokka notices the twitch and reaches up to run his fingers through Zuko’s hair again, unselfconscious like Zuko could never be. Cool fingers run down the back of Zuko’s neck, tracking the shape of his shoulders, soothing away the tension. “I suppose if I have to lose out,” Sokka finally says quietly, offering a half-smile that doesn’t quite reach his eyes. “It might as well be to you going to fuck up Zhao.”

Zuko sighs, leaning toward that smile until his temple is resting against Sokka’s, feeling like he needs something to help him stay upright. “I wish I hadn’t done it,” he admits, forcing out the words around the ball of regret in his throat. There are so many things Zuko can’t change, that he knows he can’t, but this is the one thing Zuko can’t seem to come to terms with like he can the rest.

“…What?”

“I should have stayed,” Zuko says, twisting his head so he can half-meet Sokka’s gaze without needing to put any distance back between them. “I should have—I should have taken the choice you offered.”

It’s still hard to speak treason, even when he’s already a traitor, even when no one will ever actually hear the words. It’s worth the struggle, though, for the small smile that curls Sokka’s lips, sad but warm and genuine and just for him. “It’s nice to hear you say that, even if it’s just a dream.”

“This is the weirdest dream I’ve ever had,” Zuko huffs, and he can feel Sokka’s laugh on his skin, in his blood.

“Me too,” Sokka grins, pulling Zuko a little closer even as he tenses, head tilting like something is calling for his attention and Sokka doesn’t want to give it. “Weirder than all the nightmares of Crazy Blue.”

“What?” Zuko frowns, trying to see Sokka’s face while still pressed against him. Sokka just said that like Zuko should understand what he’s talking about, and Zuko isn’t ready to let this slide into the usual unreality of his typical nightmares.

Sokka steps back though with a glance over back into the mist, fingers curling when Zuko catches his hands before they fall away. “I think,” Sokka says, lips twisting into a wry smile even as the dream starts to break around Zuko, “That I met your sister in Omashu.”

Zuko jolts upright on the side of the road, flames snapping around his fingers and then stinging his fingertips as he remembers to yank them back, his heart pounding in Azula-induced panic. The adrenaline on his empty stomach makes Zuko feel vaguely ill, but not nearly enough to distract from his confusion over how he managed to fall into a state to dream so thoroughly with Agni so high in the sky. Is he sick? Poisoned by some new plant?

That had felt…so real. Real enough that Zuko can still feel the echo of Sokka’s touch on his skin, can still feel Sokka’s fingers curled around his hands. Real enough that pain twists in his gut to have seen Sokka hurting like that, and anxiety makes him lightheaded to think of Sokka being anywhere in Azula’s orbit.

“Is all well, Nephew?” Zuko jerks at Uncle’s words, scrambling to his feet like that’s what he meant to do in the first place.

“I’m fine,” he rasps out, forcing his inner flame back down, forcing his hands to stop shaking.

“Are you sure? You seem troubled.”

Uncle’s concern grates against Zuko’s raw emotions and Zuko snarls out a wordlessly reply before stalking off to find a place within eyesight and out of earshot. He feels too open, far too vulnerable from just a fucking imaginary conversation with Sokka, but he still needs to keep Uncle in sight to make sure the old man doesn’t get up to anything.

And Zuko wants to stay in view, too, because he might have finally snapped under the stress of it all with that hallucination or dream or…whatever. Some weird combination of stress and heat and exhaustion. His mind throwing up something to make him rest. Even though it had felt real. Even though Zuko would never dream of calling Azula ‘Crazy Blue,’ which is so purely Sokka it makes him dizzy. Even though he can still feel Sokka’s almost-inner flame fading from his fire sense like Sokka is only just a few steps too far to be seen, just a little bit out of reach like always.

&#45;-

Eventually they run out of things that they can’t replenish through foraging, even if Zuko had any faith in Uncle’s judgment on whether that particular plant needed to be boiled to be safely eaten or whether it was boiling that turned it into a poison. The memory of Uncle leaning heavy on his shoulder, breath rattling in his throat, skin covered in welts, is far too fresh still for Zuko to extend him any trust.

Zuko spends the morning scouting out a comfortable, secluded glade for Jasmine while Uncle counts their coin and considers whether any of their meager remaining possessions might be worth anything in trade. Zuko hopes it doesn’t come to that. And anyway, who this far into the Earth Kingdom in the middle of what's starting to feel like a drought is going to want a *theater mask*. It’s useless for anything except looking alarming in the night, which Zuko is already using it for, so it’s not up for trade anyway.

Besides, it made it this far. They can’t just give it up now, because it’s convenient.

The town they slip into is bigger than a lot of the others they have seen, which is good. It means their faces, shadowed by wide-brimmed hats, won’t stand out so much here. And it's big enough to have a lodging house and a bar on top of the usual general store and feed shops, which means it might be big enough that they actually *could* trade something if they needed to—as long as that something isn’t the theater mask that’s inexplicably managed to survive this far with him when nothing else has except Uncle.

The size of the town turns out to be the only good thing about it, though. Zuko quickly realizes that their coin doesn’t seem to go nearly as far here as it does on the coast. Or maybe that the coin of a refugee doesn’t go particularly far at all compared to the coin of a Prince, even one in exile. Uncle’s gentle, meandering approach to haggling doesn’t seem to be having much of an effect, either, and the merchants snap and snarl about famine and conscription and summer shortages and refuse to bend regardless of how much Zuko shouts.

Uncle eventually hauls Zuko into the shade of a building to very literally cool down when he finally notices that the air around Zuko is starting to shimmer from more than just the summer sun. Zuko grumbles about going, but he’s also quietly, pathetically grateful for the excuse to end the staring contest he found himself locked into with the tiny, grizzled old woman selling salt.

“I know tempers are short in heat like this,” Uncle says with gentle understanding, as if the Fire Nation weren’t always hot and Zuko isn’t always short-tempered. “But it’s not as bad as all that. No need for anger.”

“They’re practically reaching into our pockets to steal from us in broad daylight,” Zuko snaps, purposefully not seeing the speaking glance Uncle gives him and staring at Uncle’s hands instead as he goes through the familiar motions of making tea.

“They are merchants trying to run businesses in hard times, Nephew. Not everything—”

“They’re asking almost *three times* the going price for a sack of rice! Three times!”

“Things are not the same in the interior as on the coast,” Uncle shrugs, settling himself more comfortably against the building and contemplating his teacup.

“No, the interior is where they *grow the rice*.”

“But it’s not where they get to keep the rice. The military taxes strike hard, here,” Uncle frowns, casting his eyes over the sliver of the town they can see. It’s fairly bustling by the standards they have come to know. But it’s clearly still shabby, worn down. By no means doing well.

“Trust the breadbasket of the world to fuck up their supply chain distribution so much that they starve,” Zuko mutters, dropping his head back against the wall and tipping his broad-brimmed hat forward to keep the shade over his face. “Of course everyone in the Earth Kingdom would be incompetent.”

Whatever reply Uncle would make is cut off by an overly solicitous voice suddenly calling out, “Poor dears!” Zuko glares up at the woman staring down at them with open pity on her face. “It’s so hard to be a refugee, but so good that you could keep your family together. Here, every little bit helps, I know!” She drops a few copper pieces into Uncle’s teacup, smiling benevolently.

Zuko stares at her, then down at Uncle’s teacup, half-full of tea and now also sweaty, grubby coins. “What the f—”

“What a wonderful gesture!” Uncle hastily calls out. “Thank you, madam, for your generosity. May the Spirits look kindly on you!”

The woman simpers, accepting Uncle’s thanks with a pleased little smile and turning back into the thoroughfare.

“What,” Zuko grates out. “Was that.”

“That was *kindness*, Nephew,” Uncle says wryly as he fishes the coins out of his tea and slips them into their coin purse. “People do display it, sometimes.”

“That was pity. That was her feeling sorry and—”

“—and giving us enough coin to afford some of that rice you wanted. Beggars can’t be choosers, Nephew.”

“We aren’t beggars!” Zuko snaps, which is a mistake, because Uncle just looks thoughtful as he pours the remainder of his tea onto the ground, not even seeming distressed by the waste.

“We could be,” Uncle finally muses, sitting up a little straighter and assessing the people hurrying by their resting spot.

“...What.”

“We need both coin and rest. Let’s see if we can’t combine the two, Nephew.”

Zuko stares, uncomprehending, and then with slowly dawning horror as Uncle begins begging in earnest. He calls out to anyone walking by, shaking his teacup, offering blessings and bemoaning their weary state and refugee status.

“This is humiliating,” Zuko growls, stiff with secondhand embarrassment.

“We’re hungry,” Uncle says pragmatically, calling out a blessing as a passing man tosses a coin without even trying to drop it into the cup.

“So what, you do anything for some food?”

“There is no shame in asking for help, Nephew.”

Zuko just hisses out a tight breath, trying to pull his inner flame back toward his center and away from his skin. Yes, they’re hungry. Yes, they’re refugees. Yes, they’re without resources or any particularly useful skills. But begging? Just *asking* without providing anything in return? Freely admitting need with no display of strength? It rubs Zuko raw. It goes against all the lessons on leadership and power that have been beaten in him over his entire life.

And he can’t do a single thing about it. There are too many people around to for Zuko to achieve the volume he would really need to adopt to make his feelings clear. And because the more Zuko watches, the more he realizes that he can’t even cling to the shape of the tattered honor he isn’t supposed to care about anymore. The exchanges that should be more palatable, the ones that ask for something in return—a song, a dance, an extra dose of pleading—are so much worse than the outright charity. They make Zuko’s skin itch. They remind him too much of the early days of trying to navigate life away from Caldera.

The memory sits dark and noxious in his blood as he watches the Dragon of the West shuffling for coin on the behest of some Earth Kingdom shitheads. It boils into anger, seeing his Uncle literally dance and warble for some nobody scum. It spills over into the seeping, seething rage that used to have Zuko leaving incriminating things behind in exchange for the scrolls he took, along with anonymous tips to local authorities weeks later.

Zuko fixes the faces of all these assholes into his mind and tracks where they go from beneath the brim of his hat and thinks about regaining lost power. He finally convinces Uncle to call it quits then the late afternoon sun drives all but the most irritable into the comfort of their homes. They need to rest, too, after all. Zuko has more than enough targets memorized to keep him busy tonight.

&#45;-

Uncle doesn’t ask where Zuko is going when he slips out of camp once Agni has well and truly sunk below the horizon, just like he never used to ask whenever Zuko found ways to slither off the *Wani* and back again largely unseen, and the way he never asked about Zuko’s growing collection of scrolls despite his ever-present lack of funds. Uncle spent nearly four years holding onto his plausible deniability with truly admirable determination. The familiarity of it is welcome even if the disappointed sigh is not.

Zuko is fully aware that he is a constant disappointment. He doesn’t need it to be vocalized.

The town is big enough to have alleys and multi-story structures and deep shadows, which is perfect for Zuko. The buildings are made of sunbaked clay over stone, sturdy and well insulated and full of finger- and toe-holds that let Zuko easily reach the roofs. From there it’s a matter of controlling his breathing and willing himself to patient stillness, and keeping an eye on the pub.

When the dickhead who made Uncle dance stumbles out of the building sometime later, weaving and laughing, it’s as easy as breathing for Zuko to ghost along after the glint of moonlight on the man’s dual swords. The man turns down a side alley, fingers fumbling at the ties of his pants, and Zuko wrinkles his nose in distaste. Time to end this before he needs to factor in the annoyance of dodging kicks from recently pissed-on boots.

It's gratifyingly easy to drop down from the roof onto the swordsman. Zuko’s depth perception isn’t always great, especially in his mask, but this he has spent years practicing in various corners of the *Wani*. The man crumples beneath him, shout muffled by a face full of dirt as Zuko rides his momentum forward to shift his weight onto his opponent’s shoulders, countering the man’s instinctive push back upright. Zuko’s hands are quick and sure as he grabs the hilts of the man’s swords, lunging upright and off his opponent with a knee to the back and enough force to knock what little air might be left out of the guy’s chest. Steel rings as the blades sing free of their sheaths.

Zuko turns back to the man, head cocked to the side as he takes in the drunken, half-panicked scramble backward. The moon peeks from behind the clouds with a perfect sense of dramatic timing, slicing through the alley to shine onto the grotesque visage of his mask.

“Please,” the man babbles, all his bravado and posturing gone. Something savage in Zuko stretches and flexes seeing this man reduced before him. Payment for Uncle’s shame, even if Zuko is the only one to feel the cost. “Whatever you want, you can have it. Please. Just don’t hurt me.”

Zuko smiles, slow and hard, testing the balance of his new swords with a quick, flashy twist that draws a satisfying whimper out of the man. It feels good to have metal singing in his hands again, a kind of stretching release like when a splint is finally cut from a broken limb. It feels good to have someone hanging off his wishes again. To feel strong. In control. And right now, Zuko very much wishes for the man’s coin purse. And he’ll take any snacks he has on him, too.

&#45;-

Uncle is still awake when Zuko returns. It’s a surprise, but not entirely unwelcome. He looks at the blades Zuko tosses down, and then at the small bag of jerky Zuko drops by the fire, and fixes Zuko with an unfathomable stare. Zuko stares back, face set into the scowl that passes as neutrality for him.

Uncle’s gaze shifts into quiet disappointment, punctuated with a heavy, pointed sigh and Agni’s balls, Zuko intensely, uselessly wishes that he still had Gao in that moment, that he could still send his words and his heart flying out to someone who understands.

&#45;-

Stealing to survive is much easier than Zuko expected it to be, which isn’t something that happens to him particularly often. Or ever, really. It’s different, though, when you aren’t stealing from wealthy merchants and minor nobility and regional governors. When the people you target don’t have estates and guards and mazes of rooms to be memorized.

Zuko vaguely wonders if he should be worried about the dizzying rush he feels whenever he overpowers his opponent, whenever he wins, whenever he gets to take what he wants and not care about what they want in return. It’s like his day-to-day is some half-dreaming nightmare of walking and heat and Agni’s unrelenting touch, and only then does the world snap around him into sharp focus. Is this how Azula feels all the time? It’s heady, if it is.

Zuko finds it’s a relief, too, to ask nothing of himself other than for his body to work again. His bending is a mess like always, he has no plans like always, Uncle is full of unspoken but very loud opinions like always, but *this* Zuko understands. This he is good at—blades and shadows and dramatic entrances and how to always find the light that most makes the dips and curves of his mask seem to move with life.

It’s a weird thing to be good at. Not suitable for a Crown Prince, who’s supposed to be the blazing power in front of the throne rather than the silent threat behind it. But it’s fine, because Zuko is a refugee and a traitor now, not a Prince. But not for the first time Zuko shies away from the thought that things might have turned out better for everyone if Azula had been born first, if Lu Ten had never gone to war.

&#45;-

For all that his nights feel purposeful again—if he’s going to be awake, he might as well do something productive with the time—Zuko can’t stop bristling under Uncle’s disapproval. Zuko has never been particularly adept at taking criticism, but ever since the North it’s been worse than usual, and right now it’s taking everything in him not to scream as Uncle launches into another lecture. Agni’s balls, Uncle keeps acting like Zuko should hold himself to some standard of nobility that Azula had very effectively shown no longer applied. Zuko doesn’t get to play by those rules anymore, and it grates that Uncle keeps insisting Zuko needs to.

“This isn’t how we need to survive, Nephew,” Uncle frowns when Zuko slips back to their little cave, pleased with himself for snagging dried fish this time. Meat is the hardest to come by for them, the thing his body feels the lack of the most. “You do not need to do this.”

“How did you like your jerky with dinner,” Zuko snaps, dropping the tightly wrapped fish in with their other food stores and bending his head to checking his blades for any knicks. They are almost entirely for show, but cutting down practice targets can dull their edges just as well as a real fight.

“I appreciate your efforts,” Uncle begins, and Zuko snorts because Uncle hasn’t once turned away what Zuko has brought. “But this is not a path you want to go down. This is not honorable, Prince Zuk—”

”*Stop calling me that!”*

The cave is silent for long enough that Zuko is able to pull the sparks off his fingertips, hidden in his fists but about to smoke. “Are you not a Prince anymore?” Uncle finally asks, voice careful like it rarely is, acknowledging the dangerous landscape they are suddenly walking.

“…We’re *fugitives*. We’ve been declared traitors!”

“That does not change who we are, Nephew.”

“Really? So I’m still the Crown Prince of the Fire Nation?” Zuko can tell that he’s getting louder and he doesn’t really care. “Fine. Then all of this—” he slashes a blade toward the jerky and fish and rice that he has gotten them. “—is to keep us strong.”

His words hang in the air, expecting a response, and Uncle gives him one with the air of a man knowingly stepping into hostile territory. “To keep us strong. For what, exactly?”

“For the mission.” Zuko watches Uncle’s face for any twitch of a reaction.

“…The mission.”

“We can always resume the mission and find the Avatar.” Zuko doesn’t stumble over the word, which is a faint surprise.

“The Avatar.” It’s harder when someone else is saying it, but his inner flame settles after a few breaths.

“If I’m still the Crown Prince, then that means I still have my mission from the Fire Lord, don’t I? My duty. You can’t have one without the other.” Zuko’s words are caustic, hard, even as he forces his volume to modulate in the face of Uncle’s tightening expression.

“Being a Prince is about more than doing what the Fire Lord asks,” Uncle protests, leaning forward in his urgency, face open and guileless as if being a Prince wasn’t *entirely* doing what the Fire Lord wants. Is Uncle going to try to act like he gave up his throne because he *wanted* to? “There’s more than just that *mission*.”

Zuko rocks back on his feels in surprise at the sudden venom in Uncle’s tone, at the thing as close to naked hatred as Zuko has ever heard Uncle express. “Not for me,” Zuko finally says, shaking his head. Agni, has—has Uncle only been pretending to care this whole time? About the only thing in Zuko’s life? “That mission is what I have been given. There isn’t anything ‘more’ without it.”

“Zuko, you are worth more than—”

“This isn’t about what I’m *worth*.”

Uncle takes a deep breath like he is trying to regain his neutrality. Zuko *hates* when he does that, hates when Uncle pretends that none of this matters to him when it so clearly *does*. “Then what is it about? What do *you* want, Nephew?”

Zuko snorts, involuntary. Whatever this is about, it’s definitely not about what Zuko *wants*. It never has been and it isn’t and it can’t ever be and Zuko refuses to go there with Uncle. He refuses to bare the vulnerable parts of himself, the things far too close to hope, because it’s not about any of that, either.

“Nephew,” Uncle finally sighs, looking worn and exhausted and *old.* Zuko sucks in a sharp breath against the sudden, furious twist of his inner flame as it feeds off a new kind of resentment that Uncle could look so fragile, that he might no longer be the unshakeable infallible mountain of a man from Zuko’s childhood. “The path may seem stretched, and long, and twisted, with many branches, but the badger mole—”

Zuko shoots to his feet and leaves. He’s so far past being absolutely *done* with words that just take up air and mean *nothing*. With answers that are just a way to dodge voicing a real fucking opinion. With platitudes that insist everything is fine when it *isn’t*.

It’s utter *shit*, being without honor and without a nation and still chained by the expectations of a role and a station that no one ever thought he was good enough to have in the first place. For the first time in six years Zuko can’t—doesn’t have to—slide into the shoes of a Crown Prince and pretend that they fit. But how is he ever going to figure out the rules to being whatever the fuck he is these days when Uncle keeps trying to bind him back to who he used to be?

Zuko just…needs to figure this out. He needs to figure out what he is now without constantly being reminded of the way things used to be and all the ways he fell short. Fuck, of all the ways he is still falling short of expectations that shouldn’t apply to him anymore because the past is over and done and nothing but ashes.

## Chapter 4: Into The Wild

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for an attack on a character that could be read as either straight assault or with sexual assault undertones, and for an on-screen character death (an OC, we aren't offing Zuko four chapters into this baby)

### Text

In some ways being alone is as easy as breathing because in some ways Zuko has always been alone. Even on a ship full of his crew, even in a palace full of his family, Zuko rarely walked through life with anyone at his side, and certainly not in the past three years. But Zuko walked those years with Uncle at his back or trying to tug him along or make him slow, and before with Azula always somewhere waiting to pounce. Zuko doesn’t know what to do without that weight to fight against, to counterbalance. It’s an almost sickening relief to not have to pretend in front of someone else, even as the lightness of having no expectations beyond his own feels dangerously like floating away.

Being alone is as easy as breathing. Zuko's needed lessons in how to do that right all his life.

It took days for Zuko to push down the nagging worry that when he bid Uncle a subdued farewell and led Jasmine away, he was also walking away from one of the only touchstones he has left. But Zuko knows in his head, if nowhere else, that Uncle will be fine. More than fine. The old man is genial, friendly, calm. Uncle has a way of making people like him that Zuko fundamentally does not understand, and the ability to casually lay waste to the entire region if he were truly at risk. Uncle is really only ever in danger when he is too lazy to remove himself from it. Or when Zuko is involved.

So Uncle will be fine, because Zuko is gone and even Uncle isn’t lazy to the point of being suicidal. And Zuko will be fine too, eventually. He’s finally able to set a snare that works, once he realized that a snare is just rope and knots and not some kind of magic. Zuko spent three years coiling ropes and tying knots and inspecting both for deficiencies and wear and tear. He knows what to do with those, and he’s grimly proud the first time he catches a rabaroo. And then just grim, when he realizes that he caught it but he still doesn’t quite know how to clean it to make it fit for eating. It seems more complicated than sea vultures. Or maybe Zuko just isn’t as desperate yet.

&#45;-

A sullen day of helping some trapper haul pelts toward town—Zuko is a twitchy mess the whole time, just waiting for the other shoe to drop—earns him a sullen meal of fresh-caught meat. Zuko watches the trapper clean his kill with an intensity that almost gets him thrown out of camp and has them both stalking away from the possibility of Zuko finishing the job the next day.

But it’s worth it to eat a dinner Zuko catches himself a few nights later without the persistent fear that he’s somehow going to poison himself because he doesn’t know what he’s doing, which would be truly ironic considering Uncle isn’t here anymore.

&#45;-

One thing Zuko didn’t anticipate is quite how much *time* he would have, being alone. He still travels throughout the day and now it’s only him to do the work of setting up and breaking down camp, of preparing food, of grooming Jasmine, of washing clothes. He doesn’t think he’s really figured that last one out yet, but he also doesn’t think it’s possible to be in the Earth Kingdom and not be covered in dust, so he isn’t sure how much his own ineptitude is really at fault. But once that’s done, it's just Zuko by the fire in the morning, just Zuko resting in the shade at the height of midday, just Zuko polishing his swords at night and contemplating whether there’s anything he needs to replenish enough to make leaving the rest of his supplies unguarded worth it.

Zuko doesn’t do particularly well with unoccupied time, especially when it's only his own thoughts for company. He knows that. He starts running katas again, mostly dry but sometimes live when he finds a secluded enough camping spot. When even that feels too risky—firebending and earthbending don’t exactly use the same forms—he practices with his swords, throwing his body into movement until he can finally reach that place in his mind where he doesn’t have to think.

It feels weird to train without someone there to guide him or correct his form or point out when he’s falling short. And lacking anyone to tell him that he’s wrong, Zuko just has to do what feels right, which is…unsettling. At first, it reminds him too much of when he was new to the *Wani* and would run katas dry to his room under the cover of music night because he couldn’t risk being heard and having his weakness seen, and he couldn’t bring himself to face a flame yet, even his own, but he still needed to relearn to move without falling.

Then the one day he accidentally runs a flame down the edge of his sword, mixing up his forms and leaning into the wrong instinct, and instead of being chastised again for cross-training and making things harder for himself and still being sloppy as a toddler letting his fire spill out, he just watches the flame dance along the blade. There’s no one to cringe away from here, no pretenses of competence to maintain, so Zuko just calls a little bit more fire and admires the way the flames look against the metal. If he messes up and no one sees it, is it possible to pretend that the mistake never happened?

All the training has the side benefit of completely exhausting his body and mind, too. Sleep hasn’t come easy to Zuko in years, but he can do it when his body demands it, even if he can’t ever seem to achieve a state of exhaustion that will stop him from dreaming. He dreams of swimming, of losing his grip, of finding the Avatar, of being torn apart. It would make his mornings harder, waking to clinging terror night after night, if Zuko weren’t already more used to nightmares than not.

&#45;-

Now that Uncle isn’t around, Zuko is even more careful to keep his bending under control. But eventually, even Zuko is able to realize that people outside of the Fire Nation don’t really think about fire the same way a firebender does. They would recognize jets of flame and handfuls of fire, sure. But no one seems to recognize the difference between a flame’s natural intensity and what Zuko can bring out into a cookfire, and when Agni is already scorching the air no one seems to notice if Zuko is also bending the heat around him.

It’s an embarrassingly intense relief to realize that as long as Zuko sticks to heat and not flame, he can still feed his unwelcome, persistent emotions into his inner flame until he feels like he can breathe again. On particularly bad days—most days—Zuko can spend hours focused on the heat around him, spreading it out in slow waves, or pulling it up from sun-hot pools of water, or sinking it into the earth, or holding himself cool while the very air seems to boil around him. He learns to walk almost trancelike, until finally there’s nothing left inside him to burn and he drifts back into his thoughts, weightless and empty and safe again.

&#45;-

Zuko’s eventually driven into town again. Not for his own needs this time but because Jasmine is almost out of feed and the further they get into the Earth Kingdom the less foraging she’s able to do. He glares down at the meager coins in his hand, wishing that there were enough farms around that he could just steal what he needed without it being monumentally obvious that the one stranger for miles was the one to do it.

“Hey, kid.” Zuko snaps his glare up to the man addressing him, who is *not* a merchant and therefore has *no reason* to be talking to Zuko. But who also doesn’t have that oily, calculating look Zuko has learned to get away from as fast as he can. “You looking for work?”

“I’m just passing through,” Zuko says as if that weren’t completely obvious. He slowly turns the idea of *work* over in his head, assessing the man again, looking for any deception.

“I just need some help for the day,” the man grunts, crossing skinny arms over a chest that looks like it used to be broad. “We’re rebuilding a fence.”

“I’ve never done that before,” Zuko warns.

“There’s not much to it.” The man eyes Zuko, seeming satisfied by whatever he sees. “You’d be fine. There’s dinner in it for you and the ostrich horse. A few coppers if you work well.”

Zuko hesitates, considers, and finally grunts his assent and trails the man back to his farm from a healthy distance. You can lure a lot of people to a lot of places with the right kind of promises. Zuko can’t afford to not be wary with only Jasmine watching his back.

&#45;-

There doesn’t end up being much to the work. The man—Zuko never bothers to ask his name, and the man returns the favor—was truthful that Zuko would be fine at it, since all it really requires is muscle and a willingness to keep going past the point when your body screams for you to stop. Zuko is good at that—it’s one of his only skills, according to Azula —and the dinner he earns for himself and Jasmine is perfectly adequate. Zuko isn’t surprised that he doesn’t get the coppers, though—he did his work with far too much bite and irritableness for it to be considered to have been done ‘well.’

&#45;-

Zuko learns to keep an eye out for jobs that require effort, not skill. The mindlessness of manual labor works just as well to tire his body as the mindlessness of training, even if some useless part of Zuko’s pride always bristles at the former. He tries to drown it under the satisfaction of seeing a job done, tangible and visible and worth the meal that it puts in front of him. Trading his labor for food and coin makes sense to him the way begging never did, a way of saying ‘this is what I’m worth’ and having it validated.

A half-day’s dedicated work from the former Crown Prince of the Fire Nation is generally worth a bowl of mystery stew, a hunk of stale bread, a pile of hay, and no more than five coppers. It’s strangely comforting, to finally know his value to others in terms that he can touch. And Zuko doesn’t consider being a gracious or easy work partner to be worth anything any price, which he makes very clear on every job he takes, and the way it’s met with a shrug and a glower is comfort as well. They demand nothing beyond what they ask for and Zuko gives nothing beyond what he promises.

&#45;-

“Hey, watch it asshole!”

“You watch it, fuck face, what are you, blind?” Zuko snarls, glaring as he drops the stone he’s hauling dangerously close to other man’s feet. A small crew has been working for hours to clear some stretch of land for crops or something like that—Zuko doesn’t know, he doesn’t ask questions, he doesn’t care—and the self-appointed dickwad in charge—who doesn’t even know the farm, he was just the first one to get hired—has been grating on Zuko’s temper all day.

“You got a big mouth on you for someone so scrawny, kid.”

“And you’ve got a huge head for someone so fucking stupid,” Zuko snaps. “Now get out of my way.”

“Your way? You don’t go no way around here, asshole.” Which barely makes sense, but the tone is hostile so Zuko gets the intent just fine. “I tell you what your way is!”

“You couldn’t find your way out of your own ass,” Zuko growls, tired and cranky and absolutely over having to deal with this self-important sack of dirt pretending to be a human. *One more turn*, he reminds himself. One more turn of the farmer's sand clock and Zuko can grab his food and his pay and get out of here.

“You better watch yourself,” the man threatens, looming into Zuko’s space. “You could make a lot of people mad saying shit like that. I could say you didn’t do any work, you know. I could say you didn’t earn anything at the end of the day.”

“No one here would back you,” Zuko scowls, crossing his arms. Zuko’s been busting his ass for hours even as the others dawdle toward the end of the day. Plus, he’s having a far easier time carrying rocks that really should be burning hot from the sun than the rest of them are. He’s more than earned his pay.

“No one here would go against me,” the man smirks. “Not for some scarred-up weirdo like you.”

Zuko just rolls his eyes and leaves his stone for the man to deal with, numb by this point to comments on his appearance so transparently designed to get a rise out of him. How original, both the insult and the threat. As if any of the other workers have any idea who the fuck this idiot is, let alone care enough about him to fall in line.

Agni’s flaming dick, the whole crew is a bunch of mouthy, pissy assholes today, and Zuko cannot *wait* for this fucking job to be done. It is *not* worth the meal and the handful of coppers he has waiting for him at the end.

&#45;-

If Zuko weren’t so tired from the job and having to make up everyone else’s slack so they could all get paid, he might have had the presence of mind to put a little more distance between himself and the farm after the early evening meal. If Zuko were better at reading people in general, he might have picked up on the glances and looks.

But Zuko just put his head down to indicate that no, he didn’t want to fucking talk, now fuck off, thank you very much. And Agni had been particularly hot, and their temporary employer had been particularly stingy with water rations.

Zuko barely manages to get Jasmine settled for the night in the first clearing he finds before he’s flopping down on his bedroll, exhaustion finally catching up and pulling him down into a hopefully dreamless sleep.

&#45;-

Zuko wakes to a heavy weight crashing down onto his back. The air flies from his lungs as his face is shoved into his bedroll. Zuko jerks, already thrashing and trying to find leverage as he goes from sleep to waking. But his hands are wrapped under his body, tucked awkwardly under his chest, and his legs are too tangled to find purchase, and his struggles only earn him a low laugh and a hand on the back of his neck grinding his face harder against the ground.

“I told you to watch yourself, asshole,” a voice breathes into his ear, and Zuko goes motionless, taut. “Now it’s time for us to teach you a little lesson in respect.”

Zuko begins to panic, then. Not that he was *calm*, before. But this is revenge now, not a crime of opportunity. And Zuko might be generally confident in his ability to hold his own in a fight, but he’s been caught flat-footed in the worst possible way, his hands trapped against his chest so he can’t bend, his weapons too far away to reach. And ‘us’ is very different than ‘I’. Zuko doesn’t know what this is, precisely, but he knows what it could be and he isn’t going to fucking wait around to find out.

Zuko begins to struggle in earnest, trying to twist free, trying to wiggle a hand out from against his own body where he won’t do anything but burn himself, trying to find some purchase with his legs to buck against the weight on his back. He flails with his fire sense too. He can’t do shit except raise and lower flames with his body trapped like this, but he grabs for the fire he can feel anyway. He can snuff the campfire and plunge them into darkness, and if Zuko is expecting it and they aren’t then he can use the moment of disorientation to his advantage, and—

There’s a choked gurgled and then Zuko loses what little breath he has left as the man collapses onto him, a complete, half-smothering deadweight. Fuck, this isn’t what Zuko expected, this doesn’t make it easier to—

Zuko finally registers that the weight on him is just *weight*. That it’s heavy and suffocating but not actively restraining or pinning in response to Zuko’s writhing. And Zuko can’t hear a single thing except for his own harsh breathing.

Zuko squirms, finally wrenching his face to the side. He sucks in a clean breath of air and ignores the stale-sweat smell of another person too close as he finally strains his good eye into the darkness and listens as hard as he can, struggling for any clue of what’s going on, what the play is, what the next attack is going to be.

Zuko remembers that he never bothered to light a campfire in the first place tonight.

With careful, cautious movements Zuko begins to wriggle himself free. It wouldn’t do to wake his attacker—attackers?—but Agni’s balls, he needs to get out from under the man, needs to be free to move and fight, needs to figure out how many others there are and get away, needs to restrain his panic so that he can move with efficiency and purpose and not blind terror. Zuko finally gets his arms under him enough to finally shove his torso upright, scrambling forward when the weight on his back shifts and begins to roll off to the side. Fire leaps into his hands, lighting his way to his swords and Zuko dives for them, whirling to put a tree at his back and his weapons in front of him, fire jumping and erratic and skittering up the blades as panic shreds his control.

There are three of them. He recognized the voice from the job today, but after an endlessly long stretch of heartbeats Zuko realizes that the others were there at that farm, too. Pretending not to know each other, maybe. Or else bound together by their mutual hatred of Zuko after spending half a day in his presence enough to decide to come after him in the night.

Zuko trembles with the need to get the fuck out of here, but the first attacker is near Zuko’s bag and the other two by Jasmine, and sure, they all seem to be slumped in heaps right now but that could change at any instant. Zuko can see knives and rope and clubs, and delayed terror is making his thoughts foggy, his breathing too ragged for proper firebending. He keeps his swords out in front of him and the tree at his back and waits to see what they’re going to do because he can’t seem to make himself do anything else. He could run on his own, but he can’t leave Jasmine and he can’t make himself move any closer to get to her.

Zuko doesn’t know how long he crouches there, immobile and ready to explode into motion but unable to move. But eventually he registers the frayed, scorched-out strain on his fire sense, the same way it feels when he’s been asking too much of it and his inner flame just needs to be banked low so it can rest. Numb, automatic, he flicks the fire off his swords into the campfire he never lit and releases the flames. But he’s still straining, inner fire pulling thin now with effort, so Zuko takes his first careful, controlled breath since waking. He consciously coaxes his inner fire back into the center of his chest like he hasn’t had to do since he was first learning to bend, before he learned how to keep his fire from flaring out onto everything with every jump in his emotions.

Zuko blinks in surprise to feel a slight tug back, the way it would be if Zuko were trying to pull his fire sense in tight while still holding onto the flames around him. He tries again, but still that tug. Agni’s tits, if he somehow fucked up his bending even more than it already is… Zuko follows the tug back next time, letting it act as a guideline for his fire sense to follow, trying to figure out what he’s holding onto so he can let it go. It fucking figures that his basics would be devolving so much that he’s back to a toddler’s level of control and awareness of his surroundings.

Zuko doesn’t know what to do with the fact that those guidelines keep pulling him back to his attackers. He tries to find the flame again, and again, and again, and finally huffs out a frustrated breath and just goes with it. Maybe this is some panic-trauma thing, and his brain needs him to go through the motions of letting go in order to—

Zuko’s breath stutters in shock when he actually feels his fire sense untwist. Not some metaphysical in his head thing but actually how it unwinds from around a candle, and it's only as his fire sense rushes back in that Zuko realizes just how *much* it’s been straining, and for how long. But...it wasn’t around fire. It was around…heat. Because Zuko has been bending heat instead of fire these days to stay safe on the road. And because Zuko in his panic had reached for anything he could grasp onto and he hadn’t found torches or a campfire or a candle, he had found…them.

Zuko slowly straightens, swords cautiously lowering as he stares at the slumped figures that are still not moving.

*Oh. Fuck*.

&#45;-

Zuko’s hands are trembling as he hastily packs his bag, and he doesn’t bother trying to stop them. There’s no one but him and Jasmine to see them shake and she won’t be saying anything. Agni, Zuko can barely look at the motionless figure still half-slumped on his bedroll without his stomach heaving for multiple reasons. Half of him is still waiting for the man to lurch up into another attack. The other half is little more than pure skittering panic so far past Zuko’s ability to control.

Zuko makes quick work of gathering up his things, nearly sobbing with relief when he edges around the other two men to find Jasmine blinking sleepy eyes at him. Her beak is familiar and gentle, nosing through his hair as he situates the saddle and lashes his bags in place. It’s almost enough to crack through his frantic numbness and make him cry, which Zuko can’t afford to waste the energy on right now.

Zuko gets ready to mount, glancing reflexively to check his back and hesitating when he sees the firelight flickering over the knife in one of the men’s hands. It looks like a good knife.

Zuko could use a good knife.

He teeters for a long moment, trapped between hard practical logistics and the types of emotions that Zuko doesn’t have—will never have—the time for. Practicality wins out, like it always does. Zuko learned a long time ago how to set aside his own wants in order to survive.

With shallow breaths and quick hands Zuko searches the bodies—*bodies, bodies, warm but* *cooling, fuck, fuck, fuck*. He chooses the best two knives, keeps the coins in their separate purses because it never hurts to look like you have less than you do, and wraps all the food up into one of their packs. He leaves behind the spark rocks, the spare clothing that smells too much like sour sweat, the little scraps of cloth too small to be handkerchiefs that could have been cut from clothing. Zuko doesn’t want to think about those too much, or about the little carved cat at the bottom of one of the bags that looks remarkably like the one the farmer’s kid had been playing with when Zuko left dinner.

Apparently, the rest of the work crew would fall in line after the guy after all.

&#45;-

Zuko stays awake the rest of the night. Jasmine is a warm presence at his back as he stares into the darkness, ears straining for any noises above the normal sounds of the forest. The hilts of his swords are familiar and reassuring in his hands. His thoughts are loud, too loud, all of them, nothing clear or distinct except for a humming dread and the too-sharp memory of how it felt to hold Sokka’s not-flame in his mind and deep, shuddering relief that Zuko never tried to do anything except hold it

&#45;-

Zuko doesn’t go into town for days. Jasmine seems to sense his skittish energy, moving with a bit more speed and intent than the usual pace Zuko lets her set for herself. Zuko was cautious of encountering others on the road before, but now he’s outright vigilant against it, hostile wariness singing through him. He keeps pulling them into the forest where it exists, or behind outcroppings of rock where it doesn’t, when the itching fear of being watched and seen and followed gets too much for him, worse than it ever was with Azula stalking his steps because Zuko knows what to expect from her.

Training helps, though he only touches his swords, and physical exertion in general. Zuko starts jogging behind Jasmine one day when the restlessness gets to be too much, and finds that after a certain point of tiredness he can feed his emotions just as effectively into movement as he can into firebending, so long as the only goal on the other side is to feel empty and numb.

Zuko keeps his bending pulled in tight. Almost as close as he kept it when he was still afraid of his own fire. Tighter, maybe, because this time he needs to keep awareness of more than just flames on a tight leash, and there’s no Uncle around to check him if he gets out of control.

&#45;-

Zuko runs through his supplies faster than he should, exerting himself like that when he has so little to spare. But then, he has so much more than he did before, even if he doesn’t let himself think about why, and in the end it's Jasmine needing more feed that eventually drives him back into town.

Zuko turns down the offered job, even though the farmer looks old and kindly in a way that reminds him of Uncle. Zuko passes over far more coin than he probably should instead in exchange for a sack of stale grain and the ability to get away as fast as possible. That, it turns out, has a lot of value to Zuko these days.

&#45;-

Zuko does need to work again, eventually. He knows that it’s coming and when it finally arrives, he’s cautious and skittish and categorically refuses to work with anyone except the person hiring him. But he also manages to rein back his pride and his temper into sullenness instead of antagonism and hostility.

It seems to go alright, even if Zuko is a twitchy mess all day, his fire constantly leaping just under his skin. He’s somewhat grudgingly invited back for a second day of work and somewhat grudgingly says yes when he hears how much is being offered.

Sleeping in the farmer’s outbuilding instead of under the stars has Zuko lying awake for more than just the usual reasons, disoriented and edgy without a clear line of sight, silently trying to remind himself over and over what it feels like to be within walls.

&#45;-

Zuko doesn’t feel good about this. His inner fire is restless and tight, his hands itching for the hilts of his swords. He’s in yet another no-name town, a medium-sized one this time. He has enough feed left for another two days of traveling, and fuck, maybe he needs to risk that being enough to find his way to another farm because Zuko does *not* like the look of the guy offering him work in exchange for supplies. There isn’t anything particularly wrong with the man, he’s just height and muscle and easy movement in a way that tells Zuko that the guy probably knows how to fight. Zuko doesn’t want to get anywhere near him.

Zuko needs the supplies, though. He leans against Jasmine’s side, letting her investigate the back of his head as he considers his options and traces the hilt of one of his swords. He could take the job—the man said he would be in town for another hour if Zuko changed his mind— and keep his fire close to his skin and be ready to burn his way out of any trouble, even if the reality of that would cause…more problems than Zuko’s probably prepared to deal with, in the long run. He could get back on the road and trust that they’ll be able to keep following the river and that they won’t have to go too far to find another homestead. Or…

The hilt of his sword is warm from the sun. Comforting heat balancing a sharp blade, power and assurance and control for the taking.

“Oi, traveler. Yes, you, who else would I be talking to?”

Zuko half-turns toward the voice, taking in the man—a blacksmith—in a quick glance that lets him relax away from the likelihood of any immediate threat, even if the fact that the man called out to Zuko in the first place sets him on edge. Zuko doesn’t exactly look like someone who has the coin to afford…ostrich horseshoes, or whatever it is that the man’ trying to sell, and Agni’s balls does Zuko not have the emotional energy to extract himself from a sticky sales conversation right now.

“You looking for work?” Zuko blinks in surprise. “I saw you talking with Bo, earlier. I’m Hei. You’re looking for a job?”

“I don’t know anything about blacksmithing,” Zuko says cautiously. If he didn’t want to go with Bo because of his size and strength then this guy isn’t much better for all that he’s a bit shorter and sturdier. More ‘immovable wall’ than the darting quickness that seemed to hang around the other one.

Zuko could probably get away from Hei, if he had to.

“Do you know about fire?” Zuko stares, slowly turning to fully face the blacksmith. Hei just grunts as he takes in Zuko’s scar. “Well, if you aren’t afraid of it, my wife and I could use someone to help with the bellows. My daughter usually does it, but she’s sick today.”

Zuko’s eyes flick over Hei’s shoulder into his open storefront, finding the stout, brisk-looking woman doing something behind the counter. Usually Zuko never meets any wives, outside of mealtimes. And the shopfront is open, so it’s not like Zuko would be tucked away somewhere without an escape…

He flicks his eyes to the low, cheerful glow of fire from within the shop, then back to Hei. “What would I have to do?”

&#45;-

Zuko is fascinated by the forge. The bellows are easy enough to work, particularly given that Zuko doesn’t actually need to get them right in order to make the flames rise and fall as needed. It’s easy firebending, the most basic of tasks, only different from meditating over a candle in the size of the flame and the movement of his body to maintain the pantomime.

It gives Zuko lots of time to observe, and he barely knows where to start. Hei’s casual control of the fire, the way flames are guided to a useful purpose, the couple’s easy relaxation around molten metal and flying sparks—Zuko feels like he could stay here for days and still have more to soak in.

Hei eventually notices Zuko’s curiosity and begins explaining what he’s doing, talking about tempering and quenching and shaping and which metals hold the best edge, and which become brittle when they’re overworked or overheated. It gives Zuko a sharp pang of nostalgia, and he tentatively reaches out with his fire sense, not trying to hold anything or wrap his will around it, just feeling the way the rod of iron is held at a particular temperature for working, the way heat bleeds out of it into air and water and is fed back in through the fire.

It’s entrancing, the rhythm and cycle of it. Zuko can’t stop his eyes from being drawn back to Hei, amazed over and over by the fine control this non-bender has over flame, how he manipulates not just fire but heat in a way that no one except Uncle ever seems to talk much about. Zuko can feel the part of his mind not engaged with what’s in front of him spinning off into possibilities. What could a Master firebender do with knowledge like this, of not just fire but of what fire can do beyond just burning?

&#45;-

Zuko eventually begins to see that all the coppers in the world run out quickly when no one has anything to sell. Is it always like this in the Earth Kingdom? Or has drought or famine or war made it this way.

Forest and pockets of trees and anything more than scrub starts to get harder and harder to find, farms more and more sparse, farmers more and more reluctant to give up any of what they have, even in exchange for work. Eventually, even water starts to become scarce, Zuko’s searching turning up muddy streambeds and dry ponds more often than not.

With every step he takes he can feel himself beginning to fade, slipping toward a state that’s close to feverish. Every breath is thick with dust until his throat feels so parched, he doubts he could speak even if he wanted to. He reluctantly works up the nerve to firebend again, trying to draw away heat to keep Jasmine and himself cool and grimly wishing for a waterbender, something he never thought he would want before.

Even with his bending to shield them from the worst of the heat, Zuko can feel his thoughts getting fuzzier and fuzzier. It’s harder and harder to concentrate each degree Agni takes overhead. Or maybe it’s because Zuko is bending that he feels this way. Maybe his inner flame is burning him from the inside out. Retribution for how it’s been used, or for how it’s been ignored. Both feel equally likely as Zuko slips more and more out of the present and into a muddled haze, feeling trapped within too-tight skin, burning with it until he can barely distinguish the past from the present.

&#45;-

The heat breaks with a storm. Zuko can feel it coming long before it arrives. At first, he doesn’t register what it is, too tired and fuzzy to place the snapping sensation just under his skin, to realize that it’s actually *there* and not just the memory of watching monsoons from the safety of his room as a boy. But then a bolt of lightning touches down in the distance and Zuko’s inner fire leaps in welcome.

Zuko jerks his head up, startling Jasmine to a halt as he twists to the west where he can just see the smudge of dark clouds on the horizon. Without thinking he turns her off the road, pointing her through the scrubland and toward the storm. Zuko breathes deeply for the first time in what feels like days, his skin tingling. The air coming toward them is damp and electric, Jasmine picking up her pace at signs of water as Zuko’s heart rate begins to climb higher, higher, higher, the closer they get.

Zuko slides down to the ground when the first drops of rain begin to fall. He fumbles to set out his one cup and bowl, the small cookpot, his fingertips raw from digging out a shallow indentation in the sunbaked earth to line with rocks so that maybe the water can pool there too and not immediately sink into the parched earth. He ties Jasmine loosely, strips off her saddle, and begins walking toward the heart of the storm, following the persistent tug against his inner flame.

Zuko tilts his head back as the rain starts to come down harder, catching droplets on his tongue, his stuttering thoughts latching onto the shouldn’t-be-unfamiliar sensation of water plastering his hair to his head, to the feeling of rain carving rivulets in the dust coating his body. Agni’s breath, Zuko is so dizzy he can barely walk straight from moving so quickly from barely conscious to driving alertness. His veins thrum with potential and something in him is coiling tighter and tighter, rising, wild, pushing Zuko to balance trembling between control and letting his bending tear free.

Zuko has always had to tightly control his reactions to storms before, snatching back the loose edges of his inner flame and holding rigidly to his inner walls and forcing himself to feel nothing other than an itching kind of restlessness. Zuko has always had to be visible and present on the *Wani,* has never had a moment when he could afford to let his control slip. And Zuko never had the words to describe what he was feeling before that.

Now, though, it’s just Zuko and the broad empty earth and the first lance of lightning sets him ablaze. It’s still miles off, but Zuko’s fire sense is in the storm now and he feels that bolt like it’s a hand reaching into his body and dragging fingers down his bones. His inner fire surges in greeting and instead of smothering it down, Zuko loosens his hold and lets his inner flame finally respond to the storm.

Crackling energy thrums down his limbs and Zuko’s inner fire leaps to meet it. He can feel it twining around and with the foreign energy, his muscles tensing and twitching as something outside of himself slips beneath his skin and carves out space in his core, his pulse surging to the rhythm of the storm.

Another bolt of lightning and Zuko lets out a half-cry, head kicking back to tip his face toward Agni high above the cloud. Rain beats against his upturned face, blurring his vision and slipping through his parted lips and Zuko’s blood is on *fire*, his every nerve buzzing and shuddering from the crown of his head to down to his toes.

Zuko’s inner fire twists and tugs and surges with the energy of the storm until it finally finds some equilibrium, ghostly pale flames erupting over his skin, red edged with flickering white-blue sparks. The loops of flame weave over his body without burning as his fire swirls with the energy of the storm and Zuko can only stare, fascinated, and reach out instinctively with his fire sense—no, his *heat* sense.

He shudders, choking on a gasp as he feels something in the storm reach back.

The next bolt comes immediately and sends Zuko to his knees. A shout presses uselessly against his paralyzed throat as his body clenches, pure overwhelming sensation surging through him. The lightning’s energy coils over him, around him, into him. Zuko can feel every single inch of his skin, of his bones, of his veins, of his electric-tinged fire. He can feel every single pathway of his chi, the distant edges of it within himself that he didn’t even know were there, his awareness chasing energy through his own body until he realizes that he’s chasing behind his own fire as it roars through him, unchecked.

Zuko falls back onto the wet earth, closing his eyes against the water and opening his mouth to the rain and his fire to the lightning, still miles off. He lets his flames lead him and arches into the next strike, so hyperaware that Zuko can barely keep track of the separation between himself and his flame, of where he ends and the storm begins as the air fills with static.

Zuko can feel his fire spilling out of him, rolling over the bare ground, tangled with his fire sense and heat sense until Zuko feels stretched out across the earth, pulled up into the sky, straining against the edges of his own body. Zuko doesn’t call his fire back, just lets the storm and his inner flame move him and guide him and show him the shape of himself free from everything but the wildness inside.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

So when I said Zuko's bending gets interesting...

## Chapter 5: Tear Down Your Heroes

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warning for maybe a bit more than canon-typical violence

### Text

After the storm, Zuko feels…not exactly different. He’s still covered head-to-toe in dust, worse now since he basically laid down in a thin layer of mud. The weather is just as hot and dry after the storm rolls through, and the road just as empty of other travelers and merchants and any signs of thriving. But Zuko doesn’t quite feel the same as he did before, either, in a way he can’t put into words. The tense, twisting quality of his inner flame feels a bit more like a purposeful coil and a bit less like a tangled knot, and the itching paranoia of feeling always watched now is something more like cautious readiness.

It’s like some tension Zuko didn’t even know he was carrying has fallen away, like maybe he doesn’t have to lock himself away in order to survive this, and Zuko finally pokes around his bending again with wary curiosity. The days are still just as long and empty of company and distraction except for Jasmine, and Zuko still has too many things to avoid thinking about and not nearly enough water or food to keep running behind Jasmine to silence his mind.

Concentrating on his bending is still a ready way to avoid looking at the things Zuko doesn’t want to think about. But instead of burning his emotions off into his inner flame, Zuko hesitantly tries to just concentrate on the feel of the flame, on the movement of his chi, sinking deeper into himself than he would normally allow himself without someone around to watch his back.

It’s a risk to turn so far into his fire that Zuko can’t react immediately to things around him with anything other than flames. But Zuko finds that his fire feels a little less like it’s constantly straining to slip his control like this, stretching to fill his thoughts rather than consume them. It’s still hungry, still ravenous and full of wanting. But then, so is Zuko, and like calls to like.

&#45;-

That’s the other thing after the storm. Zuko had let the lightning roll through him any way it wanted until his body still tingles in memory of it, a resonance that keeps coming back without ever losing its strength. Part of him craves it again, even as a larger part of him knows there’s probably only so much of something like that his body can take, that not all storms feel that way.

But Zuko has only felt like this one time before and he’s been avoiding thinking about it for…months, really. And now with the echo of lightning so fresh, Zuko can’t stop remembering that other time, too. Without active, tight focus Zuko’s mind keeps drifting to the storm, and then from there to another storm, then to blue eyes looking through water-logged hair, then to an alley with eager fire surging under his skin and Sokka chasing the sparks on his breath like Sokka couldn’t imagine anything better in that moment than the touch of Zuko’s fire.

It’s…inconvenient, to remember. Zuko is aware that this had never *gone away*, for him, but he thought he’d managed to work himself to some place of…bleak acceptance? Resignation over the futility of wanting anything at all when he’s barely surviving? Grim understanding that it didn’t fucking matter what Sokka’s last letter said, the one Zuko lost to the explosion and the waves, because things like that aren't for him?

But the unchained energy of the storm shivers through Zuko’s thoughts. It hovers at the back of his mind, a ghost of a feeling that refuses to stay buried, a memory of throwing away control and expectation for instinct and want and how amazing it felt to do so.

Agni, maybe this is how firebenders lose control. Not in eruptions of anger or incandescent with rage, but seduced by the siren call of their own fire.

&#45;-

Some things don’t change. Zuko still dreams, when sleep manages to catch him, of cold terror and hands that are too weak. Of finally capturing the Avatar only to realize that he’s holding a monster and can’t let go.

But when he jolts awake, screams trapped behind his lips until his throat feels raw with them, and cups fire into his palms to remind himself of where and when he is, the small flames are a comfort that they weren’t always before, just like the warmth of Jasmine nearby. That change, at least, is welcome.

&#45;-

The first military patrol in the distance down this poor excuse for a road almost sends Zuko diving for cover into the scrubby bushes, which would be both completely ineffective and completely suspicious. He wills himself to stay on Jasmine’s back, wills himself to keep his eyes on her neck instead of unleashing the glare of warning he knows will be far too gold. There are only three soldiers, uniforms nearly as dirty as Zuko’s clothes, slouched and lazy like a Fire Nation soldier would never dare to be in Zuko’s presence.

It’s the longest two minutes of Zuko’s life—or recent life, at least—as they approach along the road, talking amongst themselves and giving Zuko a bare glance of acknowledgement as they pass. It’s an even longer minute before Zuko can bring himself to release them from his heat sense, to coax his inner flame back to quiet.

&#45;-

Zuko must be getting closer to the Earth Kingdom center because this is the first town he’s come across with soldiers actually stationed in it. The town itself is as dusty and barren as all the others, which begs the question of why troops are garrisoned here in particular. Maybe Zuko is approaching the edge of the territory the Earth King feels worth defending? He doesn’t particularly like that line of thought, given his distance from the Colonies and active Fire Nation troop placements, and the number of times ‘conscription’ had been given as a reason for not having enough labor, enough supplies, enough anything.

Zuko nearly turns around and leaves the minute he realizes the troops are there. But active avoidance might pique curiosity, and Zuko needs to be as inconspicuous as a strange traveler with a bad attitude and a giant facial scar can possibly be. At least a burn is unlikely to be immediately remarkable to Earth Kingdom soldiers.

Zuko doesn’t particularly like that line of thought, either.

Zuko pins his eyes to Jasmine’s neck, straining to see out of his periphery and thanking Agni and anyone else who might be listening that the soldiers are on his right and not his left. His heart is pounding so loud he can barely hear anything except his own tight, too-fast breathing, and he needs to get himself under control because ‘panic attacks in the center of town’ and ‘inconspicuous’ don’t go well together.

Zuko isn’t surprised that the soldiers follow him with hostile, suspicious eyes as he leads Jasmine to a water trough, tying her up with blessedly steady fingers. He’s used to wariness by now. Agni’s tits, Zuko usually brings more than enough wariness for everyone when he steps into a town. But he’s surprised, as he sorts through his packs, strapping down things that could be easily stolen and hiding things that are hard to tie down, that the soldiers seem to be hostile with everyone else, too, when hostility usually feels like a special gift saved just for him.

A deep, bracing breath, and Zuko makes himself step away from Jasmine’s familiar bulk toward what seems to be the general store. He keeps his breathing controlled even as his inner flame spikes in alarm when the soldiers shove off from the wall they were lounging against as if they were all just waiting for Zuko’s move. Zuko is torn between relief to not be enclosed as he steps under the shade of the merchant’s awning and the useless wish to be able to step out of sight of the eyes on his back.

“What do you want.”

Zuko assesses the gaunt proprietor’s tight eyes, reminds himself that he can always light everything on fire and run if he has to, and manages to meet the man’s blunt words with terseness rather than anger. “Salt.”

“Four coppers a bag.”

Zuko frowns at the price. That’s more than it should be, but he’s also running low and has started craving it despite the lack of water and constant sweat. And he needs to be able to preserve anything that might wander into a snare out here. “Six coppers for two bags.”

“Fine. What else?”

“Feed grain.”

“I only got the one bag. Five coppers.”

Zuko grunts. “What about rice?”

“Two sacks. Seven coppers each.”

Zuko scowls. “That’s price gouging.”

“Bitching about it won’t make more rice.”

Zuko glares, because bitching about it used to *always* make someone miraculously find more rice to sell. But shouting doesn’t have the same impact when he isn’t a Prince with the Fire Nation looming behind him. Now all Zuko has at his back are those fucking soldiers, which is making him twitchy and nervous. Zuko can see that it makes the merchant nervous too, which isn’t helping Zuko fight the urge to get his swords into his hands.

“Fine,” Zuko mutters. “Water?”

“You and everyone else,” the merchant grumbles, “I got—” A sudden muffled giggle has the man gritting his teeth. “A few gallons.”

Zuko’s eyes flick, looking for the source of the laughter. “What about—” he finally catches sight of two children crouched around the corner of the awning, smirking to each other. “—a hot meal?”

“We don’t do that—” one of the boys pops up, hurling something before diving back behind the awning again. “—here. Aw, fuck everything,” the man mutters as Zuko hears the unmistakable sound of an egg splattering behind him.

“What the *fuck* was that, Jian,” a booming voice snarls, and Zuko pivots to bring the threat into view, heart sinking as he sees the soldiers approaching, one very clearly wiping egg off the back of his head. “You looking for trouble now?”

“No, Sir,” the merchant says hastily, ducking his head in a quick bow. “No trouble here.”

“No? Then maybe it was you.” The soldier turns furious eyes on Zuko. “You trying to start a fight, stranger? Trying to cause a scene.”

“No.” Zuko breathes deep, slow, keeping his voice neutral—Uncle would be proud—and calling his flames back from his fingertips. This would be a swords-first problem.

The soldier looks skeptical, raking Zuko with a suspicious glance, then taking in the small pile of goods accumulating on the counter, very much lacking in eggs. “You see who did throw it?”
