But Zuko can feel Uncle’s chi when he works up the nerve to tentatively reach for it, a strong, powerful, steady pulse that Zuko can’t grab onto with his fire sense even if he wanted to. The realization is a relief, enough that Zuko can focus on finding food, and gathering water, and timing his breaths to the rise and fall of Uncle’s chest so that he will be ready with tea when Uncle finally wakes.

&#45;-

“Nephew.” Uncle’s voice is rough, dry, tight with pain, one of the most beautiful things Zuko has ever heard.

“Uncle,” Zuko breathes, hastily rising to his knees. He presses the cup of tea he’s been keeping warm into Uncle’s hands, inner fire flipping anxiously as he waits for Uncle to take a sip. If Uncle is well enough for tea, then maybe Zuko can finally let himself believe he will be okay.

Uncle ignores the tea, though, in favor of carefully examining Zuko for injuries, lingering on the small cuts on his face and arms that haven’t fully healed yet from his fight with Gow. “You are okay,” he finally says, sounding undone with relief.

“I’m fine,” Zuko mutters, waving the concern away. He isn’t the one lying injured right now, and he’s feeling far too jittery over Uncle being prone to think about anything else. “How do you feel? Are you alright? Can I get you anything?”

“Ah—I have been better,” Uncle says ruefully, carefully easing himself upright position as he glances around the mostly-intact house Zuko had found for them. “But I have also been worse.”

“You underestimated Azula,” Zuko scowls, unable to hold back the criticism now that Uncle seems out of danger.

“Yes, I did,” Uncle agrees, frowning. “I will not do so again.”

“She isn’t just some spoiled princess,” Zuko presses, needing him to understand. “She—

“She’s crazy,” Uncle finishes, voice heavy. “And she needs to go down.”

Zuko pulls up short, words about Azula’s skill and focus and drive drying up as his mind goes blank. Fear flutters around his heart. No one has ever acted like they saw that in Azula, let alone said it out loud. For someone else to see it…Fuck.

But Zuko forces himself to take a deep, steadying breath and set that aside for later because this isn’t the time for thinking about that. Not when Uncle is still injured. Not when there’s tea to drink and—*Agni*, Zuko barely manages to keep from spitting it out. This tea is *terrible*.

&#45;-

Zuko works on brewing a new pot of tea. Uncle might be too nice to say it but even Zuko can tell that the first pot was trash. He concentrates on maintaining more even heat this time as he brings the water to a boil. It’s frustrating that this comes so easily to him when the actual *fire* part of firebending is always so hard. Zuko has had years of training and his fire had still become ragged and weak while Azula was able to press forward without any signs of flagging. And her affinity for lightning—Zuko clearly has his own thing for it, but of course in a way that’s utterly useless. Like always.

“Uncle,” Zuko says carefully as he finally brings the water just to the edge of boiling. “I think I need to learn more advanced firebending.” He risks a quick peek up. “If I’m going to see Azula again...”

“*Are* you going to see your sister again?”

Zuko snorts at the idea that he has a choice in the matter. “I don’t think I could avoid it.”

“Hm,” Uncle hums, frowning down at his empty cup, and Zuko cringes away from Uncle’s reluctance. He knows he isn’t good enough, but they aren’t on the *Wani* anymore. Uncle can’t keep insisting that Zuko has all the time in the world to learn. He *can’t*.

“I’m not…ready.” The words are hard to get out, and Zuko forces himself to keep going, staring down at the teapot in his hands as if he needs to focus to apply even heat. “I’m not good enough. Not for her.” It hurts to admit so plainly, makes him tense and grit his teeth and brace his body in anticipation of…something. “I need to be better.”

But Uncle doesn’t get mad or gloat or frown, just gives a single, slow nod that has Zuko practically vibrating waiting for his reaction. When it comes, Zuko can only start in numb shock. “Yes, Zuko, I think it would be good for you to learn.” A considering glance. “Would you like to start now?”

“Wha—really?” Zuko straightens, pulling his shoulders back and nearly losing his grip on the teapot. “That would be—I would—But are you up for it already? You just woke up.”

“We can start with basic theory,” Uncle says, eyes laughing when Zuko slumps again. Agni, he’s so *tired* of basic theory. “Tell me, Nephew. What do you know about lightning?”

&#45;-

What Zuko knows about lightning is apparently *not* what Uncle knows. Zuko knows that it’s wild, unchained. That it rides storms across the sky and falls where it will. That it reaches out to his fire and wraps around his body and…honestly, it’s pretty mixed up in his thoughts of Sokka by this point. Heat and excitement and the feeling of barely hanging on to trembling edge of possibility.

Uncle knows it as cold fire, coming from the energy of the world around. That it’s emotionless, sterile. That it requires utter peace of mind rather than a firebender’s usual fury. That it’s precise and deadly. That it’s about release and guidance, not command and control.

Zuko can agree on that last part, at least. Just probably not in the way that Uncle means, and he hastily forces himself to refocus on Uncle’s lecture before his thoughts truly get out of hand.

&#45;-

Zuko frowns as he considers separating energies of the universe that don’t want to be separated in the first place. It feels…rude. Cruel. Impossible. Like trying to separate out all the parts of yourself and then letting them come violently crashing back together into the single body they’re meant to live within. Is this what Sokka was asking for, when he spoke about leaving aside the Crown Prince to be just Zuko? Is that how Sokka feels—that Zuko is something deadly that Sokka can’t control, can only direct and release?

Zuko…isn’t sure how to feel about that. He isn’t sure that it would be entirely wrong.

&#45;-

Finally Zuko can’t take it anymore.

“Uncle,” he cuts in, ignoring some explanation of yin and yang and balance that’s been going on for far too long now. “What about normal lightning. Like in a monsoon.”

“What about it?” Uncle asks, eyes suddenly intent on Zuko’s face. His careful tone has Zuko feeling wrong-footed, like he's about to reveal something he shouldn’t, but he licks dry lips and presses forward anyway.

“Is that the same kind of lightning that a firebender can make? That a firebender could…” He doesn’t know how to finish. Harness? Control? Let rage through him until he’s a boneless over-sensitized mess on the ground?

Zuko thankfully doesn’t have to find the words, though, because Uncle starts nodding, expression going faintly surprised. “Many don’t notice it, and most who do can only sense an extra energy in the air that they can’t place or touch. But a strong firebender almost always feels it.” Zuko mentally trips over that particular concept. “Have you always been able to sense it?”

“Ever since…yes.” Zuko doesn’t want to get into how it started after the Agni Kai with the first lightning storm at sea. How it made him feel both anchored and alien within his own body, back when pain was still the majority of his world. Did something about that agony by fire jumpstart his bending? Make it stronger or unlock some hidden piece through suffering?

Except even before then, Zuko had always loved to watch the monsoons from his bedroom window, pretending he could feel the thunder vibrating in his chest. Azula used to slip onto the broad windowsill next to him and lean against the glass at his side, breath catching in time with his.

Maybe he’s always been strong enough to feel it, in some way or another. Just not strong enough that anyone could notice.

&#45;-

Uncle claims to be feeling well enough the next morning to demonstrate rather than just talk. Zuko is skeptical that he should be on his feet so soon, but Uncle moves smoothly, if a bit more slowly than usual, so he swallows his concern. Zuko could always do with less talking. And his worries are quickly eaten up by frustration, anyway.

Uncle demonstrates the stance and motions for generating lightning, talking through how it should feel and how the chi should move, eyes sharp as Zuko tries to mirror him. Zuko does his best to replicate the movements, but the forms don’t feel quite right—too stiff where he wants to be fluid, too loose where he wants to tense. Zuko can’t seem to force the energies apart, can’t seem to direct instead of follow.

And after so many weeks of nothing but his own intuition to guide him, Zuko chafes at having an instructor again. He’d gotten used to training being a mindless, thought-free space where he explored, where he just felt his body and chi and breath and moved in the space between them all. Now Zuko is sharply reacquainting himself with the familiar, sticky feeling of inadequacy and the way it shortens his already-quick temper.

“This is stupid,” Zuko snaps, hauling himself back to his feet after another uncalled fireball erupts from between his hands. “It’s not working!”

“It’s about achieving a state where your mind is at peace,” Uncle urges, voice soothing in a way that does *not* make Zuko feel any more relaxed. “It’s about calm.”

“I am calm!”

“…Zuko. If you want to achieve peace within yourself, you must let go of your feelings of shame.”

Zuko flinches. His thoughts immediately jump to Sokka, where he’s been fighting to keep them away from. To the Avatar, to Azula. To all the ways Zuko was weak in the face of duty before he ever broke in the North. To all the ways he continues to fall short. It’s an endless list. Agni, Zuko has failed in so many ways. “I’m not *ashamed*.” It’s a weak protest. Zuko is nothing but shame, in the end.

Uncle hums, unconvinced, and Zuko turns away, arms crossing, uncomfortable being so *seen*. “Nephew, you need to let go of the things that make you feel that way.”

Zuko is aware that Uncle is probably thinking about some hang-up he imagines Zuko has over Azula, or about his upbringing, or maybe about the constant self-doubt and self-recrimination that Zuko can sometimes admit is probably not healthy in his calmer moments. But Zuko can’t stop thinking of Sokka, instead. Even though Zuko isn’t ashamed of him, not really. Sokka is just so tied into all the ways Zuko will never be good enough. His inner fire convulses tight over the thought of letting go of him.

“How about we try something else,” Uncle suggests gently, tugging Zuko out of his spiraling thoughts. “Something that even Azula doesn’t know.”

“Really?” Zuko won’t deny that he’s pleased by the idea of knowing something Azula doesn’t. He doesn’t quite know what to do with the feeling, it’s such a novel concept.

“Yes.” Uncle’s smile is mischievous. “I developed it myself by watching waterbenders.”

Zuko blinks. He…didn’t realize that was allowed. Zuko has messed around with his bending before—who hasn’t, in secret, where instructors and sisters and parents can’t see—seeing what happens if you use flame through an earthbending form, trying out some of the old styles he saw in scrolls. But Zuko hadn’t realized that that was…okay. Legitimate.

Though Zuko is pretty sure that forms built on waterbending wouldn’t exactly adhere to Caldera Standard. But then, Zuko doesn’t have to care about that anymore, does he?

&#45;-

Uncle’s explanation is setting Zuko on edge. There’s nothing inherently *wrong* with what he’s saying, but all together? It makes Zuko’s skin itch with the urge to check over his shoulder, to put his back to a wall and scan for ears lurking in the shadow.

Uncle is talking about how fire is the element of power, how its wielders are driven by desire and will and energy. How earth is about substance, persistence, endurance. How air is freedom and peace and fun. And water is about change, adaptability and community and love.

That last one at least feels right. That feels like Sokka, rolling with whatever Zuko throws at him and holding his people tight and endlessly giving even when he’s beyond annoyed, even when Zuko is sure that he’s used up the last of what Sokka has to offer him.

But still, everything Uncle is saying feels very…Avatar-y.

“Why must one be the Avatar to value love, Nephew, or endurance?” Uncle raises an eyebrow.

“That’s not what I said,” Zuko grumbles, avoiding Uncle's eyes and examining the half-burned husk of a house that is one hard wind away from falling over after Zuko’s latest fireball explosion. Zuko hates when Uncle gets all I-know-that-you-know-that-I-know vague when Zuko isn’t even sure that Uncle knows in the first place. Agni, Zuko needs Uncle to *not* know, in this case.

“Of course not,” Uncle agrees far too easily. “Now. This technique is for redirecting lightning.” Zuko’s eyes snap back to Uncle. Is this what Zuko did in that storm? “You let the energy in your body flow—” that sounds right. “—and the lightning will follow it.” That… sounds like the opposite, but okay.

“You must create a pathway, from your fingertips all the way into your stomach.” That…fine. That’s not what Zuko experienced, but it’s not *entirely* different. “The stomach is the source of energy in your body. It is the sea of chi.” That…wasn’t where the lightning had settled for Zuko. “From there you direct it out of your other arm. You mustn’t let the lightning pass through your heart, no matter what you do.” That, finally, Zuko can agree with, had somehow sensed even as he’d been wild and uncontrolled in the rain.

Zuko watches Uncle closely, focusing on imitating the motions, on feeling the movement of his chi along the paths that Uncle describes. It comes easier than trying to generate lightning did, more and more natural with every rep until Zuko can flow through the forms smooth and unthinking as breathing.

“Excellent!” Uncle’s pleasure makes something eager and warm spark in Zuko’s chest. “Well done, Nephew.”

“Great,” Zuko grins, giddy with how fast he was able to master this, his inner flame twirling along with his exhilaration. Nothing like this has ever happened to him before. “Let’s try it for real now.”

“What?”

“With some real lightning,” Zuko says, quickly sketching the motions of it again, trying to imagine what it would feel like with that crackling power trying to break free inside him.

Except Uncle steps back, aghast. “What, are you crazy? Lightning is very dangerous!”

Zuko stares, his bubbling excitement going quiet. “I thought that was the *point*. To learn to protect myself from it.” Zuko knows better than to try to argue that the lightning hadn’t felt dangerous when he encountered it on his own. Wild, untamed, sure, but not dangerous. Not if you meet like with like.

“If you’re lucky you will never have to use this technique at all,” Uncle frowns, taking on his about-to-give-teaching-parable tone.

“I’m not going to trust in that,” Zuko scowls, incredulous. Not with Azula around. “How can I be sure I know how to do it if I don’t actually *try*?”

“I’m not going to shoot lightning at you, Nephew,” Uncle says, folding his hands firmly, going as immovable as an earthbender.

“Fine,” Zuko snaps, inner flame stung and roiling. Of course, Uncle wouldn’t let Zuko fully master this. Of course, he would continue to hold Zuko back. Of course, he wouldn’t think Zuko was actually ready, no matter how much praise he offered up. “I’ll find some other way, then.”

“You can’t just go around looking for someone to throw lightning at you, Zuko!”

Zuko pauses. Azula *is* probably far away by now, but still… “Good idea,” he murmurs, considering the sky. It seems like it might rain. “I can find my own lightning if you won’t help me.”

And maybe it’s better that Uncle not be there, anyway. Zuko wants to see if Uncle is actually right about all of this, about cold fire and sterility and calm. He needs to know if his experience in that storm was just some fluke, some other way that Zuko is broken.

&#45;-

Zuko thinks Uncle is wrong.

Jasmine brings Zuko toward the storm he could barely even say he felt when he set out, nothing but a conviction that north was the direction to travel in, similar to the way Agni pulls on his inner flame. Zuko grows more and more certain the closer they get until he finally leaves her behind in safety to scale the steep cliffside.

Zuko isn’t sure why, but something about getting off the ground feels right, like if he can climb high enough then he can find his way into the heart of the storm. Zuko shouldn’t have been able to climb so easily after the past few days—weeks—he’s been having, but the energy of the storm is beginning to settle in his muscles, skating down his bones, making him feel alert and present and alive.

The potential of Uncle being so wrong makes something inside Zuko hurt a little, though. Or maybe the possibility that Zuko’s bending is so broken, that he’s lost his way so completely, that he could stand here, strong enough to feel the storm from miles away but not right enough, never good enough, to do it the way he’s supposed to.

The late summer rain is warm, hard, quickly soaking through Zuko’s clothes, washing away the dust and dirt until he feels marginally clean for the first time in months. Zuko tips his head back, tense and shaking as the storm swirls around him, electricity buzzing through the air but never coming together, never forming. The thrumming, building potential sits on his skin, rises from his bones, pushing and pushing but never tipping him over until he feels raw with the need for something, anything, to break.

“Please,” Zuko begs when he can’t take it anymore. “*Please*. I can take it! Why are you holding back? You’ve never held back before!” He doesn’t know if he’s shouting at the storm or the world or fate or something else entirely. Zuko feels charged, simultaneously hollow and overloaded with crackling energy, his fire frantic and building and reaching but nothing is *happening*. The lightning isn’t coming, isn’t crashing through him and twining with his fire and sweeping Zuko along with its wildness.

Zuko tries reaching out with his fire sense, tries calling the lightning to him, but all he can feel is the energy of the storm. It saturates the air, so big that Zuko could never hope to hold it, so dispersed that any attempt to touch it comes back empty. And it’s getting worse, thinner and thinner, and with a cry of protest Zuko realizes that all that built up potential is *leaving*. The storm is blowing away, dissipating, burning out, leaving Zuko behind, overfull and achingly empty.

With a groan Zuko collapses to his knees, pressing his forehead to the ground, trying to steady himself as the storm tension begins to slip away. He shudders, rough breaths— dangerously close to sobs—loud in his unscarred ear as the energy slowly leaks out of him, never cresting no matter how much his fire burns for it. He feels drained in its wake, empty in a way he wasn’t before, empty in a way that lets despair seep in. Zuko doesn’t have the wildness and he doesn’t have the control and he doesn’t have *anything*.

Hot tears slip out without his permission, running into his hairline as Zuko gasps around the tightness in his chest. He isn’t good enough to generate lightning, isn’t *right* in a way that Uncle must be able to sense for him refuse to let Zuko practice redirecting it. Zuko’s strong, just not enough. He can get by with the basics, just not how he should be. He isn’t a Prince, isn’t a refugee, isn’t a thief, isn’t a hero, is barely a firebender, can’t dare to call himself a friend let alone something more.

Zuko doesn’t know what he *is* anymore. What he’s even supposed to try to be. And Agni, how can Zuko ever be worth anything to anyone if he can’t figure it out?

&#45;-

Zuko eventually burns the worst of his emotions away into his inner flame, forcing his ragged breathing to even and hit a steady rhythm that forcefully drags calm around him. Drained, Zuko stares up at the blue of the late afternoon sky. Maybe he should have just done it Uncle’s way instead of thinking that he could do anything himself. Maybe he should have tried separating the energy that was all around him instead of wanting the lightning to…show Zuko something about himself again. Ugh.

*Stupid*. Stupid, stupid, stupid, to think that there was some guidance, some self-discovery, to be had in a fucking weather pattern. It’s like he’s trying to *become* one of Uncle’s dumb aphorisms.

But Agni, Zuko should be able to do this thing if Azula can. Because Azula is not fucking *calm*, not unless she's changed that much. So there has to be another way, one that fits better. Because doing it Uncle’s way feels too much like Zuko is separating out the pieces of himself to see what’s underneath and he can’t do that, not when he keeps flinching away from the possibility of finding out that there’s nothing there. Everything in him screams against forcing apart what wants to stay together.

Zuko suddenly, intensely, deeply understands where Sokka was coming from when he wrote months and months ago about the Spirit World and about having his foundation ripped out from underneath him. Zuko doesn’t know what to cling to anymore when everything he’s tried to mold himself around hasn’t fit.

Zuko can get through this, though. He knows he can because Zuko has had this thought before. Floating at sea, caught under Agni’s merciless heat, trying to hold on and not knowing what to anchor himself around anymore. And Zuko’s answer hasn’t really changed, has it? Sokka is as out of reach as ever. Zuko is a traitor and a fugitive. And Uncle is still here. Solid and steady and happy to help weigh Zuko down when he feels cast adrift, ready with a nice little box labeled Good Nephew for Zuko to step into and hide within until he feels ready to leave it. Or maybe until Zuko finds that he can stay there forever, that with enough time and effort that box is the one that will finally be the right fit.

&#45;-

Zuko uses the long, slow ride back to the empty town to hide the broken, desperate feeling inside himself behind a familiar glower. He’s damp and ragged and fucking *dusty* again, but Uncle welcomes him back the same as always, tea ready like he doesn’t care that Zuko shouted and raged and left, or that Zuko always rejects his offered cup.

Zuko latches onto the familiarity of their roles with a fierceness that he finds distantly alarming. He might not have a mission or a purpose or a reason for being anymore. He might be nothing more than a mess that needs to do better, with no idea what he’s actually supposed to change to achieve that. But until Zuko figures it out he can focus on the happiness on Uncle’s face when he silently accepts the offered tea. He can focus on this little thing in front of him, this very important thing, and the safety to be found in expectations that Zuko knows how to meet even if they chafe.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

Has Zuko finally achieved Peak Drama? Is it even possible for him to do such a thing?

## Chapter 8: Good Enough

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for a bit more than canon-typical violence

### Text

Being a Good Nephew is harder than Zuko expected it to be, which is just typical for him at this point. Good Nephews don’t snap at their Uncles, or glower, or shout. Good Nephews drink tea when it’s offered and play pai sho when it’s suggested—of *course* Uncle found himself a travel set—and don’t set things on fire in a fit of rage. Zuko really only has a handle on that last bit, at the moment, but he doggedly grits his teeth through his third cup of tea of the day because Uncle wants him to have it and Zuko is going to fucking *try*.

Uncle is content to pick a direction for once when they left the wreck of a town behind them and Zuko is too exhausted, physically and mentally and emotionally, to press about where they’re going. It feels good to just…let Jasmine investigate the back of his head and drift behind someone for a change instead of carving the way. Their pace is slower than Zuko would set on his own. But Uncle’s still injured, and they still have nowhere to go, and it’s not like they’re a priority for Azula anyway, so Zuko doesn’t see the point in shouting about it.

Zuko suspects that Uncle is milking this wounded thing for all that it’s worth, though, even if a Good Nephew would never think that. It’s just that Uncle was more than mobile enough to train the day after his injury, so his sudden inability to walk through the whole day feels...convenient. But Zuko can’t be a Good Nephew and also ignore Uncle when he starts groaning and wincing like the worst of the Ember Island Players, and Uncle keeps doing it, so they keep stopping to look at flowers and herbs while cheerfully claiming to be resting.

Zuko can feel a scream building in his chest bit by bit every day. But he’s *trying*, so he forces himself to meditate and take deep breathes and glare at inanimate objects instead of at Uncle. Besides, Zuko has no right to be annoyed in the first place. Uncle wouldn’t have gotten hurt if Zuko had just been…better.

But Agni’s tits, Zuko *really* wishes Uncle would just say what he wants instead of dancing around it.

“The forest on this part of the hill seems so different from where we made lunch, doesn’t it?”

“We stopped two hours ago,” Zuko grinds out, flexing out his fingers when Jasmine chirps in protest at his tight grip on the reins.

“Yes, so many hours of traveling! It does stress the body.”

“We *just* had lunch.”

“A body needs fuel when it is healing. And trying to overcome the draining effects of pain,” Uncle adds on when Zuko just huffs. “It saps the energy so! Some days I even feel light-headed with—”

“Fine,” Zuko snaps, keeping a growl in his chest because Agni help him, Good Nephews do not fucking growl. “There’s jerky in the saddlebag behind you.”

“Why, so there is! Jerky is such a tough food, you know. Tasty, but so much chewing. It can be so tiring, when one is also riding—”

“You could walk.”

“Or walking! And really, it’s best savored, don’t you agree? It goes so well with a cup of—”

“Do you want to stop *again*?”

“Oh, well, of course, I don’t *want* to slow down our progress, but on such a fine day…and with my injury of course.”

Zuko pinches the bridge of his nose. “Can you last another half hour?”

“But those flowers over there look like they could be the rare Red Phoenix Orchid!”

“If you want to *stop*,” Zuko begins, really trying to be a Good Nephew—really, truly trying— when Jasmine tenses beneath them and everything goes completely to shit. Zuko jerks his head up in alarm, twisting in the saddle to try to scan their surroundings with his good eye. Uncle goes quiet behind him, also wary, but Zuko doesn’t see anything in the thick growth on either side of the path, can’t hear anything except for their own breathing and a toucan puffin calling for its—

Zuko hasn’t seen a toucan puffin since leaving the Fire Nation.

A spike of adrenaline is all Zuko has time for before the bushes explode, huge figures bursting out of cover to neatly surround them. Zuko and Uncle tumble off Jasmine’s back— Uncle looking perfectly healthy, Zuko fucking *knew* it—and fall into ready stances. Komodo rhinos snort around them, wanting to charge and chafing at being held back by their riders. Zuko scans the circle, taking in the very much non-regulation but very much Fire Nation uniforms. Fuck.

“Ah, Colonel Mongke!” Uncle calls, stepping up to Zuko’s left shoulder to offer a warm greeting as if they were all running into each other on market day and not in the middle of a trap.

“You know these guys?” Zuko mutters, taking in the easy way their attackers hold their weapons, the hard eyes, the comfort with intimidation and ambush. They’re clearly some kind of special operations group, looking and dressing like that, too coordinated to be paramilitary. Why would Uncle know them?

“They’re old friends. They call themselves the Rough Rhinos,” Uncle murmurs calmly before raising his voice to be heard by the group. “It is a pleasant surprise to meet you here!”

Zuko feels a chill of dread settle over his shoulders. Even he’s heard of the Rough Rhinos, starved as he ever was for official military news. A cleanup squad. The type of soldiers you sent out to make a mess disappear when you didn’t want questions asked about how it got done.

Fuck.

“You’re losing your edge, General, if it’s a surprise to see us,” Mongke calls back, kneeing his rhino forward a few steps in clear threat. Zuko pulls a sour face. He doesn’t entirely disagree with Mongke’s assessment that Uncle might be going a little soft, and he *hates* agreeing with the people he’s about to light on fire.

“One never knows where one will encounter friends,” Uncle smiles, unperturbed. “We were just about to stop for an afternoon snack. Would you care for some tea?”

Zuko doesn’t let himself close his eyes because they’re in an ambush and he can’t sacrifice line of sight, but Agni’s balls, *of course* Uncle would try to invite the Fire Army’s Plausible Deniability Squad to afternoon tea.

“Enough stalling,” Mongke snaps. “We don’t do tea with fugitives. Get them.”

The response is instantaneous, forcing Zuko to drop and Uncle to twist away. Zuko ignores the waver of uncertainty at the way those attacks—only two to start, like Mongke wants to gauge them before committing resources—neatly split Zuko and Iroh apart. Mongke knows what he’s doing, then, which is not great, because the Colonel had said ‘them.’ Zuko knew that he didn’t have many paths left before him after fleeing Azula’s ship, but he hadn’t quite believed until now that the Dragon of the West would be cast out with him.

Zuko stops thinking entirely when an arrow comes so close to his neck that Zuko can feel the stinging burn of its passing. An archer is trying to pin him to a tree and the man is good, staying at a distance and using his arrows to disrupt any motion Zuko makes to bend. He’s clearly experienced fighting firebenders, which Zuko will also not think about. Except to note that the man is clearly experienced with bad firebenders, worse than Zuko even, because he notches a *flaming arrow* and that’s all Zuko needs.

Even as he dodges forward, Zuko reaches with his fire sense and seizes the flame. He whips the fire backward, burning through the bowstring and forcing the archer to flinch away to protect his eyes. Zuko uses that breath of room to unleash a two-handed gout of flame that sends the archer flying into a tree to slump, if not unconscious then at least momentarily out of the fight.

Zuko doesn’t have time to savor the victory. Mongke barks a command and the rest of the Rhinos dart into the battle. Most of the soldiers make for Iroh—smart—but a nearly bare-chested man whips a sword through the air as he rides toward Zuko. It’s flashy and skilled and Zuko reacts without thinking, drawing his own swords instead of trying to stop a Komodo rhino with fire. His dual-bladed block catches the soldier off guard and Zuko wrenches one sword free to slash at the saddle as the rhino thunders past.

Zuko winces as the animal bellows in pain when his blade catches flesh as well as leather, but he can’t afford the space to feel guilty about it as the cut strap sends saddle and rider listing sideways. The swordsman kicks himself free with an annoyed shout, jumping to the ground, and Zuko falls on him in a whirlwind of blades.

The bare-chested guy knows what he’s doing, but Zuko is fast and angry and can move with his swords like they are an extension of his own thoughts. It feels good. Like cutting free, for all that Zuko is tightly focused. He keeps the man off balance, changing his levels, always in motion, his fire greedily spilling out and crawling along the blades until flames fly off his swords with each strike. The man flinches back as fire licks at the side of his neck and that momentary lapse in concentration is all Zuko needs. He snaps his wrist around, blade wrapping his opponent’s as he lunges in to wrench the weapon out of the man’s hands.

The swordsman stumbles back and Zuko lets his momentum carry him into a spinning heel kick to the temple. The man drops like a sack of rice, because only fucking *idiots* ride into a planned battle without their fucking armor on.

Agni’s tits, Zuko misses his armor. Who do the Rough Riders usually *fight*?

Zuko can only catch a glimpse of Iroh and Mongke fighting before someone comes up on his left and he needs to throw himself back and away. The new opponent is fully armored, wielding two curved knives, and despite all the weight, he’s *fast*. Zuko is immediately on the defensive. The man whips inside his guard and Zuko is fucked in close quarters with a sword. He drops both blades to free his hands to divert the knife coming for his gut, just managing to push and twist out of the way but *fuck*, he isn’t going to be able to do that again.

Zuko tries to call a sheet of flame to press his attacker back, but he’s still in too tight, desperately dodging, every step he makes to try to gain distance matched by a counter-lunge forward. Zuko sucks in a sharp breath as a sloppy block opens up a shallow cut along his forearm, his inner fire surging at the pain, instinctively reacting. Zuko’s fire sense flares out, clawing around the threat inches away and Zuko doesn’t think, just grasps onto the heat source and shouts with mingled effort and panic as he wills the struggling not-fire in front of him down to bare embers.

His attacker stumbles to the ground in a clatter of armor, suddenly going boneless in the middle of a lunge that would have laid Zuko open hip to hip. Zuko stares, numb with surprise that that actually worked. The man flails to get off the ground, clumsy and awkward, and Zuko can *feel* the surge of effort in the not-fire he’s still holding in his grip. Fuck. *Fuck.*

The sound of fire meeting fire jolts Zuko out of his dangerous distraction. He yanks his heat sense back into the confines of his own body and darts forward to yank the helmet off the disoriented soldier’s head, elbowing him in the temple to take him out for the rest of the fight. The man collapses down in another rattle of metal plates and Zuko sprints across the clearing, snatching up his swords and ignoring the fact that the bending he just did shouldn’t have been possible. Uncle had said that manipulating another’s heat didn’t work when they were conscious, and especially not when they fought back. The knife-wielder had definitely fought.

*Later*, Zuko orders himself, taking his uncertainty and delayed fear and the uncomfortable thrum that something about his bending isn’t *right* and feeding it all into his inner flame. Zuko launches a flaming kick that Mongke easily deflects with barely even a pause in snapping a whip of flame toward Iroh. Zuko reaches for the flame whip instead, trying to wrestle it out of Mongke’s control. His fire sense slides, slippery over the Colonel’s hold on the flame to latch onto Mongke himself and Zuko just goes with it and yanks, the same motion as before, trying to call the heat to his control. The Colonel’s inner flame barely moves, but Mongke flinches, his fire giving a single waver, and that moment is enough for Iroh to put him on his ass and end the fight.

“Let’s go!” Zuko shouts, whistling for Jasmine. Zuko can tell—he doesn’t want to think about how—that all the soldiers are down but still alive. They both likely took on too much risk to achieve that outcome, but apparently, neither Zuko nor Iroh can truly fight against a countryman yet, even those sent to capture them. Which means they need to get out of here.

Zuko leaps onto Jasmine’s back, hauling Uncle up behind him as they gallop away, the ostrich horse sensing their urgency.

“Seeing old friends is always so invigorating,” Uncle pants, cheerful as ever. As if they didn’t both almost get killed or worse. As if Zuko hasn’t proved to himself once against that his bending is totally and completely fucked. Though maybe Uncle didn’t notice that last part.

“It would be nice to see some friends who don’t try to kill us,” Zuko snaps, flexing his forearm to make sure the knife wound there isn’t debilitating and ignoring the fact that he might not actually have any friends who haven’t tried to kill him. He assumes that Uncle does, though.

“Hmm,” Uncle makes a thoughtful noise, like they are just out for a stroll and not fleeing for their lives. “It would be nice to see old friends, wouldn’t it?”

&#45;-

Zuko isn’t sure what the Misty Palms Oasis is or why they would want to go there, and for once Uncle is being surprisingly cagey about answering. He isn’t even giving up convoluted aphorisms and tangentially related observations. Zuko…doesn’t know what to do with that. They’re either walking into a complete shit show or a load of bull pig shit, but Zuko is being a Good Nephew, so he keeps those thoughts and his opinion of Uncle’s non-answers to himself and restrains a flinch at the idea of approaching any kind of oasis ever again.

Zuko is perfectly fine to maintain his own more brooding silence but it’s hard not to say something when he trails Uncle into a bar and sees their own wanted posters slapped on the wall. It's official, then. Azula isn’t keeping this private between siblings anymore—as private as anything between them can ever really be—and she isn’t shying away from trying to drag Uncle down, too. Though Zuko isn’t particularly surprised by that. Azula never liked the Dragon of the West. But Agni’s balls, Zuko would expect his own sister to at least know which side of his face his scar is on for his wanted poster. It’s not like she wasn’t there when it happened.

“You have friends here?” Zuko mutters as he takes in the smokey bar over Uncle’s shoulder, the greasy, sullen patrons and dirty floor tacky with spilled drink—please let it be spilled drink. “Everyone here looks like a vagrant.”

“And so do we,” Uncle says placidly. Zuko twitches. Vagrant feels worse than refugee. “It’s nice to fit right in, isn’t it? And look, pai sho!”

“…Did we just travel for days so you could gamble?”

“Of course not,” Uncle assures him, already striding toward the boards. “I don’t gamble.”

Zuko makes a strangled noise that *isn’t* a shout and exhales a burst of heat into the dirt floor, stalking in Uncle’s wake when he finally feels like he can do so without screaming. He scowls as Uncle settles at a board across from some dried-out Earth Kingdom man with a cheerful, open greeting. As if there’s no need to avoid notice or be subtle or not draw attention to themselves. As if their *wanted posters* aren’t on the fucking wall.

“Nephew, would you like to play as well?”

Zuko forgets that he’s trying to be a Good Nephew for a moment, his glare automatic and instinctive at any hint of getting roped into a pai sho game. Uncle just smiles peacefully and turns back to the board, and Zuko bites back his annoyance that Uncle was probably expecting that reaction and likely finds it amusing. And because he is *trying*, Zuko dials his glare back to a glower and slumps against the wall, keeping his good eye toward the rest of the bar because one of them needs to pay attention to their surroundings and Uncle has eyes only for pai sho.

Zuko struggles more than he should to keep his focus on potential threats, though. He doesn’t know shit about pai sho, but he’s unwillingly absorbed enough against over the years to realize that whatever game Uncle is playing isn’t normal. It isn’t a game at all, really. It’s too easy and rhythmic and structured, like a dance with tiles and board, or a call and response, each player moving through the necessary reply before moving onto the next—

*Oh.*

Oh. This…is not good.

“Welcome, Brother,” the Earth Kingdom man finally says, eyes warm in his wrinkled face. “The White Lotus opens wide to those who know her secrets.”

“What the fuck are you talking about?” Anxiety makes Zuko’s words come out harsher than he intends. This sounds like some kind of information network thing. Which wouldn’t be good but is better than some other things Zuko can think of. Agni—please don’t let this be another fancy, upscale brothel thing. Zuko thought he’d finally killed that suggestion thoroughly dead on his last birthday.

Uncle seems as unaffected as always by Zuko’s sourness but his eyes glint with a sharpness that Zuko hasn’t often seen, one that makes Zuko’s inner flame go low and careful. “I always told you that pai sho was more than just a game.”

Zuko is very much realizing that. He always thought Uncle meant that pai sho was about life, or learning skills beyond the board, but now his chest is flickering full of nervousness about what exactly Uncle could have been saying this whole time. Uncle’s been cheerfully announcing that there’s more to pai sho for *years*. Suddenly Zuko is processing that there might be a lot more to Uncle, too.

Zuko’s hands tremble as he fights to maintain a calm outward appearance, or at least his usual glower. Uncle with his letters about pai sho to friends all over the world who Zuko had never bothered to ask about. Uncle who seems to know his way around every port and local official. Uncle who spent decades of his life preparing to take the Fire Crown. Agni’s flaming dick, even at thirteen was Zuko really stupid enough to think that someone would just walk away from that so easily?

Zuko trails numbly behind Uncle and his friend, giving up on eavesdropping when it’s clear that their tone is purposefully pitched too low for him to discern with only one ear and the noise of the bar. Which is fine because Zuko doesn’t know what to do with the information he already has, sparse as it is. More fears and worries than facts, really.

Zuko doesn’t know what to do with being shut out of whatever it is Uncle is doing, either, as their new old man friend leads them into a shop across town and through a *secret* *door*. Of course, there’s a fucking secret door. Why *wouldn’t* a dusty oasis at the edge of a desert be full of secret codes and hidden rooms and the familiar made strange and alien and uncomfortable and--

Zuko might be spiraling a little here, standing immobile where Uncle left him with a half-glance of not-even-apology. But he doesn't know what to *do*. Uncle is suddenly closing Zuko out, after a lifetime of freely sharing his life and thoughts whenever Zuko could bring himself to ask. He’s suddenly leaving Zuko behind, after nominally following Zuko’s lead around the world for three years. He’s always been by Zuko’s side, and now Zuko is standing alone in an empty flower shop wondering if any of that was ever what Iroh was actually doing at all.

Zuko’s thoughts churn as he leans into a corner, right eye on the front door and head tilted to keep the secret entrance in his periphery. He tries to take calming breaths, tries to tame his fears and the sick twist in his gut back. He doesn’t *know* anything. He barely has a hint of anything. He can’t let himself run this far with so little. Just because something *could* be an explanation doesn’t mean it *is*.

Fuck. Zuko has never been good at gauging when he’s getting overdramatic and when he’s reacting with an appropriate level of drama.

Zuko rests his head back against the wall and tries to meditate to the rhythm of the torches he can feel on the other side of the stone, trying to push his fire sense into the room with Uncle even if he can’t put his body there. Something about that closeness is comforting despite his uncertainties, enough that Zuko finally manages to hit a steady cadence with his breaths, one where he can find some measure of calm but isn’t wholly lost in the flames in his grip.

Zuko doesn’t fight—doesn’t entirely notice—when his mind starts edging toward sleep instead of controlled calm, exhaustion catching up to him now that he’s finally still and in a place of marginal safety. His awareness hovers at the edge of dreaming and reality, warm from the fire he can feel beyond the wall, from the heat rising off the sunbaked dirt and the sand dunes just beyond the edge of town. Zuko feels surrounded, but not in a bad way. Cradled by fire and heat, cocooned and swimming in it, and Agni's tits, how is this entire town not full to the brim with firebenders...

Zuko's shoulders slowly unwind for the first time in…weeks, and he almost imagines he can feel an instantly familiar flicker within his fire sense, bright as always but wild and unsteady in a way that isn’t usual. Zuko’s half-awake mind reaches for it without thinking, trying to stabilize the not-flame he feels out on the sands, trying to feed it and coax it to its normal steady pulse.

&#45;-

Out in the Si Wong Desert, Sokka’s cactus juice hallucinations start to get really weird, really fast. Not that they weren’t already weird—he’s pretty sure he’s discovered twelve new colors even if Toph doesn’t appreciate his insistence. Which--fine, fair, but she didn’t care about the twelve new sounds that went with them, either, when he tried to demonstrate.

He might not exactly be perceiving the world the way it actually is. Or maybe he’s perceiving more than his un-cactus juiced mind can comprehend? Whatever it is, Sokka isn’t quite sure what he’s actually seeing and what he’s actually saying, versus hearing himself whispering directly into his own ear. But slippery as reality night be, up until this point it’s been slippery in a visual and auditory way.

Sokka suddenly feels like someone is running firebender warm hands up his back.

“Zuko.” That thought is always loud enough to sound in Sokka’s ears, regardless of cactus juice. Spirits, he doesn’t know about these hallucinations progressing to a feels-like-its-actually-touching-you stage. But if it has to happen, better for it to happen with this than when he was hallucinating twisting, smirking snakes replacing Toph’s hair.

“Why do you do this?”

Sokka’s brain fuzzes a little at a sensation like tight arms are wrapping around him from behind, holding him close and protected in the cage of a warm body that isn't actually there. Like they’re back on Zuko’s ship, united in the insane gamble they’re taking together. It’s a melancholy thought, remembering all the possibilities Sokka thought they had before them, back then.

“I deserve to be happy.” Something warm in Sokka’s chest flutters in agreement. Is there something in there? A sparrowkeet trapped behind his ribs? Do sparrowkeets eat meat? Spirits, is a small forest bird about to eat him from the inside out?

“Sokka, stop talking about birds eating people while we’re still alive, it’s *not* that bad,” a cactus snaps.

“Yet,” Momo mutters, more caustically than Sokka would have thought the little guy had the temperament for.

“I can’t wait for it to come to me,” Sokka sighs, deciding to ignore the irritableness of the local fauna and flora. “I’m going to chase it.”

A sand dune is telling him to please not run off, but Sokka waves it away because he isn’t going anywhere, not when a sensation like sparking breath on the back of his neck has his head lolling back, eyes slipping closed.

“It doesn’t have to be a person, you know. I have purpose now. *I* have the mission this time.” That warm breath slips under his skin, somehow grounding even as it makes his body shiver. “I’m not going to chase you anymore. We need to stop hunting.” The sand dune doesn’t like that. “Or, no--we can’t hunt each other, anymore,” Sokka tries to explain, fumbling his words and wondering what a pile of sand knows about it and why one would have such an opinion, anyway.

The heat under his skin stops sinking toward his bones, withdraws slightly, become a little lighter and Sokka can’t hold back a noise of protest. “No, not—well yes, I guess. I just don’t need you.”

“Sokka,” Momo rolls his eyes. “Trust me. You need us right now.”

“Well yeah,” he agrees easily. “I have a purpose, one for me. And a team. And I don’t need you or anyone that way anymore because I have my—my tribe right here.” Sokka frowns, vaguely remembering why he’s even high on cactus juice in the first place. “Even though we just lost one of us. But we’ll find him.”

“Oh, Sokka,” a dried-out husk of a tree sighs, sounding touched and fond and exasperated. Sokka hums absently in response, more concerned with the sensation of someone standing at his back, suddenly holding themselves carefully apart. “That doesn’t mean I don’t want you though. It just can’t be all I want. It just can’t be…how it was.” The heat at his back sinks a little closer. “I want lots of things. Like…” His mind is suddenly drowning with possibilities, cactus juice sending his fantasies spinning. “Like can I touch your hair? It looked really soft. Or, actually, can I touch—”

”*Sokka*,” a rockpile screams. “*Hallucinate about something else, please*!”

&#45;-

Zuko jolts back to full awareness when the secret door opens. He jerks upright, shaking his head to toss away the dizzy feeling that always comes with leaving a meditative state too fast. Or shaking off the cobwebs of dreams, maybe, even though Agni is high in the sky and Zuko doesn’t exactly trust anything to be just a dream where Sokka is concerned anymore. Zuko has the vague sensation of the sound and rhythm of Sokka’s voice in his ears but not the words. Just…impressions. Desire and melancholy and purpose, all covered with a hard resolve. And a new sense of distance that Zuko wants to throw himself across even though he knows it’s for the best.

“Nephew?” Zuko twitches, realizing he got lost in his thoughts again. Dangerous, that. Uncle is giving him a careful, considering look. “We are going to Ba Sing Se. We will travel as refugees and hide there in plain sight.”

Zuko shrugs, unsettled by his dream or imagining or whatever it was, and still unsettled on top of all that by everything that’s happened in this dried-up little town. Ba Sing Se is as good a place as any. If they’re going to continue to be refugees—he trips slightly over the thought —then that seems to be where most refugees eventually go. And Uncle seems to like the idea, his body animated with a new kind of eagerness and purpose that Zuko…doesn’t really want to think about. It’s something that Zuko *can’t* think about, not when it has the potential to yank everything Zuko is standing on out from underneath him.

Zuko is a bit jealous of it, though. Uncle has a purpose, Sokka has a purpose, and Zuko is...drifting behind Uncle like a pet goat dog.

The thought settles restless in his chest even as Zuko tries to cast it aside because a Good Nephew wouldn’t be jealous of his Uncle’s happiness. Zuko determinedly feeds the unhappiness into his inner flame and uses the fuel to stretch his fire sense as far as he can out over the desert. He’d tell himself that he’s chasing that sense of being cradled in heat, but Zuko isn’t good at lying directly, even to himself. He knows he’s looking for that not-flame again, for reassurance—even if it’s just from his own imagination—that Sokka is still alive.

## Chapter 9: On The Way To Ba Sing Se

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for some sexual content in this one

### Text

The closer they get to Ba Sing Se, the more introspective Uncle becomes. Which would be fine. Totally fine. Completely fine. Zuko even appreciates the reprieve from talk about tea and how pleasant the weather is—it’s early fall in the Earth Kingdom. There’s nothing pleasant about it. Hearing about the lessons learned from Uncle’s past is significantly better than hearing life lessons about tea or cloud shapes or whatever Uncle is usually going on about.

But they’re days from the walled city, sitting on a damn refugee ferry packed to the brim. S*o* *many people* could hear him.

“It is interesting, the interconnected tapestry that fate waves, is it not? To be returning to the sight of one’s greatest failure, this time as a supplicant with hands outstretched rather than a conqueror with fists clenched. It makes one wonder, if the first time I had only approached with humbleness and—”

“Shut up,” Zuko sighs, pinching the bridge of his nose and pressing a bowl of something attempting to be gruel, into Uncle’s hands. “Someone’s going to hear you.” Zuko eyes his own bowl with skepticism, prodding at the mysterious contents.

“I know you’re sad about selling Jasmine, Nephew, but you know we couldn’t—”

“I’m not,” Zuko snaps, even though he is, and they both know it. At least the family that bought her had looked like nice people. And she seemed as happy to bury her beak in their hair as she ever had in Zuko’s, which is *fine*. “If you want to monologue then find someone to talk to about how this awful food we’re paying for is. I ate better in the fucking badlands before I figured out how to hunt.”

“It wouldn’t take much, to be better than this,” a new voice drawls, amused and husky. “I’m not sure that bar you’re setting is all that high.”

Zuko glares up in annoyance at the interruption only to find himself looking into a pair of laughing brown eyes. Zuko blinks. It’s another teen. Zuko hasn’t seen many people his age in his travels, at least not without parents around, and especially not any dressed in such a hodgepodge of armor. Dark shaggy hair and ropy forearms and a way of chewing lazily on a stalk of wheat that puts *thoughts* in Zuko's head. The guy raises an expectant eyebrow, prompting Zuko to reply, “Um. Hello.”

That’s apparently all the invitation the other teen needs to slide closer and continue the conversation. “Are you a refugee, too?”

Zuko remembers to nod, after a beat, distracted by staring at the suddenly close distance between them.

“Me too. My name’s Jet, and these are my Freedom Fighters, Longshot and Smellerbee.”

Zuko flicks Jet’s…Freedom Fighters a quick look, taking in a thick bowl cut and an impassive face. Weird names. And they’re quiet, so much that Zuko barely noticed their presence before Jet gestured toward them which isn't something Zuko usually missed. Zuko glances their way again, briefly registering their wariness before his eyes drag almost against his will back to Jet. The other teen hasn’t looked away from Zuko. His inner fire turns a little flip under that stare, nervous and…something else.

“We’re down here eating these scraps,” Jet murmurs, continuing the conversation as if Zuko did something other than just staring mutely. “But I hear the captain’s up in his tower eating like a king.”

Jet looks like he expects some sort of reply, so Zuko defaults to a scowl. It’s apparently the right response judging by Jet’s firm nod, which is good because Zuko finds he wouldn't mind keeping those brown eyes on trained on him, regardless of how…unsettled it makes him feel. It’s not a bad kind of unsettled, he doesn’t think. Not when Zuko feels like he can ignore the phantom sound of water against iron hulls for the first time since he saw the ferry docks. Not when it feels like Jet is looking at *him,* not some idea of what he thinks Zuko should be.

There’s a magnetism around Jet that Zuko finds…interesting, even as he doesn’t quite know what to do with that interest. Zuko's been around so few people his age since he was exiled. No one, really, outside of brief interactions in markets. This is the first real attention from a peer that Zuko has *had*, outside of maybe Song. And Sokka, which--Zuko can’t let himself think about that in front of other people. And it's attention from someone who is…kind of hot.

“It doesn’t seem fair, does it?”

“No,” Zuko agrees, clearing his throat to hide his uncertainty because he hasn’t really been paying attention to Jet’s *words*. That seems to be the right thing to do again, though, because Jet smiles all slow, like he has a secret to share. It softens some of the sharp angles of his face and makes Zuko’s inner flame drop in a not-bad way. Zuko hopes Jet wears the expression often.

“What sort of king is the captain eating like?” Uncle’s question has Zuko jolting in surprise, then flushing at the fact that for a moment he completely forgot that Uncle was even there. Agni. Jet rolls easily with the interruption, though, smile turning sharp again.

“The fat, happy kind,” Jet drawls before turning back to Zuko, which makes his inner flame give another happy-nervous little twist. “So.” A smirk, an invitation to join in the secret that has Zuko’s pulse thrumming. “Want to help us liberate some food?”

“I’m in,” Zuko says almost before the question is out of Jet’s mouth, feeling an answering smile tugging at his scar as he rises to his feet, inner fire coiling at the potential for wildness. Jet doesn’t step back to give him space, and Zuko doesn’t move to put distance between them, and his inner flame curls at the potential for something else, too.

&#45;-

It feels good to break out his swords again and take to the shadows. Having blades in his hands feels right, has always felt right, even when nothing else has. Doing it with other people is new, but it doesn’t feel uncomfortable, or wrong. Just different. Jet’s friends are good, quick and quiet and able to stick to the pockets of dark that linger on any ship. And Jet seems to know the layout of the ferry, which is convenient, quickly leading them to the kitchens.

Lockpicking is apparently outside of their skillset, but Zuko’s able to step in there. Lu Ten had taught Zuko years ago—in retrospect, an interesting thing to teach your eight-year-old cousin one summer--and Zuko had plenty of practice over the years with Azula and her friends around, and then later. He makes quick work of the door and then they're in and Jet is clapping him on the shoulder, murmuring words of praise, leaning in a little bit too close.

“Thanks,” Zuko says, half-turning into the other teen instead of pulling away. Jet doesn’t pull back either, his hand still on Zuko’s shoulder, and Zuko’s skin prickles with the contact. It's just a hand on his shoulder, maybe just the sharp edge of adrenaline or the thrill of sharing a risk, sharing something like this that Zuko's never really done before, but--how would it feel if Jet touched him somewhere else?

Jet slips into the room and Zuko follows, Longshot and Smellerbee already examining the cabinets. Zuko doesn’t mind being last in. He runs his eyes along the lines of Jet’s body, the other teen’s swagger suddenly answering a lot of questions Zuko didn’t even realize he had.

They quickly gather food, picking past the moldering grains and limp vegetables to find meat and fresh greens. And if there isn’t quite the abundance Jet described, it’s certainly more and better than they were given to eat as paying customers. They quickly fill sacks with what they find and then they’re slipping out the way they came, quick and quiet again.

Zuko is lit up with the intoxicating feeling of having power and control again, something he hasn’t felt in too long. Agni, but it feels *good* to be able to actually do something right for once. And it’s all the more exhilarating to be doing it as part of a team, to have so smoothly fit into their unit. Is this what Sokka feels like, with his sister and the Avatar and the other girl?

Zuko wavers a moment, feeling suddenly weird to be thinking about that, and then feeling weirder at the way the thought feels…intrusive, almost. Distracting in a can’t-ignore way when Zuko needs to be able to ignore it, and edged with something like guilt. But then, that part isn't new. It always is.

With a hard exhalation Zuko burns that line of thought away into his inner flame, refocusing on clinging to the shadows. Sokka isn’t for him, for so many reasons, in so many ways. Zuko needs to remember.

&#45;-

Zuko watches Jet hand out food to the other passengers. Jet’s rangy body moves easily across the tightly packed deck, smiling and murmuring and approaching anyone and everyone with ease and confidence, leaving grins in his wake. Zuko envies it and drinks in the sight of it like he might somehow absorb that quality into himself by staring enough. As if that’s the only reason Zuko is staring.

Jet has a fluid charisma that seems to mold itself to whatever the situation requires and it’s fascinating to watch. Zuko is aware that Jet could use something like that for anything he wants, and what Jet wants is to help people. Fuck, he *does* help people.

Zuko remembers the heady sensation of striding into that Earth Kingdom town to save Lee, knowing he was in the right. The feeling shattered against the town’s hostility, but having a piece of it again now, the way being met with welcomes and smiles settles over Zuko’s shoulders…it feels good. Better than the power to take, even. And it’s grounding to have a purpose again, even if it’s something little and quick and already gone.

Zuko hides his surprise when Jet settles with him and Uncle in the end. Jet could have chosen anywhere on the ship to sit—anyone to join—but he drops down on Zuko’s right side, leaning against the railing with him and Uncle. There’s space between them, space that Zuko is suddenly highly conscious of. He can feel that distance, that it’s there and that it’s short. Much shorter than Zuko would normally be comfortable with. Much shorter than a stranger would usually want it to be.

Jet chitchats easily with Uncle, who’s happy to have a conversation partner more willing than Zuko usually is. Zuko *is* trying to be a Good Nephew, but some things he just fundamentally can’t seem to do. Actually engaging in discussion of pai sho strategies and tea blends is one of them. But Jet holds his side of the conversation easily enough for both of them until Agni’s light is long gone and Uncle finally settles into sleep.

Zuko and Jet sit in silence after that. It’s not awkward—despite Zuko having no idea what to say—but it isn’t restful either. Zuko is overly aware of every part of his body on the side Jet is sitting, of the casual way Jet’s leg is stretched out, of how the position pulls his pants tight over his thigh. Zuko flicks a sideways look at the wheatgrass still in Jet’s mouth. Zuko wonders what else Jet can do with that mouth, if he spends so much time sucking on—

Zuko cuts the thought off, flushing, embarrassed but also prickling all over with heat. Jet smirks without looking as if he knows exactly where Zuko’s mind is going.

“Want to find somewhere quieter?” Jet murmurs, tilting his head toward the bodies packed into every available inch of deck space.

“…Yes.”

Maybe Zuko should stay. Maybe he should hang back and assess this situation before letting himself get carried along by it. But he can’t resist, in this quiet moment, the urge to follow his wanting instead of chaining it back. Especially not with Uncle asleep and no one else there to hold Zuko accountable to being a Good Nephew. Besides, Good Nephews are still allowed to do…whatever this is, aren’t they?

Jet leads them to a quiet little pocket of the ferry, open to the air but enclosed in a way where no one will stumble onto it unless they’re deliberately looking. It’s the kind of corner Zuko used to seek out on the *Wani*, and the familiarity of it aches a little. The space isn’t quite large enough for two people, but Zuko doesn’t mind, and Jet clearly doesn’t either as he tugs Zuko in behind him and turns to face him.

“I recognized you by that scar, you know.”

Zuko stiffens at the quiet words, jerking back as his inner fire flares with alarm. Not that there’s far to go, the space is tight. A bad space for a fight, but a bad place to be trapped without help, too. Where did Jet’s friends end up? Are they nearby?

“It means you’re an outcast, like me.” Jet’s face is serious, eyes gentle in a way that has Zuko’s heart rate slowly dropping down toward its normal pace as he belatedly registers the lack of hostility on Jet’s face. “We need to have each other’s backs.”

“…Being alone isn’t always the best path,” Zuko finally offers. He isn’t quite sure what to say in response to this…empathy? Support? Or to the fact that Jet isn’t, in fact, about to expose him.

But Zuko seems to have stumbled onto the right words again because Jet is nodding, leaning back against the wall with a sigh. “Right. It helps to know someone else is there.” He studies Zuko’s reaction to that, then reaches out and gently catches Zuko’s chin, soft pressure that angles Zuko’s head so that Zuko is looking into his eyes again. It exposes the scar Zuko had automatically turned to hide, the gesture some kind of wordless reassurance. But it’s also an invitation, one Zuko can see echoed in the intensity in Jet’s eyes and the parting of his lips and the gentle stroke of his thumb over Zuko’s skin. One that Zuko seizes as he leans across what space there is between them into the suddenly-tense angle of Jet’s body.

Jet’s body feels different than Sokka’s. It slots against Zuko’s in a different way, is muscled in different places. Jet’s lips move at a different pace, too, the noises he makes more trapped in his throat than breaking free. It’s not bad, necessarily. It’s just not the same. And Agni, Zuko doesn’t want to think of Sokka right now, doesn’t want to feel the regret and bitterness over choices neither of them can unmake. So he concentrates on Jet instead, on feeling the shape of his body and the novelty of pressing against armor, on leaning into his touch, on tasting him.

They’re both quiet as they explore each other, cognizant that their privacy is a fragile thing. Jet pushes Zuko’s shirt off and Zuko makes quick work of Jet’s armor, seeking some sense of equivalency between them. The press of Jet’s bare torso against his own has Zuko sighing in pleasure, soaking in the cool expanse of skin.

Zuko keeps his inner flame locked tight, holding it low in his gut where it turns languid, slow coils. He’s shakily relieved that he can control himself under Jet’s hands like he couldn’t with Sokka. Maybe his control has actually improved in the months since. Or maybe it’s just how it is with Sokka. But keeping control doesn’t mean Zuko isn’t appreciating this, isn’t enjoying arching into Jet’s touch and feeling Jet hard for him and hearing the whispered praise as Zuko’s hands worm beneath Jet’s pants to find the hot length of him.

Zuko likes knowing that this charismatic, magnetic man who catches the attention of everyone around him chose Zuko out of anyone he could have had. He likes being able to make Jet feel good, make him come undone, being the one who puts that hazy, pleasure-drunk look in Jet’s normally sharp eyes. He likes having a space to discover and learn that feels safe instead of fraught, one that Zuko can enjoy partaking in without feeling anxious because whatever this is with Jet, Zuko knows that it’s going to be temporary. Jet will drift out of his life as just suddenly as he drifted into it. There are no expectations between them beyond mutual pleasure and that knowledge is just as electrifying in its own way as having Jet’s hands slipping inside his waistband in return.

Zuko finally stops thinking when Jet shoves him back, hooking his ankle at the same time. Zuko lets himself be taken down flat onto the deck, gasping at the sudden press of still sun-warm wood against his skin. Jet swallows the sound, weight settling on Zuko’s sprawled body in a way that makes Zuko’s head spin from trying to process so many new sensations all at once. Then Jet starts moving his lips down Zuko’s neck, down his torso, and Zuko lets out a contented sigh at how nice it feels to put himself under Jet’s mouth and hands and smirking eyes and need to think of nothing at all

&#45;-

Zuko tolerates the ferry ride far more easily after that first night. He sleeps better in those few days than he has in longer than he can remember, especially considering that he’s back on the water for the first time in months. Being able to press his hands into someone else’s heat at night helps him remember that they aren’t numb with cold anymore. And he finds that with Jet, it’s hard to think of much at all, anyway.

&#45;-

Reaching Ba Sing Se terminal is surreal. Zuko is back at Uncle’s side again, staying close as the crowd spills from the ferry. The great, arched space is big enough that Zuko wants there to be sky above him, shoulders feeling heavy to see only stone. Zuko feels oddly bereft even though he can feel Agni already climbing somewhere above them. The light without sun is odd, green, messing with Zuko’s vision on his left side though Uncle seems unbothered by it as they join the queue of other refugees stumbling toward their new life.

Zuko lets Uncle take the lead, because this kind of thing has never been his forte, and because the idea of answering whatever rapid-fire questions the intake agents are shooting out without getting snarly or tripping over a lie is probably beyond him. He watches Uncle flirt, instead, refraining from rolling his eyes, and tries not to watch Jet. Zuko can’t be like that here, not in public. And besides, Zuko needs to be alert for any signs of recognition. He isn’t sure that anyone would know him—it depends on how motivated Azula was with her wanted posters —but it wasn’t all that long ago, really, that the Dragon of the West was trying to break down these walls.

Jet saunters over to where Zuko is slouched against a pillar and Zuko feels something pleasantly surprised flutter in his stomach. Zuko is still startled each time when Jet comes to him out of anyone he could choose to be beside. Jet leans next to him, sighing as he looks over the crowd in a way that Zuko recognizes, the sound of someone who’s been carrying a heavy weight and wants to set it down but isn’t sure if they can yet.

“So, this is supposed to be our new beginning, huh?”

Zuko just grunts in response, but Jet is used to that by now, too.

“What are your plans in the city?”

Zuko shrugs, tracking Uncle as he leaves the intake agent and approaches a tea vendor. Zuko glances back in surprise when Jet tugs on his arm, urging Zuko to turn into some semblance of privacy between them, face devoid of its smirk in a way Zuko hasn’t seen often from him.

“Would you want to join the Freedom Fighters?”

“What?” Zuko blinks, inner flame going still in pure surprise. He…had been expecting goodbye.

“My crew,” Jet says, as if clarification is what Zuko needed. He isn’t quite looking at Zuko, eyes tracking the crowd like he often does when his friends aren’t close by.

“I thought you were giving that up,” Zuko finally says, quiet. “What happened to new beginnings?”

Jet tenses, face freezing, and Zuko silently curses himself for saying the wrong thing, for fucking this up right at the end.

“I just can’t leave my Uncle,” he hastens to explain. “I’m all he has.” It might be more like the other way around, but Zuko isn’t going to get into that with Jet. Besides, he doesn’t like to think too much about the reasons Uncle is still around, lately.

Jet nods slowly, still not quite looking at him, which Jet *never* does—holding direct eye contact is his thing. The other teens’ face is whiter than Zuko would have expected, too, and Zuko feels a bolt of sudden alarm. Agni’s tits. Maybe their time on the ferry meant something different to Jet than it did to Zuko. Maybe Zuko had been saying the wrong things for a lot longer than just this conversation.

“I’ll see you around, then,” Jet finally says, voice a little tighter than usual, expression a little too fixed.

“Yeah,” Zuko says uselessly, confused as Jet abruptly strides off, quickly disappearing into the crowd. Zuko stares after him a moment, feeling oddly bereft with only that for a goodbye. Which is stupid of him, because wasn’t Zuko just worried that Jet was in too deep? He shakes his head, finally making his way back to where Uncle is perched with a cup of tea and a look of pure contentment.

“They have hot tea here?” Zuko asks in surprise, glancing at the sad-looking food and drink carts scattered across the station. Zuko hadn’t felt much by way of flame around and assumed they were offering what amounted to travel rations dressed up in different packaging.

“They didn’t,” Uncle says serenely, bringing his steaming cup to his face for a deep inhale.

“Agni’s—are you trying to get us caught?” Zuko growls, tension ratcheting through his body, eyes darting for anyone who might be looking at them, or pulling away from them, or really in any way indicating that they’re aware of them at all.

“What?” Uncle frowns, glancing up at the sudden anger in Zuko’s tone, the edge of barely contained rage that Zuko has tried so hard to keep out of his voice lately.

“Firebending in public,” Zuko hisses.

“It was just heat,” Uncle protests. Just heat. As if the visible evidence of what he’d done wasn’t steaming in his hand. As if heat doesn't count. “And they were ruining such good tea with such poor steeping!”

Zuko drops his head into his hands, telling himself that he can snarl at Uncle and still be a Good Nephew if what he really wants to do is scream. Agni, sometimes Zuko doesn’t understand how this man could be a military genius. Particularly not in moments like this, when he has no common sense. And especially not when they finally settle onto the monorail that will bring them to their new home—the thought is like a fresh bruise that Zuko can’t stop poking—and Uncle tickles and coos at a little baby as if he’s nothing but a doting grandfather and not the enemy walking unnoticed into the city’s walls.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

We had to know Jet was going to come back around eventually, right?

## Chapter 10: Learning to Settle

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings in this one for some sexual content, alcohol consumption, and canon-typical violence

### Text

It’s both easier and harder than Zuko expected, to settle in Ba Sing Se.

Easier, because somehow no one asks any questions. Zuko knows he can’t lie, has been anxious about their backstory for days, but everyone just accepts them as Mushi and his cranky nephew Lee. They’re handed a job in a teashop, fulfilling almost every dream Uncle has ever had with one swipe of an intake agent’s brush. They’re handed a tiny apartment around the corner, fulfilling every unacknowledged longing Zuko has had for some semblance of privacy again. And it all happens within a day.

The city’s bureaucracy when it comes to refugees is amazing. And somewhat horrifying, when Zuko considers why it’s needed to become so efficient.

It’s hard, though—nearly impossible, some days—to be in a place without war. Zuko was born into war, raised under its shadow and trained to seize its fortunes, sent out to join it at the age of thirteen. War has been one of the few constants of Zuko’s life. He doesn’t know how to be without it, how to act, how to just…do tea, instead. Zuko doesn’t know what the rules are yet, for being nothing but a teashop server.

And more concerning, Zuko doesn’t know the rules for Ba Sing Se except that there *are* rules. The lack of knowing—Zuko is fine breaking the rules, but he wants to know he’s doing it—sets him on edge, twitchy and restless. But then, that isn’t particularly new for Zuko, even if he can’t respond with temper and shouting like he usually would.

Jet helps with it all—a thought Zuko never expected to have again and is still surprised to be thinking.

&#45;-

Zuko is longing for manual labor and doesn’t know what to make of that fact. But Agni, what he wouldn’t give right now for a fence to build or a cart to haul or some rocks to clear. Because customer service? It’s the absolute worst. Uncle takes to it like a turtle duck to water, of course, but Zuko…well, he doesn’t. He can’t even decide which *part* of all he hates the most. Probably working the register, because basic math literacy in the Earth Kingdom is as subpar as every other aspect of the entire country. But taking orders is also terrible. And the sweeping could be fine, if people just got out of his fucking way.

Zuko had pointed that out to a couple, yesterday. Which might be related to why he is back to taking orders today.

The only saving grace of being forced to interact with strangers for hours on end is that Zuko usually doesn’t have to actually *look* at anyone. His scar was noticeable but—uncomfortably —unremarkable when he traveled on his own in the Earth Kingdom. Ba Sing Se, though, is full of refugees all acting as if they’ve never encountered the war let alone felt its impacts. Zuko has so clearly been touched by it.

Zuko bristles at the pity and gentle concern and horror that follows most patrons who catch a look at his face. But he quickly learns that he can just stare at his notepad and stomp around the shop and drop tea on the tables and leave and avoid eye contact altogether. That suits him just fine for a number of reasons, and generally works except for the occasional customers who inexplicable want Zuko’s opinion on the menu—it all sucks—or his thoughts on how much tea to order—none. Or Agni, when they just sit there and force Zuko to initiate the transaction is if they don’t fucking know exactly why he’s at their fucking table in the first place.

Zuko is not going to snap another charcoal pencil in half, even though he hates them and the way charcoal gets into his fingers and under his nails and stains his hands like ash. He’s five days into customer service and down three pencils already. They don’t have that many left. But Agni, this *person* is just *sitting there*.

“Agn—What do you *want*?” Zuko finally snaps, because he might have the stubbornness to wait this person out until the shop closes but today he just doesn’t have the will for it.

“Whatever you like.”

Zuko drops his pencil instead of breaking it. He fumbles his notepad, barely avoiding dropping that too as he jerks his head up to meet a familiar pair of brown eyes. “Jet?”

“Who else,” Jet smirks, wheatgrass in his mouth, slouching in his chair as if there’s no reason he wouldn’t be here right now.

“What are you doing here?” Zuko mutters, clutching his notepad in both hands and darting quick glances between Jet and the floor, trying to find his pencil.

“Looking for you.”

Zuko blinks at that, then drops down to pick up his pencil, using the brief moment out of sight to fix his face into a neutral scowl. This is…unexpected. “…Why?”

“Can’t I just want to spend some time with you?” Jet drawls, leaning down to catch Zuko’s eyes where he's still crouched on the floor.

Zuko is alarmed. Jet had already seemed more upset than he should have been when they parted in the terminal. Following Zuko here…does Jet want more than Zuko can give? The thought makes him itch, makes his shoulders tense with wariness even as part of him thinks that it might actually be kind of…nice, to be chased for non-nefarious reasons. “That’s… fine.”

“I’m glad,” Jet smirks, leaning over a bit further as he stares at Zuko on his knees. There’s a particular glint in his eyes as he hovers just on the edge of looming and Zuko’s inner fire perks up in interest.

*Oh.*

This, Zuko understands. This, he gets. This…would be fine. As long as it stays nothing more than this.

“So…” Zuko rises to his feet, pencil back in hand, wondering what’s supposed to happen now that he’s been found. “What do you want?”

“I think you can guess.”

Zuko can, especially when Jet says it in that tone, but, “…I’m working.”

“Forever?” Jet pouts, playful.

“No…”

“So, when do you stop working?”

“Tonight.”

“Perfect,” Jet grins, eyes sweeping down Zuko’s body in a way that makes Zuko’s inner fire pulse, which is incredibly inconvenient because he is *working*. And apparently Zuko’s already over his discomfort with Jet seeking him out. Quick, how that worked out.
