“…You can’t stay here if you don’t order anything,” Zuko finally points out when Jet makes no move to get up and leave.

Jet settles into his chair like he’s staying for the long haul. “I’ll have your favorite tea, then.”

“…Okay.”

Zuko makes it all the way back to the kitchen before he remembers that he doesn’t have one.

&#45;-

Uncle doesn’t ask where Zuko was when Zuko slips back into their room that night, and Zuko doesn’t volunteer the information. He can tell that Uncle is awake despite the darkness, but he just gets ready for bed in silence and then lays there, listening as Uncle’s even snoring eventually starts to rumble through the little room. Neither of them, apparently, wants to probe at the other’s secrets just yet. Zuko is fine with that.

&#45;-

Zuko doesn’t drop anything the next day, but it’s still a shock to glare up into laughing brown eyes. “You’re back.”

“I am,” Jet agrees easily.

“…What do you want?”

Jet smirks, eyes dropping south of Zuko’s face, and Zuko huffs in…annoyance. Definitely annoyance. “The same thing as yesterday?”

“Hmm.” Jet slouches forward to rest his cheek on his fist, looking up at Zuko through his lashes. “I might be in the mood for something hotter this time.”

“…It’s tea.”

“Surprise me,” Jet laughs, like Zuko just made some kind of joke.

“…Okay.”

Jet is weird. Zuko’s sure of that, even if the guy has the confidence to get away with basically anything. But Jet pays for his tea—Zuko wonders where the coin’s coming from, Jet can’t have a job if he’s here during the days and with Zuko at night—and settles into his chair, seemingly content to watch Zuko work. Which…is fine. Jet’s stare is still a bit unsettling. But still not in a bad way.

&#45;-

When Zuko has idle moments to let his thoughts wander—something he doesn’t typically allow himself—he doesn’t know quite what to make of being found by Jet so quickly. Zuko and Uncle weren’t exactly trying to hide—not from Jet, at least. But the Lower Ring wouldn’t be the easiest place to track someone down, and Jet did it in less than a week.

But then, that efficient Ba Sing Se bureaucracy probably placed all the refugees from the same boat relatively close to each other. Easier documentation, easier transport, easier check-ins and monitoring. And it’s not like Uncle was shy about his love for tea, it came up in literally every conversation he had with Jet on the ferry.

So maybe there’s nothing to keep thinking about, really. Especially not when Zuko is more than familiar with how shockingly easy it can be to track someone down when you’re feeling properly motivated.

&#45;-

Zuko slams his broom down into its corner, finally done with the day. There are still a few customers left for evening tea—a concept that Zuko will never understand. Not that Zuko understands any of this. But regardless of its lack of sense, evening tea means that the shop doesn’t need the full day-shift crew, which is all that Zuko cares about right now. It’s been an aggravating day and Zuko is so ready to walk away from this stupid teashop and its stupid customer who don’t know what they want and all the idiots who can’t count change and the clumsy jerks who spill their tea and need Zuko to fucking clean it as if they don’t have functioning hands and Zuko doesn’t *care* if it's literally his job to clean it, it’s still shit and Zuko is *done.*

Zuko stalks out the front door and nearly trips over his own feet when he sees Jet leaning against the wall, wheatgrass between his teeth, eyes flicking over Zuko with that smirk.

“Hey,” Jet says, heat slowly entering his eyes.

“Um. Hi.” Zuko feels so wrong-footed right now. He hadn’t expected to see Jet, had been dreading a night of Uncle opining about tea as if they both didn’t spend all day already thinking about it.

“Miss me?”

“Um.” Zuko can feel a blush trying to crawl up his face. He hadn’t been bothered that Jet wasn’t there today. Not at all. Zuko is just choosing not to try to say that out loud to the other teen.

Jet grins, like Zuko’s non-answer was a whole conversation in and of itself. “You busy tonight?”

“…Maybe.” It depends on the definition of busy.

“Want to hang?”

“…Okay.” Jet’s been waiting for Zuko for who knows how long. It would be rude to turn him away. It would be rude not to follow.

&#45;-

Jet watches Zuko a lot. Nearly every day. It makes Zuko feel…not paranoid, because it’s not really a bad thing. Just constantly…overly aware. Even when Jet slips out before the end of Zuko’s shift, or hasn’t come in yet, Zuko starts to feel like someone is always watching him when he works. Like that girl in the corner, who comes in multiple times a week and peeks through her bangs like she’s trying to get a good look at his face. Or those old ladies who always come in on alternating days and whisper together, clamming up whenever Zuko approaches the table.

Though today the feeling might be edging more toward overt paranoia, because Zuko just got yanked into the back by Uncle right after snapping another charcoal pencil. Zuko might be getting better at being a Good Nephew, but Uncle still knows when to intervene when Zuko forgets. And even if they’ve never spoken about it, Uncle knows that staring has always been hard, for Zuko. That it only got worse, after his banishment.

Zuko finds that he doesn’t particularly mind the staring, though, when it’s just one person instead of a crowd. When he knows who’s doing the looking, and at least has a sense of why. Jet is a familiar face. And it’s nice to have something familiar other than Uncle to hold onto, in this place where everything is so new. Especially when Uncle is determined to throw himself into being the best Mushi he can possible be. Zuko is still actively working at being a Good Nephew. He isn’t sure how long he can be *Lee* before he slips. And Jet is some sliver of a connection to the part of Zuko that doesn’t seem to have a place in Ba Sing Se, the part that’s good at slipping through shadows and is never quite comfortable until there are swords in his hands. Zuko isn’t ready to let that go yet, even if Uncle is.

&#45;-

Jet’s apartment is small, tight for three people and especially for four. Though Longshot and Smellerbee don’t actually hang around much when Zuko is there. Which is…fine, even if Zuko does wonder where they go. Maybe they work nights. But Zuko certainly isn’t going to ask and risk them staying. Beyond the privacy their absence affords him and Jet, the pair seem awkward and twitchy in Zuko’s presence beyond their reserved wariness on the ferry. Maybe they’re also surprised by Jet’s pursuit of Zuko. Or maybe they’re feeling insecure about how much time Jet’s giving to Zuko instead of them, which Zuko really should be more worried about, but also doesn’t think he has it in him to reject.

Zuko is also never going to ask because Jet never seems particularly concerned about Longshot and Smellerbee either way. He meets his friends’ discomfort with posturing and bravado and rants about justice, and somehow that seems to relax them even as it only makes Zuko more tense. But Zuko had already noticed on the ferry that Jet can mold his charisma to match whoever he’s speaking to, and Jet would know what his friends need more than Zuko would.

And tonight, Jet seems more than happy to see them leave. He grins sly and smirk-y he uncovers a bottle of wine from beneath his pillow and dramatically pops the cork. Zuko can tell from the smell that immediately permeates the room that it's basically swill. But then, the crew on the *Wani* made moonshine in old blasting jelly vats, so Zuko isn’t really one to hold out for quality.

They sit on Jet’s basically bare mattress—could Jet afford a real blanket if he stopped buying so much tea?—pouring the wine into lopsided cups and leaning back against the wall, shoulders touching. Zuko’s used to how much Jet likes to talk by now, and it seems like this is going to be a starting-with-talking night rather than an ending-with-talking one. Zuko sips slowly, holding the wine in his mouth where Jet knocks it back like a shot, savoring the burn down his throat, seeing how long he can keep his face still and endure the taste before finally swallowing.

“And how’s your new life, fellow refugee,” Jet asks, tone biting like it always is when he gets to talking about starting over.

Zuko just shrugs, because there isn’t much to say about it, not without talking about what came before. And especially not when Jet has inserted himself so thoroughly into what Zuko’s life is now.

“This place is so fucking weird,” Jet mutters, pouring himself another cup as Zuko grunts in agreement. “They act like nothing’s even going on outside their stupid walls!”

“There is no war in Ba Sing Se,” Zuko says quietly, a phrase that was repeated over and over through their intake process. A promise, maybe, but also a warning.

“It’s ridiculous,” Jet growls. “The Fire Nation is *out there*, right now! Stealing more land every day. Killing people. Terrorizing villages. Destroying our forests and our crops! And they have all this here—” he gestures wildly, wine splashing over his hand. “—and they do nothing! They sit behind their walls and pretend that people aren’t being burned alive this very second!”

Zuko winces. He knows Jet is making a point, exaggerating like he always does, but…it’s not a light thing, to burn someone alive. It’s not quick, or easy.

“Putting your head in the sand doesn’t make the ash eaters go away,” Jet continues, glaring down into his cup. “It just gives them the whole rest of the Earth Kingdom, and fuck the rest of us, right? They act like nothing outside the walls matter.”

“It’s hard,” Zuko finally agrees. And it is, to pretend like nothing in their past ever happened. It’s jarring and uncomfortable and sometimes makes him feel like he’s walking through each day in a dream. It lights a quiet fear in his chest that one day he might forget that he ever used to be anything other than Lee.

“It’s criminal,” Jet snaps, slouching back against the wall, sullenly licking spilled wine off the back of his wrist in an absent gesture that for once doesn’t seem designed to catch Zuko’s attention.

“Maybe it’s easier for people to just…pretend it didn’t happen,” Zuko says, staring into his own empty cup.

“Is that what you want to do?” Jet challenges, voice hard. Zuko glances up to see his eyes on Zuko’s scar. “You want to just pretend nothing from before happened?”

“No,” Zuko says slowly. He can’t, even if he wanted to. “But it’s different for me.”

“Why?” Jet’s eyes narrow, his body tensing slightly.

“I’ve just…seen too much,” Zuko sighs, because he has no way to explain that putting the war behind him would mean casting off all that he is. Though he has a feeling that Jet would understand that, if Zuko did find the words for it.

“Like what,” Jet scowls, still restless with anger.

Zuko tilts his head back instead of thunking it against the wall. He opened up this line of questioning himself when he knows he can’t lie. But then—Zuko doesn’t have to wholly lie, does he? He remembers the other Lee, the real one, waiting for his brother to come home and terrorized by his own army. He thinks of the stories he’s heard from wary merchants and gaunt farmers and finds that those come surprisingly easy to his lips for all that they’re so hard to think about.

But words about barren towns and stolen men and soldiers made to die at the hands of their own countrymen only seem to rile Jet more, until Zuko finally stops talking, uncomfortable with the look in his eyes. Zuko knows rage in all its forms, and Jet’s is bordering on snapping into something worse.

Jet notices, eyes narrowing on Zuko and agitated shifting going still. Then Jet slips back into motion, shoving his cup aside and pulling Zuko down on top of him. Zuko goes without resistance, unbalanced and dizzy from the sudden shift in mood and maybe a little bit from the wine, too, but more than willing to follow where Jet leads.

Zuko wiggles a bit, settling his weight more comfortably on top of Jet and enjoying the press of their bodies together with no armor in between as Jet’s tongue slides into his mouth like a challenge. Like always, the tension falls away when it’s just them, just this, Jet stepping easily from whatever he’s thinking to focus solely on Zuko. Jet seems determined to blow Zuko’s mind in every way he can think up and Zuko doesn't really get why but he's more than happy to go along for the ride.

Jet must be more in his own head than he's letting on, though, because his noises and movements beneath Zuko tonight border on too calculated. Scripted, almost. Which is distracting and a little off-putting, but still doesn’t make it feel any less good, which...whatever. Even when Jet gets like this, Zuko can still appreciate being the focus of that kind of planning and attention. Especially when Jet putting on a show lets Zuko play a role, too, lets him keep his inner fire under control and shrug into the mantle of Lee as he explores and learns and discovers.

&#45;-

Zuko keeps waiting for the day when Jet doesn’t show up, and it keeps never happening. He still doesn’t really understand why Jet latched onto him out of everyone he could have chosen. Maybe it’s some sense of companionship, after raiding the kitchens on the ferry together. Or maybe out of a need to find someone other than Longshot and Smellerbee who will admit to remembering the war. Or a kind of kinship with someone else who isn’t entirely sold on the idea of carving out a new life like the other never happened.

Or maybe Zuko’s projecting.

But Agni, he never imagined it could be a relief to talk about the ravages of war until he’s surrounded by Ba Sing Se’s steadfast refusal to discuss the source of all its refugees. And there’s a rage and frustration in Jet that matches Zuko, even if Jet can never know the source of Zuko’s anger, and Zuko doesn’t entirely understand the boundaries and triggers of Jet’s.

Sometimes when Zuko lays next to him and listens to him growl about the Fire Nation, Zuko’s tense discomfort taken for enraged agreement, he thinks that it probably isn’t healthy to hold onto so much rage. But Jet can’t feed his into an inner flame like Zuko can. And it feels good to be allowed to be angry, to remember this part of himself. To be able to say ‘me too’ or ‘I understand’ and have someone enraged on your behalf, instead of listing all the reasons you should stop being upset.

Zuko thinks he understands better now what Sokka meant when he wrote about people pulled into the war too young and changed by it. Zuko can see the shape that Jet has been warped into, so clear and strong that Zuko can barely comprehend what Jet could have been before war got to him. Agni, how has *Zuko* been warped by it? He’s pretty sure he’s been immersed in war longer than Jet has, for all that Zuko lived a more privileged life at the start.

Maybe the fact that he doesn’t know is part of the warping.

&#45;-

Zuko falls into a rhythm, living mostly as Lee and only as himself in snatches and grabs. He meditates with Uncle as Agni crests the horizon, focusing on the pulse of his inner flame and the fire cupped in his palms. He grits his teeth through days of customer service, trying to scale back his glares and not throw anything because Uncle wants him to do this so Zuko will try, and if Zuko’s going to try then he isn’t going to fucking half-ass it. He spends his nights sprawled across Jet’s futon until Zuko needs to drag himself back to his own apartment to sleep.

It’s an odd rhythm, absent the training and guiding purpose and intensity that Zuko used to lean on. But Uncle seems content, and Zuko is…not actively miserable. And a Good Nephew would be grateful for the generosity that’s brought them this life, even if it rankles to have needed to accept it. Zuko’s skin itches whenever he thinks of all they’ve been given while providing nothing back except another body behind the walls. But then he thinks of giving back to Ba Sing Se and the Earth King, and that itches even worse.

The days blur together in their sameness, distinguished only by Jet’s creativity and Uncle’s newest tea blends. Zuko starts to wonder if this is actually how it’s going to be now, for the rest of his life. With each day it seems more and more likely that no one will come for them, or discover them, or track them down and burn away the shield of normalcy that Uncle has drawn around them.

Zuko isn’t quite sure if the thought is entirely a good one, but it at least lets him release some of the persistent tension he didn’t even know he’d been carrying over the long weeks as a fugitive. Will Zuko slowly become used to this, too? Just like he became used to trading labor for food and to living in the confines of a ship and to being Crown Prince before that, until he doesn’t remember a time when he was anyone but Lee?

Maybe. The uniformity and routine of it all is so steady that it takes Zuko completely by surprise when it all goes to shit.

&#45;-

It’s a normal shift like any other at the teashop—so it’s completely terrible and grueling and monotonous all at the same time, like the shop inhabits some fold in reality where things can be both overwhelmingly boring and overwhelmingly frustrating at the same time. Zuko is behind the register, which is marginally better than needing to take orders, but only marginally because he still has to fumble with idiots who pay their entire bill in fucking half-coppers, Agni’s tits, who *does* that.

Zuko is counting out the coins *again* because there are so fucking many of them and the lady won’t stop trying to stack them into piles when he *already has a system* when the door slams open. Zuko startles, scattering the coins on the counter as he hears multiple teacups crashing to the floor which Zuko will definitely need to sweep now, too, and *fuck this day*.

Zuko glares at the door, a snarl rising in his throat at the backlit figure standing in the doorway like it’s some kind of fucking theater drama. Then they step forward and Zuko’s glare slides into a scowl of confusion. It’s Jet. But Zuko has never seen Jet’s body shaking with this kind of tension before, has never seen the crazed, wild-eyed expression on his face.

Or no—Zuko *has* seen that look before. It's Jet’s Fire Nation expression. Zuko has just never seen it directed at himself.

*Fuck*.

“None of you are safe!” Jet screams, arms swinging wide. “The Fire Nation is hiding among us!”

Zuko grips the counter as everyone stares at Jet before glancing among themselves in…gentle concern and mild confusion?

“Right here in this shop!” Jet continues, eyes finally landing on Zuko. “They’re getting ready to attack! To—to destroy the city!”

Zuko’s inner flame shudders, cold numbness spreading out from his core as he stares down the calculating rage in Jet’s eyes. *This* is what Jet has been about. This is the reason for his focused intensity every day in the shop, for his ever-more angry ranting, for his insistence on something new every time Zuko’s back hit the mattress. He had been…gathering intel. Observing. Trying to make Zuko lose control.

Zuko is going to be sick.

“Ash eaters serve your tea every day, pretending to be one of us! Well they’re not! That old man—” Jet’s finger stabs toward Uncle. “—is a firebender!”

Zuko follows Jet’s pointing finger toward Uncle’s expression of befuddled surprise. Zuko can see the way Uncle’s weight shifts, though, in case he needs to defend himself. Zuko turns slowly back to meet Jet’s eyes, feeling like he is forcing himself through sticky honey. Zuko’s numbness fractures over the unsteady, dangerous rage rising out of his core and for once Zuko doesn’t try to fight it back or burn it away.

Good Nephews don’t stand by and let Earth Kingdom shitheads endanger their Uncles.

The clarity and purpose of anger is familiar and welcome, simple and consuming when nothing else seems to make sense anymore, and Zuko embraces it wholeheartedly. Jet snarls in response to the glare on Zuko’s face, reacting as if attacked. His hands whip back to draw his swords with a dramatic spin and it’s all the excuse Zuko needs.

Zuko vaults the counter as customers scream and scatter, grabbing for one patron’s swords and throwing himself toward Jet almost before he has them fully in his grip. Their blades catch with the clean sound of metal on metal, Jet retreating back into the space of the open street under the force of Zuko’s onslaught.

That advantage doesn’t last for long, though, once Jet gains room to maneuver. Jet’s good, which is inconvenient but not a surprise—Zuko’s seen the way Jet’s body moves, has felt the calluses on his hands that come from training, saw the casual comfort Jet had with raiding the ferry. And on top of it, Zuko isn’t familiar facing hooked swords and needing to be wary of attempts to yank him off balance and tangle his limbs as well as slashes.

Zuko isn’t concerned, though, because he is too busy being *furious*. Everything in him is boiling at the idea that this guy, this person who can be kind and considerate and fight corrupt authority on behalf of those who can’t fight themselves, would try to use Zuko against Uncle. Uncle, who wants nothing more than to serve tea and find the perfect jasmine blend. Zuko’s rage feels clean, pure, leaving his mind clear and making his parries strong enough to rattle up Jet’s forearms, making his attacks vicious and quick.

Zuko’s inner flame licks under his skin, wanting to join, and Zuko doesn’t hold it back, letting heat ride up his blades and swirl in the air around him. Not enough to shimmer and distort, Zuko isn’t totally gone in his anger, but enough to be felt. Jet is snarling, throwing insults and invectives and accusations, but Zuko saves his breath for his fire, exhaling heat until the force of it coming off his blades is like another blow behind every strike.

They clash together, both with dual blades crossed, caught straining against each other, bodies angled and aligned and it’s so familiar and so wrong that Zuko can’t stop the furious flare of his inner fire. Jet set out deliberately to use Zuko, to take away the one thing Zuko has left in his fucking life and Zuko wants to *hurt* *him back*. He holds Jet’s eyes, snarling into Jet’s crazed fury and deliberately wrapping a coil of heat around Jet that can’t be mistaken for anything but firebending.

Jet’s eyes go wide and Zuko can *see* something in him snap. Jet shoves himself away from Zuko with a scream, barely getting enough distance to unlock their blades before throwing himself back into the fight. He is barely coherent in his rage, teeth bared, attacks becoming choppy and predictable. Anger burning away his training and control, Zuko notes from the heart of his own rage. A common problem for young, volatile firebenders.

Zuko reacts like he would if he were encountering an onslaught of uncontrolled bending, gritting his teeth and weathering the storm, deflecting and dodging and leaping and dancing out of reach, waiting for the moment he knows is coming, when Jet’s wild swings cause him to overreach. Zuko darts within Jet’s guard, sliding up the curve of Jet’s arm to punch the hilt of his sword into Jet’s temple and unleash a front kick that Azula would have been proud of.

Jet flies across the street, body hitting the wall with a sickening thud. It should be enough to take him out of the fight but Zuko doesn’t relax. He knows that rage like that doesn’t let you stay down.

Jet doesn’t even get halfway to his feet, though, before green-robed figures are swooping down on him. Zuko pulls up short at the synchronized, efficient way the two uniformed men grab Jet and haul him to his feet, manacles of stone flying through the air to catch Jet’s wrists. Zuko had been so focused on the fight that he didn’t even realize any kind of enforcement had shown up. Dangerous. Though maybe Zuko wouldn’t have realized they were there regardless, because he’s pretty sure that these are the Dai Li that Uncle had warned him about. This…is not good. Zuko doesn’t need to be catching the attention of any secret police forces.

“There is no fighting in Ba Sing Se,” one of the agents—Zuko can’t tell which—intones. It sounds like a threat, with the cadence of a ritual.

“They’re firebenders!” Jet shrieks, and Zuko hides his twitch because he didn’t exactly consider, during the fight, that using his bending against Jet would finally give the other teen his evidence. “Right there! Both of them are firebenders!”

“It was just Mushi, before,” an annoyed voice calls out from behind him. Zuko jerks to the side, keeping the Dai Li and Jet on his right and taking in the crowd of customers and employees gathered outside the shop. “Now you’re saying it’s his nephew, too?”

“What, am I going to be a firebender next?” Another customer grumbles.

“There are no firebenders in Ba Sing Se,” the Dai Li—orders? Commands? States? The tone is even harder to deal with than Uncle at his most neutral.

“Yes, there are!” Jet insists, straining against their hold. “Right there!”

“They’re not firebenders, they’re refugees,” the teashop owner shouts. “They were in a sorry state, too, when they got here. And now they’re some of my best workers!”

Zuko glances over at that, catching the shadow of a shrug the owner gives him. No one would accuse Zuko of being a good employee, but Uncle more than pulls their combined weight, and Zuko isn’t about to argue against himself.

“This kid’s crazy,” a woman mutters. “We were just enjoying our tea and he barged in and started screaming and waving his swords around!”

“Who does that?” Her companion shakes his head sadly. “And to accuse two fine citizens, who are only trying to make a new life for themselves, of being firebenders?”

“It’s shameful!”

“This one started the fight?” The Dai Li ask, giving Jet a little shake.

“Yes,” the teashop owner confirms, scowling at Jet. “Lee here was just defending us when this vagrant drew weapons in the shop. They aren’t even Lee’s swords.”

Zuko glances down at the hilts in his hands. That’s true. But they have a good weight, and they took his fire so nicely. He wouldn’t mind keeping them.

“Is that true?”

Zuko looks up to see both Dai Li staring at him, Jet wordless with rage between them. “Yes,” Zuko replies, holding Jet’s eyes and watching his face twist into something alien.

“He’s lying!” Jet screams. “Lying! He was firebending just now!”

“There were no flames, child,” one of the customers says gently, and Zuko watches something in Jet break against the force of their disbelief, at the reality of his Earth Kingdom countrymen rallying around firebenders and not him.

It’s over after that, Jet dragged away still bucking and spitting with rage, glaring back over his shoulder at Zuko until he’s dragged fully out of sight.

*…I did that*. Not all of it, not the worst of it. But Zuko had very deliberately been the push over the edge, at the end, had been ruthless in his defense of Uncle and himself. He isn’t quite sure how he’s supposed to feel about it. Azula would be proud.

&#45;-

Zuko’s steps are heavy as he finally walks back toward Uncle, handing the swords off to the rather dazed man he grabbed them from.

“That’s the value of good customer service, Nephew,” Uncle murmurs just for Zuko. Zuko doesn’t know how he’s supposed to respond, can only shake his head. Yes, it could have gone so much worse if the crowd hadn’t rallied behind them and painted Jet as someone totally divorced from reality. But Zuko isn’t ready for whatever levity or life lesson Uncle is trying to introduce to the situation, not when his inner fire is burning like acid in his throat.

Zuko makes his way back to the counter, at a loss for what else he is supposed to do but shake out his apron and put on his most neutral scowl and go back to counting half-coppers. He tries to make everything about him project ‘fuck off,’ every line of his body saying that he isn’t rattled and that if he is, it’s only because of the unexpected fight.

Zuko firmly pretends that he doesn’t see Uncle watching him with concern, as if Uncle knows exactly why else Zuko might be upset about all of this.

It’s hard to count half-coppers with all the staring, though, even if it's impressed looks and grateful glances rather than the usual pity. Zuko wants to crawl out of his skin, being the center of the entire shop’s attention. He shouldn’t feel bad for defending himself and Uncle the way he did. He shouldn’t. He didn’t do anything to Jet before all this, and Uncle especially didn’t.

But Zuko can’t stop feeling it, even knowing it would be so much easier to just be angry. He can’t stop feeling guilty and stupid, so stupid, for getting them into the situation in the first place. Zuko isn’t sure how Jet found out about them, whether Zuko had slipped or some other way. But for Zuko to think that someone like Jet was pursuing him for *him*?

Zuko said it to Sokka months ago: he knows what he is, and what he looks like. It was stupid of him to believe that Jet, who could have had anyone he wanted, would be interested in Zuko. It was foolish to think that just because Sokka was interested that anyone else would be. You can’t expect the good kind of lightning to strike twice, Zuko knows that all too well.

Zuko suddenly misses Sokka with a ferocity that has heat prickling behind his eyes, which is totally unacceptable because he *cannot do this at work*. But Agni, the openness they had between them, even if only in letters. That easy acceptance…Zuko can’t believe that he could have ever thought Sokka was using him like that. He can’t believe that he ever accused Sokka of such a thing, that he ever thought someone as good as Sokka could be like Jet. Zuko was— is—so, so stupid, and Agni, how much does he have to suffer through before he finally learns?

## Chapter 11: Just A Little Bite

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

No particular warnings for this one!

### Text

Zuko tries to throw himself back into the rhythm of life in Ba Sing Se. Its new form isn’t all that different, really. Morning meditation with Uncle, days spent in the teashop, evenings spent staring sullenly at the wall while Uncle talks about tea and tries to cajole him into a game of pai sho until Zuko can barely keep from screaming. And somehow the degrees pass and it's eventually time to lay down and pretend to sleep to the rhythm of Uncle's snores. As ordinary and unremarkable a routine as Zuko can manage, when every day he wants to rage and stomp and smack customers upside the head for trying to order black tea, but not so black, please.

Zuko can't say that he’s happy, but that doesn't matter. It's never mattered. It's *safe*. And safety for Uncle is what’s important, what will always be important. That won’t change no matter how many times Zuko needs to remind himself of it, no matter how much it feels like he’s going to break in half some days trying to fit himself into a shape that Ba Sing Se can hold.

Zuko can feel himself winding tighter and tighter, but he can’t relax his guard like he would be able to if he were truly being Lee. Not after Jet delivered such a sharp lesson in how stupid Zuko can be when his dick’s involved—as if he needed another reminder. But Agni, the effort of it all is exhausting. Zuko feels like he could be back in Caldera, twitchy and paranoid and conscious of constant eyes everywhere except the security of his own room. He can’t bring himself to resent the feeling, though. It’s its own reminder of the kind of lessons that Zuko should never have let himself forget in the first place.

&#45;-

"Prince Zuko—"

"Don't call me that." The words are automatic at this point.

"—it is said that though the willow bends in the lightest breeze, the strongest of trees will break in true wind far before the willow ever creaks."

Zuko shoves the heels of his hands against his eyes until he can let out a tight, controlled breath instead of a scream. "Can you just...not. With the stupid sayings."

"There is wisdom to be found all around us, Nephew."

"Just...what do you want. Just say it. Please."

Uncle looks faintly miffed. "You seem...tense, at work, lately."

Zuko just stares at the quiet concern on Uncle’s face. "…Yes." Zuko *has* been tense. It's on purpose.

"Do you think all that tension is...good?"

Zuko blinks. "Yes?" Fuck. He tenses against the squirmy, anxious suspicion that he’s missing something that everyone else finds obvious.

"And you do you think your constant state of tension is a strain on yourself?"

"...Yes." Zuko has never shied away from hard work, and he’s so used to this it barely qualifies. Zuko’s been tense all his life.

"Nephew," Uncle sighs when Zuko continues to just stare at him blankly. "I am worried that you’re overly concerned with another—"

"Another person finding out our secret and exposing us to the Dai Li and the Earth Kingdom army, which would like nothing more than to publicly torture us as a display of power before trying to trade us to the Fire Nation for concessions?"

"...Yes." Uncle says after a beat. "That."

"Okay," Zuko nods. Just making sure they’re on the same page. "I don't think I’m overly concerned about that."

"You are *very* concerned about it, though," Uncle presses.

"Yes," Zuko agrees easily. He is. And *very* is just the right amount of concerned to be. Uncle might be throwing himself into the life of a humble refugee—Zuko desperately hopes, so strong he can barely even admit it, that ‘the life of a humble refugee’ is what Uncle is throwing himself into—but Zuko can't let himself forget that they’re fugitives. Traitors. Descended from Agni in a way that will never mean *don't worry*. Uncle might want to forget, but Zuko won’t. Not again, at least.

&#45;-

The nights are hardest in this new rhythm, which isn’t exactly new, or unexpected. Sleeping has never been easy for Zuko, but now it's even worse, like the whole incident with Jet broke the part of Zuko that let him relax. He lies awake most nights, now, staring into the darkness and pushing heat throughout his body because if Zuko doesn't do *something* he’s going to go crazy. His inner fire is restless and unused and unhappy, and he can't reach for the torches he can feel in the city all around him, he *can't*.

He lies awake longing for things he can’t have before burning them off into his inner flame. The usual things, but Zuko doesn’t anticipate the longing to be back on the road with its brutal weather and constant vigilance, walking the thin edge of survival. There was nothing good about it, but there *was* seemingly endless space in the barren Earth Kingdom wastelands, room enough to work off energy and restlessness without worrying about someone else, without needing to hold himself back lest he invite fresh concern.

Sometimes sleep manages to come despite his best efforts. When Zuko jolts himself awake in those moments, silent as always in his terror, the heat reminds him that his feet aren't numb from cold even if he can’t feel anything else, that Uncle is close and calm with rest even if Zuko can’t see him. Sometimes even with his eyes open, especially on nights when the moon is clear, Zuko can still see hands reaching up, pleading, close enough for him to grasp, just out of reach, turning electric-blue against his skin to pull him down into the endless darkness.

&#45;-

The attention required to notice everything going on around him at the teashop is different than Zuko is used to. Back in the palace there were lots of people, but not necessarily around Zuko. And on the *Wani*, Zuko always had his spaces to retreat to when he just needed to be by himself. Now, though, Zuko can’t just up and leave in the middle of work—he already tried, it didn’t go over well—and the teashop is full of so many *people*. Zuko tries to note them all, to keep track of which faces are new and which are regulars, who’s looking a little too curious or suspicious, who might be paying too much attention to Uncle. The constant need to engage is exhausting, even if Zuko knows the anxiety of not doing it would leave him exhausted in a totally different way.

And it means that Zuko is quick to notice the girl who keeps coming in and staring at him through her bangs. He vaguely remembers her doing this for a while, now. They have plenty of regulars, so that part isn’t inherently unusual. But no one has been so persistent in trying to catch his eye or get a look at his face since Jet stopped occupying the back corner, and all Zuko can think is that his wanted poster isn’t *that* poor of a likeness, once you get a good enough look.

“Uncle,” Zuko mutters, taking a tray of fresh tea and pretending he needs to readjust the weight of it. “That girl won’t stop watching us.”

“You, Nephew,” Uncle smiles, amused as he glances over Zuko’s shoulder.

”*Don’t look*,” Zuko hisses. “I think maybe she figured out that we’re…”

“Or maybe she has a crush,” Uncle replies, gently turning Zuko around and nudging him back toward the shop floor.

Zuko snorts, fixing a scowl on his face for the customers and rolling his eyes for Uncle. That’s the most patently ridiculous thing he’s ever heard. It’s much more likely that she’s discovered they’re exiled Fire Nation royalty and is now plotting how to gather enough evidence to turn them in to the Dai Li.

That's fine. She can plot all she wants. Zuko will be ready this time.

&#45;-

Zuko is not ready for the girl to ask him out the next time she’s in.

She pays for her tea in exact change, as if she’s noticed how aggravated it makes Zuko to have to count coins into people’s hands, and then quietly offers that her name is Jin and would Zuko like to join her for dinner that evening, just the two of them? Zuko gapes, wondering if the buzzing din of the shop has impacted the hearing in his good ear. He’s still gaping when Uncle swoops in from nowhere to accept on his behalf. She walks out with a pleased little smile and a bounce to her step that finally breaks Zuko from his frozen shock. He whirls on Uncle with a glare.

“What are you *doing*?”

“Sending you on a date!” Uncle says cheerfully, arranging pots and cups on Zuko’s tray. “I thought that would be obvious.”

“*Why would you do that*?”

“Why not?” Uncle smiles. “She seems like a lovely girl.”

Zuko has gone a week without snapping a pencil and he isn’t going to snap one now over this but it’s going to be a close thing. “Agn—because we are *refugees*,” he hisses.

“Refugees still get to go on dates,” Uncle says placidly, completely ignoring the fact that Zuko said ‘refugee’ but meant ‘Imperial firebenders in hiding.’

“She might be trying to spy on us,” Zuko protests, picking up his tray.

“Or maybe she has a crush.”

Zuko doesn’t have an answer to that. Asking him on a date would on the surface seem to support Uncle’s theory, and it’s not like Zuko can exactly explain that recent experience has shown that going on a date can very much be part of a nefarious plan.

&#45;-

Zuko meets Jin at sundown outside the teashop. Agni’s fading light sets a fitting tone for whatever ridiculousness Uncle has gotten him into with this, and hides his lingering discomfort. Zuko found it so much weirder to leave the apartment with Uncle knowing why than it ever did when Zuko was slipping out to see Jet and just left. It’s definitely worse when Uncle knows. He’d insisted on dressing Zuko up and trying to do something about his hair, as if Jin hasn’t been staring at Zuko for days. She already knows what he looks like.

She still asked him out.

That’s…weird.

“Lee!” Jin’s grin is big enough to see from down the street, that bounce still in her step.

Zuko takes a beat too long to remember that ‘Lee’ means him. “…Hi.”

“It’s great to see you!”

“Um. Yes.”

She laughs like he just told some kind of joke and casually reaches out to grab his wrist, tugging him along and launching into a one-sided conversation about the restaurant she’s bringing them to. Zuko just nods and makes noises when it seems like she expects a response and hopes that they’re the right kinds of noises to make because he isn’t really listening. His mind is still tripping on the easy way she wrapped her fingers around him, as if there was no need at all for caution.

&#45;-

The restaurant, when they get there, seems nice. It’s open to the night air in a way that Zuko appreciates, in a way that lets him feel a bit less hemmed in. Zuko doesn’t really know where to look, though. He should probably be looking at Jin, but being seated next to a wholly exposed wall opening right onto the street makes him twitchy and distracted. He has his right side to the street, but that means his blind side is toward the dining room filled with strangers. But if he did it the other way around then anyone could be walking by, and is the threat more likely to come from within the restaurant or without?

It is not relaxing.

“So, you work in the teashop with your Uncle?” Jin’s eyes are bright as she smooths her napkin onto her lap.

Zuko’s eyes dart around the room. “Uh, yeah.”

“Did you start there right when you came to the city? You’re refugees, right?”

“Yes.”

“How do you like Ba Sing Se?”

“…It’s different.”

Zuko’s nerves make him tight, which makes him terse, and he can tell, which only makes him feel tighter, which only makes the words harder to push out without a dripping edge of resentment. Jin easily handles the heavy lifting in the conversation and doesn’t seem to think much of his quiet or his tone, which…well, it’s not like she hasn’t seen him at work.

“So, what did you do before Ba Sing Se?”

“Traveled.”

“With your Uncle?”

“Yeah.”

“Where did you travel?”

“All around.”

“What’s your favorite thing you saw traveling?”

Zuko tries not to be a total jerk but…this is awkward. He knows its awkward, even if Jin doesn’t seem to care, and his awareness of the awkwardness climbs higher and higher in his throat until Zuko feels like it’s a struggle to breathe around it. Zuko just…doesn’t know what to do with her. He doesn’t know how he’s supposed to be right now.

“So, what’s your favorite tea?”

“I don’t really have one.”

“What’s your favorite thing about Ba Sing Se?”

“Uh…the food.” It isn’t particularly good food, but Zuko has a fresh appreciation for consistent, regular meals that he doesn’t have to literally chase down himself.

“What’s your favorite color?”

“Black.”

“That’s boring,” Jin laughs. “What’s your second favorite?”

“Blue.”

It’s not that he doesn’t like girls. And she’s perfectly pretty, with those big eyes and the mischievous smile that always seems to be sitting on her lips. Zuko just doesn’t know how to sit here and have small talk and pretend that he’s no one but Lee. Not when she wants to know about him, not just talk to him. Not when Zuko’s past is so full of treacherous ground and the façade of Lee is so thin.

“Do you like your meal?”

“Yes.” He likes most meals, at this point. “Do, uh. Do you like yours?”

“Yes! I love the noodles they do here, and their sauces are to die for, don’t you think?”

“Um. Sure.”

She laughs again, grinning like he told another joke, and Zuko ducks his head down, concentrating on his noodles. At least she seems to find his awkwardness endearing, which… is her choice.

&#45;-

Jin takes him to her favorite spot in the city after dinner once Zuko finally admits to not having one. He represses a sigh at the idea of continuing this date. Zuko isn’t sure how much more he can socially embarrass himself before he self-immolates. There’s something particularly acute about the embarrassment of being incompetent in front of a person who inexplicably likes him. It’s different than the overwhelming shame of Zuko’s other failures— that he more than knows how to burn through by now.

They turn the corner, walking close enough that it’s clear that they’re together even though they aren’t touching, and Zuko might have some thoughts about that fact except that they’ve ground to an abrupt halt, along with his feet.

“It’s called the Firelight Fountain,” Jin offers, a smile in her voice. “I think it’s the most beautiful place in all of Ba Sing Se.”

“Yeah,” Zuko agrees, clearing his throat. He can see that it really is lovely, once he shakes away the jolt of adrenaline at unexpectedly walking into an expanse of light stretching across night-dark waters. Fire dances like jewels on the pools, twining and shivering as a breeze calls up tiny waves, refracting off the polished, faceted ornamental stones. Its…breathtaking. All four elements working in harmony to make something beautiful.

Uncle would like this spot. Zuko’s going to need to find some excuse to bring him this way one night.

Zuko is content to take the moment to stare at the interplay of water and fire and earth and air, and Jin seems content to stand at his side. At some point she reaches out again, slipping her hand into his. Zuko startles but doesn’t pull away as she twines their fingers together. He keeps his eyes on the square, watching the torches and making a point of not pulling the fires into his grip. He lets them move to their own will even as he brushes his awareness against them, soaking in their comfortable flickering until his own inner flame begins to move in rhythm.

Zuko isn’t surprised when Jin turns toward him. He lets her gently tug him toward her as she reaches up on her toes, eyes catching his a moment before pressing her lips against his in a closed-mouth kiss. Zuko lets that happen, too, lets her brace her weight on his shoulder and angle her mouth against his, and it’s nice and sweet and warm and not at all what he wants.

Jin slowly pulls back after a few heartbeats, a little smile on her lips as she searches his face. “Not doing it for you, huh?”

“Uh.” Zuko is going to die of embarrassment. He knows he’s supposed to want this. Agni’s tits, some old version of him probably *would* have wanted this. “It’s not—um…”

“It’s okay,” Jin says, giving his hand a little squeeze. “I get it.”

“It’s not you,” Zuko mumbles, reaching back and remembering he doesn’t have a phoenix tail to tug on anymore and running his hand through his hair instead. “It’s just…”

“It’s not you, it’s me?” Jin teases, laughter in her voice, and something in Zuko loosens a little bit at the sound of it. At the fact that she isn’t upset, that she doesn’t need an explanation. Something about her lack of demand makes him want to provide one.

“I’m still…” He blows out a hard breath. “There was someone else. Before.” He shrugs. “Before I came here. I’m not…”

“I understand,” Jin assures him, face earnest, and for once he believes the words. “You can’t force yourself to be ready. I appreciate your honesty.” Zuko winces at that and Jin bites her lip as she catches the motion, hesitating before finally asking, “Do you have to go home?” “…No,” Zuko admits, because he’s terrible at lying even when it would give him the perfect out. “Why?” Isn’t their date thoroughly done and dead?

“I can show you some other places, if you want?” Her hand is still in his, but somehow Zuko doesn’t feel like it holds any pressure or expectation. “Being around people and having a distraction always helps me when I’m trying to get over something. Or someone.”

Zuko blinks at her rueful tone and doesn’t let himself think. “Okay.” Why not? He can always just leave. But if he leaves now…Zuko doesn’t want to spend the rest of the night sitting with Uncle when his memories lurk so close to the surface of his thoughts. And something about Jin letting him take the possibility of anything between them off the table makes Zuko feel like he can take a deep breath for the first time all night.

Jin grins at his answer and loops her arm through his, towing him along just like she did to start the night. It’s a close gesture, one that would normally make Zuko uncomfortable, but she’s so genuinely excited that it’s easy and friendly and somehow already familiar.

Zuko still doesn’t quite know what to do with himself or with her, but following along is easy enough. He knows how to do that. Jin takes him to her favorite dessert shop, the places her friends play music and dance when the weather is nice, the spots where the night markets set up on certain days, and its…not awful. Nice, even, at times.

“Why are you doing all this?” Zuko finally asks as they make their way back toward the teashop, her arm still hooked through his. The sustained contact isn’t something he’s used to, a warm press of cloth against his skin, but after the whole night, he’s able to be conscious of it without being on edge about it.

“All of what?”

“Showing me around. Spending time with me. After I…”

“After I kissed you and you rejected me?”

Zuko starts, guilty, before realizing that she’s teasing again. He glances away, hiding his face at her giggle. “Yeah. That.”

“’Cause I like you,” she says simply.

“Um.” Zuko thought his position was fairly clear after their kiss.

“And not just for *that*,” she rolls her eyes, nudging him with her shoulder.

“But…”

“But?”

“I’m kind of…an asshole?”

“Oh? I hadn’t noticed,” she grins, and Zuko is pretty sure that was sarcasm. Still, just to be safe…

“I’m rude to customers,” he explains. “And I snap a lot. And I don’t…care, really. About… things.” That was maybe broader than Zuko meant to go. He cares plenty, about lots of things. Just none that pertain to the teashop, outside of Uncle.

“Hmm,” Jin considers him. “I wouldn’t say you’re an ass. More of a jerk.” Zuko feels that like a knife to his heart, can see the shape of it written out. “Don’t worry, though, I don’t mind. Maybe I like a little bark with my bite,” Jin says serenely as they finally reach the teashop, giggling again at his startled expression. “I’ll see you soon, Lee. Okay?”

“Yeah,” Zuko says, automatic, dazed as she unhooks her arm from his. “Okay.”

&#45;-

Uncle is waiting up when Zuko slips back into their apartment, which is also weird and different than how it’s been before. Zuko half-heartedly ignores Uncle’s eager questions—

“You spent a long time away!”

Zuko grunts.

“You must have enjoyed yourself!”

Zuko grunts again.

—before finally muttering that the night was nice and pointedly grabbing his sleep clothes. Zuko’s lingering confusion over the whole thing takes the usual sourness out of his words, though. He undresses and lies down without really noticing what he’s doing, lightheaded still with the possibility that someone might like him just for…him, in all his cranky irritableness. Because if Jin could? Then maybe other people could, too. And maybe Zuko can actually believe that Jin isn’t the first time.

&#45;-

Uncle isn’t quite ready to let the subject go the next morning, speaking during the early hours when Agni has just crossed the horizon, a time usually reserved for meditation and carefully guiding his inner fire to a place where it will stay locked beneath his skin for the day.

“I am glad for you, Nephew.”

Zuko cracks an eye open, scowling in confusion. “What?”

“It is good to see you experiencing the normal parts of being a teenager. It is good to see you enjoying your youth.”

“Um.” Zuko does not want to get into—ever—how much of his youth he may or may not have been enjoying.

“You had so much put on your shoulders so young,” Uncle continues, with a rare air of melancholy.

“Uncle…”

“It makes me happy to see you living a normal life.”

“…Okay,” Zuko finally says, closing his eyes again to signal the end of the conversation.

Zuko isn’t really sure that what he is experiencing is in any way normal. But if Uncle is happy, then that can be enough for him. And Zuko isn’t actively *unhappy*, which…might fall short of what Uncle wants for him, but isn’t so bad, not really. Uncle’s happiness comes first, after all, and that’s still present, that’s still the thing that Zuko grounds himself onto. One thing that hasn’t changed, even if it feels like so much else has.

&#45;-

When Jin shows up at the teashop a few days later and asks Zuko if he would like to go dancing with her that night, Zuko doesn’t fight when Uncle says yes on his behalf again. He just frowns after her, confused, wondering if this is what friendship is. Wondering if all uncles are so eager to push their nephews toward someone else. Wondering if this is what being a normal teenager is: no real responsibilities, no purpose, just…dancing after work with someone who inexplicably wants to spend time with you.

### Text

Zuko is enduring another day of customer service, which somehow is getting harder with experience instead of easier. Maybe because the teashop keeps getting busier. Uncle’s been promoted up to making his own tea blends, which Zuko knows he’s supposed to feel happy about because Uncle is ecstatic. But Zuko can’t quite manage to be a Good Nephew in thought as well as action just yet—and even action is still iffy, to be honest. So instead, he’s gritting his teeth into something that might be considered a smile if you look at it sideways as new customers flood the shop, none of whom seem to know what they want or how to order it or drink it or pay for it without extensive help.

At least Zuko doesn’t have to take orders anymore, as of yesterday, when he snapped his last charcoal pencil for the week and got shoved behind the register instead. He glances longingly through the door to the back, where he can hear the afternoon’s dishes being washed. Why won’t they let him just do that? Who cares if cooks deal with the dirty dishes and servers stay on their floor? Who in their right mind thinks it’s a good idea to keep Zuko on the floor in front of customers, other than Uncle?

He blows out a hard breath, grasping for patience as he finally finishes counting change into the hand of some fancy woman who seems to think everyone in the shop is out to rob her, including Zuko, which really only makes him want to try. She sniffs, somehow managing to stare down her nose at him despite being a full head shorter, and pulls herself in tight to leave like she doesn’t want to risk touching anyone else in the room.

Zuko can sympathize with the desire, if not the underlying sentiment.

Zuko is relieved—more than he will admit—that the next person in line already has exact change in hand. He recognizes one of their regulars. As a bunch they're slow to learn—even slower than Zuko, somehow—but they’re finally starting to realize that exact change makes everyone’s life less awful when Zuko is the one handling their bill.

A commotion at the door—it better not be that fancy woman, Zuko is *beyond* done with her —has him glaring up, his inner fire twists in anticipation, edgy and hungry for an excuse to let out some of the jittery, tight energy that always wants to take the form of a scream by this point in the—

Zuko’s inner fire blazes up so suddenly that it almost slips out from underneath his skin. He wrenches for control as it burns so sharp and hard through him that all that's left in its wake is blank shock as he stares at the door, wondering if the stress has finally made him snap.

&#45;-

Sokka is wandering the Lower Ring, pockets full of posters that truly capture Appa’s essence no matter what Katara has to say about it. Or Toph, whose opinion shouldn’t matter anyway. He’s determined to find good places to put up the flyers even though it feels like they’re getting taken down right behind him, sometimes the very second he turns a corner.

Ba Sing Se is kind of creepy, that way, even without Joo Dee hovering at his back.

The city isn’t at all what Sokka had expected of the bastion of the Earth Kingdom. Sure, it has stunning architecture and more people than Sokka even knew existed. There’s rich culture, poetry and literature and art that he could get lost in for days. Sokka is still trying to wrap his mind around the scale of the luxury and extravagance and sprawl that requires visitors to have a dedicated *guide* assigned to them.

But walking around the Lower Ring, Sokka feels a sticky kind of discomfort at the city’s stark inequality. It goes against everything he knows about Tribe and community to be living in abundance while others are getting by with so little within the same walls. But Toph had just shrugged, and no one else in Ba Sing Se seems bothered, and when Sokka tried to say something about it Joo Dee had pointed out that everyone was cared for, even the refugees, which isn’t something most cities would do. And Sokka had thought of Agna Qel’a and promptly shut up, because he can’t deny that Ba Sing Se is doing more than the Northern Water Tribe ever did.

There’s something about this city, though, that Sokka just doesn’t *get*. How could a city of this size be so horrifyingly inept at rebuffing Fire Nation attacks that it needed a band of teens to help them out? But at the same time be so scarily competent at running the lives of its citizens that Sokka can’t even keep his flyers up for more than a few minutes? How could a city of refugees be so wary of strangers that no one will answer any of his questions, no matter how much of Yue’s earnest helpfulness he tries to channel?

Sokka’s worried—in the privacy of his own mind, only, because he’s not trying to rock the already unstable boat that is their group right now—that his inability to understand how Ba Sing Se works is increasingly becoming a problem. All of them, Sokka especially, had been fired with purpose after the Spirit Library. Yes, Appa’s kidnapping had dampened that enthusiasm, but Sokka was sure they would figure that out in no time. The temporary loss wasn’t enough to smother the spark of hope in his chest that after *decades* of slow attrition they finally have a viable opportunity to strike back at the Fire Nation and end the war.

For the first time there’s something *real* to plan for, more than just how to stay on course or shop efficiently for supplies. Sokka has thoroughly thrown himself into the effort, but all of his plans rely very much on *timing*. And Sokka can't seem to factor in Ba Sing Se’s jarring refusal to admit that a war was even occurring in the first place once you left the Outer Wall. Sokka can see the too-fast approaching moment when Aang’s need to find Appa runs up against the Day of the Black Sun, and someone is going to need to make a choice.

Sokka is already bracing himself—even if he will never admit it out loud—for the moment when Aang doesn’t choose them. The longer it takes to find Appa the more contingencies Sokka tucks away in the corner of his mind, never to see the light of day until they’re needed. Sokka might not know how to navigate the new short-tempered version of Aang they’re dealing with these days, but he can take an educated guess that openly planning for Aang separating from the group will only cause problems.

Sokka can acknowledge that he *might* be avoiding the issue, too.

He doesn’t like the idea of being at odds with Aang, and Sokka’s already overly aware that not giving the hunt for Appa his whole and total focus is a sore point. But one of the four of them needs to keep the bigger picture in mind, and if it’s Sokka’s turn to think about all of them and the fate of the world and let Aang focus on the immediate and the personal, then Sokka can do it and take whatever comes along with being the voice of reason that no one wants to hear.

Though it’s hard to stay reasonable when the good denizens of the Lower Ring won’t tell him anything more useful than the best spot in the district for tea.

The Fire Nation just attacked the walls, the *Lightning Princess* nearly broke through, and all four of them are running around shouting that the Avatar is in Ba Sing Se and looking for help. And somehow each interaction with the citizens of the city is still like talking to a clay wall—unreadable bland expressions, stoic looks, and firmly changed subjects.

*You haven’t been at it that long,* Sokka reminds himself. *This kind of thing takes time. You* *need to build trust*.

Except Sokka doesn’t have an unlimited number of days to build relationships until people trust him enough to overcome whatever it is that’s holding them back. He’s already lying awake most nights, stressing over timelines, and coordinating search efforts, and the sheer magnitude of Ba Sing Se, and all the terrible things that could happen to an animal trapped in the hands of people who don’t seem to care about the war, or lost cultures, or much of anything outside of themselves.

That tension is constant between the four of them, whether it's oppressively enveloping or an itch at the back of their minds, bad enough that even Aang was on the verge of air-smashing another set of crockery yesterday. All four of them had jumped at the idea of canvassing the city on foot and trying to get in with the locals. Everyone wants new leads, and everyone’s eager for the opportunity to get some distance from each other. Aang’s is not the only temper starting to fray as each day passes with them no closer to an audience with the Earth King than when they started.

But Spirits, when Sokka suggested the idea, he hadn’t anticipated quite this much apathy from the city’s inhabitants. Shouldn’t they want the war to end as much as the rest of the world?

Sokka can only hope that the more time they spend in Ba Sing Se, the more visible they are, the more they’ll be able to find information and help through sources other than the official channels. Joo Dee is nice, but…definitely not a straight shooter. And if Sokka learned anything from Yue—and he learned a *lot—*it’s that some things are best done the unofficial way. It helps to know the right people.

That’s what he told Aang and the others, at least, full of confidence and conviction. But the sheer scale of Ba Sing Se looms over them, and so far all Sokka has been able to get out of people is that the Blooming Petal is the best teashop in the whole Lower Ring. Which isn’t super useful in the long term, but in the short term Sokka is thirsty, parched from the dust that seems to hang everpresent in the air and the lingering summer heat that Toph insists will break soon into cold, though Sokka isn’t quite sure he believes her at this point.

Maybe if the teashop is so popular it can become a staging ground for the next phase of Operation Backchannel, and Sokka can set up shop there, maybe pretend to be a student or a poet looking for a new space to work. He can go by the name of—

He dodges a surprisingly fancy-looking woman who bursts out of the Blooming Petal as if she expects people to watch out for her rather than the other way around.

Okay, maybe the Blooming Petal won’t be a good place for Operation Backchannel, if it’s full of people like that. He needs a place with more of a local vibe, where he can become a familiar face and start noticing familiar faces in turn. Not entitlement and sniffing and people who think they’re too good to interact with others.

Sokka’s already resigning himself to more fruitless searching as he shoulders open the door, barely halfway through the motion when his feet grind to a halt.

&#45;-

Sokka might have sunstroke. Can sunstroke make you hallucinate? Maybe Toph spiked his water with cactus juice again. Maybe he needs to find a quiet corner and sit down and put his head between his knees. He might be about to pass out. He might already be passed out. The sounds around him are muffled, the ground feels like it's falling out beneath his feet even though he’s staying upright, and he isn’t entirely sure he’s breathing anymore.

But he’s definitely hallucinating.

It’s a deep and abiding betrayal on the part of his eyes, which Sokka thought were as onboard as the rest of him with the new plan to seek fulfillment through his defeat-the-Fire-Nation mission and not by throwing himself at the next untouchable, responsibility-chained royal he stumbles across. It’s really breaking the trust, to be slapping Sokka in the face with a mirage like this.

Because some projected figment of his imagination is the only explanation for why Zuko would be in front of him right now. Prince Zuko. Fire Prince Zuko. Crown Prince Zuko of the Fire Nation. Imperial firebender. Descended of Agni. Standing behind the counter of a Lower Ring teashop. In an apron. Making change. Looking pissed about it.

Please don’t let this be another Spirit thing. Sokka doesn’t know if he can handle a malicious not-Zuko again, not after interacting with the non-malicious real thing.

Someone shoves Sokka in the back with a pointed comment about blocking the door and Sokka’s brain snaps to attention as he stumbles forward. Sound starts behaving normally again, which is good, but his eyes are still fucked because the hallucination glances up and can’t-be-real Zuko spasms and sends coins falling onto the floor instead of the register. Everyone in the shop exclaims in polite surprise about it, except for that-cannot-actually-be-Zuko, who ignores the scattered coppers in favor of staring back at Sokka.

Some distant corner of Sokka’s brain points out that he’s actually quite familiar with the way Zuko’s eyes widen like that. And he’s seen Zuko’s pale face go even whiter, before, even if he does *not* want to remember the last time he saw this particular expression. Even a hint of that memory is still enough to scald.

But Sokka does know that look, whether he wants to or not. So realistically, Sokka *could* be hallucinating what’s in front of him. Some desperate conjuring of a sunbaked mind. It would be a particularly vivid hallucination, sure, but not the first time Sokka’s hallucinated Zuko. Or imagined Zuko wearing…a variety of outfits. Though usually, those two things don’t happen at the same time...

The apron is a new—and inspired—suggestion from his subconscious.

Sokka’s hallucinations—and imaginings—typically involved a significantly smaller quantity of disgruntled teashop patrons, too, now that he thinks about it. And not quite such a sizeable audience. And never such vivid scents of tea. And his feet are never sore from walking the city all morning looking for Appa, his hairline itching with sweat and grit.

Oh-fuck-is-that-Iroh pauses beside a still frozen maybe-Zuko and murmurs something with a gentle nudge that has his nephew nodding, expression completely blank, eyes still fixed on Sokka. And Sokka finally considers that maybe, somehow, Crown Prince Zuko of the Fire Nation, Child of Agni, might actually be stalking toward him right now across the floor of a Lower Ring teashop.

Sokka feels a dangerous heat kindle in his chest, one that he’s spent weeks telling himself that he doesn’t need. And he doesn’t. Need it, that is.

But oh, does he want it.

This-could-actually-be-Zuko stops a few feet away, tense and awkward as his body sways forward like Zuko expected to keep coming closer but just…stopped. Sokka can see the little extra ring of white around the gold of Zuko’s eye that means Zuko might be panicking just as much as Sokka is, and somehow it’s that possibility out of everything that gives Sokka the wherewithal to finally open his mouth and ask, in a totally normal voice, “*Zuko, what the* *fuck what the fuck what the—”*

“Outside,” Zuko snaps, breaking into motion again and tearing his eyes away from Sokka to glance around the shop. Sokka can almost hear the echo of boots on metal decking.

Though in fairness, this isn’t going to be a conversation to have in the middle of a crowd. So Sokka has no choice but to follow, really, when you think about it. It’s definitely a conversation for this shadowed alley next to the crowded teashop, instead.

“What are you doing here?” Zuko demands, spinning to face Sokka, and the question is so ludicrous and the tone so familiar that Sokka almost starts laughing.

“I’m working,” Zuko frowns, arms crossing over his apron-clad chest, and Sokka’s momentarily thrown by how much more expressive Zuko’s body language is outside of armor.

Has the Fire Prince managed to infiltrate Ba Sing Se and make himself an apparently trusted and inconspicuous member of the Lower Ring community in order to…somehow find the Avatar? Wait, is Zuko even doing that these days? Or did Crazy Blue take all that over?

“I’m looking for Appa,” Sokka says. Fuck. Should he have said that? Maybe not. But it’s not like they’re making a secret of the fact that Appa is gone.

“Yeah.”

“…You lost it?”

Sokka bristles a little at the undertone of incredulous disbelief in Zuko’s question before deflating, because, well—they did. “It’s a long story.”

“And…you think it’s here?” Zuko glances to the teashop before giving Sokka a look of side-eyed concern, like he’s suddenly worried for Sokka’s sense of spatial awareness and Spirits, only Zuko would be so *literal*.

“…Okay.” Zuko’s scowl gentles into something closer to a thoughtful frown, his eyes settling somewhere in the vicinity of Sokka’s collarbone, which really seems to be Zuko’s favorite place to look when he can’t meet Sokka’s eyes. Sokka will have to ask him why, one of these days.

He promptly stumbles over the implied future behind that thought. Spirits, he isn’t supposed to be like this anymore. He can’t control any choices but his own, he knows that, and he doesn’t want his happiness to be dependent on anyone but himself.

“So…” Zuko’s careful tone makes Sokka stop prodding at the gut assumption that he would be seeing Zuko in the future and pay attention to the Zuko in front of him now. “You aren’t trying to hunt down…us?”

“Okay,” Zuko says slowly, shoulders loosening. “Okay. Good.”

“…You are?” Zuko’s voice goes hoarser than usual, expression more open in its surprise than Sokka is used to, and Sokka seizes the moment of stunned stillness to examine Zuko back.

He takes in familiar sharp cheekbones and the line of his jaw and the scowl on his face, and Spirits, he's seen it all before but Sokka can’t get over the way Zuko’s whole face seems changed now that he’s ditched that awful hairstyle. Even tense and glaring, Zuko seems more approachable like this than he ever did mostly bald and tightly braided. Even his scar seems softer, less stark now that its edges are blurred and hidden.

Sokka wonders if it means something, for Zuko to look like this now. He doesn’t exactly think Zuko would have kept that old hairstyle because he thought it looked *good*.

“I’m always glad to see you, Zuko,” Sokka finally admits, even as a not-so-small part of him screams that he shouldn’t be saying this. Sokka doesn’t really know what is left between them after both of them did things that can’t be undone, he knows that this isn't what they are to each other anymore. But the words are still true, even when Sokka knows he should probably be feeling some sort of way about the fact that the last time he saw Zuko, all Zuko wanted was for him to leave. That all Zuko had for him then was fear and accusation and longing and a tentative trust that didn’t extend far enough to let Sokka help him.

The words are still true, though, and Sokka...isn't exactly surprised by that.

Zuko searches his eyes, somehow simultaneously tentative and intense in his uncertainty, and for a brief moment Sokka feels a misplaced jolt of adrenaline, a spike of fear that has no place here. Zuko’s sister looks way too much like him, has nearly the same eyes even if Sokka’s never seen them as open as this. The similarity was enough to shove Sokka off-balance every time they encountered her over the past weeks, and it’s apparently enough to jostle his footing now. Maybe because Azula tried to kill Sokka *quite* recently, all things considered. Maybe because she had watched that chi-blocking girl flirting with Sokka with a kind of sharp delight in that too-familiar gaze, like she already *knew*.

A slight flush rises over Zuko’s cheek as his gaze dips to Sokka’s mouth and Spirits, Sokka missed that too. The visible signs of his effect on Zuko, the cracks in Zuko’s tight control. It makes it hard to breathe without gasping.

“Sokka.” Zuko wets his lips and Sokka doesn’t even try not to stare. “Why did you come to the shop?”

“I was tired and thirsty,” Sokka says, wetting his own lips, and his stomach *swoops* at the way Zuko’s eyes track the movement. “I didn’t expect you. This.” He waves his hand to take in the shop and the Lower Ring and Zuko and the *apron*. Something a little lower than his stomach *swoops* at that apron and the way it hugs Zuko’s body, so different than the military dress Sokka is used to. “Are…are you and Iroh here for the Avatar?”

Zuko shakes his head, gold eyes intent, and Sokka can suddenly feel the heat radiating off him, his skin prickling under the warmth.

Sokka sucks in a shaky breath. “Are you and Iroh here for any nefarious plans?”

“No,” Zuko huffs, and Sokka sets aside the mixture of relief and regret in Zuko’s tone to think about later.

Sokka opens his mouth for another question—what if they have plans that *they* don’t think are nefarious, but that *Sokka* would—but Zuko kills whatever words Sokka is trying to gather by taking a deliberate step forward.

“Sokka,” Zuko murmurs, like Sokka has never heard him before and *Spirits,* Sokka can feel the heat of his name on his face and the huskiness of Zuko’s tone in his dick. “Do you really want to talk about my uncle right now?”

Sokka takes a long breath to think of all the reasons he really, really should talk about General Iroh in this moment. And in that pause the much louder part of Sokka’s brain, the part that’s always thrumming in the background, lunges forward and takes the reins.

“Fuck no,” he breathes, grabbing Zuko’s shoulders and closing the space between them, the solidity and warmth and realness and actually-here-ness of Zuko surging from his hands through his entire body.

He tilts his head up for Zuko’s mouth—not quite as far away as he remembers without needing to work around the bulk of armor—and Zuko surges down to meet him, crowding Sokka back against the alley wall, hands on his chest as their lips crash together with more enthusiasm than art.

Sokka’s last thought before everything except *Zuko* leaves his head is that he’s so fucking happy he volunteered to canvass the Lower Ring today.

Sokka shivers at the taste of Zuko, at the way Zuko lets out a tight noise against his mouth as Sokka chases the familiar flavor of smoke and spice. The sound vibrates from Zuko’s chest into Sokka’s as they press closer and closer until Sokka is dizzy from the feeling of being pinned between the stone wall at his back and the hard muscles of Zuko’s body. Zuko’s hands are wandering down Sokka’s sides, making every inch of his skin tingle with the need to be the next spot to be touched. Sokka’s other hand skims down Zuko’s back to palm his ass--holy *shit--*and haul him closer, and Zuko lets out a choked gasp at the sudden friction and *fuck*, Sokka *loves* this no-armor thing.

Zuko pulls back slightly, searching Sokka’s face as they both pant for breath. Sokka drinks in the sight of Zuko’s blown-out pupils and wet lips, the way his skin is flushed with desire up to the edge of his scar. Whatever Zuko sees must reassure him, or urge him on, because Zuko’s mouth is on his again in a heartbeat and Zuko’s fingers are determinedly finding their way under the edge of Sokka’s shirt. Sokka presses into the touch and pulls Zuko closer, unable to stop the noise that leaves him as Zuko’s thigh slides between his own to rub up against Sokka’s hardness. And *Spirits,* that's Zuko’s erection pressed against Sokka’s hip, big and eager and *there* in his Earth Kingdom outfit like it never was in Zuko’s old uniform.

Sokka grinds down, seeking friction, and Zuko buries his face against Sokka’s neck and exhales hot and sharp and grinds back. Zuko’s body and hands are demanding, wanting, sending pleasure and heat singing through Sokka’s veins. Sokka thought he remembered how good it was before, but his memories are *nothing* to the feel of having the real thing in his arms and moving against his body and sinking teeth into Sokka’s neck.

“*Zu-*ko,” Sokka moans, eyes sliding half-closed as his head drops back. Zuko makes a tight sound against his neck, then a hot tongue is painting the column of Sokka’s throat, and *Spirits,* Sokka is going to *die*. Just expire on the spot from his inability to process so many things that feel so good.
