## Chapter 16: Uncomfortable Questions

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

References to some sexual content in this one!

### Text

Zuko doesn’t really sleep without dreaming anymore, which means he doesn’t really sleep. He dreams of too many different things for any single one of them to ever start to feel mundane enough to be worth enduring without a fight. The air being ripped out of his lungs. Blue fire clashing with red. The bright claws of the Ocean. The *Wani* breaking apart around him, but this time with the crew on it, too. A hand outstretched, wreathed in flame.

Zuko jolts awake in the darkness, heart buzzing and muscles locked and chest tight with the weight of his held breaths. It’s easier tonight, with the moon hidden behind clouds, to convince himself to finally relax enough to start breathing again. The cloudy sky is probably why he could fall asleep at all in the first place, really, though he definitely won’t be doing that again, His head feels thick and achy with tiredness, but his body hums with adrenaline and a high-edged panic that he knows from experience won’t fully dissipate until morning.

Zuko flexes his hands open and closed, stretching out sore muscles. Sokka is a new addition to his dreaming. Zuko’s surprised in a resigned way that it’s taken this long for him to make an appearance. Zuko can remember the dream vividly, because he always can. The cold crush of icy water, one hand wrapped around Uncle’s wrist, the other clasped with Sokka’s. Straining as they tug in opposite directions, both insisting that they know the way to the surface, Zuko’s grip slipping the entire time.

Zuko shakes the last of the phantom ache out of his fingers and forces his breathing to match the rhythm of Uncle’s snores until his body finally recognizes that he is not, in fact, about to lose everything, wishing all the while that his subconscious could have a bit more fucking subtlety sometimes.

&#45;-

Zuko is trying to be better, again, at the teashop. To be the Good Nephew that Uncle wants him to be when Zuko is here, even if he can’t be that person anywhere else. It’s half-assed and the bare minimum and it shouldn’t be the struggle that it is, but Zuko wants—*needs*— Uncle to stop trying to figure out what’s wrong with him. Beyond the benefits of not being a total nightmare on his coworkers’ willingness to overlook his overly long breaks and cooperate in Zuko’s shift trading, Zuko needs the probing and prodding to end. The ongoing questions mean Uncle is discontent, which is unacceptable, especially now when Zuko no longer has the ability to slam his door against it because Zuko no longer has anywhere to go that Uncle can’t follow.

The constant *concern* would normally be enough to drive Zuko to a very loud breaking point, but all Zuko can muster lately for it is a burst of sharp annoyance and a dull, persistent aggravation. His inner fire is too much drifts of lazy, playful sparks to readily flare up like it used to. Which Zuko would be worried enough about to bring up to Uncle—he’s never felt or heard anyone talk about anything like it before—if there was any way to do so without also bringing up Sokka.

Besides, it’s fine. His bending still works. That’s all he really needs. And Zuko’s sure of that much, at least, because he spends most of his time in the teashop bending these days. Practicing moving heat within his own body, spooling it down his arms or letting it settle in his mouth against his tongue. He spends his shifts sunk into awareness of the temperatures all around him. Pots of tea boiling and steeping and cooling and being poured into cups that absorb and insulate, creeping into his fire sense as they fill with heat. Steam curling in the air, shivering and dissipating under cooling breaths. The warmth of the benches that sit in the sun, the heat transferred by bodies to worn wood.

Zuko holds it all within his awareness, only half-present in the mechanics of doing his work, which is apparently the amount of presence that allows him to strike the right balance between functional contributor and tolerable human being. Zuko doesn’t give that much thought, though, enough to have any particular feelings about it. His attention is too consumed by the movement of heat, by taking delicate control of this temperature and then that one, and then that one over there. Playing with how precise he can be, how wide his hold can go, body moving automatically through the motions of being a Good Nephew and mind entirely caught up in Sokka.

&#45;-

Zuko is pretty sure that Sokka no longer needs Zuko to guide him along the maze of alleys from the teashop to the apartment, but every time he still lets Zuko pull him along by the hand anyway. That knowledge sometimes makes Zuko even more flustered than thinking of any of the things they’ve done together involving far fewer clothes, Zuko’s mind spinning around everything it could mean.

Today, though, Sokka might be letting him do it for a much more prosaic reason.

Zuko eyes him over his shoulder as Sokka lets out a second jaw-cracking yawn in as many minutes. “We haven’t even done anything yet for you to be tired from.”

Sokka snorts, rolling his eyes. “I’ve been waking up at the ass crack of dawn since I’m not training in the afternoon anymore. Sorry I’m not a weird magic morning person like you are, Jerkbender. That shit isn’t natural for the rest of us.”

Zuko takes a moment to focus on Sokka’s tone—amused, teasing—and not his words— annoyed. “Sorry?” Waking up at dawn has never bothered him—he’s usually already awake —but Zuko did at some point in his time at sea notice that some people aren’t a fan of it. Zuko had attributed all of Sokka’s sleeping on the *Wani* to illness. Apparently not.

“No apologies necessary, man,” Sokka says, expression turning wolfish as he gives Zuko’s ass a sudden squeeze and laughing when Zuko startles. “It’s worth it.”

Zuko blushes, at Sokka's laugh and touch and at the way those words paired with Sokka’s unconscious physicality make Zuko’s inner fire lurch in his chest. Zuko ducks his head, hiding his face even though he knows Sokka can already see the redness there. The way Sokka touches Zuko without ever seeming to think that he shouldn’t—it always makes Zuko breathless, flustered, a little bit dizzy around the edges. And when Sokka says things like that at the same time—Zuko is surprised he’s even still standing, with the way Sokka can flip his world around without even seeming to try.

&#45;-

“What if we—” The words slip out without permission as Zuko tries to turn his shirt right-side out without taking his eyes off the effortless way Sokka is redoing his wrist wraps. “What?” Sokka prompts, glancing up through his loose hair, apparently not needing to look to finish tying off the linen strip.

“…Nothing,” Zuko says, shaking his head as something anxious seeps into his chest with Sokka looking at him so expectantly. Things are perfectly good, perfectly comfortable, the way they are now. Zuko doesn’t need to say anything, definitely doesn’t need to change it. “Never mind. It’s a dumb idea.”

“What is it? I’ve liked all your ideas so far,” Sokka says, waggling his eyebrows.

“It’s…not that kind of idea,” Zuko hedges, turning back to the shirt in his hands.

“Oh. Well now I’m even more curious,” Sokka says, but Zuko can see out of the corner of his eye that some of the relaxation has left Sokka's shoulders, and that just sparks even more of Zuko’s own tension. Fuck. He shouldn’t have said anything. Stupid, he should know to just stay quiet.

“It’s nothing.”

“Tell me.”

"It's really nothing."

"So it's not a big deal to tell me, then."

Zuko hangs a moment between not wanting to mess this up and not being able to deny Sokka anything within his power to give. He sighs. “You said you were waking up earlier than you want? So you could train?”

“Yeah,” Sokka grumbles, pulling a face as he starts gathering his hair back for his wolf tail. “Katara is giving me a lot of shit for it still, too. She thinks it’s hilarious.”

Zuko…is not going to ask about that. “What if we trained together? Then you wouldn’t have to wake up early all the time, and you could have someone to train with, and—” Zuko risks a glance to see that Sokka has gone completely still halfway through twisting a tie into his hair. Shit. “Or—never mind. Sorry. Forget it. It’s a bad idea. I shouldn’t have—”

Sokka's lunge is so unexpected that Zuko can only yelp in surprise as he crashes into him and sends them both sliding sideways off the low futon. Zuko flails, anchoring onto and bracing against Sokka’s forearms as Sokka pins his shoulders to the floor, alarm ripping down his spine as every instinct Zuko has screams for him to fight back, to find his feet, don’t stay down, never stay down, get up, get up, *get up*.

Except—Zuko's tripping mind is struggling to process, but Sokka looks anything but upset.

“Swords!” Sokka cries, half on top of Zuko and uncaring of the hair falling into his face, leaning into him and pinning him and…not attacking?

“…What.”

“You know how to use swords!” Sokka whisper-shouts, fingers digging into Zuko’s shoulders, but not painfully. Zuko’s body is slowly realizing that it maybe isn’t about to fight, and as his adrenaline eases back Zuko’s able to register that Sokka is practically wiggling on top of him in…excitement?

“Um. Yes?”

“Wait, Spirits,” Sokka breathes, something like awe coming over his face as he looks down at Zuko, which does something sharp and bright to Zuko’s chest. “You know how to use *two* swords.”

“The dao, yeah…”

“Fuck *yes*,” Sokka crows, shoving off Zuko’s shoulders to sit back on Zuko’s thighs as suddenly as he lunged at him in the first place. “This is going to be *awesome*! I never got to try out swords before. Oh man, where can I get one to practice with? I get to use one, too, right?”

“I have two,” Zuko finally manages to say, dizzy from the force of Sokka’s enthusiasm and the sudden drop-off from panic. From part of him being something that Sokka could look at with all that admiration.

“Right. Right! Yes!” Sokka grins. “Spirits, Zuko, this is going to be *great*!”

Zuko can only offer a half-shrug in response, dazzled all over again into silence. He should maybe get off the floor, or at least all the way onto it, with his legs still half on the bed and Sokka sitting on them. He should maybe try to say something back, help with figuring out schedules and timing and what Sokka already knows.

But Zuko’s too shaky with relief, and enjoying too much the sound of Sokka’s excited planning and chatter to try voicing more than occasional wordless agreement. Agni, Sokka doesn’t even seem concerned with the fact that training together means changing their arrangement. So Zuko guesses he shouldn’t think about it too much either. It’s just a little bit, after all. Not really a big difference, just putting their bodies to a different use. Even if the thought of having Sokka in a new part of his life makes Zuko quietly lightheaded, his inner flame flipping small and quick in his chest. But Sokka just looks wholly, purely delighted by it all, so Zuko is content to lie there and take it in and ignore the fact that he should really be getting back to work. Whatever trouble he gets into will be worth it, to have helped put that kind of smile on Sokka’s face.

&#45;-

“Did you have a nice conversation with Minji, Nephew?”

“…It was fine,” Zuko says, scowling at the tea on his tray. All three pots are supposed to be the same blend of black tea, but the pot in the middle is bleeding off heat faster than the others, so it isn’t going to steep the same. Zuko shifts his hand underneath the tray and carefully sends a tongue of heat upward.

“What did you talk about?”

“I was trading shifts,” Zuko says absently, brow tight in concentration until—yes—there— the temperature levels out and all three are in sync again.

“Why?”

“Why what?” Zuko glances up in surprise at Uncle’s neutral-but-holding-a-lot-back tone. Zuko hasn’t heard that one in a while. Wariness prickles the back of his neck as he belatedly registers the lack of tea in Uncle’s hands, the full orientation of his body toward Zuko. Uncle is here to talk, not just to fill time.

“Why did you want to trade shifts with Minji?” Uncle repeats patiently, eyes sharp on Zuko’s face.

“I just wanted some different time off,” Zuko mutters, glancing around for Sung-min. Zuko can’t bring this order out until the last pot of tea is here, and he would really like to walk away now.

“What do you need the time for?”

“Why do you care?” Zuko glowers at Sung-min’s back. “You never cared where I was before.” Agni’s tits, Zuko had barely spent a week in Ba Sing Se before he was disappearing with Jet without a backward glance. Uncle’s sudden interest sits new and uncomfortable on Zuko’s shoulders.

“I have always cared, Nephew,” Uncle says quietly, seriously, absurdly, and Zuko’s inner fire flares jagged with how much he doesn’t want to hear it.

“How many nights did I just walk away after work again? Remind me when you ever said anything about it,” Zuko snaps, voice low because otherwise it will be a shout, and Good Nephews don’t fucking do that.

“I wanted to give you your space,” Uncle protests, hands moving like he wants to reach out even as Zuko shifts to put his tray more firmly between them.

“And now you don’t?” Zuko challenges, concentrating on the irritation tightening his shoulders to steel himself against Uncle’s sadness. “What? I don’t get space anymore?” All those nights when Zuko was falling into bed with someone who would probably have happily slit his throat, and Uncle decides he wants to know *now*?

“You seem more distracted of late,” Uncle defends, and Zuko barely notices as Sung-min edges up to set the last teapot on the counter before darting away. “As if you have a lot on your mind. I thought you might be feeling…burdened.”

“I didn’t realize Lee wasn’t allowed to *think*,” Zuko hisses, snatching up the last bit of his order and ignoring the way Uncle flinches from his sudden vehemence, so close to the tone of Zuko’s old rage, as he stomps away. Of course Uncle decides to pry when it’s probably the least Zuko has needed watching since they came to fucking this city. Impeccable timing, as always. Zuko’s barely even left the *street* the past week, for fucks sake.

For Zuko’s whereabouts to suddenly be so important, for Zuko’s absences to suddenly be so inconvenient that Uncle needs to pry…it’s not like Zuko was a model fucking employee before and is now messing up. He went from begrudgingly functional to distractedly functional. Why would Uncle care about *why*? All he cares about is tea and pai sho and—

Zuko’s muscles lock, for a moment, before he forces himself to keep setting tea down on the table.

*Enough*.

He doesn’t want to think about this anymore. He doesn’t want to give weight and attention to things that will do no one any good to bring up. He just needs to firmly ignore the fact that Uncle never bothered to ask before what Zuko got up to after work like Zuko ignores everything else. And Zuko can continue to extend Uncle the same courtesy, of never asking back because Zuko had been—still is—too afraid of what he might hear, after the desert.

&#45;-

Zuko manages to trade enough shifts to end up with more consecutive time away from the teashop in the afternoon a few days a week, which doesn’t improve Zuko’s distraction when he's there. More time with Sokka for training and everything else just means more material to be distracted by. Zuko thought that maybe all the extra time would make things start to feel routine, would let the novelty finally wear off, but instead it feels like there’s constantly something new to discover and get lost in.

The luxury of time itself is something to get lost in, too, Zuko learns, and one that never seems to grow old. Maybe because with time they’re able to burn through the urgency that always drives them when they first come together, like maybe both of them are secretly worried the other won't actually be there this time. But with time now, the desire is still there, as strong as ever but more patient, more willing to be savored instead of needing to be sated.

Being with Sokka when it's like that can be slower, quieter, more deliberate. Different, but still good. Like honey in the afternoon sunlight, sweet and slow and warm. Like the fire in Zuko’s veins bleeding out in strands of heat. Like the pulse of Sokka’s chi, setting the tempo of Zuko’s breaths.

&#45;-

For all that he’s wrapped up in Sokka every moment he can manage, Jin still drags Zuko out after work. It’s harder to find time now since he started picking up some of Minji’s shifts on top of Sung-min’s, but Jin is a woman determined when she sets her mind to something.

Zuko remains quietly flustered and confused that she seems to have set her mind to him, even as he appreciates the time with her when they can manage to make it happen. They walk around the Lower Ring or explore the night markets. Sometimes she drags him to a performance or dance or masquerade—Agni’s tits, Zuko didn’t know whether to laugh or cry the first time she put a mask in his hands—her arm always looped through his with enough familiarity by this point that he doesn’t notice it as much anymore. Jin always has something in mind, and Zuko is more than content to hand her the reins and trail in her wake and have that be all that’s expected of him.

“Are you even paying attention?”

…Maybe a bit more is expected of him than just that.

“No,” Zuko admits, because he genuinely has no idea what she’s been talking about, zoning out to memories of the afternoon, the sounds Sokka had made, the way his body had shuddered and clenched and moved in rhythm with Zuko’s.

“At least you’re honest about it,” Jin mutters, with a little shoulder bump so he knows she’s teasing.

Zuko just shrugs rather than hazard an answer. He isn’t sure if she’s figured out yet that he’s a miserable liar, but he isn’t about to point it out proactively if she hasn’t.

“You’ve been daydreaming all night, Lee.”

“…You can’t daydream at night,” Zuko says, because she clearly wants him say something and, like always, he has no idea what.

“*Fantasizing* then, if you’re going to be pedantic about it.”

“Um.” Zuko definitely doesn’t know what to say now. That’s…pretty much what he’s been doing.

“Ha!” Jin exclaims in triumph. “I knew it!”

“How,” Zuko complains, dangerously close to whining. Agni’s balls, it’s not like Zuko’s ever been talkative, before. Why is everyone suddenly able to tell that he’s being untalkative in a new way?

“Why else would you have told *me,* your only friend—” Zuko doesn’t even try to deny it. “— that, for the first time ever, you couldn’t come out because you had work?”

“…Because I had work?”

“Because you’re freeing up your time to be with your beau!”

Zuko cringes as Jin’s delighted shout draws glances and curious looks from around the night market. “Don’t say that.”

“What? Your beau?”

“Yes, that. Never say that again.”

“What should I say instead, then?” Jin pokes his side. “Your gentleman caller? Your lover? Your—”

“Why do you need to call it anything,” Zuko grumbles. Why does everyone need to *name* everything and make it fit into little boxes. Why can’t it just be…whatever it is?

Jin cocks her head, her expression quieting at his aggrieved tone. “Don’t *you* want to call it something?”

“Not really.” It’s never felt all that great, when it’s been done to him. Refugee. Traitor. Exile. Failure. Disappointment. How could they put words to whatever it is between him and Sokka without introducing expectations about how it’s supposed to be and judgments of whether it’s right and enough?

“Why not?”

“It doesn’t need—There’s just…a lot of history. With us." Zuko huffs out a frustrated breath. "It’s complicated. There’s nothing to call it. Nothing really fits.” Which is fairly standard, for Zuko. The things he does rarely seem to fit where they’re supposed to.

“Oh,” Jin says slowly, her mouth forming an O as she draws out the word. “Is this…your person from before? That you were hung up on?”

Zuko eyes her sidelong. “...Yes.”

“…So getting over him is going great, huh?”

Zuko snorts out a surprised half-laugh and Jin bursts into giggles beside him, the sharp edges of Zuko’s tension and frustration soften in the face of her humor. “It’s hard because Ba Sing Se was supposed to be a new start,” Zuko admits. “A new life.”

“And here’s your old life, looking all cute?”

“A piece of it, at least,” Zuko sighs, ignoring the rest of her words. As if something as small as ‘cute’ could ever describe Sokka.

“You know, Lee, you can start over without leaving everything behind,” Jin says sagely, looping her arm a little firmer through his.

Zuko makes a noise in the back of his throat that comes out sounding exactly as skeptical as he feels about that statement.

“Everyone is shaped by where they came from,” Jin says. “That doesn’t go away just because you crossed the walls. Even if the Cultural Authority would like it to.”

“Careful.”

“I know,” she sighs. “Anyways. It’s the choices you make now that matter, right? That’s how you get a new start, by choosing new things.”

Zuko just grunts, which Jin takes in stride. Her words sound pretty, but he isn’t sure that they’re right. And he doesn’t think that anyone who knows Zuko’s history would agree with her. Some people can make new choices and have that be enough to start over. But Zuko’s past is still out there. Actively hunting for him, tempting him in the moments when his resolve wears thin, falling into his bed. Zuko can make all the choices he wants, now. That won’t let him escape the ones he’s already made, the ones that keep pulling him back every step he tries to take forward.

&#45;-

Zuko can feel Uncle’s eyes as he looms just a half-step too far into Sung-min’s space for comfort, holding his silence until the man stutters out hasty agreement to trade a shift with Minji before running away, which lets Zuko shuffle his free afternoon to the day after tomorrow. Uncle’s stare makes his skin itch, which Zuko doesn’t need right now. He’s already irritable and frustrated over having to wait a day longer than he expected to see Sokka again because Sokka’s schedule had changed.

“I don’t see much of you anymore, Nephew,” Uncle comments from the stovetop where he’s measuring leaves into multiple pots of tea.

“What are you talking about,” Zuko grumbles from his spot folding napkins at the counter, refusing to look up from his work. “You see me every day.”

“I see you, yes. But we used to spend much of our days together,” Uncle muses, giving one of his teapots a critical half-turn.

“Because we work together.”

“And before that, because we traveled together,” Uncle says with a surprising degree of nostalgia, as if he longs for the days of chasing rumor and fleeing for their lives.

“Sure,” Zuko agrees cautiously. Uncle almost never talks about what came before Ba Sing Se, and Zuko is suddenly hyperaware of every coworker in the room, every ear that could catch a stray comment and bring it straight to the Dai Li.

“And now you work different shifts.” Uncle sighs, wistful, and Zuko doesn’t know what to do with that. “And you spend evenings with your friend. The girl, Jin?”

“You *told* me to go out with her,” Zuko snaps, forcing his hands to unclench from around a freshly laundered napkin, carefully smoothing out the creases with heat-warm fingers.

“And it is good that you have a—friend.” Zuko doesn’t miss Uncle’s delicate, searching pause. He pointedly doesn’t react to it.

“Then what are you complaining about,” he asks flatly, finishing the last of his napkins and staring down at the counter, pressing his hands against the wood so they can’t curl into fists.

“I miss the time we used to have together.”

“The what?” The taste of smoke dissipates with Zuko’s surprise. “The time in the *teashop*?”

“Yes,” Uncle sighs. “Such nice days together.”

“When we barely speak because we’re working?”

“There’s much contentment to be found in companionable labor,” Uncle says, and Zuko can only stare because who in their right mind has never thought Zuko was *companionable*? “Are you with Jin, then, during the afternoons?” Uncle asks, skipping back in the conversation far enough that Zuko needs to scramble to catch up.

“No,” Zuko admits, carefully controlling his expression to a neutral scowl instead of a defensive one.

“Hm. But you still feel the need to change shifts?”

“…Yes.” Zuko wishes that Uncle could just ask what he wants to ask, instead of dancing around it until Zuko barely has a picture anymore of what information he needs to be protecting.

“I see.” Uncle is silent for long enough that Zuko wonders if that’s the end of it, but then he speaks again, quiet enough that Zuko needs to strain and shift his good ear around to hear. “You know, Nephew, I may seem to smother you. But it’s only because I want what is best for you.”

“What?” Uncle…thinks Zuko is switching shifts to get away from him?

Which…*would* be a big change. Uncle has always known where Zuko was. Has always had an eye on him, except for those weeks when Zuko traveled the Earth Kingdom on his own, and even then, Uncle found him again like he’d been just out of sight the whole time. Always there, always watching, always ready with words and advice and judgment and opinions on what Zuko could have done instead.

Zuko thought he understood why Uncle has always been there, but maybe… maybe he’s never bothered to find out. Maybe he’s always just assumed, and never actually known.

“I am always here, Nephew,” Iroh murmurs, gentle and kind and caring.

“Yes,” Zuko forces out, eyes still pinned to the counter, to the hands he is forcing flat and cool against the wood. “I know.”

Zuko closes his eyes, reaching for some semblance of calm as Uncle finally lets the conversation end. Fuck, Zuko can’t feed his sudden flare of resentment into his inner fire fast enough to not feel it, too busy already trying to burn away a wave of self-loathing for still being unable to accept what Uncle chooses to offer him, and beneath it something thin and sticky that might be fear.

Agni's balls. It was easier before Zuko ever thought he could ask questions back.

&#45;-

Sokka wishes he were spending the afternoon with Zuko instead of stealing servants’ uniforms with Aang from the back of a laundry cart—gross, gross, gross—all for the plan Toph and Katara cooked up between them. Infiltrating a party at the palace to try to plead their case to the Earth King sooner rather than later isn’t the worst idea Sokka’s ever heard— it would, admittedly, be hard to top ‘what if we purposefully make the Avatar so mad that he enters the Avatar state for vengeance’—but he doesn’t like just how much it relies on sheer bravado. They know so little about what they’re getting into, for all of Toph’s confidence in what they’ll find.

Besides, self-assurance is her usual state. Toph being confident isn’t exactly an effective measure of whether something should be done or not.

Though rushing home to get ready in time, the uniforms stuffed into his bag, to find Katara and Toph all done up like rich Earth Kingdom aristocrats, makeup and fans and everything… Sokka pointedly nudges Aang’s open jaw closed, rolling his eyes when Aang still can’t stop staring, hearts in his eyes.

Well then. Maybe this will work after all.

Sokka quickly disappears into his room to wiggle his own uniform on over his clothes, carefully smoothing the fabric over his chest to press any wrinkles and bunches out. The gesture awakens the faint heat of Zuko’s hands on his body, something Sokka could think he just imagined if he didn’t know the marks were there.

*Sometimes confidence is all you need*, he reminds himself, taking a deep breath and trying to blow out the nerves starting to jangle along his limbs. Fake it until you make it. Until you’ve learned enough that the confidence can be real. If it’s good enough for the Fire Prince, then it's good enough for the fancy servant Sokka is about to pretend to be.

A fancy servant named…Etan. No, Eto. A real aw-shucks kind of guy, who hails from the Middle Ring. Born to refugee parents, excited for an opportunity to attend University one day if only he can meet the qualifying exams, who loves steamed buns and—

“Let’s get a move on, Sokka!’

“Coming,” Sokka shouts back to Katara—no, to…Sedna. An Upper Ring aristocrat new to the society scene and ready to dazzle. She loves horticulture and tending her garden, and…

&#45;-

Sokka doesn’t know what he expected an aristocratic party in a palace to be, but somehow it wasn’t this. There are so many people—he didn’t even realize there *were* this many fancy people in the city—and it’s such a large space. Spirits, the villa Ba Sing Se gave to the Avatar and his entourage might actually be *modest*.

And everyone, including the other servants, acts like he’s practically invisible. Which should be useful, for gathering intel, but instead wastes his absolutely perfect cover story. Plus, it makes actually getting close enough to anyone to hear anything way too hard.

A nobleman sweeps by as if Sokka isn’t even there, proving his point and forcing Sokka to execute some quick footwork to avoid dumping his tray of…puffs…all over the floor.

“Nice,” Katara murmurs, lips barely moving as she pretends to look over his tray. “Where’d you learn that?”

“Where’s Toph?” Sokka’s eyes flick over the room as he tries to channel some of Zuko’s Fire Nation attitude and act like he belongs here. Or maybe that anyone who thinks he doesn’t belong here is a fucking idiot, if he’s channeling the Fire Prince. “And just training.”

“New stuff?” Sokka hides a smile at the animation in her voice even when it's quiet. Katara, of all people, always appreciates the excitement of having something new to practice. “And she got pulled into some kind of conversation about…something.”

“Ah,” Sokka grunts, finally finding Toph’s surprisingly small shape in the crowd. “And yeah, Zuko showed me some things.” Should he say that name here? Is it a common one? Sokka takes a quick second look around to make sure no one is close enough to overhear. “He knows swords.”

“Oh,” Katara frowns as she finally picks up a puff and pretends to survey the crowd, doing an excellent job of appearing to ignore him like only a little sister could. “I guess I knew that.”

Katara leaves it at that, and Sokka has to fight back the urge to fidget away the anticipatory tension that shot through him and now has nowhere to go. He’s pretty sure a waiter isn’t supposed to show that much emotion. Or any, really.

Katara reaches for another puff, using the gesture to steal a glance at his face. “So…things with him are…good?” The question sounds like she can barely make the words make sense together. Sokka can sympathize with the feeling. It happens a lot, around Zuko.

“Yeah, they’re…they’re good.” ‘Good’ seems far too bland to encompass it, but Sokka doesn’t know that he has any other words he can give her without thoroughly embarrassing them both in the attempt.

“That’s…good.”

“Yeah.”

A drawn-out silence, then Katara’s shoulders sag before she visibly remembers that she’s supposed to be a fancy rich person who's never slumped a day in her life. “This is weird,” she mutters, casting her eyes around the room again. “Talking about you and him—it’s so weird.”

“Yes,” Sokka says with a quiet, rueful laugh. “Trust me. I know.”

“You’re being careful?” Katara’s voice is tight with worry as she flicks out her fan to hide the matching expression.

“I am,” Sokka says firmly, making sure his voice doesn’t waver. “I promise.”

“I just…the idea that you’re trusting him. After everything…”

“I know,” Sokka says, glancing away from the room to study the set of her shoulders, the proximity of her hand to the waterskin at her belt. Katara has been surprisingly close-mouthed about this whole thing so far and Sokka doesn’t want to make her stop if she finally has something she needs to say, even if she’s choosing less than stellar time to say it.

Though it’s not the absolute worst moment. Sokka has no idea what they’re looking for really, and neither does Katara. Toph is their expert on this particular hunt, in her element across the room charming some collection of matronly, well-dressed women.

“He tied me to a tree!” Katara finally bursts out, miraculously quiet as she glares at the crowd over her fan. Sokka winces even though the look isn’t directed at him.

“I…remember.” And some part of him is wholly, completely, wildly inappropriately jealous that when it happened to him it was just *Jet* doing the tying.

“Are you sure, Sokka?” The anger seems to sweep out as quickly as it came, leaving only worry behind. “That he’s really different?”

“Yeah,” Sokka says, the word ringing with conviction even though if you asked him, he still can’t quite put his finger on *how,* even though it's been nagging at the back of his head nearly since that first afternoon. It’s more than just the fact that Zuko’s sole driving purpose is no longer trying to capture Aang. Maybe it's that Zuko had always been a ball of barely restrained tension and seething emotion before Ba Sing Se but now, Zuko seems…thinner, somehow. Not physically—though that, too. But like there’s less to hold back? Even though whenever Sokka tries to pin it down exactly Zuko still seems to be full of so *much.*

Sokka isn’t sure that the change is entirely a good thing, either. It’s not like Zuko seems any more relaxed, outside of those moments after sex, for all of that feeling inside Zuko to not be fighting to get free anymore. And while Sokka thinks he does pretty well for himself in bed if Zuko’s reactions are anything to go by, he doesn’t exactly think he can claim to have fucked Zuko so well it's mellowed him out.

“How do you know?” Katara’s voice is suspicious and edged with hardness as it breaks through his thoughts. He starts, guilty, yanking himself back into the present. Spirits, they’re on a secret infiltration mission. Now is *not* the time to start daydreaming. "How can you be sure?"

“How do—I don’t know, Katara,” Sokka shifts his tray to his other hand in lieu of throwing them up in exasperation, and to hide his discomfort that he doesn't have an explanation for her. “Because I’ve spent time with him, enough to tell?”

“Sorry, sorry,” Katara mutters, trying to belatedly wave her tone away and sneaking him an apologetic look as she grabs another puff “I didn’t mean to…I know that you—I just—” She sighs. “He isn’t plotting, right?”

“I don’t think he would tell me if he was,” Sokka points out dryly. “It wouldn’t be a very good plot if he did.” And Sokka doesn’t think Zuko could be so boneless on top of Sokka in those moments when they’re sticky and tangled and still coming back to earth and also be plotting. That seems like too much of a deception, for someone so hilariously bad at lying.

Katara waves away his joke with her fan. “But you don’t think he is, right?”

“No,” Sokka says, forcing himself back to seriousness since Katara seems to need to hear something specific to be able to unwind. If having him verbally confirm a lack of plots is what she needs, Sokka isn’t going to withhold it from her.

“And he hasn’t like…asked you to come to the Fire Nation side or anything.”

*…Fuck.* “Not…exactly.”

Katara slowly turns toward him, eyes narrowed. “…What?”

“Not recently?”

“*What*.”

“I said no,” Sokka mutters, defensive. Now it’s his turn to examine the crowd. What an interesting bunch. What fine robes.

“When?” Katara whisper-shouts, cold and low and dangerous as a blizzard sweeping in off the sea.

“The North,” Sokka sighs, rolling his head to try to loosen the sudden stiffness in his neck. He had…really hoped this would never come up. Ever. It’s not like it had been a real question, a real choice.

“I—what—how—why would he think you would say *yes*?”

“I mean, I asked him first. So.”

Sokka glances up into the sudden silence to see Katara staring at him, stunned. He hastily holds out his tray as cover for her gaping. “You…asked the Fire Prince. To join the Avatar. In the middle of the invasion of the North.”

“Well, it’s not like he was leading it,” Sokka mumbles, annoyed at his own prickliness around the conversation. It hadn’t meant anything back then, not really, and it makes him feel stretched too tight inside his own skin for Katara to act like it means something now.

“Tui and La, Sokka!”

“What!”

“You asked him—and then—He asked you to become a—a what? A Fire Nation spy for him?” Katara’s face is openly aghast, which is not how she should be looking at his tray of food if he doesn’t want to get yanked off the floor by the head servant man.

“And I said no,” Sokka snaps. He is *not* doing this shit again. The whole reason to even tell them about Zuko in the first place was so they could avoid this exact conversation.

Katara tosses her head, scoffing. “*Crown* *Prince Zuko* doesn’t take ‘no’ for an answer—”

“He does from me.” Sokka is deeply satisfied at the way she pulls up short, and then deeply horrified when she suddenly turns scarlet even through her makeup. “No, no, no,” he denies as she stares at him in shock, reading *far* more than Sokka ever meant into that statement. “That’s not—I wasn’t—ugh. Can…can this conversation just be over? Please?”

“Yes,” she agrees hastily. “Yes. Let’s just…”

“Take a turn around the room?”

“Great idea. Great. Let’s…yes, let’s do that. I think I see Joo Dee.”

&#45;-

Aang, predictably, is the one to blow their cover, because if there’s one thing that Toph hasn’t fully grasped yet it’s that an airbender cannot be repressed for long. After a lot of staring from the assembled rich people—in both entertainment and threat, Sokka thinks—they find themselves making the actually-not-that-long walk from the palace back to their villa, still without having been able to speak to the Earth King.

“So…do we need to worry about the Dai Li?” Katara wonders. Sokka glances up from the careful watch he’s keeping on Aang’s dejected rock kicking—Toph’s rock kicking is much more enthusiastic—to see something like reluctance on her face.

“Maybe,” Sokka acknowledges, feeling more intimidated than he would like by the idea that the Dai Li might have just shown themselves to be an object that even Toph can’t move.

“Does that mean that the Earth King isn’t actually going to help us, then?” Aang cuts in, voice high with upset.

“I don’t know if I would say that just yet,” Sokka soothes.

Toph snorts. “I don’t know that I *wouldn’t*.”

Sokka takes a deep breath, trying to project assurance and calm toward Aang’s restless fidgeting. “I think it wouldn’t hurt to know a bit more about the Dai Li. At the very least, they seem important to how Ba Sing Se works.”

And it wouldn’t hurt for Sokka to look a little more headlong at the possibility that Ba Sing Se might not support the Avatar, too. Everyone they’ve talked to so far has been scared or creepily on-script or both, and none of the four of them have been able to dig up a whiff of what everyone is so worried about. Maybe Ba Sing Se’s ever-present Cultural Authority is the unspoken threat hanging over everyone’s head, holding the city back from helping.

## Chapter 17: Locked Fault

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for some light sexual content in this one, and reference to child abuse

### Text

Training with Zuko is difficult, probably more than it should be. Not that Sokka expected Zuko to be casual about training, because Sokka doesn’t think Zuko knows how to be casual about anything. But Zuko seems unsure how to teach beyond just…demonstrating a full kata and then staring expectantly. Which is less than helpful.

Sokka can acknowledge that it also doesn’t help that the majority of his formal training from the Northern Water Tribe—solid, focused on ceding and retaking ground and wearing your opponent down—doesn’t exactly provide a great foundation for Zuko’s Fire Nation style, all quickness and changing levels and far more flipping off the ground than any non-airbender should have reason to do.

Mostly, though, training is hard because Sokka can’t get his mind out of the gutter when Zuko is around.

Sokka finds it embarrassingly difficult to concentrate on what Zuko is saying while also staring at his body in motion. And Sokka can never seem to remember exactly how he’s supposed to hold himself after Zuko adjusts his arms or legs into position, his body swaying toward Zuko and breaking form before Sokka even realizes he’s unconsciously trying to sink back into the heat of him.

Sokka knows it should be easier to ignore than it is, since they almost always come to the courtyard to train by way of Zuko’s futon. Or the wall right inside the apartment door, or sometimes the floor between. But there’s just something about Zuko's unconscious confidence, that only seems to bubble up when he has a sword in his hand, about the flex of his muscles and the lines of his body that Sokka should be trying to imitate, not cataloging for future alone time, that Sokka can't help but get lost in.

Zuko is saying something about grips, and hilts, and Sokka is pretty sure he should be paying attention because Sokka’s pretty sure he should pay attention to everything Zuko says. But Sokka can’t quite seem to hold onto the words, consumed by Zuko’s forearms flexing as he demonstrates different ways to hold a sword, by the veins over the back of his hands, and Spirits, Zuko even has *thumb* muscles, and those calluses…Sokka has felt those on his body, in his body, anchored on his shoulders, and suddenly all he can think about is how it felt when Zuko—

“*Sokka*.” Zuko’s voice breaks through Sokka’s daze, loud and exasperated and sounding like he’s repeated himself a few times already.

“Huh?”

“You aren’t paying attention at all, are you?”

“I am paying *lots* of attention.”

“To what I am saying?”

“Ah.” Sokka clears his throat. “Then no. Missed…most of that.”

“Agni’s tits, what were you even—” Zuko catches the look in Sokka’s eye and snaps his mouth shut, nonplussed. “…You’re something else.”

Zuko scratches the back of his neck, blushing all pink and adorable and it’s enough to send Sokka’s brain skipping happily off toward the gutter again, so distracted he almost misses Zuko’s next words.

“Do you need to blow off steam so you can focus?”

“…What was that?” Sokka is suddenly listening *very* intently. That almost sounded like— “Do you need to get off so you can pay attention,” Zuko repeats, as if it's a perfectly normal question to ask a person.

“Um, maybe?” Sokka laughs, incredulous, waiting for the joke. Except Zuko just shrugs in agreement and tugs Sokka’s sword out of suddenly lax fingers. He sets both weapons on the paving stones and pushes Sokka back, amusement warming his eyes when Sokka can only gape and stumble in front of him until his knees hit the bench and Sokka collapses down to sit, clumsy with shock.

“You going to help me out here?” Zuko asks, giving Sokka’s legs a pointed tap.

Sokka is still failing to catch up with what's going on, but he manages to collect himself enough to belatedly spread his knees as Zuko drops down between them. And Sokka might have no idea how exactly this is happening, but he is *wholly* onboard as Zuko makes quick work of freeing his already hardening cock. Sokka’s body clearly has much more of a clue than his brain does.

Zuko pauses with one hand wrapped around the base of Sokka’s erection, flicking a considering glance up through his lashes that makes Sokka’s mouth go dry.

“You can’t make a lot of noise out here,” Zuko warns, giving Sokka a slow, almost absent stroke.

“I can be quiet,” Sokka hurries to say, already gripping the sides of the bench to anchor himself. “I can be so quiet. The quietest. Nothing but quiet. You won’t even know I’m here.”

Zuko raises an eyebrow. “Sokka. You’ve never been quiet a day in your life.”

Sokka opens his mouth to protest, indignant, except Zuko’s firebender hot mouth is suddenly around him and the sound Sokka makes is…not the quietest. Nor are any of the ones that follow at the feel of Zuko’s silent laughter vibrating through his dick.

&#45;-

Sokka actually can focus on what Zuko is saying, afterward, which is both a nice bonus and an embarrassing statement on how much of Sokka’s mind is wrapped up in nothing but Zuko when they’re together, even when Sokka is pretending otherwise. Sokka would feel weird about the whole thing if he weren’t pretty sure that Zuko is amused by it all. Zuko’s mouth hitches into a barely-there half-smile when he’s laughing at something, even though he doesn’t usually let the sound out. That little hitch is there for the rest of the training session.

Sokka keeps waiting for Zuko to suggest some reciprocity—Sokka is *more* than down for some reciprocity—but Zuko doesn’t bring it up even when they’re done for the day, just leans back onto his arms, face tilted up to the sun as they both get their breath back from flying through the last kata at double-time. Zuko’s eyes are closed, so Sokka takes the opportunity to stare as much as he always wants to, enjoying the sight of Zuko flushed with exertion. His hair is long enough to clump with sweat, which Sokka still can't get over, his shirt damp and pulled tight across his chest, and Sokka can see a bead of sweat crawling down the side of Zuko’s neck before Zuko brushes it away.

“It’s cooler in the shade over here,” Sokka points out. This particular corner rarely gets direct light and can always be relied upon to be marginally more comfortable in the persistent, dry Earth Kingdom heat.

“This is nice, though,” Zuko says lazily, as if he weren’t currently baking himself. Sokka continues to be amazed that Zuko doesn’t seem to ever tan much, with the way he always seems to find his way into the closest available patch of sunlight. Sokka had quickly realized that the most sure-fire way to get Zuko to cuddle on top of him—which Sokka adores, even if he still hasn’t figured out how to ask for it—is to lay down in the square of sunlight that streams in from Zuko’s window. He isn’t sure if it’s a firebender thing or just a Zuko thing, to always want to bask in the sun’s rays and never seem to burn, but either way, Sokka is happy to use it to his full advantage.

“Days like this make me miss the cold,” Sokka mutters, fanning his sweat-damp shirt away from his body. “Toph keeps saying it’s going to get colder, but I don’t know if I believe her anymore.”

“It will,” Zuko assures him. “It won’t be like the South, though. There’s nothing like that.”

Sokka hums in agreement, because even winter and snow won’t be the same with so many trees and houses and people.

“The first time I went…it was something else. Amazing.”

“What, when you wrecked our village? That was spring, that barely counts,” Sokka scoffs, even though he knows that it’s a rare day in the South that won’t kill you if you aren’t careful.

“I didn’t wreck it,” Zuko protests, cracking open his unscarred eye, shoulders relaxing when he sees that Sokka isn’t actively upset.

“You knocked down my watchtower, Zuko.” Sokka says dryly. “And Gran Gran. And me.”

“Well, one of those things deserved it.”

“Hey!”

“And anyway, that wasn’t my first time.”

“It wasn’t?” Sokka hand pauses its fanning in his surprise. “When were you there?” He’s suddenly caught in the idea that Zuko could have crossed his path earlier. Before they ever found Aang, maybe even before the warriors went away, before…he feels light-headed with the possibilities of it.

Zuko hums in thought, unaware of the ways Sokka’s thoughts are spinning as he tilts his head back toward the sun, eyes slipping closed again. “Right after I turned fourteen, I think.”

Sokka swallows as a whole new line of thought joins the mix. Sokka can barely wrap his mind around the idea of Zuko at fourteen. Was he just as tall? Or did he shoot up more recently? Sokka thinks Zuko moves too fluidly to have been the victim of a recent growth spurt, but Sokka is also aware that Zuko is the kind of person who would refuse to let something like his hand suddenly being six inches further from his torso than it used to be hold him back. It’s hard to hold onto the idea of Zuko as anything other than what he is now, really. Spirits, Sokka can barely wrap his mind around Zuko being *relaxed*, and he's looking at it right now. “What were you doing there?”

“Looking for the Avatar, what do you think,” Zuko says, only a little bit sharp.

“In the South Pole?” Sokka wants to laugh at the idea of scouring the South for anything other than seals and penguins. They barely have people, anymore.

Zuko cracks his eye open again. “It’s where he was, wasn’t he?”

…Right.

“So you thought the South was amazing,” Sokka prompts, shamelessly changing the subject.

“Yeah.” Zuko says, gaze distant, clearly seeing something other than Sokka. “It was…harsh. I’m pretty sure a bunch of us almost died. A few of the crew would have definitely lost fingers if Uncle wasn’t there.” He sounds rueful and almost…fond? “We didn’t have any of the right supplies, none of the right clothes. We had no idea what we were doing. We almost got the ship stuck in the ice on the way back out.” He breathes out a noise that would probably be laughter, for someone else.

“And…you liked that?” Sokka can barely understand Zuko, sometimes.

“It just…was what it was,” Zuko shrugs. “It was cruel and uncaring. It didn’t pretend to be anything else.”

Sokka really doesn’t understand Zuko, sometimes.

“When the storm stopped, everything was snow and ice and totally untouched, like people had never been there before. And it was night, so the stars reflected back up like the snow was glowing…”

*Oh. That makes sense.*

“That was nice,” Zuko finishes softly, blinking himself back to the present with an almost shy look for Sokka.

“Yeah,” Sokka agrees. “It is.” Sokka and Katara used to climb up onto the roof of their house, if they could slip out without waking anyone, to look out and see the tundra like it was lit from the inside. Something warm blooms in his chest at the knowledge that Zuko has seen that too, seen it and carried the memory of it with him ever since. “Did you ever go back?”

“You were there for it.”

“I meant before that,” Sokka rolls his eyes.

“No,” Zuko says, giving Sokka a sideways look and rising to his feet. “We almost died. Some people got upset about that.” Sokka bites back a laugh at how disgruntled Zuko still sounds over it. “It took a lot of convincing to get us South again.”

&#45;-

There's a new Joo Dee and it’s weird.

It’s quiet after dinner, a tense moodiness that none of them felt entirely comfortable displaying in front of their new guide. They had finally managed to stop asking about the old Joo Dee, which made the new one happy. but Sokka can tell that none of them have stopped thinking about it. Did something happen to her? Because of them? Is this a warning, in some way? Or would she have been replaced regardless, moving on to a new assignment, or just… upgraded to the newer model?

“Did anyone find any more leads, today?” Sokka finally asks, even though the fact that no one has volunteered anything yet is a clear ‘no.’

“I talked to some of the people doing the actual fishing, not just selling the fish, in the Outer Ring,” Katara says glumly. “But it’s nothing I haven’t heard before.”

“I got nothing,” Toph says, falling back into a disgruntled slouch. Aang just shakes his head, ripping dried fruit into bits for Momo, and Sokka can’t tell if it’s because he’s trying to fight off anger or tears. Maybe both. Sokka understands the feeling. He’s acutely aware that they’ve gotten nowhere in finding Appa, beyond waiting down the days to their audience with the Earth Kingdom. And neither of the Joo Dees would give them a straight answer on when, exactly, that audience is scheduled for.

“Everything we do just goes nowhere,” Aang bursts out, voice choked. “Whoever we talk to, wherever they live, no matter how promising it seems it all just ends up at the exact same place!”

Sokka takes a deep breath to prepare to soothe away Aang’s frustration and pauses, something about Aang’s words nudging at the back corner of Sokka’s brain. He takes a giant, purposeful mental step back and tries to shed all his bias and assumptions and think through the bigger picture, beyond just today and this week, all the way back to their first steps into the walls.

“You’re right,” Sokka says slowly. His brain is running with Aang’s outburst as a literal statement, shifting around and repositioning the past few weeks of dried-up leads and evasive answers and stymied attempts to get around Joo Dee, and a picture is starting to come together with a shocking amount of clarity. “It *does* all seem to come back to the place.”

“Yeah, nowhere,” Toph mutters.

“But in the same *way*,” Katara breathes, straightening, restrained excitement in her voice. She can see where Sokka is starting to go. “Sokka, do you think there’s some kind of, I don’t know, orchestration behind it?”

“What?” Aang frowns, sitting a little more upright at the siblings’ sudden energy. “What do you mean?”

“I don’t know,” Sokka answers her. “It would be a huge conspiracy. There’d have to be so many people involved just to track us, let alone to run interference and get ahead of our leads.” Zuko occasionally makes offhand, sideways references to Caldera enough that Sokka has picked up that the capital is full of ministers and officials all reporting up to progressively more important ministers and officials. Is the Earth Kingdom the same way? Is everyone part of the net of bureaucracy?

“That would be a *ton* of administration,” Toph says, echoing his thought, her kicking foot stilling as she starts to consider the idea.

“Ba Sing Se seems good at that kind of stuff,” Aang points outs.

A tense silence settles over them, and Sokka can practically feel them all hesitating on the edge of saying something that he’s only ever glanced at sideways in the back of his mind in the dark of night when no one is around.

“So…we need to actually investigate the Dai Li?” Katara finally asks. “Not just maybe, but —actually do it?”

“I think so,” Sokka says quietly, skin already prickling like fresh eyes are watching from the shadows.

Aang is nodding, but his face is still twisted in uncertainty. “What does that even mean, though? How do you investigate a Cultural Authority?”

“It’s investigating Ba Sing Se’s government,” Toph shrugs, like that’s an easy thing.

“That’s saying we want to investigate the King, though,” Aang protests. “And we can’t even *see* him!”

“No.” Sokka is still trying to pull the outline of an idea together, but, “The government in Ba Sing Se is way more than just him. There are all those ministries, and councils, and edicts, and bureaus…”

Katara is nodding. “A whole system across the city, for everything.”

“So we investigate that,” Toph says, relaxing back like it’s settled. “An administrative network that big will have government contractors for everything.”

“We can start with contractors and find our way in,” Sokka suggests, the bones of a plan finally slotting together. He makes a mental note to ask Toph what a contractor is later. “Everyone keeps saying the Earth King loves animals. So there’s got to be someone in that palace in charge of it, right? They’ve got an agency for everything.”

“Pets,” Katara puts in. “And animals as entertainment at parties?” Toph nods in confirmation that yes, that is a thing that rich people do. “And labor at the palace and in the government buildings.”

“Kitchen suppliers?”

“That too,” Katara agrees reluctantly, as unhappy as they all are putting ‘Appa’ and ‘kitchens’ in the same thought.

“Where do we even start,” Aang asks, brow furrowed. “If there’s some kind of conspiracy they’ll notice if we just started looking for them.”

“The new Joo Dee seemed like she wanted to be extra helpful, today,” Katara points out, ignoring Sokka’s sudden awestruck murmur of ‘*New Dee’*. “I bet she’ll be happy to help out first thing tomorrow.”

&#45;-

“Can you just. Explain this some other way,” Sokka bites out, trying to swallow back frustration that he can’t understand how to work out the spinning move that Zuko seems to throw himself into so easily. While Sokka would normally enjoy the sight of Zuko doing how-can-this-be-used-in-a-fight acrobatics, watching Zuko just demonstrate over and over and over isn’t helping Sokka see how to do it himself.

“Um.” Zuko scratches the back of his neck uncertainly. “It’s a firebending move I modified, so you just—” He turns into the twist again, a whirlwind of blades and feet and elbows, before giving Sokka a your-turn-now look.

Sokka blows out a hard breath. “So clearly this isn’t working for me,” he says, forcing his annoyance to stay annoyance and not tip into anger. “Can you just…do it slower, or something?”

“Um, I can try…” The spin is marginally slower but not nearly enough for Sokka to figure out how Zuko’s weight is shifting from back to front like that, and when the rotation starts, and how his sword does *that* without cutting his own stomach open as he finishes the twist.

“What if you explained it instead of just doing it,” Sokka suggests, crossing his arms and then promptly dropping them back to his sides and trying to keep the irritation off his face, because Zuko will think he's upset with *him*, and Sokka *isn’t*, he's just…upset that Zuko thinks this is so easy it doesn’t even need to be taught, when Sokka has no idea where to even start.

“Okay, um…How?”

“I don’t know!” Sokka throws up his hands, frustration sparking. “How about however you got taught!”

Zuko flinches, which Sokka *hates* causing, shoulders tense and eyes on the ground. “…This is how I learned it.”

“You…” Sokka’s irritation stutters, loosening its grip to make way for surprise. “Someone just did it? And you had to copy them?”

“…Yeah,” Zuko says, looking baffled and wary by Sokka’s confusion. “Sorry. I don’t know how…” He trails off as Sokka shakes his head.

“No, that’s—no. Don’t apologize.” Sokka frowns. Maybe this is just how Zuko learned *this* move, because it’s more advanced? Maybe he’s too far removed from the beginner stuff to remember that? Except, hadn’t Zuko said he was still on the basics a few months ago? “Is that how you learned everything?”

“Uncle talks a lot, I guess,” Zuko finally offers, shoulders inching downward as he seems to realize that Sokka isn’t mad.

“But Iroh didn’t train you your whole life, right?”

“No, not until—” Zuko gestures toward his face, avoiding Sokka’s eyes. “—you know.”

None of this makes sense. “So someone would just…firebend. And you would need to do it?”

“…Yes,” Zuko says, like it’s so obvious he doesn’t understand why Sokka would even need to ask.

“And that works?”

Zuko’s face darkens into a scowl. “Azula never had any issues,” he mutters, testy, and Sokka can only stare because he’s seen Azula in action. She is definitely the prodigy Zuko described her as, and if *that* is his standard for whether something is an effective method of instruction or not…

“What happened if you couldn’t do it?” There has to be more, some breakdown of the move or explanation or grounding in theory.

But Zuko goes motionless in a way Sokka hasn’t seen in Ba Sing Se, voice suddenly harsh. “You just had to get it.”

“But what if you couldn’t,” Sokka presses. “What if it was like me now, and I can’t figure it out from just watching. What happens next?”

Zuko is silent for long enough that Sokka starts to feel uncomfortable, his jaw clenched, eyes fixed at his feet before finally rasping out, “I wouldn’t do that.”

“What?”

“I *wouldn’t*,” Zuko snarls, intense and pulled in tight and eyes snapping up and Sokka suddenly feels like he’s on Zuko’s ship again. “Not to you. Never to you. Okay? You don’t—I wouldn’t—”

"That—" Sokka's adrenaline is spiking at the urgency in Zuko’s voice, his body snapping to readiness at the clear edge of something that sounds a lot like anger but looks a lot like fear. “Okay, that’s good," Sokka says, forcing his tone to go low, his words to stay easy. "I believe you. I do. Zuko, I do.” Sokka ignores his racing heart and keeps up a steady murmur, more tone than substance until Zuko finally settles back into twitchy, fidgeting motion again.

Fuck. Sokka doesn’t like this, doesn’t like one bit feeling this uncertain about whatever buzzard wasp nest he just kicked up. He doesn’t entirely know what he’s assuring Zuko about, what he’s saying he believes but…his eyes flick to Zuko’s scar, stark against his bloodless face. Sokka can imagine.

Sokka forces himself to take a deep breath, to relax and loosen because Zuko is strung tight enough right now that Sokka doesn’t trust him to read the difference between anger at him and upset on his behalf. He puts on as open an expression as he can manage, taking a slow step forward and staying purposefully at ease when Zuko immediately pins him with a warning glare.

“Can you show me again?” Sokka keeps his voice gentle, even. “And maybe, if you come closer—”

“I don’t—I don’t think I can—” Zuko cuts in, flushing, eyes back on the ground. “Not—not now…”

“No, not for that,” Sokka hurries. “Just—if you come closer, behind me, and…” He keeps his tone confident and soothing as Zuko cautiously approaches and ignores the prickling of his skin as Zuko’s heat brushes along his back, because that is thoroughly unhelpful right now. “And if you move my body as you move yours—yeah, like that, and then—yeah, pull me— yes, perfect. Perfect.”

Sokka keeps his words low and even and constant, a steady stream until he finally hears the harsh edge of Zuko’s breaths even out, until eventually he feels Zuko’s tension unwind as much as it ever does. Sokka keeps speaking, though, quiet assurances and nonsense until Zuko has moved them through the motions over and over and over again, enough times to finally shake off whatever memories were riding him. Enough for Sokka to actually be able to complete the spin on his own, by the time he has to leave, which puts the ghost of a smile on Zuko’s face even if Sokka suspects that he’ll never be able to bring himself to actually use this particular technique ever again.

&#45;-

Sokka glances up as Aang flops down at the breakfast table, taking in the dark circles under his eyes and the tightness of his features and the uncharacteristic lack of enthusiasm for the day. Sokka hates how Aang seems to be wearing himself down against Ba Sing Se’s bureaucracy the longer and longer they spend in the city. It must be getting bad, for Aang to be looking like this.

Sokka would normally let Katara field whatever mood this is, but she and Toph already left for some girl’s thing and it’s not like Sokka can just sit here and let Aang…brood. An airbender isn’t meant for brooding.

“The porridge is good this morning,” Sokka offers, which is…really a stellar start. Just great. Yue must be laughing at him.

“Thanks,” Aang mutters, staring at the pot for longer than is strictly necessary before finally reaching to serve himself.

“How’d you sleep,” Sokka asks around a mouthful of his own breakfast, feigning casualness about as well as Toph does.

“Okay,” Aang grumbles, wiping a stray bit of porridge off the table.

“And how are you?”

“Okay.” A little more snappiness this time.

“You sure about that?”

“I’m angry all the time,” Aang says tonelessly as he stirs honey into his bowl.

“That sounds about right,” Sokka sighs, because he isn’t Katara and he has no idea how to cheer Aang out of a mood like this.

“I wish I wasn’t, but I don’t know how to stop,” Aang says, words tight like he’s mad about that too. Sokka winces in sympathy. He’s more than familiar with the way resenting your own emotions makes having them so much worse.

“Why do you need to stop,” Sokka asks his bowl, making a show of deciding if he should sprinkle in more nuts.

“Anger isn’t a healthy emotion to hold onto. It distorts the mind and tethers the body to negative thoughts that you should let go to achieve balance.” Aang intones, clearly quoting.

“I wouldn’t say you’re holding onto it,” Sokka says after a brief struggle, not trying to debate pacifist free-from-all-materialism philosophy from his own position of being totally willing to throw down to defend his stuff. “It seems pretty justified, to me.”

Aang looks up in surprise, spoon pausing halfway to his mouth.

“It’s okay to be angry, Aang.” Sokka isn’t sure if the airbender needs to hear it, but it can’t hurt to remind him.

“Maybe,” Aang frowns, skeptical. “You’re used to it, though.”

“Huh?”

“Zuko’s angry all the time,” Aang says, giving his porridge a moody stir.

“Oh,” Sokka takes a moment to mentally prepare for the shift in topic. “Well. Sure. But…not as much, anymore.” He takes a moment to consider their afternoons. “Anger isn’t really the, um, dominant emotion.”

Aang blushes slightly but rolls his eyes. “That’s good, right?” He asks around a mouthful.

“Yeah.” Though…also weird.

“You don’t sound sure,” Aang says, a neutral observation that lets Sokka choose what to share, instead of pulling it out of him. Sokka gives him a sideways look. How did Aang get so good at turning the tables on a heart-to-heart?

“No, I…I’m not upset about it, or anything,” he says slowly, trying to sort out his thoughts and aware that he isn’t really managing to convey the issue. “It’s just…Zuko isn’t as angry anymore.”

“And that’s a bad thing?” Aang wrinkles his face in confusion.

“I don’t know.” Sokka pokes at his mostly empty bowl. “I guess I’m not all that convinced that he stopped having reasons to be.” Just like Sokka doesn’t entirely believe that Zuko is truly any more relaxed, for all his lack of crackling tension.

“Maybe he just learned a more productive way to deal with it.” Aang sounds guilty for not being able to do that himself, and maybe a little jealous of Zuko’s emotional maturity.

Sokka considers, briefly, the idea that Zuko might have learned healthy coping mechanisms in the past few months. “…Yeah, no. I don’t think that’s it.”

But it’s definitely *something*. Zuko doesn’t shout as much, or stomp around, or slam doors. And it’s not like Sokka *wants* him spitting mad and on the verge of losing his shit at all times. It just...Zuko demanded your attention, before, whether you wanted to give it to him or not. And now he seems…muted, somehow, outside of when they’re crashing through his bedroom door. Entirely capable of fading into the background and being overlooked, but maybe not entirely willing.

Sokka used to be unable to tear himself away from all that passion Zuko seemed to feel so strongly, but he's startled to realize that he even misses the way Zuko could never seem to express it all, and the way Zuko would crash through life, feelings spilling out over everything despite his best efforts to hold them back. Shining bright and impossible to look away from even as he blinded.

“Do you think Ba Sing Se changes you,” Sokka asks abruptly, setting his bowl down a little more forcefully than he intended.

“What?” Aang startles, fumbling his grip on his own breakfast.

“Do you think that being in a place like Ba Sing Se makes it hard to stay true to yourself?”

“How so?” Aang frowns.

“It’s so…insulated. Protected,” Sokka tries his best to explain even though he has less a fully formed thought to share and more a nagging worry.

“Like there’s nothing outside the walls?”

Sokka nods in relief that Aang gets it. “Yeah. And we know that it’s there, but…Do you think you can still become complacent? Without even realizing it? Like you just…start not remembering anymore that there’s more out there?”

“Maybe,” the Avatar says after a long moment. “Would you know, though, either way?”

Maybe not, and Sokka suddenly finds that he doesn’t want to say that, for risk of reigniting the anger that Aang seems so afraid of.

Is that what happened to Zuko? Could it be happening to them, too? The four of them spend their time training and exploring and waiting for the Earth King to let them know he’s ready to see them, day after day after day. Sokka isn’t entirely sure that’s the approach they would have taken months ago, back when they scoured the coast of the North Pole to force their way into a city that didn’t want to be found.

Sokka is afraid that the answer is yes, because sitting here in front of far more food than they could ever eat, in a house far bigger than they could ever need, Sokka can’t think of what else they can *do* in Ba Sing Se other than this. They’ve already divided up the city, already search every day for hours, already follow every lead they can no matter how small in case this is the one thing that finally brings them to Appa, in case this is the critical piece of information that will let that last part of Sokka’s plan fall into place.

Sokka doesn’t have any other ideas than this, and that fact makes fear settle low and festering in his stomach. He thinks the answer might be ‘yes.’

&#45;-

“Oh, wait. Hold on.”

Sokka pauses in the doorway, glancing back in confusion because they have all their clothes back on, they have Zuko’s swords, they have water. They should be good to go train.

“I almost forgot,” Zuko says, digging around his corner of the room. “Here.”

Sokka stares at the packet in Zuko’s hand, pulse reacting to the familiar word. “You got me food?”

“Yeah,” Zuko shrugs, like it’s nothing, waggling the bundle when Sokka doesn’t move to take it. “It’s jerky.” A pause. “Meat.” Uncertain, now. “You were hungry last time…”

“You’re always feeding me,” Sokka murmurs, equal parts exasperated and confused and wondering as he finally reaches out to take what Zuko is offering.

“What?”

“Nothing,” Sokka sighs, shaking his head. Of course Zuko wouldn’t be marking all those moments like Sokka does. “Thanks.” He watches the familiar relaxation of Zuko’s shoulders as he unwraps the bundle and takes a bite. “It’s good.”

Zuko grunts in satisfaction, intent gaze finally leaving Sokka’s face as he shoos Sokka out the door.

“Wait,” Sokka says around a mouthful as he starts down the narrow, dim stairs. “Did you get this just because I told you once that I liked meat?” Sokka can hear Zuko’s shrug, in the rustling of fabric, can easily picture his so-what confusion. “What do you want, then?”

A thinking silence, then Zuko brushes barely-there fingers over Sokka’s shoulder. “You.”

Sokka glances back and rolls his eyes, even as his pulse flutters at the reply. “I meant to eat.”

Zuko’s glance is shy, quick, molten. “…You.”

“I meant *food*,” Sokka protests, face on fire like Zuko clearly wanted, playing up his indignation because it makes Zuko’s mouth curl into an almost-smile. He ignores the warm, happy thing in his chest. It’s probably just the sun, as they step outside. Or something like that.

&#45;-

Zuko glances at the new shift schedule on his way to grab the latest order, checking to make sure all the trades he negotiated last week will still work and nearly tripping over his own feet as he registers what he’s reading. Zuko turns toward Uncle with enough sharpness that Sung-min spins right around in the doorway and heads back to the floor with his tray of dirty dishes.

“Your shift changed,” Zuko accuses, narrowing his eyes at Uncle’s broad back.

“Hm. Yes, it did,” Uncle agrees placidly, measuring leaves into one canister of tea, then another.

“Why,” Zuko demands, not even trying to keep the hard edge of anger out of his tone. Good Nephews get to be upset when their Uncles try to disappear without saying anything.

Uncle turns to give him a considering look, the silence stretching long enough that Zuko starts to wonder if Uncle is actually going to refuse to share his whereabouts as some kind of life lesson. “There is a pai sho tournament,” he finally says. “In the Middle Ring. I’ve been invited to participate.”

“…Pai sho,” Zuko repeats numbly, tensing against the ribbons of dread weaving between his ribs.

“Yes,” Uncle smiles. “It is a great honor, just to be recognized.”

“Because of your pai sho.”

“I never dreamed I would receive an invitation to a tournament!”

“To play pai sho.”

“Yes, Nephew.” Uncle shoots him a mostly-happy-but-a-little-bit-confused glance at Zuko’s repetition. They both know Zuko doesn’t like repeating himself any more than he ever did. “Would you care to join?”

“No.” The response is automatic, tight, as Zuko watches Uncle open a new order of tea leaves. When would Uncle have become known to anyone in the Middle Ring, let alone to someone with the clout to invite him to a pai sho tournament? Did that somehow happen in the teashop without Zuko noticing? When Zuko wasn’t here? Zuko thinks of the last pai sho gave he saw Uncle play, the one back in that oasis town, and feels ill.

Uncle is quietly humming as he begins laying out the leaves for all his blends, as if he doesn’t notice that the world is trying to tilt off its axis. Zuko braces against the earth-shaking feeling, the finally-impossible-to-keep-ignoring whisper that maybe Uncle has been living his own life this whole time, parallel to Zuko’s instead of part of it.

The sensation is more than shock that Uncle’s world doesn’t revolve around Zuko. It’s a crack in the bedrock that Zuko rebuilt his life on, to actually consider that Uncle might have had his own reasons for wanting to attach himself to a globe-trotting quest for the Avatar. There are too many fragile things balanced on that foundation for Zuko to be able to afford questioning its strength, for Zuko to allow himself to start wondering if the reason Uncle has been concerned lately about Zuko’s shift trading is because Zuko suddenly being around in the evenings and not the afternoons is…inconvenient, to Uncle’s life.

*Enough*.

Zuko can’t do this. Not at all, and especially not here. He forces his snarl into something more like a scowl and grabs his tray, stalking onto the shop floor and ignoring Sung-min’s flustered squeak of surprise. He can’t afford to think about Uncle potentially rearranging his shifts so that Zuko isn’t an inconvenience, without even planning to say a word to Zuko about it. So Zuko will just think about making Uncle’s absence convenient for him, instead.

&#45;-

“What are you doing tomorrow night,” Zuko growls as he grabs Sokka’s hand and hauls him into the alley, needing to get the fuck away from the fucking teashop as fast as fucking possible.

“What the—why?” Sokka jogs a few steps to keep up. “What’s going on?”

“Uncle is taking the day off work tomorrow and won’t be back until the next day.” Zuko is aware that he sounds distinctly less than pleased about it.

“What’s he doing?”

“Some pai sho thing.”

“All day?”

“And all night,” Zuko hisses, and he should probably try to act a little more excited about the fact considering what he’s trying to ask.

“Why--Oh. *Oh*. Ohhh.”

Zuko huffs out a reluctantly amused breath. At least Sokka got it, anyway. “Are you busy?”

“…Not anymore.”
