Okay? You’ve never—Zuko, breathe. Breathe for me, okay? Can you do that?”

Zuko…can’t do that. He can barely register that Sokka…isn’t mad? Is gripping him with urgency, not with anger? Is…is saying it's fine? That everything has *been* fine?

“I trust you, Zuko,” Sokka says firmly, thumbs drawing gentle circles over Zuko’s wrists. “And your control. I'm not asking to stop. Not unless you want to.”

The words don’t hit at first, but when they do Zuko sags forward over their hands, folding himself around the burning relief in his gut and barely managing to quiet his desperate gasps for air. Sokka isn’t asking to leave, or for Zuko to go. Zuko still isn’t sure *what* he’s asking, but as long as Sokka is staying Zuko can figure it out. It will be fine, as long as he isn’t leaving. But…

“You shouldn’t.” Zuko finally forces out, voice low and harsh with he is uncomfortably aware is unshed tears. “Trust me. Fire…”

“I shouldn’t?” Sokka’s words are quiet, almost conversational, thumbs still circling the bones of Zuko’s wrists. “You know, I didn’t even know firebending could be about heat and not just flames, not until you showed me.” Sokka shifts to grab one of Zuko’s hands, tracing the shape of his fingers and the lines that thread across his palm. “Do you remember that first time? When we were on the ship, and you brought me dinner?”

“I remember,” Zuko whispers. He remembers everything that involves Sokka, especially from back then when everything was a ‘first’ to be treasured and hoarded and protected.

“You sat down on the floor with me,” Sokka continues anyway, the quiet awe in his voice making Zuko shudder. He is already stretched too taut to be able to absorb something so unexpected. “And you concentrated on that bowl, and held it in your palms, and like it was no big deal did a thing I didn’t even know was possible. It was amazing.” Zuko flushes at his words, something in him cringing and bewildered to receive admiration for something that was…nothing. “Even in just those few days, seeing what you could do with heat at the start and what you could do with it at the end? You got so much better by the time...And now?” Sokka laughs, self-conscious and wry. “Zuko, you’re so good at it. Your control is incredible. I trust you.”

“It’s just a parlor trick,” Zuko mutters, squirming and glad for the darkness to hide his discomfort even though he’s pretty sure Sokka can feel it anyway with how they are sitting tangled together. “I only learned because I couldn’t do real bending.”

“What does that mean?” Sokka almost never lets statements like that go, and Zuko should have known better than to make it in the first place if he didn’t want to explain.

Zuko sighs, looking for words. “After I was…banished. I couldn’t firebend for a long time. Too long.”

“Because you were injured?”

“…Because I was afraid to,” Zuko forces out, words matter of fact despite the familiar throb of shame whenever he thinks about it. He tries to focus on the feel of Sokka’s fingers continuing their slow massage over his hand, instead of the memory of desperately needing to escape his own inner flame.

“That makes sense,” Sokka says quietly, and Zuko can’t help shifting restlessly, away and then immediately back because he doesn’t want to pull away. He knows Sokka probably means the words as an assurance, but it’s still nearly unbearable to remember that he’d ever been so frightened of his own fire in the first place.

“It was awful,” Zuko mutters. He can feel the memory of the stares like they’re still on his back, the murmuring too quiet to hear when his ears were still ringing day and night, the way each flinch would send his hard-fought balance reeling again. “It’s not like I was any good to begin with, and then—” Zuko forces himself to take a deep breath before his agitation stokes his inner flame any higher. “It’s dangerous, too, not to bend for a long time like that. Things don’t…sit right. Inside you.”

“Fire is hungry.”

Zuko grunts in acknowledgment, relieved that he doesn’t have to explain that part, at least. The way unused fire coils and grows and takes on a life of its own, desperate for anything to consume until it starts to feel like it’s eating away at the borders of your very self. “I couldn’t —I could barely even be within touching distance of a candle, for a long time.”

Which was hard. The *Wani* had been full of tight corridors and torches and other firebenders and dark spaces that needed to be lit. Zuko had only been saved by his affinity, honed by years with Azula, for finding the places that no one else ever went.

“So Uncle taught me about heat,” Zuko continues, taking a forcibly even breath through the memories of what that learning actually entailed. “It’s still fire sense, but different enough that it was fine. It’s not as…in need of restraint. Usually.” Because Zuko can manage to fuck anything up, as it turns out, given the opportunity. “And I could barely even touch a fire without…panicking. Even if it was far away from me.”

And no one in their right mind is willing to be around a panicked firebender for long. Zuko had been acutely aware of the limited tolerance he was working with when it came to his crew. He could be a nuisance or a frustration as long as he was useful in some way, but he could never let himself become a *problem*.

“So Uncle just…kept teaching me. And eventually, I learned. It’s barely good for anything, though. It’s not like anyone needs to keep warm in the Fire Nation.” And now all Zuko uses it for, outside of Sokka, is *tea*. “But…I got used to it after long enough. Enough that I could touch the heat of a flame. And then the flame itself. And eventually I could use my own fire, again.”

“That was very brave,” Sokka says and Zuko scoffs. Nothing about those months was anything other than a grim, shameful slog back toward bare competency.

“It was,” Sokka insists. “A lot of people have experiences like that and never get over it. There was an old man in my village. He fell through the ice when he was young. It happens, sometimes. The ice is weaker than you think, or you don’t realize you’re walking over an old air hole. Decades later, he still couldn’t bring himself to walk out onto the ice, even in the heart of winter. A lot of people never get over the things that happen to them.”

Zuko might be able to appreciate Sokka’s words more if he actually *was* over what had happened to him. Still, he allows himself a spark of warmth over the fact that Sokka tried, that Sokka might think of him that way, even if it's not true.

Zuko turns his hands, gently dislodging Sokka’s grip so that he can take Sokka’s hand in his own, now, his turn to trace the roughness of calluses and the length of Sokka’s fingers. Sokka's skin is cool as always against his own and a tendril of familiar heat slides underneath Zuko’s skin, wanting to reach out and change that fact.

Now…might be a good time. To mention this. Since they’re already neck-deep in uncomfortable revelations, the past few days. And since Sokka wanted to talk about consent. And control.

“About the heat stuff,” Zuko starts, not really knowing how he’s going to continue but sure that if he doesn’t get the words out now then he’ll talk himself out of saying anything at all again.

“Yeah?”

“I have something to tell you.”

“Okay,” Sokka says. His voice is easy and relaxed, but Zuko can feel the nearly imperceptible twitch of his hand.

“I haven’t known how to bring it up,” Zuko admits, glancing somewhere over Sokka’s shoulder because even in the darkness he can’t quite bring himself to look Sokka in the face for this. Sokka and Zuko talk a lot, but the landscape of things they mutually skirt around is vast.

“You can tell me,” Sokka assures him, and Zuko ruthlessly orders himself to stop stalling.

Zuko dives in, not allowing himself to think about what might come from this because if he does then he’ll never be able to say it. “Do you remember when you were sick, on the *Wani*?”

“…Yeah,” Sokka says after a surprised beat. “I mean, not like the actual stuff, I was pretty out of it. But that it happened, sure.”

“You had a fever.”

Sokka nods, heard and felt more than seen.

“And we needed to get it down.”

“The frogs.”

Zuko half-smiles at the audible distaste in Sokka’s voice before forcing himself to continue. “And before that. We tried other stuff. Like medicine. And…bending.”

“What?” Sokka’s hand twitches again under Zuko’s fingers. But doesn’t pull away. Zuko fights the urge to preemptively cling.

“You were too hot,” Zuko explains, hating the sudden smallness of the words, hating the way his inner fire is going thready and uncertain at the edges. “And…I know how to transfer heat.”

“…Okay.”

“I spent a long time trying to keep your fever down. Trying to kind of…siphon off the heat, I guess, from where it was coming from.” Zuko can feel the flutter of Sokka’s pulse in his wrist as it picks up speed. He swallows down the anxious lump in his throat and forces himself to finish. “And after I stopped, I could still…feel that.”

Sokka is silent for a long time. Long enough that Zuko has time to swing wildly between fear and tentative relief and back toward hysteria again.

“Zuko,” Sokka finally says, words slow and precise. “I’m not a bender. And I’m definitely not a firebender. I don’t know what that means.”

*Fuck*.

“Oh—Sorry. Okay. So…” Of course Zuko can’t even confess his sins the right way. “Firebenders have an inner flame. You know about that?”

“Yeah,” Sokka replies, in a way that really means ‘kind of,’ which Zuko is familiar with since he does it all the time.

“Most people have…something.” Even Zuko can tell that wasn’t exactly helpful. “It’s not all the same, but everyone has…chi, I guess. And bending is about the movement of chi, and channeling it, and following it.” Zuko glances up, even though Sokka can’t see it, and Sokka nods, even though he doesn’t know Zuko is looking. “There's this move called the breath of fire, where you turn your bending inward and move your own chi to raise your heat. And what I did with you was…the opposite.”

“Turning your bending outward…”

“To move your chi,” Zuko finishes through a sticky web of nervousness, licking suddenly dry lips and bracing himself for Sokka’s reaction without having any idea what that reaction might be.

“And you can still feel that? My…chi?”

Zuko nods, sharp, getting ready.

“What…Zuko, what does that mean? I don’t—is it bad? Are you okay?”

Zuko lets out a small, unhappy noise that Sokka still doesn’t get it even while a corner of him trips over the fact that Sokka would be worried for him, first. “It means I can feel you the way I can feel fire.”

Sokka is silent, waiting.

“The way your sister can feel water.”

Sokka’s hand goes stiff in his own, and Zuko thinks with tight sadness that Sokka's finally starting to understand.

“What…Zuko, I’m not a fire. What does…I don’t understand.” Zuko *hates* the edge of uncertainty and concern in Sokka’s voice, hates that he’s the reason for it, the reason that Sokka is suddenly sounding off-balance and unconfident.

“I can show you?” Zuko offers. He doesn’t have any words left and just—he needs Sokka to *understand* so that they can get to the part where Sokka *reacts,* and Zuko can figure out if he’s destroyed this thing between them before even figuring out what it is.

“I—yes, okay. Okay. Show me.”

Zuko feels a bolt of relief that Sokka still trusts him enough to allow Zuko this, especially when Sokka doesn’t fully grasp what ‘this’ is yet except that it makes Zuko nervous. Zuko gently disentangles their hands, kindling a small flame so that Sokka can see clearly. His eyes sting at the sudden light, Sokka’s worried face appearing cast in flickering gold and shadow.

Zuko raises his other hand to hover over Sokka’s chest and lets his awareness stretch out beyond his own skin. Sokka’s not-fire is right there, bright and vibrant as ever, blazing across Zuko’s fire sense. He wraps his control around it, painfully careful, and takes a moment to sync his breathing before coaxing the brightness to grow in time with his inhale, settling it back down to its normal intensity on his exhale, just like he would with a candle.

Zuko devotes his full focus to unwinding his fire sense then, spooling it back beneath his skin and extinguishing the flame in his palm with the withdrawal. The darkness sweeps back in and Zuko waits, feeling the stillness of Sokka’s body pressed against his own like an ache in his bones.

“That—I—you’ve done that before,” Sokka finally says, the words tight with something like recognition.

“Yes,” Zuko whispers, hunching over as the edge of…accusation?...in Sokka’s words twists in his gut.

“All the way—Spirits, even back at the abbey?”

“I didn’t…I wasn’t sure, back then.” Zuko hates that he can’t deny it. “I thought I was imagining it.”

“You—fuck. Fuck, Zuko.” Sokka shoves his hands through his hair as Zuko flinches from the words, the panic buzzing in his ears making it hard to concentrate on Sokka’s tone. “What the fuck.”

“I’m sorry,” Zuko whispers, ragged, offering what he can. “I didn’t—I didn’t know that that would happen. I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to…”

“Can you control me?” Sokka’s voice cracks and Zuko feels it like a knife. “Like how you can control fire? Can you make me—”

“No! No, no, no,” Zuko rushes to assure him, needing to make sure Sokka understands and cursing that he needs to rely on words right now when they’ve never come easy. “I can’t make—it’s not—I’m just…attuned. Really attuned. I…I can find you, if you’re within the range of my fire sense. I can feel you.” He pauses, licking his lips before handing over the only thing he has left. “You can…I think you can fight it.”

“…How?” Sokka’s voice is cautious in a way that makes Zuko want to haul Sokka into his arms and tuck him against his chest and never let him go. He wishes he knew if that would be welcome, right now.

“I…I’m not sure,” Zuko admits, hating himself for never pressing Uncle on this, for not being ready to give Sokka what he needs. “Uncle mentioned it, once.” And Colonel Mongke had definitely resisted. “We can practice?”

“Okay,” Sokka sighs in something that might be relief. “That’s—alright. That’s good. Can… can other firebenders do this?” Sokka sounds like he’s trying not to be terrified of the answer.

“I don’t think so,” Zuko hedges. “It’s…a heat thing.” And for all its uselessness, no one knows heat quite like Zuko does. “I can try to stop it,” Zuko offers, guilt preemptively prickling down his ribs, because he isn’t actually sure if he *can*. “If you want. I’d…have to actively think about it. But I can try. I can do it.” For Sokka, he’d make it happen.

“No, it’s…fine.”

Zuko nearly collapses back in relief that Sokka isn’t pushing him away, the fact that he would fall away from Sokka the only thing keeping him upright. Zuko doesn’t know if he should take Sokka’s uncertain words the way he is hearing them, as a reassurance and, but everything in him is melting under a wave of intense gratefulness. Including his self-restraint. “I wasn’t sure if this was why…”

“What?” Sokka prompts when Zuko trails off as his mind catches back up with his tongue.

“…Nothing.”

“Zuko.”

He sighs. “Why you liked…heat?”

Sokka snorts, surprising them both with his sudden amusement. “Zuko. Trust me,” he says dryly, seeming to set aside the last of his worry. For now, at least. “I liked that *way* before I got sick.”

“Oh.” Zuko blinks, curiosity and surprise and the return of Sokka’s levity chasing away most of his lingering fear. “That’s…good.”

Sokka breathes out another amused noise before reaching for Zuko, hauling him forward until Zuko is sitting fully in Sokka’s lap, clasped hands between them, breathing in Sokka’s leather-metal-sunshine-tea scent. The tea is new, but it still helps something in Zuko’s chest unwind, still evens out the edges of his inner flame.

“Thank you for telling me,” Sokka whispers against his neck, lips barely brushing skin.

“I’m sorry it took me so long.” Zuko turns his face into Sokka’s hair, nuzzling at the border of soft strands and bristly undercut.

“Some things are hard to say,” Sokka murmurs, and Zuko sighs in acknowledgment, sagging, because there is so much still that he can’t bring himself to give voice to.

## Chapter 22: Compromised

### Text

The man is back.

Zuko goes immobile for a beat when he sees that *fucking* man. The one who distracts Minji, or flusters her, or bothers her, or whatever the fuck it is that he does to her that Zuko absolutely refuses to deal with today.

Zuko whirls back into the kitchen with a snarl and Minji stutters to a halt, stopping in her tracks as Zuko looms in front of her.

“Give me that.”

“What?” Minji frowns, flushed and already fucking *distracted*. Zuko growls and snatches the tray from her hands. He ignores her gasp of surprise, or outrage, or whatever it is he doesn’t *care*. Zuko cares about not having yet another shift with her fumbling and making mistakes and being off her game when Zuko is still fighting for his equilibrium after everything with Uncle and Sokka. Uncle who he still can’t entirely look at straight on. And Sokka who still wants to do this thing they’re doing, who said things were okay, but who also didn’t *stay.*

No. Minji cannot be off her game today. Zuko is already off enough for every single person in this fucking establishment.

Zuko stomps out onto the floor, tray in hand. The shop’s regulars recognize his expression and fall back in front of him like a wave as he walks up to the man’s table. The guy looks up, a sneer twisting his features when he sees Zuko instead of Minji, and *fuck that.* Zuko sets his face into a glare and stares him in the eye and holds the tray straight out and drops it onto the table a bare inch beneath the height where things will start to shatter. Zuko figured out that distance his first week.

Cups leap off saucers. Half-steeped, boiling tea sloshes out of its pot, spilling over the now-disgustingly soggy pastries and onto the table. The man scrambles back to avoid a lapful of scalding chai sencha blend because on top of everything else he *always* orders the most absolutely disgusting custom pots that make Uncle nearly *cry* to mix for him.

“What the fuck, man,” the guy sputters, the entire shop frozen, staring at the wreckage.

“Enjoy your *tea*,” Zuko growls, slapping a single napkin onto the table and putting every single piece of feeling he’s ever had about tea and life and everything else into the word.

&#45;-

It’s one of the rare mornings when Sokka and Katara are together instead of trying to divide the sprawling expanse of Ba Sing Se between them. One of Katara’s list of government contractors had turned into a potential lead, and by silent agreement, neither of them had wanted the other to go without backup to confront what could just be an exotic pet dealer to the wealthy or might be some kind of black-market smuggler. Assuming they can find the guy, of course, because so far, his operation is nowhere to be found.

Which does seem to suggest smuggler.

“It’s not even late morning,” Sokka grumbles as they stare down another empty warehouse. “How’d they move all this stuff between yesterday and today?”

“Someone tipped them off.” Katara’s tone is grim.

“As if we’re even worth giving a tip about,” Sokka sighs, scrubbing his hands over his face. His cynicism creeps out when Aang isn’t around. “You said there’s one more place he’s been doing business out of?”

“Yeah. Let’s go.”

“If we woke up early to look at a bunch of empty lots…” Sokka mutters, not even bothering to finish the thought as he scowls down the passing alleys just in case a massive air bison is tucked into one.

“You’re cranky this morning,” Katara comments.

“I’m not—” It’s not even worth finishing the protest. Sokka is cranky. There’s no reason not to be. “This is just such shit. I can’t believe we got up early to find nothing, *again*.”

Katara gives him a sideways look. “Why are you so tired? You didn’t get home *that* late last night.”

“I didn’t sleep well,” Sokka admits. “I was just thinking, I guess.”

“Don’t hurt yourself.”

“Fuck you, too,” Sokka replies without rancor. He really set that one up for her.

“But seriously,” Katara glances around a corner with the wariness they’ve both learned in Ba Sing Se. “Did things go okay?”

“Yeah, I guess,” Sokka sighs, not quite sure what to say between the crippling embarrassment and the nearly yelling at Zuko’s uncle and the whole I-can-maybe-kind-of-control-your-life-force thing. Zuko is expecting him back, so… “It was fine.”

Katara makes a skeptical little noise in the back of her throat, because Sokka sounded about as convincing as he feels. “Just making sure.”

“I appreciate it.”

“I want you to be happy,” Katara adds, a reminder for both of them before she starts taking them down a series of surprisingly narrow alleys for the Middle Ring, pausing at each intersection to check her direction against the sun.

“Thank you.”

“And I want you to be safe,” Katara says over her shoulder, hands on her waterskin as she darts around the corner, braced for a fight.

“I’ve noticed,” Sokka says dryly as she waves the all-clear. Katara’s always-ready protective anger is one of the few constants in his life lately, it feels like. “I am trying, you know.”

“I know,” Katara mutters, giving him a quick, guilty look. “I’m sorry if I’m being overbearing. I just…it’s hard to step back.”

“I know we’re both used to spending all our time together, but—"

“I don’t think you’re being yourself, with this,” Katara cuts in. “It worries me.”

“…What do you mean?”

“You aren’t planning, Sokka,” she sighs, halting at the next intersection to face him full on. “You always plan, even things that don’t need it.”

“That’s not tru—”

“What did your servant character when we infiltrated the palace want to study at university?”

“Zoology, obviously. Why?”

“You plan *everything*,” Katara repeats, rolling her eyes. “But with Zuko—” She manages to say the name without tripping over it, for once. “—you aren’t…you don’t seem like you’re thinking ahead.”

“I’m being careful,” Sokka protests, splitting his gaze between her face and the alleyways behind her, because he’s a *careful* kind of person. “I don’t tell him any eclipse stuff, and he doesn’t—"

“I know, I know,” Katara assures him. “I know you wouldn’t slip with any of that. But…are you being careful with you?”

“…What do you mean?”

“Sokka, Aang might be fine, and we might be fine, and the mission might be fine, but *you* still might get hurt. And you aren’t acting like you’re looking ahead to see it.”

Sokka shifts, uncomfortable. She…isn’t exactly wrong, which makes the earnest concern on her face that much harder to stomach. Sokka’s been very actively *not* letting himself think too far forward, in fact. Planning ahead skirts too close to admitting that he wants things that he can’t let himself hope for, and Spirits, fuck, he is starting to sound like Zuko. Shit.

“Katara, I don’t know what I’m doing.” Sokka finally says, tugging restlessly on his wolf tail. “I’ve never done…this, before.” It still doesn’t feel comfortable, admitting to Katara that he doesn’t know what he’s doing.

“Yue..?”

“It wasn’t the same.” He cuts her a quick glance, but her expression is quiet, expectant, waiting for more. “I was …” He waves a hand through the air. “Hurting too much.”

Katara digests that, rocking onto her toes, for once not immediately letting lose with sharp-edged protectiveness even though they both know Zuko was the reason he was hurting. “Are you still?”

Sokka blinks. “I…don’t know.”

“Maybe you need to figure that out.” She studies his face, then gives his wolf tail a gentle flick before turning back to the alley. “You can’t wall your feelings off forever.”

“It’d be nice,” Sokka mutters to himself, wincing when Katara catches the words anyway.

“You won’t be happy if you do, Sokka.”

“I won’t be happy if I stop and get hurt, either.” He isn’t going to fight her on the walling himself off part, not with the number of jokes Toph’s been landing about his ability to actually keep his emotions out of it like he said he would. Spirits, he’s an idiot.

“Well, one way you definitely won’t be happy, and the other maybe you will be. Your choice.”

Sokka stares at her back, vaguely disgruntled to hear something that feels so huge and tangled summarized so succinctly. He's the one *in* a...whatever he's in. When did Katara get so smart about relationships? And when did he get so dumb, to actually end up in a place where he’s making this choice again? And over Zuko, again. Spirits, Aunt Wu really read him right because apparently he has a real taste for self-inflicted idiocy. Like once his heart learned the shape of opening up to Zuko, Sokka lost his ability to hold it back when it already knows the way.

“Come on,” he finally mutters. “Where’s that warehouse again?”

Katara refuses to move, though, crossing her arms and ignoring his shameless attempt to change the subject. “It’s not just that, Sokka.”

He sighs. Isn’t ‘that’ already enough? “What do you mean?”

“It’s not just that you could get hurt. I don’t want you to get caught by surprise by other things, either.”

Sokka doesn’t even bother to ask this time, just lets her see his confusion.

Katara presses her fingers to her temples, blowing out a hard breath, her I-can’t-believe-I-have-to-explain-this pose. “What are you going to do if we have to fight his sister again? Or when we have to fight his father? Are you going to be able to do what you have to?”

Sokka can’t help the annoyance in his tone. “The plan comes first, Katara. I know that.” And Sokka would *love* to fight Zuko's father.

“Yeah, but—Sokka, if you don’t think ahead about that stuff, and consider it, and prepare yourself for it—are you going to be able to *do* it, when it happens? There’s a reason you over-prepare for everything.”

Sokka is still frozen in place when Katara sets out again. He belatedly gets his feet moving to scramble after her as a trickle of dread slithers down his spine. She’s…talking about things like yesterday. Where even though Sokka planned incessantly the night before, he still couldn’t come up with anything when Iroh asked him the most basic of questions, not when it was a question Sokka had been avoiding even within his own mind. But Katara is also talking about being…compromised. About being so deep underwater, regardless of his intentions, that Sokka doesn’t even notice the weight of it has changed him. Not until it’s time to act and he realizes he can’t. About being in so deep that Zuko is pulling Sokka off his axis without even meaning to, without either of them noticing until Sokka tries to find his balance.

Spirits, has it already happened?

Sokka’s been reassuring himself that he doesn’t need to get involved any deeper than he’s comfortable with, that he can walk away at any time if he needs to no matter what Toph says. But Sokka also just engaged in a deeply uncomfortable conversation with Zuko’s surrogate father figure because not doing so didn't seem like an option. Fuck, Sokka just found out that Zuko’s been sitting on the fact that he can control, to some extent, some…*thing* inside Sokka, the way he can control fire. That Zuko can *find* it, which…Spirits, all the way Zuko could have used *that.* And Sokka didn't walk away*,* even though he is *very* aware, much as he wishes he wasn’t, that one of the things Zuko can do with fire is *put it out.* Some part of Sokka still can’t stop flinching from the idea of being that vulnerable to Zuko, is maybe a little bit grateful that neither of them was particularly in the mood last night after all that talking. Sokka’s been vulnerable in so many ways to Zuko before, even in ways that involve fire—*especially* in ways that involve fire. But Sokka *chooses* that, and trusts Zuko to stop and…

Apparently, Sokka trusts Zuko to stop this, too.

…Shit.

Some part of Sokka that tries to be coldly logical points out that it’s far past the point where Sokka can try to claim that he *hasn’t* been changing and adapting and adjusting all along to make this thing with Zuko continue to feel okay to hold onto. Volunteering to be practiced on instead of running from what could be an eclipse-plan destroy vulnerability, deciding to bring Iroh spiced buns and get in his good graces instead of just suggesting another place to hook up where Iroh can't find them—these aren't sudden abberations, they're a pattern of behavior. They're what he's been doing this whole time.

Spirits, Sokka's been so wholly focused on not taking another blind leap when really he should have been watching for the slow slide that’s been happening whether he wanted it to or not. It’s almost even scarier for its gradualness. Sokka can look back and see each step of the way but somehow still stand here and have no idea if he is falling with Zuko or on his own again.

Maybe Toph wasn’t only teasing.

“Tui take it,” Katara suddenly mutters, echoing his feelings so perfectly that Sokka feels a momentary burst of alarm that she’s somehow in his head. He jolts back to the present—is that another sign that he’s compromised, being so distracted on a mission?—to see that their latest alleyway has dumped them out into a broad, open, empty square.

Sokka presses the heels of his hands to his eyes, shoving aside the weight of yet another dead end with practiced resignation. At least they both know what comes next, by this point.

“You want to canvass the square or try to talk to people?”

Katara gives him once-over. “I’ll take the people. You aren’t fit to talk to anyone yet.”

Sokka grunts in acknowledgment before beginning a careful sweep of the space, moving methodically over the cobblestones, looking for scraps of fur or slips of paper or any detritus left behind that might give them a hint of where to go next.

He doesn’t turn up anything more than splinters of wood, but Katara manages to find out that the Dai Li were seen in the area the night before, shortly before the whole operation moved.

“Moved where?” Sokka sighs, because that isn’t exactly something they can act on. Confirmation of what they already suspect, but they don’t really need more of that.

“I don’t know,” Katara folds her fists under her arms in frustration. “No one would say, if they even had any idea in the first place. Just something about a lake.”

“Right, just dump all animals into the lake,” Sokka mutters. “Hide ‘em all at the bottom until you need them. Makes perfect sense. Let’s dive right in.”

“Alright, Sarcasm Guy,” Katara rolls her eyes. “Let’s get back home. You need lunch. And maybe Toph and Aang found something.”

&#45;-

Practicing resisting Zuko’s chi-bending—Zuko doesn’t want to call it that, keeps insisting that it might not be chi, that its heat and close to fire. But Sokka refuses to keep being referred to as a ‘not-flame’—is more difficult than Sokka expects it to be. He was bracing himself for needing to control his anxiety and any potential fear at being so in someone else's control, because Sokka doesn't exactly think Zuko would draw a difference between fear in the abstract and fear of Zuko himself. He was ready to suck it up because he needs to learn to resist this and Zuko needs to learn what he's doing, even if Sokka is more than a little uncomfortable being an experimental bending test case.

And some part of him expected it to be difficult, too, for the usual reasons practicing anything with Zuko is difficult—because he's close, and warm, and so cute when he’s concentrating that it’s nearly unfair, and it’s all so *distracting*.

It *quickly* becomes apparent, though, that the real difficulty is the fact that Zuko actively moving the not-flame inside Sokka—shit, even he’s thinking of it that way, now, dammit— feels absolutely amazing. Zuko’s careful, intent stillness and singular focus on moving something beneath Sokka’s skin? The way Sokka’s body falls into rhythm with Zuko’s without him even needing to try? The liquid-feeling heat that Zuko kindles inside him and moves, like a kick somewhere between Sokka’s gut and his chest that he feels from fingertips to toes? Fuck, even just the knowledge, in those moments when he can be comfortable with the implications, of being so intimately within Zuko’s hold? The awareness that he’s been there for *months*, because now that Sokka is learning to recognize the feeling he spends more than one restless, achy night thinking of all the other times he's felt it.

Both of them agree that this particular kind of training needs to happen in private, after the first time. And Sokka can't deny that he's a little disappointed when Zuko immediately and resoundingly, at great volume, rejects the suggestions to bring this into bed. Sokka doesn't push against the hard, sharp edge of Zuko's refusal, even if he thinks he might daydream for the rest of his life about what it would feel like to move inside Zuko while Zuko tugs at his chi, to feel Zuko inside him in two ways, about what it could be like for Zuko to pull that not-flame brighter and higher in time with—

Well. Sokka is actually relieved, once he gets over the disappointment, that Zuko is willing to shut the suggestion down so decisively rather than bend around any of Sokka’s wants and desires. It's a reassurance after yesterday to get some evidence of that. And because it's only hearing the note of warning and genuine fear in Zuko’s voice that it occurs to Sokka really think about the fact that just because Sokka is the only one Zuko seems passively attuned to, doesn't mean Sokka's is the only almost-inner-flame out there that Zuko could control.

&#45;-

Sokka dawdles at the breakfast table past when he would normally leave for the day, waiting. Waiting longer than he expected, actually. He already ran through his schedule for the day, thought through the next books he needs to track down at the library for the invasion plan, noodled over some poetry he’s playing around with, and somehow—Sokka knows how— ended up daydreaming.

He caught Zuko at the tail end of a shift yesterday, interacting with a customer on his way out the door, and it had been…hilariously painful. Sokka has viewed Crown Prince Zuko as untouchable and strong and resolute for so long, and Zuko is all those things. But Zuko is also comically bad at dealing with strangers, and the fact that he works in customer service? Sokka couldn’t help but smile, watching the abrupt, awkward, short, uncomfortable way Zuko tried to extract himself from conversation with someone who just wanted to tell him how much they appreciated his help with the menu.

Sokka had ruefully considered, as Zuko visibly started edging backward, that Zuko might have actually been better at social interaction when he had all that stiff and shouty Prince stuff to fall back on. At least then Zuko could pretend to be above it all, or lean into etiquette and stuffy propriety. Watching Zuko fight down the urge to blow off a well-meaning middle-aged lady who clearly just wanted to pinch his cheeks? It's…endearing. The same way his prickliness is endearing, and his outrage over what Sokka is pretty sure is perfectly normal coworker behavior is endearing, and his earnestness and the full attention he gives anything he does, and—

“Save it for your bedroom, Lover Boy,” Toph grumbles as she slouches down at the table across from him.

Sokka is so deep in his thoughts that he openly startles despite sitting here waiting for her. And then he registers her words and flushes. For once Toph’s pointed call out is coming when he *isn’t* thinking about sex, just about…how much he likes Zuko.

…Next time he should probably just think about the sex.

“What?” Toph pauses with a piece of fruit halfway to her mouth. “Too flustered to say anything back?”

Sokka would like to just…not engage in any of this right now, not when he’s been waiting for her all morning and needs to get this done before he talks himself out of it. “Can I ask you a favor?”

Toph takes a giant bite, speaking with her mouth full as she sets one foot in the table with a studied kind of insolence. “You can *ask*.”

“You can hear my heartbeat?”

“I think we’ve established that by now.”

“So you can tell if I’m reacting to something, even if I don’t show it?”

Toph shrugs. “If you’re in range.”

“And how big is your range?” Sokka presses, hoping it's big enough for this.

Toph scowls in his general direction, openly suspicious. “Why?”

“I need your help,” Sokka admits. “With a plan I can’t ask Katara or Aang for help with.”

Toph takes another gigantic bite. “Why not?”

“Because you would do what needs to be done no matter what else was happening,” Sokka says, staring down at his clasped hands and watching from the corner of his eye as Toph goes still. “And I don’t know if they can.”

“What kind of plan,” she finally asks, slowly sitting upright and pressing both feet to the floor.

“The kind of plan where maybe someone needs to decide that you guys can’t trust me anymore. My judgment or decision making or whatever.” Toph’s eyebrows shoot up in surprise. “In case I’m…compromised.”

She wrinkles her nose in distaste for the idea. “Wouldn’t you know?”

“I hope so. But. Just in case. It’s good to have a plan.” And because Sokka has a sinking feeling that a big part of being compromised is not realizing that you are, and maybe not wanting it to stop once you do.

“It’s not magic,” she finally says with none of her usual bluster, openly unhappy. “It’s got its limits. I can’t read your mind.”

“I know.” *Thank the Spirits for that.*

Toph takes a deep breath, rubbing her palms over her legs. “Okay. Fine. What were you thinking?”

Sokka gives himself a moment to sag in relief, since Toph can’t see it. Then he starts sketching out his plan for how and when Toph would take him out of the equation, if it ever comes down to it. If it ever seems like Sokka can no longer see the choices that need to made or do the things that need to be done or put the Avatar's mission above all else. He hopes it will never actually but needed, but knows that it's always good to have a contingency, just in case.

&#45;-

Sokka is invited over for dinner. With Iroh. And Zuko. Zuko and Iroh. And Sokka. All together. Eating.

It's an invitation that Zuko delivers with eyes just a bit too-wide and voice just a bit too unsettled, and that Sokka receives with just a bit too much stunned silence. Zuko’s clearly still in no way comfortable with the two parts of his life finally coming together. Sokka can sympathize, but he braces himself anyway and accepts the invitation and walks to the Blooming Petal the next night like he’s preparing to head into battle.

He’s stupidly grateful that Iroh had suggested the Blooming Petal for dinner and not the apartment, because Sokka isn’t sure if he can ever be in that room with Iroh ever again. It’s a gesture that’s meant to make the night easier, probably. An offer of seemingly neutral ground that is thoroughly the General’s territory. A reminder, maybe, and a warning, possibly, of the extent of Iroh’s control over the spaces his nephew occupies.

Sokka shows up bearing spiced crackers—the closest thing he could find to fire flakes—and a small jar of fire peppers that he’d needed to wheedle Toph into helping him track down in the specialty stores in the Upper Ring. It’s a gesture that’s meant to recognize his status as a guest. An offering intended to cause that quiet, flustered pleasure of Zuko’s face because Sokka knows that fire flakes are his favorite and that he misses the tastes of home. It’s a reminder of his own, maybe, of the influence Sokka has over Zuko’s happiness. That Iroh might know Zuko, but that Sokka knows him too.

The General watches the exchange, making all the appropriate noises of thanks and excitement, offering a neutral smile when Sokka catches his assessing eye over the width of Zuko’s shoulders. Part of Sokka can't help hovering wary and ready for combat even as he indulges in a burst of satisfaction over being able to put that surprised half-smile on Zuko’s face.

Apparently he and Iroh are both still feeling each other out. And apparently they’re both hoping that Zuko won’t notice that he is the object of the borders Sokka and Iroh are trying to draw for each other.

“Nephew,” Iroh calls when Zuko stutters between going to Sokka’s side or his uncle’s as they move to the kitchen, all open uncertainty to anyone who knows how to read the set of his shoulders. “Come help me prepare the meal.”

Zuko relaxes at having a clear task, moving to trail Iroh toward the counter. Sokka follows, reaching out to skim his fingers whisper-light over Zuko’s palm, an echo of a clasped hand.

“Is there anything I can help with?” Sokka is passably decent at cooking, by this point, enough to be able to get through most prep work without having Katara chase him out of her way anymore.

“A guest cannot work, Master Sokka,” Iroh smiles, all amusement and hospitality. “Sit, sit! Enjoy your tea!”

Zuko shoots Sokka a sideways glance, like he’d prefer that the answer be ‘yes’ but isn’t going to say it in front of his uncle. Sokka hesitates. Is he reading too much into the General trying to draw a line around Sokka that says ‘visitor’?

Zuko shifts, deliberately drawing Sokka’s attention. He is angled toward Sokka, his gold eyes shy and intent as he pulls his apron over his head even though the shop is empty and he doesn’t have to wear it. But then, Zuko knows how much Sokka loves that apron and the sight of Zuko in it. It’s Zuko’s own quiet gesture toward the shared thing between them, like he’s plucking a chord for only Sokka to hear. A reminder as Zuko joins his uncle at the prep table, even if he doesn’t mean it as one, that Zuko can draw his own boundaries.

Sokka sips his tea and fidgets—beneath the table—his way through Iroh’s small talk about the weather and the city and tea varietals. Half of Sokka’s focus is going toward trying to appear confident and not nervous and not like an idiot in front of the General. The other half is centered on watching the way Zuko and Iroh interact. It’s unreasonably fascinating and reminds Sokka a bit too much that Zuko grew up in a palace—or a nest of dragons, fucking Aunt Wu and her poetic phrasing—and not necessarily in a family like Sokka understands it.

Sokka takes in the way Iroh keeps a careful eye on Zuko, watchful and assessing. Zuko always keeps Iroh in his periphery, too, especially when his uncle’s back is turned, tracking, gauging. Zuko seems comfortable with Iroh on his left side, but he’s still in almost constant motion that might appear restless and agitated if Sokka hadn’t already picked up the way Zuko’s pivoting and sharp turns always happen to open up his field of vision.

Sokka notes the way Iroh uses suggestion and calm observation and twisty sayings that must be some Fire Nation thing because Sokka can barely figure them out, anything except outright asking to get Zuko to do what he wants. And Zuko bristles and scowls and hisses protests and biting comments, shoving his uncle back with words even as he keeps Iroh close with ready compliance in the midst of his snarling.

It's...illuminating. Of what, Sokka isn't entirely sure yet. But definitely something.

When they finally settle to eat, the food is Earth Kingdom rather than Fire Nation and absolutely delicious, which Sokka is simultaneously delighted and slightly miffed about. Iroh *would* be a good cook, on top of everything else.

“Here, you want to—” Zuko gestures with his chopsticks, leaning over without prompting to show how Sokka can put all the various components into a single dish. Sokka smiles, warmth blooming in his chest at Zuko’s focus on ensuring Sokka gets the best meal possible, even if it means intricately explaining how to eat food Sokka’s been chowing down on for weeks by this point. Sokka glances up when his bowl is finally prepared to Zuko’s satisfaction to find Iroh watching them, expression quiet and thoughtful in a way that makes Sokka inexplicably want to blush.

“So Master Sokka, have you been exploring much of Ba Sing Se?” Iroh asks, all open and friendly once they are settled.

“A bit,” Sokka hedges after remembering to hastily swallow his mouthful instead of speaking through it. “There’s so much of it, it’s hard to know where to even start.” Particularly when you’re hunting for an air bison.

Iroh hums in agreement, smiling. “Do you have a favorite part so far?”

“Well,” Sokka says slowly, automatically seeking out Zuko as he considers his words and whether there’s some deeper question here. Zuko is staring down at his food, but his unscarred ear is cocked like he’s interested in Sokka’s answer. “The libraries have been really great.”

“You are a lover of literature, then?”

“Poetry,” Sokka admits, just managing not to jump when Zuko’s foot hooks around his ankle beneath the table and oh, Sokka is suddenly deeply delighted that the Blooming Petal uses chairs and benches instead of low tables and cushions.

“Oh? Do you have a favorite style?”

Iroh is an excellent conversationalist, as it turns out, especially when it comes to keeping up a three-sided discussion of poetry when one side does little more than grunt and offer various shades of scowl and grumbled comments when words are required. He knows about Fire Nation authors, which Sokka would have expected, but also about Water Tribe works that Sokka has never heard of before, quoting passages of unknown words set to a familiar, rolling rhythm that has Sokka quietly aching for nights around the fire back home. They find common ground in Earth Kingdom poetry, and Sokka forgets to hold onto his wariness as he falls into a debate of meter and style, and whether departing from traditional forms shows a lack of ability or an abundance of creativity, and whether the third Earth Kingdom transcendentalist movement even existed or was just the burgeoning abstract rationalism period hitting its stride.

“My nephew, of course, much prefers theater, to poetry,” Iroh smiles, unbothered by Zuko’s immediate glare.

Sokka looks to Zuko in surprise, catching the end of a side-eyed glance before Zuko ducks his head and grabs for more rice. It’s a statement intended to demonstrate Iroh’s familiarity with Zuko, maybe, showing off one of the little private things he knows about his nephew. But it’s also potentially an offering of sorts to Sokka, of this thing that makes Zuko happy that Zuko would never think to volunteer.

Sokka watches, bemused, as Iroh prods his nephew into more active participation by shifting the topic to recent productions of classical works. At first Sokka doesn’t think it’s going to be much of a discussion. Getting Zuko to talk about something when he’s feeling stubborn is harder than finding an air bison in Ba Sing Se, and Zuko has been far too edgy and tense to be in a talkative mood all night.

But then Zuko starts using more and more words—each of them more and more exasperated —in his replies and spending more and more time actually looking at his uncle instead of the table. Iroh, Sokka realizes, is deliberately making a series of increasingly outlandish statements until Zuko’s sense of outrage won’t let him keep quiet anymore. And Zuko grumbles and rolls his eyes and scoffs and never actually tells Iroh to stop what he’s doing as Iroh listens attentively and observes closely and accepts every inch that Zuko offers without ever drawing attention to it.

Sokka bites back a frown, trying to get a handle on what he’s seeing. It almost feels like Zuko’s annoyance with his uncle is…habitual. Not that flashes of it aren’t real, of course. Sokka’s eyes flick between them as they snarl and hum their way through a debate on adding ballads—"the stupidest thing I’ve ever heard in my life” and “a wonderfully creative display of modern inventiveness”—to political comedies. But Sokka is starting to see that both Zuko and his uncle have certain deep patterns of behavior. Starting over in Ba Sing Se—or whatever Iroh is calling it—didn’t reset their tendencies toward each other, even though Sokka can also see from the outside that for Zuko, at least, those habits don’t sit easily anymore.

Not that Zuko would ever say it. Both him and his uncle, Sokka thinks as he looks back over the night, are far too set into the habit of avoidance to lay something like that out so plainly.

Sokka sits back and sips his tea as somehow the conversation shifts and Zuko and Iroh start going back and forth over table manners, of all things. With Zuko chastising Iroh, which isn’t what Sokka would have expected. Is this some kind of royalty thing, the way uncle and nephew interact? Or a Fire Nation hierarchy thing? Maybe it’s just a Zuko and Iroh thing.

Sokka sighs to himself, thinking that both of them would probably benefit from a few more good, air-clearing talks. Sokka might even suggest it, if he didn’t know that it would kill Zuko dead on the spot to endure another one so soon.

&#45;-

“Would you care for a game of pai sho, Master Sokka?” Iroh asks, waving both Sokka and Zuko back into their seats as he starts gathering the empty dishes from dinner. “It has been a long time since we last played.”

“Ah, sure,” Sokka blinks, faintly surprised that Iroh is suggesting that the night continue even. Sure, the wariness between them had slowly started to fade over the course of the meal, but it’s not *gone*. “Can I help clean up?”

“No, no,” Iroh smiles, eyes bright with…mischief? “I can take care of it, and then get the board. Enjoy some tea with my nephew.”

Sokka cuts his eyes over to Zuko, who’s bright red up to his hairline at the comment. Yes, definitely mischief.

“Are you enjoying your tea?” Sokka murmurs once Iroh has bustled himself off across the room, gathering the dishes from dinner and from cooking and humming to himself— probably more loudly than necessary, but Sokka appreciates it—as he gets to cleaning.

“Shut up,” Zuko mutters, but the foot he has wrapped inside Sokka’s ankle gives a little tug and there’s no extra tension beyond what's usually there in the line of his shoulders.

“So,” Sokka takes a sip of his own tea just to see the flash of Zuko’s scowl. “Classical theater, huh?”

“So. Poetry, huh?”

Sokka grins, wanting to kiss the half-annoyed, half-teasing expression off Zuko’s face and not at all trusting Iroh to keep his back turned considering the man’s historical sense of timing. “Do you want to play pai sho?”

“No.” Zuko almost has the response out before Sokka finishes the question, and Sokka bites back a startled laugh at his immediate prickliness. “It’s a two-person game.”

“You could be on my team,” Sokka suggests, leaning his head against his fist and twisting in his chair so he can finally wrap his foot behind Zuko’s ankle in turn now that he doesn’t have to have perfect posture for Iroh anymore.

“No,” Zuko repeats, a little more insistent. Sokka can feel the hint of tension in the calf he’s now rubbing beneath the table, can see the barest stiffness in Zuko’s arms as he fiddles with his teacup. More than just annoyance, the way Zuko is always a little annoyed around tea… Discomfort?

“Do you not like pai sho?”

“No.” Zuko’s face is incredulous, like he can’t believe he needs to be asked.

“Do you not like pai sho more than you don’t like most things?” Sokka amends, grinning when Zuko has to take a beat to parse through the sentence before hitting him with a glower.

“I don’t want to talk about it,” Zuko finally mutters, shooting a quick glance toward Iroh, who’s still busy with cleanup. The tension is moving into his shoulders.

Sokka eye’s that tension. “Should I not play?” He asks slowly, trying to sort back over the conversation and figure out when, exactly, Zuko started to move from normal levels of vibrating annoyance to active stiffness.

“You can. It’s fine.” It doesn’t sound fine.

“I don’t want to do something that will upset you,” Sokka says, feeling like he’s echoing his words from the courtyard. Zuko’s sudden alarmed attention says that he hears it too.

“You won’t,” Zuko finally mumbles after seeming to reassure himself in whatever he sees on Sokka’s face even though his hands are still twitchy, restless. “It’s not that, it’s…”

“It’s..?’”

Zuko sighs, sitting back in his chair, arms crossed defensively even as his leg presses closer beneath the table, knee-to-knee now. Sokka tries not to be distracted by the contact. His hands itch to slip beneath the table and touch.

“Uncle has just…always had pai sho,” Zuko finally mutters, shooting another wary glance toward Iroh. “It’s his thing. Just his. Not…ours.”

“And that’s a bad thing?” Sokka is careful to keep his voice neutral, because he’s trying to understand and he can see that Zuko is already braced for judgment.

“…I hope not.” Zuko’s eyes drift to Iroh’s back again, something like concern or worry or maybe even fear shadowing his face. Shit, Sokka wishes he were seated on Zuko’s right, so Zuko couldn’t turn the unscarred side of his face away and hide his expression.

“Zuko,” Sokka eventually asks, pulling Zuko’s attention back from whatever he’s brooding on. “What do you want?”

“You.”

“That’s not what I meant,” Sokka says, but he really should have expected it by now, and the warm burst in his chest that goes with it. He considers what he can see of Zuko’s face, what he can read in his posture, in the press of his leg against Sokka’s. “Do you want me to stop the game? To play? To pretend it's fine?”

“It *is* fine,” Zuko says, seeming to deflate with the words, his crossed arms loosening as the tension just…leaves, all of a sudden, Sokka blinking and rapidly reassessing to make sure he didn't just make up the last few minutes. “Just…play. He’ll be happy.”

And Zuko will always default to making others happy, when it comes to the ones he cares about. Sokka holds back whatever thoughts he has on the matter, though, as Iroh finally returns to the table, pai sho board in hand.

“Nephew, do you mind bringing over the tea?” Zuko hesitates. “And maybe some of the pastries left from today?”

Sokka bites back his smile as Zuko moves for food, not tea, sharing a quick glance of amusement with Iroh. It didn’t take Iroh long to notice, apparently, that Zuko has a thing with Sokka and food, even if Sokka still isn't sure that *Zuko* has noticed it it.

Sokka helps Iroh set up the board, relying on half-remembered instructions from months ago and quiet prompts when Iroh catches him hesitating. They begin to play as Zuko returns to the table, setting down tea near Uncle and a plate of pastries near Sokka—Sokka really shouldn’t laugh, but he wants to—before hopping up on the counter along the wall instead of returning to his chair.

Sokka glances over, questioning, but Zuko just braces a foot on the arm of Sokka’s chair and layers his arms on his upraised knee, resting his chin on top. He catches Sokka’s look and just gives a little shrug. “It’s your move.”

Sokka shrugs and turns back to the board, deciding to take his cue from Zuko’s relatively relaxed shoulders and Iroh’s calm tea-sipping and just roll with it. It’s nice, he realizes, to be able to look at the board and throw himself at a problem that doesn't feel as fruitless or fraught as his more recent challenges. To brush his shoulder against Zuko’s calf if he wants to, which he does. At some point in the game, Sokka realizes his hand is wrapped loosely around Zuko’s ankle, but neither Zuko nor Iroh acts like they notice, or care if they do, so Sokka doesn’t move it. It’s weirdly calming to play this game again. It’s quieting, to bend his mind to a problem whose consequences don’t actually matter, and sip tea, and have Zuko sitting warm and relaxed at his side, not involved like Sokka might have wanted but content to observe and be present.

“Nephew,” Iroh comments at one point, teasing clear in his voice when Zuko lets out an absent little hum as Sokka takes a bite of pastry. “I didn’t realize you cared so much about pai sho, to want to watch a whole game. I am delighted to discover this.”

Sokka grins, holding back his laugh so Zuko’s glare won’t get turned on him. Zuko pins his Uncle with a glower before pointedly leans forward and moving one of Sokka’s tiles for him, clearly some kind of gesture that Sokka is going to need to get the backstory for later. And… it’s actually a good move. Better than the one Sokka would have made, which seems to surprise none of them more than Zuko.

## Chapter 23: Know Your Place

### Text

Chronically-on-time-Katara was late to meet Sokka at the library, such a small, innocuous thing to lead to this: Sokka skidding into a dodge as a small boulder flies toward his face in one of Ba Sing Se’s many back-alley courtyards, the ones that Sokka would think they were pure accidents of city development if there weren’t so fucking many of them. And if it weren’t Ba Sing Se, where nothing is allowed to happen by accident.

“Took you long enough,” Katara shouts as she sweeps a rope of water out over his body, giving him time to pop back to his feet as her—their—attackers jump back.

“How’d I know you were going to piss someone off,” Sokka calls back, sending his boomerang flying behind a vision-obscuring spray of mist. “You were just supposed to be looking at lakes!”

“One of the four of us has been getting into a fight at least once a week,” Katara grunts, sending a shower of ice shards to pin the sleeves of the man Sokka has just knocked prone, taking at least one earthbender temporarily out of the equation. “We’re overdue!”

“That’s not how probability works!” Sokka throws himself wide of a cloud of stinging dust, eyes slitted to try to hold onto some semblance of visibility.

“It is when there’s a shadow organization working against you!” A rain of water flattens the dust cloud into a thin layer of mud, and Sokka just grunts because…fair point.

“Why don’t you water whip them?” Sokka uses his boomerang to deflect a chunk of cobblestone in a suspiciously manacle-like shape flying toward Katara’s wrists.

“Give me your waterskin and I will. I don’t have enough left on my own.” She launches a disk of ice, her whole body moving in a fluid wave as she purposefully misses the initial hit in order to pull the disk back into a strike from behind.

“I don’t have any left,” Sokka admits, using the empty skin in question to force the third earthbender to fall out of his stance to avoid getting a waterskin to the face.

“What? You *drank* it all?”

“I was thirsty!”

“You were in the library looking at *maps*!”

“Yeah, Fire Nation maps! Planning!” Sokka trades places with Katara in a set of quick, tight footwork that lets him throw his weight behind a punch to the second earthbender's face as the idiot attempts to try some hand-to-hand combat instead of bending. “It's hard work! And it's dusty!”

“I was walking around in the sun all morning and *I* still had water left!”

“You were at a *lake*!”

Both siblings jump into the air as the ground suddenly heaves beneath their feet. Sokka stumbles on the landing but manages to use his falling momentum to put his weight behind his boomerang as he sends it spinning toward the last earthbender’s ankles. The woman yelps in surprise, the ground stilling as her stance breaks.

“Fine,” Katara huffs. “We’ll work with what we have. I’ll cover you.”

“But I don’t have a boomerang anymore.”

“*I’ll cover you.”*

Sokka sighs and drags a scroll case out of his bag, falling into rhythm with Katara with the ease of long practice. She continually breaks the woman’s stance so the earthbender can never truly ground herself to throw a fully realized attack while Sokka disrupts the woman's aim and vision so that she can never fully pin Katara. They move around each other, flowing and giving and ceding ground, slowly advancing across the courtyard, dodging and deflecting projectiles along the way.

“Ready?”

“Go.”

Sokka pivots hard, sweeping his leg over the ground to kick up a sharp spray of grit, startling the woman backward. Sokka’s already turning the motion into a spin as Katara shoves out a dense wall of fog peppered with ice shards. The earthbender shoots up a column of earth, effectively blocking the ice and breaking the fog and providing an excellent axis for Sokka to pivot around to wallop her in the throat with his scroll case.

It’s a very fine scroll case, thick leather over a rigid wood frame, with delicate stitching and the memory of gold-paint designs that someone must have scraped off before the case landed in the third-hand markets. Sokka is vaguely embarrassed by how much he loves it, even when he has nothing much to put inside it beyond his own half-written thoughts. It makes a satisfying *thwack* as it connects with the earthbender’s neck. The woman wheezes, eyes wide in shock as she folds forward, instinctively raising her hands to her throat. Sokka encourages her to continue on down with an elbow to the side of her head and a sharp knee to the face.

“Unconscious,” Katara pants, eyeing their three prone opponents and calling the pools of water accumulating around the courtyard back toward her.

“All of them?” Sokka glances toward pinned-by-ice-man as he retrieves his boomerang from where it’s half-buried in the ground. Sokka doesn’t remember either of them taking him down but yup, he’s definitely unconscious, too.

“Friendly fire, I think.”

“Rough.” Sokka takes a deep breath, heart still pounding too loud in the quiet that always seems too large once the fighting stops. There isn’t even noise from the street filtering to them, as if everyone normally on the other side of the shops has cleared the area. They probably have. “Katara, what the fuck.”

She pulls a face, a mixture of reluctance and self-castigation. “Someone was pretending…I thought someone needed help. It doesn’t matter.” She waves the entire almost-successful ruse away, which Sokka would very much like to spend some more time on, her eyes narrowing on him. “You’re hurt.”

Sokka glances down, suddenly feeling the sting to match the thin line of red soaking into the blue of his tunic. “It’s fine.” It doesn’t hurt, much.

“Let me take a look,” Katara says, stepping forward and already rolling her water into a familiar healing-ready globe.

“Ew,” Sokka says, eyeing the water in distaste. “I don’t want your Ba Sing Se alley water. Who knows where that’s been?”

“It’s not—it’s just *water*.”

“That’s been on the *ground.* Besides, we need to get out of here.” There’s no way a fight like theirs went unnoticed and Sokka doesn’t particularly want to stick around to wait for the authorities. Or to find out that they were just fighting them.

“Let me just make sure you’re okay first,” Katara insists. “None of them are moving, we have a minute.”

“Katara, it’s fine.” Sokka focuses on shoving his scroll case back into his satchel, relieved that the wooden frame seems uncracked. “Let’s just leave, we don’t want anyone showing up.”

“Sokka.” Her tone has him rocking to a halt. “Can I please see your ribs to make sure you aren’t going to bleed out on the street?”

He looks back down at his side, which isn’t bleeding *nearly* enough for that concern in his non-professional but often-wounded opinion. He doesn’t want to waste time, and besides… “Do I need to take my shirt off for that?”

“…Yes?”

“Then no.”

Katara opens her mouth, then slowly closes it, expression somewhere on the border between suspicious and horrified. “Do I even want to know?”

“No,” Sokka says decisively. “No, you do not.”

“…Fine. Let’s go back.”

“Great idea,” Sokka says, waiting for her to catch up before hustling back toward the street. If they can find crowds then they can relax. Sokka isn’t quite sure of all the rules of engagement their mystery enemy adheres to, but it’s become clear enough that whoever they keep clashing with doesn’t want to be caught *or* seen. “Did you find anything?”

“No,” Katara says, the words distracted as she focuses on covering their retreat while Sokka casts his eyes over the path forward, both on the lookout for threats. “Just water.”

“Why the hell did they jump you, then,” Sokka bites out, blowing out a frustrated breath that they just did all that for what sounds like no reason at all.

“I don’t know, otherwise I would have said,” Katara snaps. “But we have to be close to something if they did, right?”

“We could be right on top of it,” Sokka mutters. “It won’t matter if we can’t figure out what that something is.”

Sokka shows up that afternoon with bruises on his arms that Zuko didn’t put there, which Zuko is absolutely sure of because he doesn't leave bruises like that, and almost never anywhere that visible. Zuko’s inner fire snaps to attention, going quiet in a way that feels far more coiled than calm.

“What happened?” Zuko demands, coming to a stop a few paces away and dragging his eyes over Sokka’s neat wolf tail and exasperated face and scuffed up arms and scraped knuckles.

“It’s not a big deal,” Sokka says, stepping forward and reaching like Zuko is just going to take his hand and drag him off to bed when he looks like *that*.

“Have you seen yourself?” Zuko steps back, giving Sokka another once-over and crossing his arms to tuck his hands away.

“You sound like Katara,” Sokka mutters, like it's bad to sound like a healer when someone is *injured.*

“Fine,” Zuko grunts, turning back toward the teashop. “Wait here.”

He ignores Sokka’s wordless protest and dramatic grumbling, and then Sung-min’s startled yelp when Zuko bursts back into the kitchen.

“You’re back,” Sung-Min gasps, sounding more than slightly panicked by the fact as he casts a desperate glance toward the shift calendar.

Zuko pauses, a roll of bandages and a jar of antiseptic ointment in hand. “Why are you being weird?” He glances suspiciously around the kitchen. Is something going on? His inner flame, already taut and sharp-edged, pricks to wary attention.

“I’m not being weird! You never come back. *You’re* being weird!” Sung-min's eyes go wide, then he claps a hand over his own mouth, staring at Zuko.

“…Okay.” Zuko isn't going to deal with this now. Or ever. He stalks back out into the afternoon sunshine to find Sokka still waiting in the same spot, leaning back against the alley wall like his bare arms aren’t mottled with slowly rising bruises--and is that a shadow, or is the side of his tunic suspiciously blotchy and dark?

“It’s really not that bad,” Sokka insists, eyeing the supplies in Zuko’s hand.

“It was just a scuffle.”

“A scuffle,” Zuko repeats.

“Just, you know. A thing.”

“A thing.”

“Yeah.” Sokka’s fingers are tapping against the back of Zuko’s hand, restless, and why is he being so *dodgy* about it?

Zuko moves on to Sokka’s torso, where there’s some bruising but none that produces more than a wince or grumble when Zuko probes at it. “Can I ask you a question?”

Zuko pauses in the middle of his cool-down kata, glancing over to where Sokka is sprawled in a patch of sunlight. Sokka’s nominally stretching, but they both know he’s mostly watching Zuko, which makes Zuko feel jittery and overly aware of his limbs. Not in a bad way, though. “Sure.”

“Imagine you’re in a fight,” Sokka starts, leaning back onto his arms and propping one booted foot onto the other.
