Zuko nurses his dessert after dinner, not because he particularly cares for it but because he knows Sokka is going to want it halfway through the pai sho game. He’s hopped up onto what’s become his usual spot on the counter, eyes on Sokka as Sokka helps Uncle set up the board while telling some story about a volcano and fortune telling and clouds. Which, to be honest, Zuko isn’t entirely following beyond the rhythm of Sokka’s voice and the fact that clouds are on Sokka’s mind this evening.

Zuko is still feeling loose and…vivid, after the storm and this afternoon. Like everything is too sharp and intense, but in a good way. He might still be a little bit drunk on how the last edges of lightning are sitting inside his inner flame. And maybe on the memory of Sokka looking at him like Zuko was something to be in awe of, too.

He wishes he could hold onto the feeling and let it fully work through him, let it settle until it feels like it’s seeping into his bones, but it’s not something Zuko can do in front of Uncle. But even feeling this unrestrained, even if it’s less than he could be, means that Zuko still hasn’t fully shrugged back into his control, or into the way he’s supposed act in a room that has Sokka and Uncle together.

He can’t help thinking about where he would have been during Sokka’s story, when usually Zuko tries not to put his past and Sokka into anything approaching the same space if he can help it. It was shortly after Sokka left the *Wani*, from the sound of it. Before the shirshu incident? Maybe. Zuko would have been on the coast then. Resupplying and pretending that he hadn’t just sent his heart out in a scroll tube with no idea if it would ever come back to him.

Zuko probably hadn’t even been a day’s journey away, if he’s remembering the maps correctly. Less, if he traveled by Komodo-rhino instead of on foot. A few scant hours from Sokka that whole time. And the Avatar. Both of them, in an isolated town with no allies, beset by distractions, swayed by manufactured predictions…

Watching Sokka make the opening moves of the pai sho game, Uncle sipping tea, thinking about who he used to be—Zuko feels like the ghost of his old life as never been so close, or so expectant. Like he’s never been so aware of his three touchstones, the ones that gave him purpose when everything else was gone, the ones that continue to tug at him, suddenly all within reach and impossible to hold next to each other.

When Sokka leans back in frustration halfway through the game, glancing at his empty dessert bowl in annoyance, Zuko’s mostly-full one is at the ready. Zuko soaks in the pleased surprise on Sokka’s face, the absent way Sokka runs his fingers over the skin of Zuko’s ankle where his foot is propped against Sokka’s chair. Zuko concentrates on the way it makes things in him relax and other parts of him spark and shiver, and wonders if any one of those anchors on their own could ever be enough to ground him.

&#45;-

Zuko slips out again that night, masked and wearing black and restless with more than just the aftereffects of lightning. He’s moving more purposefully this time, maybe. Looking for something, possibly. Maybe he’s always been looking, ever since he started taking to the roofs at night. Maybe he’s just only now letting himself acknowledge it.

Because Zuko has always enjoyed being like this the most when there is a goal in mind. Has felt the most alive slipping through shadow and pitting himself against architecture and observation when there’s some possibility of success to strive for, something to retrieve or set himself against. Agni, did he ever really think it would stay just burning off energy for the sake of it? Did he really think it ever was?

Zuko knows the kinds of places people try to hide what’s valuable to them, what they don’t want found. Especially rich people, powerful people, people who think they’re above consequences and rules. Little things and big things, objects and secrets, things that could take down a person’s whole world or just disrupt their life. Zuko has always been better than he should be at making his way to those kinds of things.

And Zuko has spent far more time tracking down sky bison—and finding them—than Sokka ever has.

Zuko doesn’t let himself think about the impulse, or the reason beneath it. He can’t let himself wonder which of the pieces of himself are behind this particular urge. Instead, Zuko takes a moment to settle the swords crossed on his back. He thinks about how something like a sky bison would be huge, how there’d need to be a special kind of concealment for what basically amounts to a multi-ton ball of heat.

Zuko leaps across the gap to the next roof, letting his heat sense spill out with the motion and wash across the city before him, touching and cataloging and seeking, with Zuko following behind.

## Chapter 25: Infiltrate

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

No particular warnings for this one

### Text

The four of them are all at the house, one of the few mornings each week they take to train together. Toph is putting Aang through his earthbending paces across their private courtyard while Sokka cools down in a broad patch of sun. He moves absently through stretches he picked up from Zuko, watching Aang’s lesson like he has any idea what’s going on.

Katara comes up behind him, silently offering a waterskin and a packet of bread and cheese. Sokka accepts both, drinking deeply, his appetite waking up now that food is in front of him. He keeps half his attention on Katara, though, because she’s still standing there and fiddling with her necklace like she has something she’s working up to saying.

“Have you been hearing any weird stuff when we’re out in the city?” She finally asks, quiet, eyes fixed on the training session like maybe she isn’t talking to Sokka at all. She has significantly more than half his attention, now.

“Maybe. What kind of things?”

“Like people saying someone else has been asking around about the same kind of stuff as us, lately.”

“Or that someone else came by recently?”

“Something like that,” Katara confirms, chewing on her lip. “How long since you noticed it happening?”

“A bit now.” Sokka reaches for his toes, frowning as he tries to think back to when it first happened. “A couple of weeks, maybe.”

Katara grunts in acknowledgment. “What do you think it means?”

“I don’t know,” Sokka sighs, silently counting through the stretch. “All we know for sure is that it sounds like someone else is out there, doing something that looks a lot like searching for Appa.”

“And what we suspect?”

“That there’s a new threat we need to figure out,” Sokka says quietly, hesitating as he wonders just how much to voice when he hasn’t even been sure there was anything to have thoughts about in the first place, until now. “Either a new person, or the D—the enemy changing strategies.” They don’t say that name in the house the Dai Li have given them, in a space Joo Dee freely walks through.

Katara nods, looking grim and resign, like nothing Sokka said was particularly surprising to her. “Do we need to start officially buddying up, when we go out?”

“…Probably,” Sokka sighs, reluctant because he knows how doubling up will cut down their collective efficiency, which means more time searching and less time for other pursuits and plans. But they need to be safe against whatever new danger is within the city. It doesn’t need to be stated out loud that there’s only a slim chance that anyone else hunting Appa would be doing it for reasons that were good.

&#45;-

The chill night air is a welcome relief as Zuko and Jin break free of the swirling crowd, Jin deftly finding an open spot of ledge to jump up onto out of the way of the dancers. The music has turned slower and romantic, which is just the type of song Zuko prefers not to dance to if he can help it. These monthly masques that Jin’s friends throw are Zuko’s favorite of the impromptu dances and theater productions and concerts that she always seems to know about. And not for the reason he knows Jin has probably assumed.

“You were pretty snappy with the drink vendor, earlier,” Jin comments, still more than a little breathless from their last reel.

“So?” Zuko is pretty snappy with everyone.

“I just think it’s funny. Most people working a job like yours develop a customer service voice.”

“A what?” Agni, is this some new thing he’s supposed to be doing at work that no one has told him about?

“You know,” she sits up a little straighter, suddenly adopting a high, bright tone. He can imagine her wide, guileless eyes even through her half-mask. “Oh gosh, let me help you with that! Silly me, that mistake is clearly all my fault.” She slumps back, her normal tone returning. “That kind of thing.”

Zuko stares. “People do that on purpose?” He shudders when she nods, glad for his own mask to hide his discomfort. “Never do that again.” It freaks him out to hear her like that, like she has a whole separate personality she can shrug on and off. He recognizes the rhythms of it, too, from the way Sung-Min and Minji speak when they’re working the floor versus in the kitchen. It’s always been frustrating, like Zuko has more coworkers than he actually does when Zuko is already bad enough at reading people that he can barely handle the two of them to begin with.

“Most people in customer service do that,” Jin laughs. “You don’t, though.”

“…No.” Not unless you counted the entire concept of Lee.

Jin hums thoughtfully. “Your version is more like not yelling as loud as you want to when you get mad.”

Zuko stays silent, watching the dancers and the way torchlight scatters over their lacquer masks. She isn’t exactly wrong.

“That’s going to be hard you know, in the Upper Ring,” Jin says with a feigned casualness that has Zuko snapping to attention. Jin is not one to feign much of anything. “They aren’t going to like that.”

“What do you mean,” Zuko demands.

“You haven’t heard?” She sounds genuinely surprised, hesitating now like she regrets bringing it up. “Word on the street and at the Blooming Petal is that your uncle is making quite the name for himself with his tea blends.”

“So?”

“So, chances are, he’s about to be recognized for it.”

“What does that mean?” It almost sounds like the word should be capitalized, the way she says it, like being recognized is an official and formal event. Zuko shifts, uneasy, as he thinks about what it could mean for it to be applied to two Imperial firebenders in hiding.

“It means Mushi might have his own teashop in his future. And not in the Lower Ring.”

Zuko takes a long moment to digest her words. Uncle would be beyond delighted. But it would come with a lot of attention, and Zuko isn’t sure he likes how many eyes something like that could bring them. Or the kind of disruption it would bring to the fragile balance of Zuko’s life.

“You hadn’t heard?” Jin asks, voice gentle in a way that makes it clear that he should have.

“No,” Zuko bites out, hating that he’s unsure if it’s because Uncle wouldn’t want to speak of things that weren’t certain yet, or whether he thought Zuko wouldn’t care that their whole life was about to be uprooted again just because the reason for it was tea.

“I guess it’s not a sure thing, yet,” Jin says, barely sounding convinced by her own words.

Zuko cuts her a glance, through his mask. “How did you know, then?”

“I’m just wise in the ways of the world,” Jin sings, making a show of loftily surveying the crowd until he rolls his eyes and elbows her to get her to stop. “For real, though,” she settles back into her normal tone. “Servants talk, especially when you get them out of the Upper Ring and they’re feeling snooty. You can learn a lot, that way.”

“…Like what?” Zuko has spent years thinking about all the different ways to dig out certain types of information, almost always from the outside. What would someone like Jin try to learn? How would she go about it from within?

She purses her lips beneath her half-mask, considering, before suddenly launching into the latest Upper Ring rumors. It’s light and frothy and even a little scandalizing, though more in the realization of the kinds of things she can find out about the city’s elite without them knowing. Zuko tries to just take it all in as nothing more than gossip about the lives of people he knows nothing about, barely more than fiction. But he can’t help hearing the political undercurrents beneath the rumors, can’t stop thinking about what all the bits and pieces Jin offers up would mean for administration, the courts, the military.

Zuko tries to focus on the music and the dancers even as his mind keeps poking and prodding at how a system like the one Jin is sketching out could meld with Fire Nation ways. What would need to be burned away and replaced, if Ba Sing Se were ever to be the jewel of the Fire Nation’s empire? What would it mean for the city, for a Fire Nation governor to rule here one day, or even just for the Colonies to establish stronger relations with the heart of the Earth Kingdom?

They’re things that *Lee* should have no reason to think about. Or Zuko, for that matter, these days.

But he still can’t stop himself from noting how all of Jin’s stories seem to center around resources—squabbling for them and maneuvering to control them, even if it harms the collective good of the city. Different than the Fire Nation, where fighting for position rarely involves the physical goods themselves, than it does the ability to decide what is done with them.

It all seems so…petty. So stupid to be worried about, when there is a world at war outside the walls. But then, there is no war in Ba Sing Se, and maybe this is what flourishes within the walls in its absence. And maybe this is what prevents the war from actually ending and making the mantra true.

Zuko used to want the war to end as quickly as possible. It wasn’t even that long ago, really, that he held that up as a goal to strive for. He wonders though, as Jin hops down to dance again as the music picks back up, if that is still the case. Or if there are some outcomes now st that would outweigh the loss of lives like the 41 or the northern fleet. If maybe now there are some ends that justify just a few more sacrifices.

&#45;-

“Are you *sure* you don’t want to play?” Sokka asks Zuko beneath the sounds of Iroh cleaning up dinner. “We can be on a team.”

Zuko screws his face up at the suggestion. “Definitely no.”

It’s a cute expression, even though it probably shouldn’t be, and Sokka wants to lean over and kiss it right off his face. It’s probably a good thing that Zuko doesn’t sit next to Sokka like this when the actual pai sho is happening or else Sokka would be constantly distracted.

“Teams could be fu-un,” Sokka sing-songs, already knowing that Zuko will say no and take his usual perch the minute Iroh comes back. After so many dinners ending the same way, Sokka has started struggling to picture Zuko anywhere in the room except in that spot. It makes his mental image of Zuko’s workdays interesting, when he can’t seem to move Zuko off the counter.

“I’m no good,” Zuko says. “You don’t want me on your team.”

Sokka raises an eyebrow at the familiar echoes underneath the protest but decides not to chase them with Iroh nearby. “Did you ever learn?” Sokka is positive that Iroh would have tried to teach him.

“There’s no point,” Zuko shrugs, which is not a ‘no,’ and Sokka decides not to call him on that, either. Zuko is persistently and weirdly dodgy around his discomfort with pai sho, even as he keeps insisting that Sokka play the game.

“Why not?”

Zuko shifts under the scrutiny, playing absently with some of Sokka’s tiles. “Some people are just suited for certain things.”

“What do you mean?” Sokka keeps his eyes fixed on the board, giving far more of his visible attention than necessary to setting up the game. He’s learned to give Zuko breathing room in little ways, for things like what this conversation seems like it could turn into. Hopefully, Iroh has a lot of cleanup to do.

“Like…you’re suited for helping Aang and planning. And Azula for being a great firebender. And Uncle is a pai sho genius.”

“And you?”

“Nothing much,” Zuko says simply, letting the tiles fall back onto the table. Sokka hazards a glance, something in his stomach dropping when he sees no resentment or tension in Zuko over the statement. Like it’s just fact. Not even that Zuko is good at nothing, but that there is nothing he ever *could* be good at.

It’s moments like these where Sokka wonders what the fuck Iroh has been doing for three years. Or else what a thirteen-year-old Zuko was like, if this is where he is now nearing seventeen.

“I don’t know why you always do that,” Sokka finally sighs, letting his handful of tiles drop to the table in frustration.

“Huh?” Zuko looks startled that Sokka would be upset by anything he had said, which is just…the most Zuko thing.

“You don’t give yourself any credit.”

“For what?”

Sokka closes his eyes at the genuine confusion in Zuko’s tone. “For everything, Zuko. You’re a genius with swords. You’re an amazing bender. You’re such a perceptive person you figured out how to get yourself out of laundry duty when you were just a kid. You know all about politics and power and how the system works. You’ve been through shit that would crush someone else, and you’re still fighting. I don’t know why you sell yourself so short.”

Sokka gets nothing but silence in response, but when he opens his eyes it's to see Zuko staring at the pai sho board, frozen wide-eyed and stunned. Sokka suppresses a sigh and doesn’t press for any kind of reply. He probably shouldn’t have sprung something like that on Zuko with no lead-in, not with Iroh nearby and limiting what either of them can do or say. If they were alone Sokka might try to coax out a response, maybe temper difficult words with easy touches, but now Sokka can only look at Zuko’s face, waiting for his eyes to finally flick up and see Sokka’s sincerity.

Zuko’s shocked expression cracks a little, something achingly vulnerable underneath, and Sokka immediately slides to the edge of his chair to lean into Zuko’s side, trying to be solid and steady and silent and not throw any more surprise shots at Zuko’s sense of balance, pressing close until Iroh finally returns to the table.

Iroh walks over slowly, dessert and tea in hand, eyes moving between them like he can physically see the mood in the air.

“Nephew,” Iroh says jovially, which is *not* the tone Sokka would have taken. “I haven’t seen you look like that since we had to sell Jasmine.”

Zuko immediately glares, annoyed, and Sokka blinks as he realizes that Iroh had purposefully made a comment designed to incite and annoy Zuko and get him back onto familiar footing. But also…

“Jasmine?”

“An ostrich horse that was with us in our travels, until we reached Ba Sing Se and needed to board the ferry,” Iroh explains as he pours out three cups of tea.

“Yeah, the ferries were strict,” Sokka says. Zuko’s face twitches with some mix of emotions Sokka can’t identify before they disappear beneath a scowl. “But wait. I thought you guys were strapped for cash. You spent it all on a ride?”

Zuko suddenly seems to find the table intensely fascinating. “Um.”

“Hmm,” Iroh sets a cookie on his plate, half an eye on Zuko. “A nice turn of phrase. Yes, we were rather ‘strapped for cash’ then.”

Sokka slowly turns to face Zuko. “…Did you steal an ostrich horse?”

“Maybe,” Zuko mutters, sullen and defensive.

“…Was it named Jasmine when you stole it?”

“No,” Iroh says with relish when Zuko just glares. “No, she was not.”

“Oh,” Sokka can feel a smile growing on his face, laughter caught in his chest. “Oh wow. An ostrich horse companion, that you came to own through disreputable means and named Jasmine and traveled with, and were forced to sell when you finally reached your destination because you couldn't bring her the last step of the way. It’s like a play.”

Zuko glowers even harder, pink climbing up the unscarred skin of his cheeks.

“My nephew misses her very much,” Iroh discloses, as if it weren’t perfectly obvious from the way that Zuko never talks about her.

“Just play already,” Zuko grumbles, shoving up from his seat and stalking to the counter. “You’re never going to end the game if you don’t start.”

&#45;-

It’s one of those nights that’s neither dark nor light as the moon peaks in and out of deep intermittent clouds. It makes trailing the Dai Li difficult, with their dark robes that seem designed for night cover. Zuko needs to keep one eye on his footing and one on his surroundings and another on his targets and the sky, and that’s just way more than he has to work with. Zuko can stop worrying about visually finding the Dai Li once he comes across an agent, at least. They’re usually on a rooftop, which was an unsettling discovery, but Zuko can follow them easily enough once he finds them as long as they stay above ground and within the range of his fire sense.

The problem—one of many—is that the Dai Li *don’t* tend to stay above ground. There’s some kind of underground network of tunnels or hideouts in the city, beyond what could be explained by the public sewer systems. Earthbenders would have an advantage there, and escape routes would be sparse. Zuko is still trying to feel out the shape of it, trying to be cautious and methodical about investigating even though everything in his gut is telling him that there’s no way he will find the sky bison above the earth, in Ba Sing Se.

Assuming that the Dai Li really have the creature, of course. Sokka seems to believe it even if he won’t say it outright. And Zuko can think of more than a few reasons why the power behind Ba Sing Se’s throne might like to hold the Avatar’s leash. Factor in Sokka’s grumbling about still being blocked by the local bureaucracy, and needing to slip an escort, and the Dai Li start looking like a better and better culprit.

An organization that adapted to secrecy and shadows would hold a prize like Appa at the heart of their power, under its direct control. It would know the risks of involving too many people in a secret like that. Zuko just needs to figure out where, exactly, the heart of the Dai Li’s power lies. Wherever it is, Zuko is willing to bet that it won’t be above ground where Sokka’s been looking.

&#45;-

Jin was right. The news—promotion?—comes through an official messenger, dressed far more finely than any resident of the Lower Ring would ever be. The woman is all robes and flash and scrolls and seals and the kind of pomp and circumstance that Zuko knows you only get to engage in when people believe in the power behind your ceremony.

Uncle is ecstatic, like Zuko knew he would be. The chance to open his own teashop is, apparently, truly a dream come true which…probably shouldn’t be news to Zuko. He already has a name picked out, even: The Jasmine Dragon. Which Agni’s tits, why not just call it The Place Where Firebenders Are?

But the residents of Ba Sing Se know nothing about the Dragon of the West, or his dreams, Zuko reminds himself. And Uncle has wanted this for years.

It’s disquieting, to think that the goal might always have been this.

The owner of the shop tries desperately to keep them. It’s vaguely amusing, to see the way the man tries to talk Uncle into staying with offers of reduced hours, as if Uncle would be happier being *less* involved with tea. And it’s completely horrifying to have that energy directed toward Zuko when it becomes clear that Mushi will be taking his ticket to the Upper Ring and not looking back. Zuko can only stare in frozen shock at the owner’s offer of double pay and half the hours. The economics of the move make no sense—how could it be sustainable without severely underpaying another part-time worker, the labor costs would get astronomical otherwise and it’s not like Zuko adds a lot of inherent value. Zuko is so confused by the math that it takes him a long moment to register the man’s sweating tension and to realize that it’s really a last-ditch bid for Uncle. Everyone in the shop knows that Mushi is devoted to Lee. If Zuko stays, so will Uncle.

Zuko shifts uncomfortably around the realization that he has the power to block Uncle’s dream, if he wants to. It would be easy. All Zuko would need to do is dig in his heels and kick up a fit and take his reduced hours and refuse to let things change, beyond suddenly having more time for Sokka. And Agni, Zuko has had enough of change. He is perfectly fine, for once, with how his life is now.

But Zuko couldn’t do that to Uncle, no matter how badly he is failing at being a Good Nephew these days. Besides, even if Zuko had more time for Sokka, he’s pretty sure that Sokka won’t have any more time for him.

So. The Jasmine Dragon.

It will mean more work for Zuko, which he isn’t looking forward to. But the Upper Ring also means being closer to Sokka, which…Zuko doesn’t know if that’s a good thing or not. To be physically closer, yes. To be closer to Sokka’s real life and all the people that come with him…Zuko’s control has never exactly been the best. It’s been hard enough being in the same city separated by two walls and hours of tram tracks. If they turn out to only be a short walk away…

Jin is going to be the one who is far away now, Zuko realizes as he forces himself to think about something else. And that is something that Zuko can be purely sad about, even if she grins like she’s trying to show off every one of her teeth at the announcement.

Zuko wonders how Sokka will take the news. His inner fire shivers, slinking low. Fuck. He’s too afraid to follow that thought to think about how sharing this news might go.

“Sokka, are you okay?”

Sokka freezes at the sound of Aang’s voice, halfway through another lap through the streets around their house. He looks up with a visibly guiltily cringe—dammit, there goes playing it cool—to see Aang sitting on the sweeping roof of the front porch, waving down like Sokka didn’t just hear him shouting.

“Why wouldn’t I be okay?” Sokka calls back, reluctantly turning his steps into the entry courtyard. There’s plenty of space—more than enough—for pacing here, too. Sokka just… kind of wanted to do it where the others wouldn’t see.

“Because this is your fifth time walking by and not coming in.”

Or maybe Sokka needs to do his pacing out of the Upper Ring entirely, next time. “Were you watching me?”

“Not at first,” Aang says cheerfully, hopping off the roof to land in front of Sokka in a gentle puff of air. “But then you kept on walking.”

“I was just thinking about some stuff,” Sokka mutters as they walk inside, ignoring Katara’s automatic “Don’t hurt yourself” from the front living room. The worst living room for sitting but the one with the best view of the street.

“Make sure you clean up before dinner, if you were *thinking* about things that needed privacy, lover boy,” Toph drawls from the front living room, because apparently Sokka wanting some time to himself is a full Team Avatar concern.

“I wasn’t thinking about *that*,” Sokka scowls. And if they thought he was, then why were they all *watching* him.

Toph just grins. “You are now.”

“Now we all are,” Katara grumbles. “Thank you, Toph, for that.”

“Any time, Sweetness.”

“*Anyway*,” Sokka cuts in, heading off whatever might follow that particular tone at this particular time of day, when they’re all started to get irritable before dinner. “I’ve got a bit of news—”

“Did you finish your carving?”

“—about Zuko.” Sokka is just going to act like Toph isn’t even there, how about.

“Need help picking out a ribbon?”

Katara’s eyes widen in alarm, because apparently she hasn’t joined Sokka in Toph-ignoring just yet. “Sokka, what is she talking about?”

“Sokka,” Aang says, solemn and grave at his side, placing a steady hand on his arm. “I would be happy to look at ribbons with you.”

“What ribbons? What carving? Sokka?”

“*We* will be *happy*—” Aang continues, with a quick speaking glance toward Katara. “—to help you with whatever you need.”

“I will be *happy*, Aang,” Katara snaps. Sokka wonders what argument is happening above his head right now. “But I’m still allowed to think it’s a bit early for something like that!”

“The monks always taught that there are no boundaries or fixed shape to the way that someone loves—”

“And *I* said that’s great, but it doesn’t change the fact that they’ve only been dating in person for—"

“You can’t put your own timeline on the pace of someone else’s—”

“Certain things need to be done the right—”

“To say that one way is right is to say that all other ways are—"

“Zuko’s teashop is moving to the Upper Ring!”

Sokka stares at them all in the ensuing silence, because what the actual fuck have they been talking about when he isn’t around? Toph abruptly breaks into a loud cackle that the three of them ignore, which is what Aang and Katara *should have done from the start*.

Aang finally snaps his mouth shut. “Zuko’s what is what?”

“Oh, are we actually listening to me now?” Sokka waves away whatever Katara is about to say. “Whatever. The—I don’t know how it works, but Zuko’s uncle is really good at making tea, I guess.” Toph lets out an explosive giggle-snort. “And so he’s been offered his own shop to run. In the Upper Ring.”

Aang searches for words for a long moment, finally settling on a rather squeaky, “Where?”

“They’re not sure yet,” Sokka sighs, tugging on his wolf tail. It’s a mess today, but he can’t seem to stop pulling it apart and gave up three laps ago on putting it back together “They don’t get moved for a few more days.”

“I swear,” Katara starts. “If this was all some kind of long con—”

“Then we can all be suitably impressed by everyone’s acting ability,” Sokka says loudly, glowering until Katara subsides with a half-apologetic wince. Iroh’s excitement had been real, and strong enough for Sokka to realize that the General’s usual genialness was its own kind of mask. A different kind of Fire Nation public control.

“So just to be clear,” Toph says, shit-eating grin firmly in place. “Sparrowkeet is about to move to be closer to Sokka?”

“He—that’s not—that’s not *why*.”

“Sure. Of course not.”

Sokka opens his mouth to protest further before remembering that engaging with Toph is never a good idea. “Right.” He turns to Aang and Katara. “That’s what I wanted to share. Zuko just found out.”

“What does this mean?” Aang asks, expression somewhere between thoughtful and hesitant, which are just two of the many emotions Sokka is feeling right now.

“I don’t know,” he admits. He isn’t sure if Aang is talking about what this means for Sokka’s relationship, or for the eclipse, or for Appa, or for Zuko himself. But whatever it is, Sokka’s answer is the same.

“It means the Dragon of the West is really good at tea,” Toph says, with a tone that makes it clear this should be the only logical conclusion. “I can’t wait to try the stuff.”

The new shop—the Jasmine Dragon—is…nice. It’s huge, compared to the Blooming Petal. The ceilings are tall, the architecture bright and airy and grand. There are round tables instead of long ones running the length of the room, chairs instead of benches, a spacious kitchen, even a courtyard and a paved garden for when the weather is nice. The honeyed wood blends with the warm tones of the masonry, and the whole place already smells pleasantly of spices and herbal things.

It’s…an improvement.

“Do you know what was here before?” Sokka asks, turning a slow circle. His fingers trace the intricate scrollwork running around the windows. The craftsmanship is gorgeous.

“Some kind of wellness food shop, or something,” Zuko offers from across the room. He is leaning against the counter, arms folded as he watches Sokka take the place in. “Drinks to make you age slower, that kind of thing.”

“…What?”

“Rich person stuff,” Zuko says, as if he’d never been one. He half-shrugs at Sokka’s sideways look, eyes skating away as silence falls between them.

The shop is quiet like it probably never will be again once it opens, only the two of them now. Sokka had met Zuko down at the apartment like usual and they’d ridden the tram together, since Zuko didn’t know how to tell Sokka how to get here and Sokka felt…weird, for reasons he didn’t want to question right now, about waiting for Zuko to come to him at the monorail station.

It’s probably for the best that Sokka had gone down to the Lower Ring, too. It had been something of a marvel to travel with Zuko, even for such a relatively short trip compared to all their other traveling, even if Sokka hadn’t been able to wholly enjoy it. He’d spent most of the trip focusing on projecting calm and teasing and light-hearted enjoyment, because Zuko had looked like he was on the verge of vibrating out of his own skin the further and further they went from the Lower Ring.

Sokka knew in the abstract that Zuko liked habits and predictability and knowing the world around him, but he doesn’t think he truly appreciated how much until he was watching the rug get yanked out from under him. For someone who traveled the world for years, Zuko is remarkably anchored to certain touchstones in his life, apparently. Or maybe Zuko is just out of practice with the feeling of the ground being unsteady beneath you.

“So what do you think,” Zuko finally asks, not quite looking at Sokka in that way that usually means he has something on his mind he’s trying to work his way around to voicing.

“It seems nice,” Sokka says, pretending to be engrossed in the window carvings to give Zuko space to sort out of his thoughts. He isn’t sure what Zuko is after, but that wasn’t a very Zuko kind of question.

“Is it…okay?”

“For what? It seems perfect for Iroh.” For Zuko, on the other hand…

Zuko’s eyes finally shift to Sokka’s face, the usual sign that he has worked himself around to the point he is wanting to make. “What about for you?”

“…Huh?”

“Is it too…” Zuko waves a hand before crossing his arms again, chewing on his lip. “Sokka, I don’t know where you live. Is this…alright? That this is here?”

“Oh.” That. “I—yeah. Of course it is.” Some corner of Sokka’s brain has been poking at that question ever since Zuko told him the news. Maybe longer, if you count useless daydreams. Sokka won’t say it isn’t a bit of a relief that the Jasmine Dragon is still a decent walk from their house, even if it’s close enough that Sokka is still going to have to warn the others away from the Eastern district if Zuko wants to avoid run-ins.

But just because Sokka appreciates the bit of distance doesn’t mean he wants Zuko to stay in the Lower Ring. Sokka is undeniably nervous to be so drastically changing this thing they have, but he can also recognize that it isn’t what they have that’s changing, just the context all around them. Moving from one teashop to another, from the Lower Ring to the Upper Ring, from indulging in half-daydreams, half-nightmares about running into Zuko while out canvassing the Lower Ring to ones about running into Zuko closer to home.

It’s weird to need to consider things like that, to think of Zuko being part of the polish and shine and extravagance around here. Sokka had gotten used to Zuko’s prickly, rough-edged presence in the Lower Ring where that kind of habitual surliness was tolerated, if not exactly welcome. In the Upper Ring, though…Sokka is a bit worried for how Zuko is going to handle the transition. He has a vague idea that a Prince should fit in better up here than down there, and he has a very firm idea that that will not be the case.

“It’s not just—” Zuko starts, shifting against the counter before trying again. “The shop is here. But we have rooms here, too…” He’s worrying at his shirt-cuffs, shoulders hunched like he actually thinks Sokka would protest the idea of him being so close every day. *He* wasn’t the one spending hours on the tram.

Before he can say that, though, Sokka gets caught on a very different idea. “…Rooms? Plural?”

“I—” Zuko glances up, words dying as he catches Sokka’s expression. “Oh.” He licks his lips, eyes flitting down Sokka’s body. “Yeah.”

Sokka holds Zuko’s gaze, slowly sauntering across the room, watching the way Zuko’s shoulders relax and his eyes heat and a different kind of tension starts winding through his body. Good. “You should show me those, too.”

“Yes,” Zuko says immediately, pushing off the counter before hesitating. “There’s nothing in them, yet.”

Sokka grins. “When has that ever stopped us?”

Zuko finally accepts a few days later that wherever Sokka is staying in the Upper Ring, it’s outside the range of his fire sense. He doesn’t know whether he’s relieved or disappointed. He can still hold onto the thin edge of safety provided by not knowing. But he still needs to feel that moment each time when Sokka steps outside of his reach, fading from his awareness.

It was easier when there was never the possibility in the first place that Zuko could know.

Now when Zuko slips out at night, he very deliberately doesn’t let his first sense spill beyond what is needed to move safely until he’s well past the boundaries of the Upper Ring. At least not until he has no other alternatives, because Zuko doesn’t need any more tests of his control in his life than he already has. Embodying Lee has become so much more difficult, with upper-class customers and their expectations for pleasant service to go along with their tea. Navigating a room of nobility and political elites should, in theory, be something comfortable and familiar, but Zuko doesn’t know how to fade into the background the way he’s supposed to.

Zuko can add it all to the list of things he’s inept at.

Knowing that he can still feel like himself for a few hours under his mask in the dark of night helps Zuko get through the days that feel newly long, for all that Agni’s touch on the world is growing briefer and briefer. It helps to know that this one thing at least is still the same, even if Zuko can’t go out every night anymore. Partly because he needs to hold himself back from the temptation to turn his searching toward the Upper Ring, and maybe toward something other than a sky bison, if he lets himself loose too much.

But an at least equal if not bigger reason is that it had taken less than a day for Sokka and Zuko to add together new physical proximity and a newly private room and come up with Sokka staying the night.

Not every night, of course. Not even often enough to qualify as frequent. But it’s possible now, where before it wasn’t, and Zuko clings with both hands to the fact that after dinner and pai sho, he and Sokka can sometimes slip upstairs and pull the world tight around them, until it is just the two of them in their space again with no thoughts or worries for anything except each other.

&#45;-

Sokka is up before Zuko, which would be a rarity if it weren’t for Zuko’s nightmares. Sokka had known they were bad, from napping in the afternoons, but at night…well, they’re something else, at night. And now that Sokka is awake in the predawn light, rubbing slow, soothing circles on Zuko’s back to keep him in some state of dreamlessness, he can’t help *thinking*. Sokka really wishes he could just snuggle back into Zuko’s warmth and go back to sleep, or at the very least focus on how nice it is to have his own personal firebender as the nights get chill. Even a few weeks ago, Sokka probably would have been able to drift half-awake and thinking of nothing much beyond the feel of Zuko pressed against him.

But there’s something about being with Zuko in the Upper Ring that makes Sokka’s everyday concerns much more present and intrusive and loud, like they weren’t before. Or maybe it’s just that time is running short, or that he and Toph and Katara and Aang are finally feeling like their clues are coming together. Maybe there’s just more on Sokka’s mind in general now than there was the first time he stepped into the Blooming Petal.

But Sokka is pretty sure that something about the act of going to the Lower Ring to see Zuko had become a ritual of sorts. A routine where Sokka shed things like eclipses and missing companions and anything outside the two of them, and then picked all those things back up again on his journey home.

And now Zuko is here. It’s not bad—this part in particular is pretty excellent. But Zuko hasn’t felt quite as distant as he used to from Sokka’s normal life. And Sokka hadn’t realized how much purposeful separation he’d been keeping between his time with Zuko and everything else until it suddenly collapsed. Or how that separation gave him much-needed space from his thoughts, too.

Sokka is finding it increasingly hard to set aside the concerns of his normal life, especially in the quiet moments like this when Zuko is passed out, wiped from helping Iroh open the new shop. And he is starting to kind of hats that he can’t stop his mind churning. His thoughts travel all too easily from the half-spoken fears that fell from Zuko’s unconscious lips to all the warnings they’ve been receiving lately in their hunt, all the metaphorical stones they’ve found already overturned. All signs point to some other person—persons?—being on the chase for Appa too. Aang might be willing to be all broody and frustrated and ‘let them come’ about it, but Sokka can’t stop remembering Zuko all those weeks back pointing out that Appa would be great bait, for an Avatar.

Spirits, what are they going to do with another enemy in the city? They can’t even get a handle on the one they already have—and Sokka can admit that the Dai Li are their enemy in the privacy of his own mind, even if he still isn’t willing to take action against a group like that without hard proof. What happens if there’s another adversary out there, already so close? There’s only so much the three of them can do to watch Aang’s back.

Zuko stirs then with the abrupt wakefulness that comes with the sun rising, breaking Sokka out of his thoughts. Sokka smiles at Zuko’s murmur of pleasure when Sokka doesn’t stop rubbing circles on his back, letting himself get momentarily lost in the sound. This, at least, still chases away everything except thoughts of Zuko. Sokka cranes his neck to see one gold eye slitted open, peeking through disheveled hair and blankets.

“Good morning, beautiful,” Sokka whispers, just so he can see Zuko roll his eyes so hard they fall closed again. Zuko turns his face into the pillow, but he doesn’t shrug Sokka’s hand off, and his body stays heavy and relaxed. Which is all Sokka is ever striving for, when Zuko wakes from the bad dreams he never seems to remember so long as Sokka can keep his subconscious locked onto other things.

&#45;-

Zuko is aware of the way proximity seems to bleed Sokka’s life into his own even if he doesn’t know what to do about it. Zuko appreciates how easy it is to train with Sokka now that Zuko doesn’t need to work back-to-back shifts in order to have the time. And Zuko can acknowledge, in the privacy of his own mind when it’s just him and the night is dark and no one is around to see his face, that he loves the way Sokka just pops in. Sokka swings by the Jasmine Dragon in the mornings and afternoons, sometimes for a snack, sometimes just to say hello and give Zuko a smile. The easiness of it sets something warm and strong burning in Zuko’s chest, more intense and consuming than Jet’s hours of staring ever could kindle.

But it’s also surprisingly dissatisfying to realize that there were places in the Lower Ring that they can’t call theirs anymore. And somehow the casual feel of the whole thing now that they both don’t need to set aside specific time makes Zuko even more achingly aware that for all he is getting pulled more and more into moments of Sokka’s day to day life, Zuko is distinctly not a part of it. Not the real parts, anyway.

Zuko might see Sokka more and might have a little part of each of Sokka’s days to call his own, but Zuko isn’t part of what Sokka *does*. Zuko is just…what Sokka does, when Sokka’s real life is on hold. And that’s fine. It is. Usually. Zuko adores the easy conversation between them and the way he can hoard new things again, little tidbits that no one would ever think to mention but that Zuko cherishes because they are *Sokka*.

Other times…other times it’s hard to hold onto Lee, when Sokka is constantly, wordlessly, implicitly expecting him to be Zuko. Those times Zuko feels like he’s fraying at the edges, trying to remember what the rules are anymore to who he is trying to be. Those are the times when it’s all too easy to forget what it is, exactly, he’s supposed to be trying to be in the first place.
