“So, why’d you never mention Jasmine,” Sokka asks around what sounds like a mouthful of muffin.

“What?” Zuko glances up from his sweeping to make sure that Sokka still has food in front of him, relaxing when he sees there’s more than half the plate left.

“Your nice ostrich horse,” Sokka says, resting his chin on his fist. “The one you stole, and then lovingly named Jasmine after your Uncle’s favorite tea.”

“Shut up,” Zuko mutters, focusing on the crumbs caught under the table. He’s handling closing today, since Uncle covered opening, so it's empty except him, and Sokka watching.

“I’m just saying.” Sokka takes another bite of muffin. “It seems like you were really fond of her.”

“What are you, jealous?” Zuko snaps, as if Sokka doesn’t know by now that he bites back hardest when someone pokes too close. “She was an ostrich horse.”

“A loyal, faithful companion. At your side through thick and thin. Through the good and the bad. And to leave her, forgotten—”

“I didn’t *forget* her.” He spent—spends—far more time than he probably should, when work is slow, wondering what her life is like these days.

“No, you just never talk about her.”

“Because she’s an *ostrich horse*.” Zuko glares in exasperation, huffing when he sees the teasing tilt to Sokka’s smile. “We sold her to a nice-looking couple, anyway, so she’s fine. They couldn’t take the ferry for some reason.”

“Hmm. Is that how you got to Ba Sing Se? On the ferry?”

“Yeah,” Zuko grunts. The less he can talk about *that* whole experience with Sokka, the better. Zuko isn’t ashamed of it, he just…doesn’t particularly like to think about when, exactly, Jet started pretending.

“We kind of just walked in,” Sokka offers, redirecting Zuko away from things best left unconsidered.

“They let you do that?” Zuko can’t imagine the vast bureaucracy of Ba Sing Se letting anyone within the walls without requiring all forms filled out in triplicate.

“Well, not exactly,” Sokka hedges. “But the walls were under attack at the time, so I guess they made an exception, because, you know, priorities. And then, well—Aang.”

Zuko’s broom slows. “…Under attack?” He hadn’t heard of any kind of military mobilizations after the attack on the North. News doesn’t exactly reach him directly, anymore —if you could call what he used to receive ‘direct’—but something like that would have been known outside the walls before it happened. Zuko doesn’t think he arrived so much earlier in Ba Sing Se than Sokka to have missed something like that.

“Yeah,” Sokka says through the last bite of his muffin. “Didn’t I tell you about that?” “…No.” Zuko carefully props his broom against a table. He has a feeling he is maybe going to want to sit down, for this.

“Oh yeah, it was *nuts*,” Sokka says with a combination of enthusiasm and horror. “Ba Sing Se’s defenses are beyond incompetent, as it turns out. They basically only have the walls going for them.”

“Well. Yeah.” That’s not exactly hard to pick up, from Uncle’s stories about the siege. But stone walls are rather flame resistant, and with enough earthbenders you can do plenty of damage when you can always fall back behind walls. And especially if you can trap your enemy between them.

“Which would have been totally fine,” Sokka continues, “If they didn’t have a wall-busting drill basically designed specifically for the purpose. It was actually really cool, the way they used the rotational force of the—”

“Hold on.” Zuko would normally love hearing Sokka ramble semi-rhapsodic about topics that Zuko has no hope of understanding, but there’s a nagging shard of premonition low in his gut that he can’t ignore. “Who is ‘they’?”

Sokka pauses in the middle of reaching for another muffin, eyes widening as they flash toward Zuko. Zuko rarely asks direct questions about things that skirt close to being Avatar business. “Uh, a real serious knife-y girl—”

That could be anyone.

“—and a super cheerful flirty chick—”

Okay, okay, maybe it was just—

“—and your sister.”

*Fuck*. Zuko’s flinch is automatic, the sudden surge of his inner flame feeling more like bravado than strength as his heart begins to pound triple-time. He is peripherally aware of Sokka straightening from his slouch, trying to catch his eye, but he can’t—he just—*fuck.*

“You didn’t know?” Sokka frowns, looking startled and taken aback.

“No! I—how would I know?” Why would Sokka expect Zuko to be fully brief on Azula’s activities? Did Azula *say* something to him to suggest that? “*When*?”

“Literally right when we got here,” Sokka says, and Zuko can tell Sokka is trying to make his voice calm because he doesn’t want to freak Zuko out, which Zuko normally appreciates, but that ship has fucking sailed. “You’re upset?”

“Yes, I’m upset!” Zuko shouts, incredulous. Why the fuck is he the only one? “Azula is trying to get into the city!”

“I mean, we stopped her,” Sokka points out, far too casually for someone who has met Azula before.

Zuko braces his fists on a table, forcing himself to take a few deep breaths that do nothing to calm his spinning thoughts. “Did she say anything?” Agni’s tits, he doesn’t know if he wants the answer to be yes or no.

“I don’t know,” Sokka says slowly, holding himself like he thinks he might be walking on eggshells. Which he is, because *Azula*. “It was a while ago.”

“Sokka, please,” Zuko pleads, the words scraping his throat with their naked urgency. “Try to remember. Did she say anything?”

“Um, she, uh…she laughed kind of, like, meaningfully at one point, I guess…”

“What was happening?” Zuko demands, ignoring Sokka’s side-eyed confusion.

“Uh…we were trying to stop them, and they were trying to fight us, and the cheerful pink girl —”

“Ty Lee,” Zuko supplies absently, trying to build the scene in his mind.

“You know her?”

“Obviously,” Zuko says, waving the question away and scowling at Sokka to get back on track.

“…Right. So uh, anyway…Ty Lee. She said a flirty thing, and your sister…laughed.”

Zuko narrows his eyes. “A flirty think to who?”

“Um. Me?”

Zuko stares as he tries to play out interaction. “And what did you do?”

Sokka shifts in his chair, looking vaguely like he thinks he might be in trouble. But Zuko couldn’t give a shit about who Sokka may or may not have flirted with before walking into the teashop. Zuko needs information. “I just kind of…waved back and said hi?”

“And then Azula..?”

“And then Azula laughed. And maybe muttered something like ‘of course’?” Sokka hesitates, like he isn’t sure whether to share. “And like…she has this type of laugh that makes it sound like she knows all this stuff about you that you don’t even know about yourself?”

“I’m familiar with that one,” Zuko says, mind racing down too many different paths to even count. “Was it more delighting in your misery? Or mocking you for being in the situation in the first place?”

Sokka blinks, starting to look about a quarter as freaked out as Zuko feels. “Um—the mocking. I guess.”

“Okay,” Zuko nods, trying to pull his inner fire back toward his center. “Okay. Is that all?”

“I don’t know.” Sokka tugs at his wolf tail, blowing out a frustrated breath. “It was a fight. You know how people just say shit in battle.”

“Like what.” Azula never just ‘says shit.’

“You know, normal fight stuff.” Sokka waves his hands like he’s reaching for the words. “Like ‘follow them’ and ‘you won’t get away’ and ‘the Avatar is mine,’ that kind of stuff. Then they split up, so I don’t really know if she said anything to Aang after that.”

Zuko closes his eyes. Agni burn it all.

“I—Zuko, are you okay? Why do you care so much? What’s going on?”

“*Fuck*,” Zuko whispers, without opening his eyes. Maybe if he never opens them again, he can just…pretend that he isn’t fucking *weeks* late in hearing about this.

“What*?* What is it?”

This is not good. This is so not good. Zuko had considered, obviously, the possibility that Azula wouldn’t chase him, but would take over Zuko’s mission instead. He had expected it, really, after the fight in that no-name dried-up town. But that had all felt abstract, something that was part of his old life, outside the walls. Something that was no part of Lee, or the Zuko he was with Sokka, because Ba Sing Se was separate from the rest of the world.

It can only be an abstract concern, though, if Azula doesn’t already know exactly where her prey is. It can only stay outside the walls if *Azula* does. And she has known the Avatar is here from the very start. And she said herself, she wouldn’t let them get away. Zuko knows from long experience that Azula doesn’t let things she considers hers stay out of sight for long without checking in. She would be trying to get in the walls. Agni’s flaming dick, Zuko and Uncle got in easily, just by looking ragged and tired and having enough money to get on the ferry. Azula might not be one to readily give up her creature comforts to masquerade as a refugee and follow that exact path, but Zuko knows more than anyone how coldly practical and unsentimental she can be, when sufficiently motivated. She could already be here.

“Zuko.” Sokka’s sharp voice breaks through Zuko’s spiraling thoughts, dragging his eyes off the floor onto Sokka’s tight face. “What’s going on in your head? You’re kind of freaking me out, buddy.”

“You aren’t safe.” Zuko’s lips feel numb. “You aren’t safe.” The thought is dominating, loud, ringing like a gong in his unscarred ear.

“What?” Sokka sits back, brow twisting. “What do you mean?”

“If Azula—she’s going to—she might already *be* here—”

“Zuko,” Sokka interrupts with something close to gentleness, which is *not* what Zuko needs now. “I think we would know if the Lightning Princess was running around Ba Sing Se.”

Zuko stares, stunned that someone so perceptive could be so *blind*, finally waving his hand to take in the Jasmine Dragon. “Would you?”

Sokka snaps his mouth shut on his reply, staring back, blank-faced. Remember who he is talking to, maybe. Remembering who Zuko used to be. “That’s different.”

“How.”

“You aren’t trying to cause problems.” As if Zuko has ever needed to *try* for things to go wrong.

“Neither will Azula until she’s ready.”

Sokka sighs, slumping back and running a hand over his face. “I think we’d notice if Crazy Blue was around.”

“She wouldn’t be direct,” Zuko tries to explain. He needs Sokka to understand, the words flying off his tongue as he thinks them. “Azula knows that you can throw yourself at the walls for years and only break yourself against them. She wouldn’t try that again.”

“So then there’s nothing to worry about,” Sokka concludes, words surrounded with softness in a way that has Zuko bristling.

“That doesn’t mean she won’t get in,” Zuko argues, hearing the desperate rasp to his voice and hating it. “That just means she’s going to be…efficient about it.”

“Efficient?”

“Yeah,” Zuko says, not knowing where the words are coming from but needing to say them because he doesn’t have *time* to find the right ones. “She didn’t try a siege, she tried a wall breaker. She didn’t come with an army, she can with her friends. She isn’t going to just outright attack, she’s going to…sneak.” Zuko remembers Azula as he last saw her. It still feels weird to picture her grown-up face with that distinctive makeup and sharply perfect hair and bright, dazzling armor. No, Azula hasn’t forgotten how to go unnoticed.

The length of the silence finally registers, and Zuko braces himself as he glances up at Sokka’s expression, heart sinking. Zuko has seen this one often enough, on Uncle and his crew and everyone else, to know what it means. “You don’t believe me.”

“I didn’t say that,” Sokka hedges.

“You didn’t have to,” Zuko bites back.

“No, Zuko, hold on.” Sokka shoves back from the table, taking a few quick steps across the shop before pulling up short against the edge of Zuko’s glare. “I believe you. I believe that you’re worried about this. That you think this could happen. And I’m sure you’re right and that she will try. But Zuko, Ba Sing Se has been holding out against the Fire Nation for decades.”

“We got in,” Zuko says softly. Two sons of Agni’s blood, welcomed into the heart of the Earth Kingdom and given a teashop because they asked. Azula will turn this place to ashes, if she wants to.

Sokka doesn’t see it the same way, though. “But you aren’t exactly trying to tear shit up, Zuko. Unless this has all been a long plan to poison some rich person’s tea or something.”

*“No!”*

Sokka’s shoulders slump, hands coming up in a soothing gesture as his face immediately twists with regret. “I’m joking, Zuko. I’m just joking.”

“Not about that,” Zuko warns, voice hard. Never about his reasons for being here. Not when Zuko barely has an idea himself, lately.

“Fine,” Sokka agrees, fiddling with his wrist wraps. “Just…I think you have a lot of history with your sister, Zuko. And a lot if it is bad.” That is…not wrong. “And I think that might influence how you react to things, is all. It doesn’t mean your reaction is bad, or wrong, just…I think sometimes you see her in a particular way that isn’t how everyone else does.”

*That* Zuko can’t argue with. It’s undoubtedly true, even if it’s not true in the way he thinks Sokka means. Zuko could push this, could try to lay it out and make Sokka understand, could walk him through Zuko’s entire history with Azula and all that it means for this moment in the present.

But Zuko is already feeling uncomfortable with how close Sokka is edging to humoring him. He knows from years with Uncle the difference between being indulged and being believed. Zuko doesn’t want that to infect what he has with Sokka with that. And Zuko is painfully aware, suddenly, that he’s running close to territory that he doesn’t let himself touch. He’s skirting up against the parts of Sokka’s life that Zuko isn’t a part of, that Zuko can never let himself be a part of because he doesn’t trust what he will do with himself if he is.

“You’ll be careful,” Zuko finally says, not quite able to bring himself to look Sokka in the face, aware that Sokka will read the words as an acquiesce or admittance when they’re anything but.

“You sound like Katara,” Sokka half-smiles, and Zuko doesn’t have the space inside himself left to feel any kind of way about how he is probably the thing Katara tells Sokka to be careful of. “I promise that we’re careful. But we can’t hide away forever.”

No, they can’t. Zuko knows from experience that Azula will always find you, in the end, no matter how well you hide yourself away. All you can do is prepare.

&#45;-

Zuko is visibly anxious that night as he and Uncle share dinner and Zuko knows it. He can’t keep his focus on what’s in front of him. He keeps messing up the heat distribution on his pan, which he hasn’t done in months. He can’t remember where the plates are. He can’t keep his anxiety from spilling out, like some part of him needs there to be tangible markers of the mess he feels inside.

“Is everything okay, Nephew?” Uncle finally says as Zuko tosses another pan of over-crisped vegetables and under-heated eggs into the garbage. “I can’t help but notice that you seem distracted this evening.”

“Sokka said Azula tried to break into Ba Sing Se,” Zuko says in a rush, like the words have been sitting on the back of his tongue all evening waiting to tumble out. Which they have.

“Ah.” Uncle blinks, looking taken aback by the topic. He takes a moment to martial his thoughts or cue up his aphorisms or whatever as Zuko stares at him, expectant. “It has been a while since you have seen your sister.”

“…Yes.” Since Uncle has seen her, too, and Zuko doesn’t see how it's relevant except to make them both equally in the dark about her movements.

“And even longer since you have truly had a chance to talk with her.”

“I—yes?” They’ve exchanged words. And Azula always wrote letters, even if Zuko didn’t always write back. And why does it matter, it’s not like Azula would ever outright tell anyone her plans, not even Zuko.

“I imagine it’s unsettling,” Uncle continues, seeming to find momentum in Zuko’s agreement. “To realize that Azula is taking on a mission of her own, now. To confront the fact that your little sister is no longer the young girl—”

“What are you talking about?” Zuko cuts in, nearly losing the feel for the heat under yet another pan in his confusion. “I’m ‘unsettled’ because Azula tried to get through the walls! She almost succeeded!”

“She didn’t, though.”

“Because she was only at it for fifteen degrees,” Zuko shouts, trying to shove away the sharp sensation of the ground tilting beneath his feet. He feels like he’s going fucking crazy, for no one else to care about this. Agni, Zuko gets Sokka not understanding. Sokka doesn’t know Azula in any meaningful way. But he thought Uncle would.

“The walls of Ba Sing Se are nothing to underestimate,” Uncle says after a pause. He looks drawn, worn, eyes unfocused as he stares at something Zuko can’t see, and Zuko abruptly remembers all that Uncle has lost here.

Bit still, “Azula is nothing to underestimate, either.”

“I know you have a history with her,” Uncle sighs, and why does everyone keep *saying* that. “But I think we always knew that the Fire Nation would come again for the city. It is not a surprise that they would send one of the royal line, to prove themselves before the nation and the world. Though she is young, I would think, for the responsibility…”

Zuko stares, immobile, before jerking around, signaling the end to the conversation. This isn’t about his fucking *feelings*. This isn’t about him being replaced, or overshadowed, or whatever the fuck everyone seems to be dancing around like Zuko is some barrel of blasting jelly about to explode. It’s about the fact that Azula has set herself the goal of getting into the city, where her primary mission and secondary goals have all been sitting, complacent. It’s about the fact that Azula doesn’t fail at the things she sets out to do.

And for Uncle to act like it’s about *growing up* and *feeling inadequate* and not immediate preparations and defensive maneuvers…it hurts Zuko like a brand, to stare down how little Uncle truly knows her.

Everyone seems to be telling Zuko to calm down, to not be scared, and none of them seem to see that they aren’t nearly scared enough. Zuko *knows* Azula, more than anyone else ever will. And with a cold flicker of his inner flame, Zuko realizes that he has never gone so long without hearing from her in one way or another. It makes him feel untethered and dangerously adrift, to know that he will only hear about what she is doing after the fact, through gossip and rumor and offhand comments.

Though from what Sokka said…maybe Azula has been sending Zuko messages, in her own way. Ones that she knew her brother, at least, would understand as long as they made it to his ears.

&#45;-

Zuko barely waits for Uncle to head to bed before he’s slipping out his window into the very conveniently located tree next to his bedroom. Uncle had opted for the smaller room with the view of the street, instead of the garden, saying something about being used to city noises now.

Sometimes Zuko wonders how much Uncle knows—or suspects—behind his purposeful ignorance.

Zuko doesn’t have time to waste on wondering tonight, though, or any to spend on being cautious. If Azula is in the city, Zuko doesn’t have time for anything. She will have a plan and it will be intricately thought out and completely controlled beyond anything Zuko could ever hope to match. All Zuko can do is what he’s always done: barrel forward until he finally crashes into a wall he can’t burn through.

Caution has never sat all that comfortably on Zuko’s shoulders, anyway.

It’s a cloudy night, deep shadows hiding the moon as Zuko slips along the roofline. It’s much harder in the Upper and Middle Rings to move like this, but then Zuko is more used to dealing with estates and perimeter walls than the crowded togetherness of the Lower Ring. It’s colder without so many buildings to act as windbreaks, though. Or maybe it’s colder because it’s that time of year, because time passes even if Zuko refuses to directly admit it. Zuko leans into his breath of fire against the chill, prioritizing avoiding stiff limbs and fumbling fingers even as the draw on his inner flame takes more concentration and energy to maintain.

The Upper Ring is full of Dai Li agents—Zuko had been unsurprised that they would monitor their own the most, and then not surprised at all—but it takes Zuko a few hours to find an agent on her own in the Middle Ring, and then another of following her at the edge of his heat sense before she moves underground. Zuko watches, pressed flat against a curving, artistic rooftop, as she slips into a manhole cover, silently thanking Agni that she didn’t just open a hole into the street like they seem to do in the Lower Ring. Then he slips off the roof and into the shadows at the base of the building, casting his fire sense downward.

It’s a strain, trying to sense anything through earth and rock. But as he carefully approaches the manhole cover his fire sense finds a pocket of open air to flow through. It’s not much, but it’s enough at least for Zuko to know that there isn’t anyone on the ladder—please let there be a ladder—on the other side.

Zuko carefully levers up the heavy stone cover with a sword, wincing at the damage it’s probably doing to the blade. He holds his breath for any sign of movement, slowly relaxing when his lungs start to call for air and nothing moves on rooves or the street or down below. Zuko takes a quick moment to confirm that the cover can be opened from the underside without earthbending. Then he slides into the yawning darkness and pulls the opening closed behind him.

Zuko freezes on the ladder, carefully controlling his breath and straining all his senses for movement or puffs of fresh air or anything to give him a clue about his surroundings. The darkness is intense, but as his eyes adjust Zuko realizes it’s not absolute. There’s a faint greenish glow past his feet. Zuko concentrates on silently moving toward it, dropping into a broad, clearly well-used tunnel.

It looks old, and like it’s been shored up in places, visible signs of fresh earthbending over dusty, stacked stone. Maybe it’s some earlier version of Ba Sing Se, covered by time and built over by later generations, still stretching beneath the thriving city. Or maybe it was always meant to be a secret beneath the earth. Regardless, if it’s as vast as Zuko thinks then it’s the perfect kind of unseen system for a secret police network to move around a city. And the perfect kind of place to hide secrets.

Zuko casts his fire sense outward, finding the heat of his agent again. With all senses peeled he begins to trail her again, hyperaware of the way sound can echo in a space like this. It’s hard to sense direction underground, especially as he twists and turns through the tunnels, especially without Agni tugging at him from above. But Zuko is almost certain that they are traveling outward, under the walls and toward the true heart of the city.

## Chapter 26: The Ashes in Your Wake

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

No specific extra warnings for this one!

### Text

Sokka stalks into the Jasmine Dragon as Zuko is finishing up his shift, trailed by the scent late autumn and a mood that Zuko doesn’t want to tangle with. Zuko takes one look at Sokka’s tight shoulders, the tic in his jaw, his restless fists, and sharply readjusts his expectations for the afternoon.

“Training,” Zuko half-asks, half-orders as he pulls Sokka into the privacy of the staff-only half of the building where it will be more contained if Sokka decides to lose his shit.

“Spirits, yes, please.”

Zuko leads Sokka out to the enclosed courtyard attached to the teashop that Zuko had immediately and wordlessly claimed as his own, glaring in preemptive warning even though Uncle hadn’t challenged it. For the first time in years, they had plenty of space for both of them.

Zuko tries running Sokka through some warmup katas to start, the kind where you can really throw your effort behind the punches and kicks if you need to work something out. Zuko does them a lot. But it quickly becomes apparent that Sokka’s concentration is completely shot. Sokka can’t seem to go more than a minute without muttering something to himself, too low for Zuko to hear with his scarred ear and the whoosh of his own controlled breaths. Whatever is distracting him, it’s enough that Zuko can tell at a glance that Sokka won’t be able to find the rhythm needed to make the kata’s steps anything other than a mess.

Zuko bites his lip as Sokka stumbles out of another easy spin. “Do you want to just…hit something?”

“As long as it’s not you,” he says, scrubbing at his face with rough hands.

Zuko…appreciates the sentiment. Sokka doesn’t have the patience or concentration right now for sparring, and Zuko considers what they can do that involves hitting things while talking about whatever it is that’s bothering Sokka at the same time, since he clearly wants to get it out judging by all the dark muttering. “Wait here.”

There’s a storage room in the back of the Jasmine Dragon where Zuko and Uncle had dumped all the things the old wellness shop had left behind. Zuko is pretty sure he saw a broken-off broom handle—perfect for swinging and smashing—and a bucket of little sandbags—perfect for heating to put on sore muscles, but more specifically for being smashed. It’s amazing the kind of crap that people accumulate and leave behind.

“What do we do with all that?” Sokka frowns when Zuko re-emerges, still in the exact spot Zuko left him in.

“Whatever you want,” Zuko shrugs, setting down his bucket and shifting uncertainly. He always wants to just burn things away with mindless physical activity when he can’t burn them directly into his inner flame, but maybe Sokka is different? “You can just kind of…” Zuko tosses a little bag into the air and gives it an off-handed smack with the broom handle. They both watch as it arcs away, skidding to a halt against the cobblestones.

“Or we can do something else,” Zuko hedges when Sokka just keeps staring, unmoving. “I guess we—”

“No,” Sokka says, making grabbing motions with his hands. “That. I want to do that.”

Zuko puffs out a relieved breath, quickly passing over the broom handle and setting himself up a few judicious paces away with the bucket. Sokka scowls down at his own hands for a moment, positioning and repositioning them around the wood before finally giving Zuko a nod, still looking dissatisfied. But when Zuko tentatively throws a sandbag into an easy toss, Sokka immediately turns his hips behind an air-whistling swing, sending the bag shooting against the far wall of the courtyard.

Sokka stares for a second, then grunts in satisfaction. “Again.”

Zuko settles in, perfectly content to help Sokka burn off whatever is bothering him. Sokka’s grumbling and muttering gets louder and louder the more he exerts himself, though, and Agni, Zuko really wishes he was better at this kind of thing. Sokka might need to vent more than he needs to hit something, and Zuko doesn’t quite know what to say back. Should he agree and affirm? Be calmly reasonable? Challenging? Zuko isn’t used to Sokka being so… bitter? Sokka can certainly be bitingly realistic when he wants to be, and sarcastically cynical, but this feels different somehow, more upset, and Zuko isn’t exactly good with emotions to begin to know how he’s supposed to respond.

“I’m just so fucking *tired* of the whole thing,” Sokka finally bursts out, emphasizing the words with a harsh slash of the broom handle.

“Hm.” Zuko refrains from pointing out that Sokka should keep his feet braced a little wider to fully leverage the power of his core. He is pretty sure Sokka already knows that.

“We just keep coming up empty every single time.”

“Mhm.”

“And yeah, not every clue is a good clue, not everything is going to pan out. But it’s the fucking *waiting*.”

Zuko grunts.

“All the fucking administration and ministries and the councilor of this needs to check with the chairman of that. How can anyone *function* with this much bureaucracy? It’s like you need to submit formal documentation to wipe your own ass.”

Zuko cocks his head. It’s a colorful image. He’s sure Ba Sing Se considered it at some point. “And I get that not everything works the way you want it to, and there’s different cultural shit to deal with here. But Spirits, it’s *ridiculous*!” Sokka throws out his arms so wide that he almost misses his next swing. “We’re here with critical fucking information about the war and they care more about the king’s fucking party schedule staying on track!”

Zuko hums. That sounds about right.

“It’s all feasts and giant houses and clothes. Like if they just keep giving us fancier shit and more medals and honors, we’ll just forget about the fact that we’re on a deadline here.”

Well, people usually do.

“They just don’t *do* anything.”

Zuko is pretty sure that Ba Sing Se is doing plenty. They just don’t want Sokka to see any of it.

“I mean, fuck, ignore Appa, ignore me, but ignore *Aang*? Who ignores the Avatar?”

Zuko takes a deep, bracing breath. His next toss stays steady.

“It’s not like everyone needs to *like* Aang, but to just act like the Avatar isn’t even there? To act like the *war* isn’t there? How does that help anyone?”

It helps those in power retain their power. People in control don’t like change or uncertainty, in Zuko’s experience. War and the return of a centuries-old spiritual bridge bring a lot of both.

“I mean, fuck, no one does that! The rest of the Earth Kingdom doesn’t do that! Omashu doesn’t do that!”

Well, Omashu is a Fire Nation territory now, last Zuko heard. So. It would be a little hard for them to pretend like the war wasn’t happening.

“Just give me something to *fight* against. I can’t deal with all this waiting anymore. We just plan and plan and do *nothing*.”

Zuko can understand that particular feeling. Especially if you leave out the planning bits.

“Spirits, at least the Northern Water Tribe *did* stuff, even if it was dumb. At least Zhao did things you could react to. Fuck, *you* did stuff when you didn’t have to. At least we could do something back. At least we knew the things we were doing were *worth* something.”

Zuko…is glad he could be of use? His next sandbag flies a little unsteady until Sokka sends it across the courtyard.

“But no, Ba Sing Se’s King just sits on his throne and goes to his parties and doesn’t care that time is running out! Who just sits at home when there is a war on! My Dad never just sat at home! Chief Arnook got up off his ass! I bet the Fire Lord isn’t—”

Zuko can’t hold in a flinch, his next toss off the mark enough that Sokka stutters to an abrupt halt, finally noticing what he’s saying and to who.

“Sorry,” Sokka immediately pants, knuckles white. “Sorry. I know we don’t…”

Zuko shrugs, staring down at his almost empty bucket, trying to reel back in his thready inner flame. “It’s fine. It’s…fine.” He glances up at Sokka’s disbelieving scoff. “It’s in the past.” Even he can hear the lie in the words.

Sokka frowns, weight shifting like he’s on the verge of pushing. He ends up giving a grudging nod, though, spinning away to begin kicking sandbags back across the courtyard and accepting the boundary Zuko is drawing. Zuko can’t talk about…that. Not when Sokka is in a mood like this.

They gather the scattered sacks in silence, Zuko using the moment to try to settle himself. Without speaking they move back to their former places, Sokka with his feet braced a little wider this time. Zuko makes himself comfortable on the cobblestones and starts tossing bags into the air again, relaxing into the rhythm and the sound of wood cutting through air and sand slapping against stone. He watches Sokka wallop sandbags until they run through two more buckets and Sokka is physically exhausted, sweaty clumps of hair sticking to his neck, fingers slow and stiff when he finally uncurls them from the broom handle.

“Better?”

“Kind of.”

“Not really,” Zuko translates, because he can still see that keyed-up energy rattling through Sokka’s body.

“It’s just…a lot, today,” Sokka finally sighs, the words half apology, half explanation.

Zuko bites his lip as Sokka starts into another round of broody staring into the distance. Just how much of a break does Sokka need from everything today? “Are you still staying for dinner?”

Blue eyes blink into focus on Zuko’s face with enough surprise that Zuko’s inner fire is already settling before Sokka speaks. “Yeah. Yeah, of course.”

His words are tired, but Sokka slips his hand into Zuko’s like he never considered doing anything else. Zuko takes assurance in that as he tugs an atypically wordless Sokka up the back stairs to the washroom in the living quarters. Sokka is tired and stressed and Zuko just…wants to wrap him in something comforting, something luxurious to make the day a little bit better. A private bathroom with indoor plumbing is one of the purest forms of indulgence Zuko can think of after years with little more than communal spaces and politely averted gazes.

Zuko starts the water running in the tub before he begins to strip the sweaty clothes off Sokka. Zuko isn’t trying to start anything, not with Sokka still in the mood he’s in. But Sokka is physically exhausted and mentally strained and dirty, and Zuko can’t do anything about the first two but he can help with that last one.

Zuko keeps his hands steady as he peels away Sokka’s clothes, holding back the heat that instinctively wants to rise to any point of skin that touches Sokka’s. Sokka is uncharacteristically docile throughout, watching with an exhausted curiosity as Zuko tests the water, going along with it as Zuko gently dumps him into the tub. The sound Sokka makes at being surrounded by warm water goes straight to Zuko’s groin, and Zuko shoves it firmly away—something to remember later, when he’s alone, maybe—and sets himself to massaging Sokka’s tense shoulders with heat-warmed hands instead.

Sokka sighs and groans in pleasure as Zuko works out knot after knot and makes sure the water temperature never drops below where Sokka likes it. It’s not exactly what Zuko had in mind for the afternoon, but it still leaves Zuko feeling content in its own way as the sky begins to streak with the coming night. And the effort earns Zuko a tired, appreciative smile and the relaxation of Sokka’s body into his hands, which is all Zuko really needs, anyway.

&#45;-

Sokka’s discontent seems to slip back on along with his clothes, as if getting himself presentable to the world means dragging back on his stress and worries as well. Zuko doesn’t like to see it, and likes even less his own tension around it. He knows on an intellectual level that he doesn’t need to be wary of Sokka’s anger like this, but Zuko still can’t stop the anxious, tense winding of his inner fire around his spine at the sight of it. And Zuko can tell that Sokka notices him reacting, and can tell that it makes Sokka upset, which just makes Zuko react more, and just…fuck everything. Zuko always somehow manages to make things worse.

Uncle glances up, expression mild and questioning when they enter the kitchen without Sokka’s usual energy and chatter. Zuko just shrugs behind Sokka’s back and grabs an entire box of sample cookies from a local baker, shoving it into Sokka’s hands and then shoving Sokka into a seat. Sokka scowls at the treatment but grumbles out a garbled “thanks” around his first bite.

“Maybe you can tell us which you like best, Master Sokka,” Uncle suggests from where he’s prepping ingredients, a second cutting board set up for Zuko. “We are trying to decide what to stock in the shop.”

Sokka grunts, but nods after a moment and begins to eat with a little more thoughtfulness and consideration. Zuko lets out a slow, controlled sigh of relief that Sokka is at least okay enough to focus on a specific task. That it’s maybe just Sokka’s thoughts that are bothering him, and nothing else.

Dinner comes together quickly, thankfully simple enough that Zuko can concentrate on his pan even through his distraction. Sokka still seems tense when Zuko walks plates over to the table, but possibly a little less caught in his own head. Zuko will take it. Especially when his blue eyes, when they drift up, fasten onto Zuko’s face with an automatic warmth that makes Zuko’s inner fire flutter and flip.

They settle to eat in silence, which Zuko has never had any problems with and particularly not tonight. And he is tentatively starting to think that they might actually manage to get through the meal without any flareups when Uncle makes the mistake of trying to find a neutral topic of conversation. Fuck everything. Uncle should know better. Years of traveling with Zuko should have taught Uncle that neutrality is a losing proposition when one side is already angry.

“I welcome your thoughts on the baked goods, after dinner,” Uncle says, eyes thoughtful on Sokka over his cup of tea in a way that Zuko always hates when it’s directed at him. “I am finding that the tastes of customers in the Upper Ring are quite different than at the Blooming Petal.”

Sokka flicks up a look that would probably be an eye roll, if he were in a lighter mood. “I’m sure the nobles around here are totally different kinds of people than the peasants in the Lower Ring.”

“Not different kinds of people,” Uncle replies like an Agni-burned idiot, as if he can’t hear the edge in Sokka’s words that has Zuko straightening in alarm. “Just different tastes.” “They’re definitely all about luxury, up here,” Sokka snorts. “That’s about the only thing. Luxury and themselves and parties. Nothing close to running the things they’re supposed to be in charge of.”

“A trait of the upper class not unique to the Earth King, unfortunately,” Uncle comments, and Zuko wants to drop his head onto the table. The solution to Sokka’s mood is clearly to *not* *engage*.

“I guess you would know,” Sokka mutters to his plate, clearly intending to be heard. Zuko winces. Apparently, Sokka burned off his physical energy, but none of his eagerness for a fight with someone with authority.

Uncle responds as if Sokka’s moodiness weren’t there. Which is his go-to conversational approach with Zuko, really, but Zuko is quite sure it’s not a one-size-fits-all strategy for dealing with angry teenagers. “It is a regrettable fact of life in most communities, certainly, that those with power become concerned primarily with their own influence and how to keep it.”

“Not in the Water Tribe,” Sokka bites out with a kind of resentfulness that has Zuko wishing he could manage to unfreeze himself enough to press his foot against Sokka’s right now.

“No?” Uncle raises an eyebrow. “I have always found the Northern Tribe to be very…set, in their ways.”

“Um,” Zuko says, his inner flame beginning to flutter with something close to panic. He is fairly certain this line of conversation is about to go completely to shit and isn’t quite sure how to stop it.

“Oh?” Sokka’s knuckles are white around his chopsticks. “Spend a lot of time with the Northern Water Tribe?”

Uncle takes a thoughtful bite of food, ignoring the way Zuko is glaring ‘please shut the fuck up right now’ at the side of his face. “I have studied widely and met many people. I traveled much in my younger days.”

“Really,” Sokka says flatly. “Spend any time in the South?”

“Just with me,” Zuko jumps in, because he can see the barbs around that question even if Uncle seems determined it ignore them.

Sokka’s gaze lingers for a moment on Zuko before snapping back to Uncle. “Is that right?”

“Yes,” Uncle says easily. “I regrettable was never able to visit the Southern Tribes, before…” Zuko can see a flicker of understanding cross Uncle’s face. Too late.

“Before what?” Sokka presses, forearms braced against the edge of the table, looking like he’s ready to shove to his feet at any moment.

“Before Fire Lord Azulon decided to move against them,” Uncle finishes, words heavy.

“Is that what you call it, in the Fire Nation?”

“There are many things it could be called,” Uncle says, which is *not* the right answer. Zuko winces again. Sometimes he wishes Uncle were a bit less focused on *teaching* in every conversation.

“And what do *you* call it?” Sokka asks with deceptive softness.

“Um, maybe—”

“Something that was allowed to happen because of war,” Uncle says, steady, calm. Zuko knows Sokka well enough to know that calm is not what he needs right now. “Something that otherwise would never have even been considered, let alone approved.”

“Oh yeah?” Sokka’s voice is acid, and Zuko’s inner fire wavers in response. “I call it attempted genocide. But I guess if it's round two, maybe it loses some of its novelty.”

Uncle sighs, eyes sad as he sets aside his chopsticks. “Terrible things happen in war, because —”

“You think I don’t know that?”

“—because war is a terrible thing. It moves anyone caught in it away from harmony and balance, away from their spiritual—”

“Um, maybe we should just—”

“Is that how you can sit here?” Sokka snaps, and Zuko can see the tic is back in his jaw. “Just focus on your spiritual balance or whatever and tell yourself everything is fine?”

“War drives people to do things that no one would be proud of,” Uncle replies, grave. “We have all done things that we regret.”

Zuko can’t quite swallow back a noise of alarm. He doesn’t need to see the snarl in Sokka’s eyes to know that that was the wrong thing to say. Uncle might not know Sokka’s particular history, but how can he be this blind to keep pressing forward like this? Uncle *knows* about the Southern Raiders.

“Really?” Sokka sits back, and Zuko can see his fingers twisting viciously into the hem of his tunic beneath the table. “What do *you* regret?”

Zuko closes his eyes, because fuck *everything.* Sokka doesn’t know Uncle’s history, either.

“Many things,” Uncle finally says, words quiet in a way that Zuko can recognize as a warning, but that Sokka won’t. “Too many things.”

“Can—”

“I don’t get how you can just sit here like this,” Sokka grinds out. “And act like everything is okay.”

Uncle takes a sip of his tea, a deliberate pause to give breath and space that Zuko can see is lost on Sokka, whose fingers clench at the delay. “It is behind us now,” Uncle finally says. “All we can do is try to move forward.”

Sokka’s breath hisses out with deceptive control. “Why does everyone keep saying that. You don’t just get to put things behind you and pretend that they didn’t happen and force other people to pretend with you.”

“The past can be like quicksand, to the unwary mind,” Uncle replies, as if any of them needs an aphorism right now. “It’s all too easy to become mired in regrets and things already done, and miss the way forward as a result.”

“So you just get to act like you didn’t do any of the things that came before? Like they didn’t happen?”

Zuko goes motionless, seeing the dangerous ground they’re suddenly standing on. But Sokka is fixated on Uncle, and Zuko is almost positive that Sokka doesn’t realize all of what he just asked.

“I remember what came before,” Uncle says softly, setting his teacup down with careful precision. “But those things do not need to define me, now, unless I let them.”

“No?” Sokka’s hands spasm in his lap, and Zuko wants to reach out and take them and lead him from this room, but Zuko can’t even get his lungs to work right, let alone get his body to move. “You did things that have consequences, but you’re ready to move on so everyone else needs to too?”

Uncle picks his words slowly, and with no more understanding of his audience. “I think everyone moves on, as you say, at their own pace. But eventually everyone needs to do so in order to continue growing. The caterpillar cannot become a butterfly unless it—”

“Let’s—”

“You don’t get to just do that,” Sokka snaps. “You don’t get to dictate healing to everyone else. Not when you’re the one who did the damage.”

“War is complex. I don’t think any party is blameless—”

“But you’re the only one trying to pretend it doesn’t matter to you anymore. You’re the one pretending you’re someone you’re not!” The words are for Uncle, but Zuko feels them like a punch to the throat.

“I have changed,” Uncle sighs. “I am no longer the man I once was.”

“Have you, Mushi? That’s great for you. Maybe everyone else hasn’t. Maybe they’re dead, so they never got the *chance* to change.”

Zuko…*really* needs to find a time to tell Sokka about Lu Ten.

“There has been needless death, on both sides.” Uncle says after a heavy pause. “No side is fully blameless, or fully culpable. But to stay mired in personal grief is to stay mired in a moment of war, to never let yourself move past that time and experience the rest of life.” “Oh, I’m sorry that my grief is holding you back from experiencing life. How *inconvenient*.”

Sokka’s words are raw and bleeding and Zuko’s breath catches over the open pain in them, even Uncle sits back, looking faintly startled, under their intensity. Is Sokka…is he still talking about his mother? He doesn’t normally act like that wound is so fresh…

“Grief is never convenient. For anyone.” Uncle says it like he’s finally noticing that he and Sokka have been having two very different conversations. “No one wants to feel it. It can be overwhelming and crushing. But eventually, it has to lessen, or you must become strong enough to bear it. Or else you cannot go on.” Uncle pauses, but apparently can’t resist an opportunity to offer oblique and unasked-for advice because of course he can’t. “It is not uncommon, for grief to become anger. It is easier to be strong when one is angry.”

Zuko pinches his eyes closed. Anger is easy, Zuko knows it. There’s a reason he burns everything into rage when it starts to feel overwhelming because rage, at least, he knows how to deal with. But you don’t *say that to an angry person*.

“My anger is perfectly valid,” Sokka growls, words like brittle iron. “It’s not some—some *mask* because I don’t want to admit my emotions.”

“I didn’t say that,” Uncle frowns.

“You didn’t have to.”

“Maybe we…” Zuko blinks in surprise at getting more than one word out as two pairs of eyes suddenly land on him. “Maybe we should…talk about something else?”

Maybe Zuko should have been more prepared with something actually worth saying, because Sokka’s eyes are slits of icy blue. “No. You don’t get to decide when people need to be over things because it makes you uncomfortable.”

Zuko jerks in surprise. “I wasn’t—” Was he?

Sokka makes a wordless noise of frustration. “Both of you are acting like you can just leave things behind. Like all the stuff you did doesn’t matter anymore because you don’t want it to and everyone else is just supposed to go along with it.”

Sokka is glaring at Uncle, but Zuko is the one feeling the ground tilt beneath him at the words. Isn’t…isn’t that what he and Sokka *do*? Isn’t that exactly how they’ve come this far? By not talking about the shared minefield of their past beyond the parts they already know are safe?

“I didn’t…”

Sokka slumps back, sounding suddenly exhausted. “What? You didn’t what, Zuko?” It’s like the animating energy is leaking out of him, and even feeling like he doesn’t know where to stand, Zuko wants to reach out and yank Sokka close against his chest, seeing him looking so worn down.

“There is no clear black and white in war,” Uncle jumps in, frowning at Sokka in a way that Zuko doesn’t need and doesn’t want. “There never is. But that does not mean that people are not allowed to move forward, and grow, and find a new place for themselves—”

“A fresh start in Ba Sing Se,” Sokka cuts in, acid.

“People are allowed fresh starts.”

Sokka grunts, staring at Uncle’s hard yellow eyes before turning to Zuko. “Do you agree?”

“What?” Zuko isn’t sure which side he’s supposed to be agreeing with. Both feel like a trap.

“Do people get fresh starts?” Sokka asks, the words coming out like raised fists. “Can they do whatever they want and then decide one day to wave their hands and start fresh and act like it didn’t happen?”

Zuko really wishes he knew what was going on in Sokka’s head, because every answer that bounces frantically through his mind feels wrong. “I—maybe? Things can be—different.” Zuko isn’t good enough to do this just with words, doesn’t know how to open himself up like he needs to when Uncle is here.

“So you get to act like the past never happened?”

Uncle steps back into Zuko’s foundering silence. “There is a difference between acting like it never happened and never—”

“You did things.” Sokka grips the edge of the table, tendons straining. “Both of you. You made choices.”

“I didn’t *have* a choice,” Zuko says, stung into speaking before he has a chance to think about the words. “Not like you.”

“What does *that* mean?”

“You got to—decide. For yourself.” Zuko shifts, unable to relax with Uncle across the table to hear this but unable stop the words now that he’s started. “How to be and how to act and what you wanted to do. If you wanted to stay or go. You got to choose all—” He waves a hand, gesturing toward…everything. “—this.”

Sokka takes a deep breath, fingers tapping against the tabletop. “And you didn’t?”

Zuko glowers, hyperaware of the way the expression pulls at the stiff skin of his scar. “No.”

“That’s a load of shit,” Sokka finally says, voice perfectly level.

*“What*?” Zuko is peripherally aware of Uncle stiffening in a way that would normally have Zuko trying to figure out how to get out of the room, except Zuko has been feeling like that since dinner started. He’s a bit numb to it by now.

Sokka turns toward him in response to his tone, facing him full on and no longer making Uncle the center of his focus. It does not, for once, feel good. “You could have walked away from it all.”

“No, I—”

“Yes*,*” Sokka cuts in. “You could have. Maybe you didn’t have great choices. Maybe you didn’t have a lot of them. But you *had* them. No one ever made you chase the Avatar.”

“Yes, they—”

“*No*.” Sokka’s hands flex, palm up, like he wants to reach for Zuko but is holding himself back. Zuko's inner flame feels like it wants to burn him from the inside out. “They put something you wanted in front of you and told you one way to get it. You chose to take what they offered.”

“That’s not how it works,” Zuko growls. Not for a Crown Prince. Not for one that wanted to stay alive, anyway. He turns to Uncle for confirmation, but Uncle is damningly quiet. Looking at the way Uncle stares into his tea instead of meeting Zuko’s eyes, Zuko abruptly remembers that Uncle probably never wanted to chase the Avatar in the first place. Not really.

Sokka notices Uncle’s silence, of course, his tone going softer but words still relentless. “You didn’t just end up here, like some rudderless boat on a tide. You made choices. You chose to play within the rules they set instead of trying to find new ones.” He pauses, waiting for Zuko to respond, to challenge. But Zuko doesn’t know what to say, and Uncle is finally staying quiet. Agreeing, maybe. “Those choices have consequences. You don’t get to just walk away from that.” A sudden slashing look toward Uncle. “Neither of you.”

Zuko can feel himself going lightheaded in a bad way, inner fire scattered as he falls back toward the kinds of certainties that used to ground him, the ones he doesn’t get to hold onto anymore. “My *choices* were to do what I had to do to stay alive. And to protect my people, and try to regain my—”

“It’s not just about *you.*” Sokka shoves his hands through his hair. “The things you do affect everyone *around* you. You wouldn’t just—just set a spark in a village, and walk away, and think that because you can’t see it anymore the fire isn’t there.”

Zuko folds his arms around himself, hands tightening with frustration. “I *told* you before, I didn’t mean to do that.”

“It’s not just about burning down a town on Kyoshi, Zuko, or wrecking an abbey, or hurting someone’s feelings. People *died*, okay? People died.”

“…What?”

“My *friend* died,” Sokka says, voice cracking in a way that makes Zuko’s inner flame ragged with the need to reach out, to hold, to comfort. Zuko feels like he’s being strangled by the sudden understanding of all he didn’t know he needed to be careful of.

Uncle makes a quiet, sad kind of ‘ah’ and Zuko remembers, finally, what Uncle said those months ago on the raft. He remembers a glimpse of the pale-haired girl before running after Zhao. A…friend. “I didn’t mean…”

“It doesn’t matter what you *meant*. It *happened,*” Sokka says, voice aching, and Zuko can finally hear the pain and sadness beneath the anger. He should have known it was there in the first place, should have realized sooner, it's not like Zuko isn't familiar. “And you don’t get to just walk away from it. You made choices. And you might not have felt you had other options, and it might not have led directly to Yue dying. But *fuck* did you play along.” Sokka turns an overly bright glare on Uncle, words suddenly venomous. “And fuck did you make sure she saw the way.”

Zuko’s mouth is too dry for words, even if he had any to say, his mind nothing but a useless clamor of too many protests and pleas and useless comforts he wouldn't know how to offer in the first place. Uncle’s deep, shaky breath is loud in the heavy quiet as he marshals his thoughts, because Uncle never could let a silence live too long.

“The loss of a single life is always tragic, yet the loss of a Great—”

“Shut. Up.” Sokka’s words are precise, hard. “You *traveled there on his ship*. You *knew* what he wanted to do. And you didn’t stop it.”

“I tried—”

“How hard?” Sokka hisses. “Really, as hard as you could?”

Uncle is damningly quiet, so Sokka turns back to Zuko, the hardness leaving his face but none of that aching pain. “And I get that you had reasons. I do, I heard them. But reasons don’t mean there aren’t consequences. Reasons don’t make it all *okay*.” He sighs, scrubbing his hands over his face, voice going low, words clearly just for Zuko now. “I know we don’t talk about this stuff, but Spirits, don’t…please don’t act like just because things are different now that they didn’t happen the way they did before.”

Zuko searches for words, for a response, for an action, for anything. “I wasn’t…”

“You don’t get to walk away from it just because *you’re* ready to. Not without dealing with it, not expecting everyone else to just walk away with you.” Sokka turns a scowl on Uncle. “And sayings it’s all just ‘*behind you*’—” Oh, Zuko realizes far too late. Sokka hates that phrase, specifically. “—isn’t dealing with it. It’s just telling yourself a convenient lie.”

Finally, no one replies, Sokka’s words hanging between them. Without the fight, Sokka sags, like the last of his energy is gone now that he has nothing to brace himself against to stay upright.

“I think I should leave.”

“*What*?” Zuko jerks in alarm, half out of his seat before he even realizes he’s moved.

Sokka makes a ‘settle’ gesture with his hands but doesn’t take the words back. “I’m tired, and I’m frustrated, and I’m taking it out on you.” The words are said to Zuko, not Uncle. An apology of sorts, only offered to one of them.

Zuko reaches for the first thing he can wrap words around. “You were going to stay the night…”

“I know,” Sokka sighs. “I just…I’m not fit to be around people right now. I don’t want to say something I’ll regret.”

Zuko flinches at the implication that that hasn’t happened yet. “*Sokka*…” His hands twist, wanting to reach, to anchor, but Zuko suddenly isn’t *sure* like he would have been before all this that his touch will be welcomed.

Sokka’s eyes catch the movement, and he pauses. “Zuko…it’s fine. I just need some space tonight.” His hand on Zuko’s shoulder is solid, meant to be reassuring, but Zuko can’t speak. When has a request for space ever *not* preceded something awful and terrible and conclusively final?

Zuko doesn’t push back, though. He just gets up in silence and walks Sokka to the door, painfully aware of the few inches of distance between them full of cold air instead of playful warmth. Painfully aware of Uncle studiously staring down at the tabletop as if he suddenly can’t see or hear, giving what little privacy he can far too late. Painfully aware of the ache in his chest as Sokka walks down the street, growing fainter with every step until he disappears entirely from Zuko’s fire sense, leaving Zuko tense and upset and alone and scared because he needs to fix this and he doesn’t know how to undo what’s already been done.

&#45;-

Sokka wishes Zuko were still in the Lower Ring, because then they never would have had that particular fucking conversation with *Iroh* there, and Sokka would have been able to keep his cool and check himself and not let himself get goaded by Iroh’s fucking condescending *placidness*. And even if they did, Sokka would have had plenty of time to cool off and get his thoughts in order before coming home. As it is, he’s still actively upset when he stomps across their veranda, and Toph is already on her feet before he finishes crossing the threshold.

“What happened,” she demands, braced like she’s about to start hurling boulders.

“Nothing.”

“Sokka, I can *hear* your heartbeat right now. What happened?”

“It’s *fine*,” Sokka snaps. “I’m not hurt, I’m not sad, I’m just angry, and I’m allowed to be, so back off!”

Toph just wrinkles her nose and crosses her arms.

“Why are you angry.” Katara’s voice comes from behind him, quiet and dangerous. Sokka closes his eyes. *Shit,* he didn’t realize she was there. And it’s no use glaring at Toph for not warning him.

“It doesn’t matter,” he mutters, turning to get them both into his line of sight, wondering if he should just turn around and go back outside.

“Yes, it does.”

“No, just—”

“You’re my brother,” Katara folds her arms. “You matter to me, so your emotions matter to me.” Sokka feels like she’s using some kind of mantra as a weapon right now. “Why are you angry?”

Sokka struggles for a moment, then sags. He doesn’t have the energy to fight this, and he knows by now that at least one of the others will dig in and make it a fight. It’s an aggressive kind of caring. “Just…something with Zuko. And I *don’t* need you going all vigilante or whatever over it.”

Katara makes a noise of outrage. “Vigilante?”

“You do kind of do that,” Aang says, grimacing in apology as he comes into the room from behind Toph.

Katara glares, crossing her arms. “Sorry for trying to protect the people who matter to me.”

“Sometimes they don’t *need* protecting,” Sokka mutters.

“Well, sometimes they deserve it anyway.”

Sokka snaps his mouth shut, momentarily struck dumb. He wants to be annoyed by her interference, but he’s also…touched. It’s hard to hold onto his frustration when Katara still thinks that way even with her not-always-concealed concerns over what he’s doing and who he’s doing it with.

“I appreciate that,” Sokka finally manages to say. “But I don’t need you fighting my battles for me here. There’s no battle to fight.” Not anymore, anyway.

“You sure about that?” Toph asks skeptically. “Because you came in looking for one.”

Sokka sighs. “That’s just…I don’t know. I think we had a fight.”

“How do you not *know*,” Toph snorts.

“What did he do,” Katara demands.

“Nothing,” Sokka says, pressing the heels of his hands to his eyes. “And I think it might have been my fault, anyway.”

Her eyes narrow. “Then what did *you* do.”

Sokka blows out a hard breath. He really just wants to go lay down right now. “I was in a bad mood. And Iroh said some things. And I should have just changed the subject. But I didn’t.”

“What kind of things?” Aang asks, frowning at whatever he sees on Sokka’s face.

“Just…philosophical things. Life stuff.” War stuff, but he doesn’t want to say that to them, even though they all know that 'life stuff' and 'war stuff' are basically the same when you're living in war. “But I was thinking of Yue and I just…couldn’t let it go, even though that wasn’t what he meant. Not really.”

The silence is long and Sokka bites back another sigh because Spirits, he bet he just made Katara even more confused than she already was, to be this worked up over something that involves both Yue and Zuko. But Sokka is still so *mad* about the North, when he lets himself be. And so viscerally enraged by Iroh acting like the damage of war is something abstract and distant, a fucking thought exercise, when Sokka knows for a fact that it’s personal and raw and lives somewhere in the middle of your chest.

“What did Zuko have to say about it,” Aang finally asks, aiming right for the heart of things.

“Not much,” Sokka bites out, and sees that Aang at least realizes that that *is* the problem, as much as Sokka can be entirely sure of what the problem is today except for everything. “Sometimes he can be such a…”

“Rage monster?”

“Anxious mess?”

“Stubborn dick?”

“An *oblivious ass,”* Sokka finishes, glaring at all of them for managing to spark his defensive instincts when he wants to just be *mad.*

“Isn’t that all the time,” Katara asks dryly, earning a bark of laughter from Toph.

“No,” Sokka grumbles. Or maybe, but not in a way that bothers Sokka.

Katara makes a skeptical noise. “I’m pretty sure that's what Princes are like.”

“Oh, for sure,” Toph confirms.

“Well, Zuko isn’t a Prince anymore,” Sokka says, vaguely surprised by how bitter the words taste.

Aang hums quietly. “Isn’t he?”

“No, he’s just—” Sokka waves a hand. So many things that Sokka doesn’t know how to wrap it up in words for them.

“What,” Katara presses, because of course she would.

“Nothing.”

“You gotta finish when your heart sounded like that about it,” Toph says, because of course *she* would.

“No.”

Toph raises an eyebrow, accepting the challenge. “He isn’t a Prince, he’s just…”

“A firebender?”

“In hiding?”

“Yours?”

Toph grins. “That’s the one.”

“Shut up, Toph,” Sokka mutters, looking away and confirming the answer for all of them.

Katara makes a dissatisfied noise in the back of her throat. “That’s who he is with you, maybe.” She pins Sokka with an exasperated look. “Who is he to everyone else?”

“I…don’t know.” Lee? A nephew? Something more? Zuko will fold himself into whatever shape pleases most, once he decides you’re worth pleasing. Sokka has known that for months. He just…hasn’t fully grasped what it could mean beyond himself and Iroh, still, what it means for the majority of people *not* in Zuko's so-small-it's-barely-there inner circle.

“…Why does this always happen in front of all of you,” Sokka finally complains, glaring at them without heat. “Every time I have something on my mind, here you all are, prying and asking questions, and just…”

“It’s because we’re supportive of your relationship and invested in your happiness,” Aang chirps, and that is *definitely* a mantra if the way Toph mouths the words is anything to go by.

“…Great. Thanks, I guess.” It’s a nice sentiment. A little concerning, maybe, that they seem to talk about his *relationship* so much. And it feels a little…much, in application. But nice.

“Do you want a hug?” Aang asks hopefully, bouncing on his toes.

“What?”

“You need a hug,” Aang decides.

“Um.”

Sokka gets a hug. And he can admit, as the air is squeezed out of him by three sets of arms, that it feels good to be surrounded and supported and held up by people who love him. Even if it makes his own arms feel strangely empty, like they’re missing the width of a fourth set of shoulders.
