## Chapter 27: Doing Better

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

No particular warnings for this one

### Text

Zuko is working the morning shift, which would have been great if Sokka had stayed the night. Zuko loves sharing the quiet moments just around dawn with him, loves the sight of him barely awake and sleep-soft and half-smiling over breakfast. It feeds his inner flame in a way that carries throughout the day, smoothing the normally rough edges of his temper into something that might even be called mellow, if you looked at it sideways and squinted.

Sokka didn’t stay, though, and Zuko spent the night in the tree outside his window, blatantly hiding from whatever Uncle might try to say to him and from the words no good nephew would ever say, too ready on his tongue for anything else. So instead, Zuko is feeling strung out. It's barely into the morning rush and he’s already prickly from lack of sleep and jerky with lingering anxiety and preemptively angry about nearly everything around him. He’s so simultaneously out of it and overly aware of every little thing that when the front door slams open, Zuko startles so bad that the tea he’s pouring sloshes out over the table and only a quick bit of bending prevents it from being scalding as it falls onto the old lady he’s serving.

Zuko spins toward the door with a snarl as the woman exclaims in outrage, glare freezing only partway formed when he sees who’s standing in the doorway. For a wild second he wonders if he’s dreaming, maybe still in the tree having a nightmare, but no—the scent of too many clashing perfumes is too strong, the wet drip of spilled tea too loud, Zuko’s heart pounding against the inside of his chest with far too much force.

Katara is visibly braced for a fight, taking up far more space than she logically should be able to in the doorway, expression murderous as her eyes land on Zuko. Zuko’s body locks. He hasn’t seen Katara since that no-name town, with its dust and sun and flames and fighting against everyone and Uncle injured and helpless and Katara trying to get closer and Zuko needing her to *leave*.

Knowing that Katara is theoretically in the city and actually standing across from her are, as it turns out, two completely different animals, and he’d barely managed to tame his inner flame when it came to the former. Zuko’s heart is beating triple time, inner flame wild and roiling, mind racing around everything in the room. Zuko can’t firebend in the Upper Ring, and his swords are in the kitchen near the back door, and he can’t defend himself with anything except his body and the tray in his hands. And all around him is tea. Liquid, that she can use however she wants, that she can turn into whips or darts or suffocating, drowning weight. The knowledge is a vice around his lungs even as his adrenaline surges in readiness.

A distant corner of Zuko’s mind wonders where Jin and Sung-Min are down in the Lower Ring right now, because Zuko might be about to pass out. They were so shockingly great about it last time.

With a harsh gasp—has it really only been a few dozen too-fast heartbeats?—Zuko manages to risk a darting glance over her shoulder. Agni’s *tits,* it’s nearly impossible to see from the dimness of the shop into the brightness outside. Zuko’s toes tingle with numbness, his fingers feeling clumsy as he tries to get a useful grip on his tray. Is the Avatar going to show up, too?

“You,” Katara growls, taking a single step forward.

Zuko makes a choked, gurgling kind of noise.

“*You*,” she snarls again, eyes narrowing, clearing expecting…something, from him. Zuko scrambles, trying to find his balance as he stares down her half-familiar face, something about seeing those specific features twisted with anger doing nearly as much to unsettle him as everything else.

“Uh.”

“You upset my brother.”

Oh, fuck. Fuck, fuck, *fuck*. Did Zuko completely misread Sokka when he left last night? He thought…he didn’t think they were *good* but he thought they were *fine.* Sokka *said* he was fine. But Agni, he also said he wanted *space*, and he’s never asked for that before, and now Katara—

“I will freeze your ass to a wall and leave you there *forever* if you ever do it again,” she growls, and Zuko’s body goes cold. “I’ve done it before, and I’ll do it again.” Her hands flex, like she can’t wait for the opportunity, and Zuko chokes back a gasp as the puddle of tea on the floor inches into his periphery.

Zuko can’t reply, can only stare, heart pounding in his throat, hands white-knuckled around his tray as she whirls around and storms out as abruptly as she came. The sudden absence of violence makes him stagger. The air seems to sweep back into the room with Katara gone, and with it Zuko’s awareness of sound and his panicky inner flame and things other than her. The patrons are all staring at him, murmuring, wealthy and gawking and entertained and it reminds him—

Zuko’s stomach heaves, nausea clawing up his throat. He needs to get out of here, needs to get away, needs to go, needs to—

Uncle is suddenly at his side, broad and calm and enveloping warmth, quiet strength that lets Zuko suck in one breath, then another, then another. Uncle isn’t supposed to be here. He isn’t supposed to be working yet. He’s supposed to have the morning off, has no reason to be here if he wasn’t watching Zuko without telling him. But Zuko can’t feel anything but relieved as Uncle gently transfers the tray out of Zuko’s hands onto a table. “I think the new stock could use some sorting, this morning, Nephew.”

Zuko walks woodenly off the floor and into the back, body reacting even if his mind is nothing but unhelpful buzzing. He slips into a supply closet they don’t use, though, instead of the stock room, pulling the door firmly shut behind him. Then he drops to the floor like the bones have suddenly been yanked out of his legs, back solidly pressed into the corner so he has solid wood on both sides. Zuko puts his head between his knees and finally, finally lets his body shudder with pent up terror, sucking in lungful after lungful of air until he can feel his own extremities again, until he can hear in his unscarred ear over the sound of metal rending and soldiers drowning and the Ocean wreaking vengeance.

&#45;-

Agni has moved more than a few degrees across the sky when Zuko finally manages to calm down enough to leave the supply closet. He doesn’t go to the stock room, though, or the kitchen, or back to the floor like he should, but he thinks Uncle will forgive him, today, for skipping out on work. Zuko hasn’t done it in a while. He’s probably overdue.

Zuko slips outside without knowing where he’s going. He just…needs to be in the sun. He knows he can’t go on the roofs during the daylight, not like he could in the Lower Ring where everyone just ignores everyone else’s weirdness as long as it isn’t actively harmful. And Zuko can’t draw attention to himself that way, anyway, not when he’s on the roofs so much at night.

Zuko sets off instead into the streets, for once grateful for their breadth and the lack of residents when normally the waste of it all would be another vaguely annoying thing about the Upper Ring. He isn’t sure what he’s looking for, exactly, until he finds himself in one of those lovely, manicured to death parks dotted throughout the Upper Ring. Even with winter on the horizon, the space is still green and full of life, showcasing the best of the Earth Kingdom’s flora on the last edges of autumn.

Zuko immediately finds the right kind of tree, still half-covered with leaves and with plenty of low, sturdy branches just above his head. Hauling himself to the top is a familiar comfort, something he used to do when he was trying to hide from Azula, something that would always work because she didn’t have the patience yet, back then, for checking every tree in the palace gardens.

The fresh air helps clear the acrid taste off the back of Zuko’s tongue, and he forces himself to concentrate on the absence of water or salt in the gentle breeze, on Agni’s touch even if it’s not as intense as it would be in the summer months. He settles himself into a crook of branch and trunk, resting his head against living wood and trying to think of absolutely nothing. He listens to leaves rustling, distantly appreciating that they’re all changing colors with the season, reds and oranges and yellows. It’s like being nestled in a nest of fire, but with none of the burning hunger, none of the necessity to control or contain. Zuko centers himself around the idea, around the sight and sound of it, and finally, finally manages to unwind enough to think.

Fuck.

For Katara to storm in like that…Zuko knows Sokka was upset last night, but *fuck*. Zuko still isn’t even entirely sure what Sokka was upset *about*. Obviously Zuko heard the things Sokka said, but…Zuko is worried he didn’t *hear* them, through his own too-fast heart and instinctive defensiveness in the face of anger. Not the way Sokka intended them to be heard.

Zuko just wants to know what to do. How to fix whatever he messed up, how to make it better. Though the idea that Zuko could somehow make Sokka’s friend dying *better*…it’s laughable, that anything Zuko could do would be enough to fix that. To think that Zuko could be enough to…

*No.*

He isn’t going to think about that. He isn’t going to start thinking about the empty spaces in Sokka’s life and how Sokka could be trying to fill them. He isn’t going to go there and start questioning ‘why.’ That kind of thinking has never brought Zuko to a good place when it comes to Sokka. Zuko’s foundation is built too closely around certain beliefs to be able to question them now without consequence. To question them when he has no need to actually think that way, when it's just the fear he can't shove away threading into each of his thoughts.

Flailing, Zuko anchors himself around the one thing that he is absolutely sure of from yesterday: that Sokka needs Zuko to deal with it. To face the things that Zuko did in the past, and the things that Zuko didn’t even realize he did, and somehow make them right.

It’s not something Zuko lets himself do often, especially these days, and it’s overwhelming, vaguely nauseating, to think back over years of hunting the Avatar. Year after year of intimidating and bribing and stealing and doing whatever he thought he had to do to survive and keep moving forward. To look at all those things he felt like he had no choice in, and to consider whether some other path was actually open to him. The one that Uncle was always looking toward, maybe, or the one that Sokka seems to see. And to try to take a step sideways now, after all of it is done, and see not just the threats he was responding to or the things he needed, but the collateral damage he left along the way.

Some of it Zuko can feel good about, in a vindictive, savage kind of way. The fucked up, messed up people he managed to get into the eyes of some authority figure that would actually care enough to do something about them. Things stolen from people who never should have had them in the first place. Most of it, though…Zuko’s chest feels sticky and tight. Agni, Zuko doesn’t even *know* all of it. He didn’t know about the burned village on Kyoshi. He knew *of* it, intellectually, academically, but not the way Sokka knows it. He didn’t know about the girl. Yue.

And that just makes it worse, doesn’t it? That Zuko could have done horrible things to so many people and not even *known*. When has a lack of knowledge ever absolved him of anything? When has not knowing ever been an excuse?

Agni, it’s shameful in a way that burns in his gut, in a way his inner fire can’t consume, that Zuko could have clung for so long to being the Fire Prince and still acted like his actions didn’t affect others, when Zuko should know more than anyone that ever breath a Prince takes has impact. That was one of the first lessons he ever learned, the one he never really needed reminding of even when he got it—that every moment, every thought, every decision matters when a Child of Agni is the one making it.

Sokka is right, of course. Zuko needs to…atone, or something. Somehow. Not just start over or move on, like Uncle seems to want for him. Zuko needs to find some way to fix what’s already been done, what Zuko didn’t do right the first time, if he can ever hope to be worth… more. Worth Uncle’s hopes and wants, maybe. Worth being who Zuko wants to be, to Sokka.

It feels huge, though. Impossibly large and scary in an entirely new way. Or maybe an old way, one he thought was behind him. Because nestled in a cocoon of leaves in the Upper Ring of Ba Sing Se, with Uncle probably waiting for him to turn up around dinner, Zuko doesn’t know how *Lee* could ever be the one to make anything better. And coming off the close edge of a panic attack, he doesn’t know how what he has to offer as just Zuko could ever be enough.

&#45;-

When Sokka walks through the door of the Jasmine Dragon in the afternoon like he said he would, Zuko needs to brace himself against the counter to stay upright. His knees are boneless with relief that Sokka is here, looking tired but smiling when he finds Zuko in the room. Zuko is glad he’s already sagging against the countertop, because that would have been enough to take him out all on its own.

“Hey,” Sokka says, leaning against the customer side of the counter on his elbows, mirroring Zuko’s pose. The position puts him thoroughly into Zuko’s space, filling Zuko’s eyes with the sight of tan skin and Zuko's nose with the scent of leather and sunshine and metal.

Zuko licks his lips, can't help a quick glance to see if anyone else is coming in behind him. “Hi.”

“It’s good to see you,” Sokka says, almost shy, eyes tracing over Zuko’s face.

“Yeah,” Zuko agrees, breathless, refocusing on Sokka and measuring the scant inches between them. It would be easy, to lean forward and close that distance. That space.

“I’m—” Sokka leans back slightly, biting his cheek, which is not the development Zuko wants. “Look, I’m sorry." Zuko blinks. What. "I started a whole thing the other night with Iroh, and then I started bringing you into it. I shouldn’t have—”

“You were right.” The words stumble out of Zuko’s mouth like they’ve been waiting to trip free all day.

It's Sokka's turn to blink. “What?”

“You were right,” Zuko repeats, slower this time, deliberate, forcing himself to hold Sokka’s eyes when most of him would just really like to hide. “I need to do…better.”

Sokka opens and closes his mouth a few times before frowning, slowly nodding. “Okay… okay. Thank you.” He searches Zuko’s face. “Are you…okay?”

Zuko absolutely does not want to think about or talk about Katara, so he just shrugs. “I’m fine.” It’s not a lie now that Sokka is here, as warm and steady as ever, almost like nothing ever happened at all. Something in Zuko unwinds at the familiarity of that kind of pretense. He didn't think it was Sokka's style, but Zuko is happy to seize on to it all the same.

Sokka hums, an equivocal noise, reaching out and catching Zuko’s hand, light, easy for Zuko to pull away if he wants. “Hey—you’d tell me, right? If you weren’t? If you needed something? I know I was upset, earlier, and that’s not—I don’t like the way I handled it. But I’m not going to let something like that get in the way, not without trying to work on it.”

Zuko hesitates. ‘Something like’ Zuko’s entire past, or ‘something like’—

“A fight, I mean,” Sokka clarifies, seeing the question on his face. “Or whatever that was.”

“It was a fight,” Zuko mutters, eyes dropping to the pulse at the base of Sokka’s neck. Zuko knows enough about fighting, both with and without weapons, to recognize one when he’s in it.

“Yeah,” Sokka sighs, chewing on his cheek again. “I—I could have said things better. I *should* have said things better. And chosen a better time, and just…I knew I was in a bad mood, and I thought I had it handled, and I just—didn’t. And I don’t mean for it to be an excuse, it’s still—I still shouldn’t have let it happen. So. I—I’m really sorry for how I said what I said. And that I didn’t give you an opportunity to say anything back.”

Zuko…doesn’t know what to do with that.

Sokka gives his hands a gentle squeeze, ducking to catch his eyes. “I know you said I was right, but—Zuko, you’re sure you’re good?” He searches Zuko’s face, frowning, and Zuko doesn’t know what to do with that kind of close scrutiny right now, either. Is he looking for some reaction to Katara having been here? But Sokka would just ask outright, wouldn't he? If he wanted to know? “We can still talk about stuff. I know I was…mad, but I promise, I’ll keep my cool. I—if you have something to say, I want to listen.”

Zuko clears his throat, the words still coming out thick, low. “I’m—I’m good.” He wasn’t, before, but with Sokka in front of him now, as open as ever, he is again. Or at least is starting to be. And he doesn’t know what he would want Sokka to hear, anyway, not when he doesn’t even have anything to say to himself yet.

Sokka lingers another moment over Zuko’s face, the intensity of it nearly enough to make Zuko blush on its own, before finally relaxing. “Alright. But I’m here if you change your mind.” He runs his thumbs over Zuko’s palms, slow and too careful to be an absent gesture as he takes a deep breath. “Do you…”

Zuko isn’t usually the one who needs to prompt. “Do I what?”

Sokka blows out a hard breath, pulling a face before saying all in a rush, “Do you think I need to apologize to Iroh about it? Or talk to him?”

Zuko flinches from the idea so immediately that he nearly pulls his hands out of Sokka’s grip, grabbing back onto them with more than a little desperate urgency as Sokka startles. “No.”

Sokka hesitates, mouth parted in surprise. “But—”

“Please,” Zuko cuts in, wincing at the idea of Sokka dragging it all back up again, or the potential teaching moment Uncle might still see in it, of the possibility of Katara coming back. “Just…leave it.”

“I…okay,” Sokka says, searching his face, a slight frown on his brow. “If you think that’s best.”

“I do.” Zuko so, so does.

“Alright. Well, then…What do you want to do now? Today, I mean. Together.”

Zuko meets Sokka’s eyes in surprise, momentarily blank. It’s not a question that gets asked often, usually because Sokka has a plan, or because they’ve worked out the details the last time they saw each other. Is this Sokka trying to make sure Zuko actually feels comfortable, or letting him set the pace or something? Is this Sokka not being sure exactly how they slot back together? “Whatever you want.”

“Zuko,” Sokka chides without heat or force. “What do *you* want?”

“You.” Sokka rolls his eyes but smiles at the familiar routine, and the sight of it makes Zuko’s inner flame flip low and warm in his stomach. “What do you want?”

Sokka pauses for a moment like he needs to think. Zuko doesn’t usually ask back. “Just for you to be yourself,” he finally says, words soft and intimate and serious in a way that Zuko isn’t prepared for.

Zuko’s thoughts stutter. That…Zuko *really* doesn’t know what to do with that. But…Agni, he wants to hear it again, he realizes. He wants to hold it close, treat it as something fragile and precious, and maybe hold it up to the light, later. Now, though, Zuko stares down at their clasped hands, a flush trying to climb up his face, suddenly overwhelmed in a whole new way. Sokka seems content to stand at the counter with him and wait, his thumb moving over what skin he can reach in the kind of slow, steady rhythm that Zuko likes.

When words come, they spill out before Zuko has time to register what they’re going to be. “Do you like to dance?”

Sokka’s thumb goes still against the back of his hand. “What?”

Sokka isn’t entirely sure how he got here, but as darkness stretches over Ba Sing Se he finds himself back in the Lower Ring with Zuko, standing close to his side for warmth and just because he can. They’re in a seemingly random intersection of roads and alleys that form a broad, irregular space. Musicians are setting up instruments at one end, someone is trying to do something aesthetically pleasing and probably dangerous with candles and streamers hung from buildings around the perimeters, and carts and blankets and wares are being set up along all the connecting streets.

Sokka finally finds his voice, still a little high with surprise. “A night market?”

“Kind of,” Zuko says, looking at him sidelong. His hair is almost long enough to start falling into his eyes, Sokka notes in a still-functioning corner of his brain. Sokka wants to press his face against it, feel the strands against his own cheek. “Only if you want to.”

“I *love* shopping.”

“Yeah,” Zuko agrees, smiling, shy, and Sokka feels like he’s about to burst, squeezing Zuko’s hand like somehow that alone can convey his enthusiasm and excitement and whatever else it is that’s beating in his chest. Spirits, Zuko *remembered*—not that Sokka thought he wouldn’t, but—Zuko saw this thing and thought of *him* and Sokka just…could be warm forever, feeling like this.

An excited voice interrupts whatever dangerously sappy thing Sokka is probably about to say. “Lee, is that *him*?”

Zuko freezes a bit but doesn’t drop Sokka’s hand, fingers curling possessively over his and *oh*, Sokka didn’t quite realize he wanted that until it happened. Huh. Zuko turns toward the voice in a way that half-blocks Sokka from view, which could be an accident, but knowing Zuko and his general caginess is probably deliberate. Sokka enjoys a quick moment of staring at the triangle of Zuko’s back before peeking around his shoulder, bemused, to see a big-eyed girl smiling ear to ear peeking back at him.

“Jin.”

“Answer the question,” the girl orders, apparently unbothered by Zuko’s curtness.

“Yeah, *Lee*.” Sokka nudges him from behind. “Answer the question.” Has Zuko been… talking about him? Spirits, is Sokka going to just combust before whatever Zuko has planned for the night even begins?

Zuko scowls over his shoulder, the kind that Sokka has come to recognize as habitual annoyance rather than genuine frustration. “Yes.”

The girl—Jin. Zuko knows her name and it’s Jin*—*lets out a noise that could only be called a squeal of delight. “It’s so good to finally meet you,” she shouts, unceremoniously shoving Zuko out of the way to get a better look at him. “Lee’s said so much about you!”

Sokka can’t stop his involuntary, surprised glance toward Zuko. Who does not, he notices, seem bothered by Jin’s casual touching despite Zuko’s usual prickliness around his personal space. “He has?”

“Well, for him,” she shrugs, sticking her tongue out at Zuko, who just huffs and rolls his eyes in response.

Sokka…mentally upgrades Jin a number of levels, in his evaluation of how close Zuko is to her. “Ah.”

“I’m Jin,” she says, turning back to Sokka. “But you already know that.”

“I’m Sokka.” He shrugs at Zuko’s wince. Why should he use a false name with her? It’s not like anyone knows who Sokka is once you get him away from Aang. And besides, maybe he would be prepared with an appropriate backstory if Zuko had *ever mentioned her once*. It’s like the ostrich horse all over again, except even worse because ostrich horses don’t generally try to engage you in conversation.

Sokka supposes, in retrospect, that considering Zuko’s closed-mouth approach to anything he remotely likes, he should take it as flattering that Zuko was so determined never to mention him to Iroh until he was forced to.

“Sokka!” Jin exclaims, trying it out. “Great name! This is so great, I didn’t think he was *ever* going to bring you.”

“I didn’t know if he liked dancing,” Zuko mutters, defensive.

“You could have *asked*.”

“Yeah, Lee, you could have asked.” How long has this girl known about Sokka, to say something like that? And what exactly does she know? She still calls him ‘Lee’, but Zuko is also willingly interacting with her, which isn’t a thing he does for many people.

“Well, he’s here now,” Zuko grumbles, and Jin just grins like she can also see the pleased ghost of a smile on Zuko’s lips as he says the words.

“You’re lucky you got here early,” Jin says with a quick glance toward the darkening sky. “There wouldn’t be any masks left if you’d waited much longer.”

Wait. “Masks?”

Jin pauses. “Didn’t he tell you?” She turns to Zuko. “Didn’t you tell him?”

“…I told him there’d be dancing.”

”*Lee.* Oma and Shu, how you even function sometimes.” She turns back to Sokka, shaking her head in exasperation. “It’s a masquerade. We put them on every month, to go along with the night market.”

“A masquerade,” Sokka says slowly, sorting through the quick and dirty rundown on types of fancy parties that Toph had given them weeks ago. “Like…” He waves vaguely toward his face.

“Yes! Don’t worry, I grabbed some when I saw you guys. Here, what colors do you want?” She holds out three half-masks, lacquered and trailing ribbons, identical except for the color. Sokka stares at the deep red, blue, and green, then flicks a glance toward Zuko, who’s looking at the selection like it vaguely pains him. It’s a little on the nose.

Sokka waits for Zuko to notice him looking, then reaches out and grabs the red one without breaking eye contact. Zuko’s gold eyes flicker, his lips parting, before he grabs blue. Sokka’s throat is suddenly tight with anticipation to see the mask against Zuko’s skin, to see his firebender in Water Tribe colors.

“And I will take green,” Jin says, cheerful and loud and reminding them of her existence. “And ignore whatever eye fucking you two are doing!”

Sokka flushes, nearly dropping his mask as his fingers go clumsy with embarrassment. Spirits, he isn’t used to being with Zuko around *people*. Zuko just snorts out a laugh, though, giving her a look that’s exasperated and *fond*. Sokka freezes, seeing it. He’s pretty sure he can count on one hand the number of people Zuko is fond of and still have enough fingers left to count all the people Zuko tries not to shout at.

“Is this okay?” Zuko asks quietly, breaking through his thoughts, and Sokka realizes he’s been still while Jin is already fastening the mask over her eyes.

“Yeah,” Sokka assures him, fumbling with his own mask. “This is…” He trails off, struck suddenly by the familiarity of doing something like this with Zuko. He can see the same memory in Zuko’s eyes before the blue mask is drawn over them. He can read the same degree of not-sure-how-to-feel-about-this-but-definitely-feeling-everything in the set of Zuko’s shoulders.

“*Wow*, you two,” Jin says, breaking into their staring again. “You really just live in your own world, huh? Lee, I’m surprised you could keep it together at the Blooming Petal if this is what you were always thinking about.” Sokka is grateful for the mask that hides the extent of his second blush as she shakes her head. “Dancing first, or food?”

“Food,” Sokka and Zuko say at the same time.

“He’s always hungry,” Zuko adds, teasing, maybe, but mostly sounding weirdly pleased about it.

“You don’t get these bad boys by starving yourself,” Sokka grins, flexing his arms. He can tease back just as well, and he likes knowing that Zuko’s skin is pink across his cheekbone even if he can’t see it.

“Food it is, then!” Jin proclaims, linking her arms through both of theirs and towing them forward. Sokka watches Zuko barely react to the contact or the closeness on his left side. Jin is definitely on a short list, and Sokka’s mind spins around what it could mean for Zuko to bring him to a place where Sokka could meet her. “They need to get warmed up anyway before the music really gets good. So, Sokka. What do you like to eat?”

&#45;-

When Zuko had suggested dancing, Sokka hadn’t quite known what to expect. And then he saw the night market and thought that ‘dancing’ was just a vague descriptor for the overall exuberant vibe of whatever this monthly party is—and yes, Sokka is a little miffed that Zuko’s been coming to them and Sokka hasn’t even known they existed. But then the musicians hit their stride, and Jin is pulling them toward the teeming square, and whatever it was that he expected, it certainly wasn’t that Zuko would actually dance, and be *good*.

Sokka definitely isn’t. He’s desperately grateful for the masks as he realizes that no, ‘dancing’ means exactly that. The masquerade must let everyone look like idiots in a crowd without feeling self-conscious about it. Except…the people here know what they’re doing, and Zuko has nothing to be embarrassed about. He moves through the steps—Sokka can’t get over the fact that Zuko even *knows* the steps to Earth Kingdom dances—with the kind of grace and assurance Sokka only associates with sword training. Zuko is somehow always on the beat when Sokka keeps getting lost in the melodies, gently guiding when Sokka usually has to forcefully pull instruction out of him, tactile and close in a way Sokka is only used to when it’s just the two of them.

They do eventually find a rhythm together, once Sokka gets over being flustered by his own surprise, because if there’s anything Sokka can do by this point it's match Zuko’s body with his own. And once Sokka manages to relax enough for that, the whole thing is surprisingly fun. Nothing like the stuffy, formal steps he’s glimpsed in the Upper Ring. This is all spinning and whirling and stomping, always linked by some brush of fingers or held gaze, always coming back into each other’s arms.

“So. This is a thing you do, huh?” Sokka asks during one of the songs where the drum is pounding the beat clear enough to vibrate through his boots so that even Sokka can’t miss it.

Zuko shrugs, candlelight making his mask seem mobile, alive. “Jin likes to dance.” And Zuko likes Jin, even if he would never say it, the same way he’d never say it about anyone.

“It doesn’t seem like it would be your thing.” Too many people too close, and too many expectations of touching.

Zuko considers for a moment. “It’s like…fighting, I guess.”

“Huh?”

A quick smile flickers over Zuko’s lips at Sokka’s eloquent confusion. “It’s the same kind of stuff.” Zuko’s hands slip from where they’re loosely on Sokka’s shoulders down to his hips. “Reading the other person.” He takes a step back and Sokka steps forward before he even realizes he needs to. “Avoiding.” Zuko smoothly moves them out of the way of another couple. “Closing distance.” A tight spin that ends with Sokka’s back somehow pressed against Zuko’s chest. “Rhythm.” The last whispered into his ear, raspy and hot.

Then Zuko shrugs and steps back and Sokka nearly stumbles, unexpectedly needing to support all his own weight again. He turns back around to face Zuko, somehow managing not to throw himself at him and very aware of the way his heart is definitely beating out of time with the music, now.

“Sounds more like something else,” Sokka says, clearing his throat and trying to find his balance, the words coming out far too strangled for levity.

Zuko grins, sharp and wicked and quick. “And that.” He tugs Sokka in close again as the song changes, a slower tempo, a harder beat that thrums in Sokka’s chest. “You know about that, too.”

“Yes,” Sokka agrees, a sigh against Zuko’s throat.

“So you just feel the rhythm the same way,” Zuko murmurs, rolling his hips in time with the music in a way that makes Sokka lightheaded. “And go with the rest.”

“I…can do that,” Sokka gasps, turning his face toward the feel of Zuko’s breathy laughter over his neck and letting the beat and the movement of Zuko’s body carry him through the song.

Sokka is breathless and flustered and maybe visibly in need of a break when the song abruptly transitions to a faster tempo. He is half-hard in a really embarrassing way considering the crowd, but how was he supposed to *not* be with Zuko grinding against him like that, breathing hot little bits of instruction into his ear.

He stumbles after Zuko toward a place to rest, still getting used to the way the half-mask limits his vision. Sokka hops up onto a ledge next to Zuko, deeply grateful that he manages to scramble up and strategically drape his tunic over his lap before Jin weaves her way out of the mess of dancers to join them.

“Enjoying yourself?” She asks, eyes bright behind the deep emerald of her mask.

“Ah—yeah.” Too much, probably.

“Mhm. I’m sure,” Jin says, tone knowing in a way that has Sokka squirming in embarrassment. “You don’t usually stay for the slow ones,” she adds to Zuko.

He shrugs. “I decided to mix it up.”

Her grin reminds Sokka a little bit of Toph, which is slightly terrifying. “Are you tired, then?”

Zuko’s eyes flick toward Sokka. “No.”

“Do you mind if I borrow Lee, then, for this dance?”

“It’s a new one,” Zuko hedges, but Jin just waves that away.

“I’ve been practicing.”

“I haven’t.”

“You never do. You saw it last time, you’ll be fine.”

“It’s fine,” Sokka says before Zuko starts looking for another excuse. “You go.” Zuko hesitates, half-off the ledge already. “I’ll have just as much fun watching, promise.”

“Thanks, Sokka!” Jin grins. “Remember to keep it in the bedroom!”

Zuko and Jin are already disappearing into the crowd by the time Sokka’s brain catches up to her comment. “Hey!” That isn’t—they don’t—they haven’t even *talked* about that, outside of the one time when Zuko was definitely lightning-high which shouldn’t even count. And if Sokka fantasizes, in the privacy of his own mind, about what it might be like for Zuko to put on a show for him, to watch Zuko stroking himself for Sokka’s pleasure—then that’s Sokka’s personal business and *not* what he meant!

Any outrage quickly evaporates, though, watching them dance. It’s easy to pick out Zuko despite the masks and the crowd, because Sokka can always find Zuko in a space, regardless of who else is in it. They twirl and jump and whip around each other, and Sokka is speechless at the idea that Zuko just *saw* this last time, a month ago, and now can *do* it like all the other couples, looking like he’s known the steps forever.

It hits Sokka that this is another kind of training, maybe, for someone who spent his whole life needing to be able to replicate a set of bending forms after only seeing them once. But it’s a kind of training without pressure, or expectation, because there might be steps to this dance but there doesn’t seem to be a single correct way to do them. No one seems to stick to it completely, and everyone brings their own style and flair in their own way.

Watching Zuko dance with Jin reminds Sokka of the lightning storm, her cheerful, sassy energy meeting Zuko’s sharp-edged focus. Watching this is seeing Zuko loose and relaxed in the kind of setting that Sokka thought Zuko would never even voluntarily enter, let alone enjoy. Watching this is realizing all over again just how confined and controlled Zuko is in his normal life, and wishing just as helplessly that Sokka knew what it would take to let Zuko always look this free.

## Chapter 28: Found Out

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for sexual content in this one

### Text

Sokka is tired of lakes. He’s also tired of ponds, puddles, wells, depressions of land that happen to hold water because it rained last night, and outdoor fish enclosures. He doesn’t know how many more bodies of water they can waste their time exploring in the hunt for Appa, but Sokka also doesn’t know how to look Aang in the eye and tell him that he thinks one of their last major leads has run dry.

Pun, for once, not intended.

Sokka sigh as he stares down yet another lake—it’s incredibly generous to call it that, but they’re almost out of options—in the Middle Ring. Sokka is partnered with Aang today, for all the good it does either of them. Aang doesn’t exactly need his help, and Sokka doesn’t exactly have anything to do. Mostly he watches their surroundings while Aang waterbends, looking for…something. Anything that feels out of place.

“This one is taking forever,” Aang complains as he drags another heap of solidified trash out of the water.

“I would help if I could, buddy,” Sokka mutters. He can tell at a glance that the trash has been at the bottom of the lake far longer than Appa has been missing, but he gives it a dubious poke with a large stick just in case. He glances up to see Aang giving him a considering look. “I’m not about to go swimming in there.” Not with how much junk Aang has hauled out.

Aang waves that away. “I could make you an air bubble so you could stay under longer!”

“A what,” Sokka asks flatly.

“I did it for me and Appa,” Aang says enthusiastically. “So that we could be underwater and still breathe.”

Sokka isn’t going to do it. He isn’t. But he still can’t hold back his reluctant curiosity. “How did you move, though?”

“Waterbending!”

“How would *I* move? Hypothetically.” Definitely only hypothetically.

Aang pauses, mouth open, considering. “Maybe I could make the air bubble just around your head?”

Sokka frowns. “How much air could that hold?” Drowning in bad air under a lake isn’t how Sokka wants to go.

“Hm…it could be a really big bubble? But leave your arms and legs free to swim?”

“Like a turtle?” Sokka asks dryly.

“Yeah!” Aang grins. “Just like that!”

“I’ll pass.”

Aang deflates, pouting. “I promise I won’t mess up and let the air bubble collapse, though! I’m much better at it now.”

“…You’re not really selling it, man.”

“You’re sure?”

“Yeah…” Sokka says, the word trailing off as an idea suddenly tickles at the edge of his thoughts. Aang and their surroundings fade away as the urge to sketch worms into his hands, making his fingers itch until he casts around for a good stick to draw in the wet sand of the shore. “Hey, Aang. When you do that air bubble thing—how deep can you go before the water pressure becomes an issue?”

Zuko knows he’s fucked before he even gets home. It’s too late. Or too early, rather. He got caught too long in the tunnels where he can’t feel Agni’s pull as easily, especially at night, and lost track of time. And then he almost got caught in the tunnels, stumbling onto a pair of Dai Li agents. The only reason Zuko got away without revealing his bending or getting captured is because he clearly caught them by surprise as they went off duty. They were in the heart of their own power, relaxing from a night’s work, no longer hovering on the edge of constant wariness.

Zuko, on the other hand, is always ready for a fight.

But fights take time, which Zuko already didn’t have enough of, and he hauls himself from the underground with grey streaking the sky. Approaching dawn makes it harder and harder to reach the Jasmine Dragon without being seen as servants wake up and merchants prepare for the day, especially in the Upper Ring, where there’s no excuse of evening shift work to fall back on. Which means going slower and slower, having to be more and more cautious. Zuko manages to lose the Dai Li on his tail, to cling to what little shadows remain along the gated estates of the Upper Ring, but it's Agni’s energy sizzling through his blood that gets him the last of the way back.

So Zuko isn’t surprised, to slip up the back stairs of the Jasmine Dragon on silent feet and find Uncle waiting in the hallway.

“Nephew.”

“Uncle.” Zuko can hear the wariness in his own voice, the extra hoarseness of exhaustion.

“A late night, I see.”

Zuko glances down at himself. Swords in one hand, mask in the other, cowl loose around his neck, head to toe in clothes that Uncle wouldn’t have seen since they were on the road, covered in dirt and dust like Uncle also wouldn’t have seen since they were on the road. There’s no point in trying to lie, even if Zuko were any good at it.

“You’ll join me for some tea, perhaps, instead of morning meditation.” The words are mild, and not a question.

“...Okay.”

“Don’t take too long cleaning up.”

Uncle heads toward their little kitchenette, and Zuko needs to wait for him to turn the corner before he can manage to unlock his muscles enough to go to his room. He sheds his swords, his mask, with a silence that is too habitual to set aside even now, tripping off the close-fitting, dark clothes that have no place in the life of a tea server and hissing through his teeth as bruises and scrapes pull.

He twists to see a mottled landscape of ragged, darkening skin along his life side, and with a clenched jaw he forces himself to prod carefully over the purpling marks and tackiness of recently clotted cuts. It shouldn’t have happened—*wouldn’t* have happened, if he was actually at the fighting weight he should be. But that went away in the Earth Kingdom and certainly hasn’t come back on Lower Ring rations. And nothing is really actively bleeding anymore, at least. It hurts, but not in a way that suggests broken ribs or internal injury. He can feel grit underneath his fingers, though, the kind that gets pressed deep into your skin when you take a glancing blow from a small boulder.

Agni’s balls, cleaning this is going to be a bitch and a half to deal with.

Zuko slips into an old shirt for now, then ducks into the bathroom to give himself a quick rinse with a wet rag to take the worst of the dust and dirt off his arms. He glances longingly at the tub. He hasn’t felt this grimy since they got into Ba Sing Se and he absolutely loathes the memory of it. But he can hear the kettle already beginning to whistle—Uncle must be helping it along—so he resolutely turns his back on the luxury of a hot soak and splashes his face from the sink instead.

Zuko blinks water from his eyes, meeting his own gaze in the mirror as he braces over the sink. The circles under his eyes are dark in a way that could be exhaustion or could be a recent punch to the face. Time will tell. His scarred eyelid is drooping more than usual, a sure sign that he’s at the end of his reserves. His skin is pale, even for him, hair clumped in ragged bunches with sweat and dirt.

This…is fine. He looks better than he feels.

Zuko hears the sharp sound of porcelain cups being set on wood and forces himself to move.

Uncle glances up as Zuko walks in. He’s already seated, the chair across from him pointedly pushed halfway out. “Thank you for joining me.”

Zuko grunts, hovering in the doorway. He didn’t exactly have a choice in the matter and doesn’t have the patience right now for the pretense that he did.

“Will you sit?”

Zuko eyes the chair and thinks about how much he would need to shift his torso to get into it, and how easy it would be to relax once he’s there. He shakes his head, barely a movement, but he knows Uncle will see it. He would probably stiffen up too much, anyway, if he let himself sit. And needing to lever himself up again…

“Hm.” Uncle’s eyes flick to Zuko’s left side like he knows Zuko is favoring an injury. Which Zuko is, and not subtly. Agni. He’s too tired to put energy into trying to hide it when they both know it’s there. “You have been going out at night.”

Zuko darts a look toward Uncle, then lets his gaze fall back to the floor, giving the barest hint of a nod.

“For a while now.”

Another glance, another nod.

“Not to see Master Sokka.”

Zuko looks away, scarred side toward Uncle, the side that only shows his emotions in the tensing of his jaw and the press of his lips and the stiffness of his shoulders.

“Why.”

Fuck. Uncle almost never cares about *why*.

“I needed to clear my head?” Zuko tries, which…technically isn’t a lie, if you consider how all this started.

Uncle just gives him a flat look, though. “With two swords, a mask, and a fight?”

“…There isn’t always a fight?”

Uncle sighs, setting his tea down un-sipped. “How badly are you hurt?”

“I’m fine,” Zuko says, automatic.

“Then you’ll let me see,” Uncle challenges, tone mild, words a trap.

Zuko considers kicking up a fuss, but he already turned down an offer to sit when he’s visibly dead on his feet, so he isn’t exactly making a strong case for his fine-ness. He vaguely tries to recall if Sokka left any hickeys on that part of his chest recently before giving up the effort. Uncle has seen far worse than a few love bites, when it comes to that, and Zuko is too bone-deep tired to do more than sigh and lift the edge of his shirt and do his best to hold back a wince at the motion.

Uncle frowns, taking a long look. “Earthbenders.”

Zuko can’t bring himself to meet Uncle’s eyes when he sounds like that, old and full of regrets and fears. “Yeah.”

“You need to clean that dirt out.”

“I know,” Zuko agrees quietly. It was one of Uncle’s first lessons, the first time Zuko stepped foot into the Colonies. Earthbenders are dangerous in more ways than the obvious. You can survive the crushing blows, but infection can be just as deadly.

“Sit,” Uncle orders, rarely-used force in his voice as he leaves his tea behind to get out the medical kit. Zuko contemplates resisting, because he isn’t sure he’ll be able to get back up if he sits down and he doesn’t want to sleep at the table. But it will be easier if he doesn’t have to twist his side in order to clean it…Zuko sighs, and sits.

“Where are you going?” Uncle asks as he begins to lay supplies out on the table.

“Around.”

“Zuko.” Zuko startles, suppressing a flinch and actually meeting Uncle’s eyes in his surprise. He hasn’t heard his name here, outside of Sokka’s mouth in…ever, maybe. “Where are you going?”

Zuko runs a fidgety hand through his hair—gritty, dusty, greasy, ew—before forcing himself to be still. “Really, just…around. There’s no specific place.”

“You are looking for something, then.”

Zuko hesitates, and Uncle’s hands pause where they’re cleaning out the top of the scrapes along Zuko’s ribs. His expression pleads with Zuko to not question his intelligence right now.

“Yeah,” Zuko admits, fixing his eyes on the bundle of gauze set on the table and trying to breathe through the panicky flutter in his chest over where this conversation is going to go.

“What is it?”

“You never cared before.”

“You never came home looking like this before.”

That is not…strictly true. In Ba Sing Se, yes. But you can hide a lot under armor, and Zuko has been doing this for a long time. Not that he’s going to point that out if he can avoid it. “Appa.”

Uncle frowns. “Excuse me?”

Zuko sighs. “The sky bison.”

His reply is quiet, the silence after deafening with unsaid words. The drip of water from Uncle’s cloth into the bowl is excruciating, Zuko’s inner flame and shoulders winding tighter and tighter with each drop, with each too-fast heartbeat that drags on without a response.

“You are searching,” Uncle finally says, words careful and precise. “For the Avatar’s sky bison?”

That…doesn’t sound any better when someone else repeats it. “Yeah,” Zuko mumbles, forcing his fingers not to fidget. “He’s missing? They had posters up, for a while..?”

Uncle deliberately sets down his washcloth, taking a deep breath. “Zuko. Why are you looking for the Avatar’s spirit animal?”

“Um. Because he’s missing?”

“Why are *you* looking for him?”

Zuko winces at the weight of years of judgment and disapproval in the question, even braced as he is against the paused debriding of his scrapes. He opens his mouth, searching, before slowly pressing his lips together when he remembers that he has no idea what to say. Zuko doesn’t exactly have an answer straight in his own head, let alone one that he can share with Uncle.

Zuko could say that he’s searching because Sokka needs it, which would be true but not entirely so. He could say he’s looking because control of the sky bison means control of the Avatar, which means power, or at the very least being able to bait him toward a specific path. Which is accurate, but not the whole of it either. He could say that it’s because he has the slim chance of making something right, though what, exactly, or how, he isn’t sure. He could say that it’s because if Appa is actually missing and in Ba Sing Se, then Azula is sure to become involved eventually if she isn’t already. He could say it’s because he feels like a ghost of himself without a purpose to make him feel solid. That he can’t stop clinging to what little he has left because he’s afraid, so deep inside he can barely admit it, that too much of himself has already faded away.

What he does say is, “I don’t know how to stop.”

The words are hoarse and exhausted and far too revealing of far too much, naked in a way Zuko doesn’t like to be with anyone other than Sokka. They feel like they fought their way out of his chest, clawed their way up his throat, as bloody and ragged as the rest of him.

Uncle lets them hang in the air for an endless moment before picking his washcloth back up, hands as gentle as they can be over Zuko’s ribs. “Nephew. You are not constrained by the choices of your past. You can walk a different path.”

As if Zuko were stuck on just one. He isn’t sure if the noise that rips free of his throat is closer to a laugh or a sob or a scream. There are so many different paths in front of Zuko that he has no idea where to even find stable ground in order to decide which to take. Zuko feels like he could be buried by them all, and still he can’t seem to find one that lets him hold on to all that he wants.

He is selfish, maybe, for thinking that someone like him would get to keep all those things.

“You can stop this, Zuko,” Uncle urges, and Zuko closes his eyes as the words ricochet through his chest. “You don’t have to do this.”

“…I know.” Except any choice he makes now feels too much like picking a side. Like picking one single path and closing off possibilities that Zuko isn’t ready to let go of, yet. Ang Agni, Zuko doesn’t know how he can decide without inserting himself into something that he’s supposed to stay out of, something he doesn’t know how to be part of anymore.

“The life we have here, the possibility of a second chance—that is not something to take for granted. That is not something that everyone gets, Nephew.”

Zuko nods, bracing as Uncle digs out a particularly deep piece of gravel. He should be grateful. He knows that. He shouldn’t ask for more than he already has. He shouldn’t struggle against giving any of it up when what he has is already far more than he deserves.

“Trying to pursue the Avatar, and hold onto our life here…you cannot do both.”

Zuko takes a deep breath as the piece of gravel comes loose, concentrating on the weird sting-burn-relief of something foreign pulled free of his skin instead of the frantic twist of his inner flame.

“Nephew.” Uncle waits until Zuko makes reluctant eye contact. “Any attempt to capture the Avatar, to return to that part of your life—it jeopardizes everything we have rebuilt here. *Everything*.”

Zuko flinches from all that is encompassed in that ‘everything’ that means so much to Uncle and so little to Zuko. Zuko knows he’s putting it at risk, he *knows*. And it hurts, hard and cold in the pit of his stomach, that Zuko knows it and still can’t stop himself. Zuko has never liked this life the way Uncle does. Not enough to truly take steps to preserve it. Not when—

“Does he know what you are doing?”

—not when Zuko already puts it at risk every moment he can’t be Lee, every moment he spends with Sokka.

“…No,” Zuko admits, fully aware of how damning it sounds to be doing this thing and keeping it from Sokka. To have insisted, when Uncle found out about them, that what he had with Sokka had nothing to do with the Avatar, and to still be searching, as if Sokka and the Avatar have ever been separate.

Uncle’s hands pause again, heavy on Zuko’s skin. When he finds his voice, his words are edged with disbelief, disapproval. “Zuko. You cannot move against the Avatar and hope to keep things as they are with Sokka.”

Zuko stares at the table until his eyes burn and forces his inner flame to move in time with his lungs and not his thudding heart. He is well aware of that fact. But he can’t stay as he is now —on the periphery of everyone’s life, taking and taking and giving nothing back.

“You need to *choose*. You cannot be everything to everyone.” That hits hard, deeper even than Uncle’s believing that Zuko could be with Sokka while actively plotting against him. Except—how much does it really matter, if it’s *active* or not? “You need to decide the path you are going to walk, for your own sake.”

Zuko looks away from the judgment he can see on Uncle’s face, finally choking out, “I know.” Knowing and doing, though…

Uncle takes in his profile a moment, then sags so abruptly that Zuko startles, jerking to catch him before realizing that he’s just slumped, not falling.

“I know, Nephew,” Uncle says, voice haggard. “I do. I know how hard it is to let go of something that used to define you. I know how difficult it is to walk away from a goal when it feels like it is just within reach. When it feels like achieving this thing is all that you are supposed to want, or be. But Zuko—do not repeat my mistakes. Do not wait until it is too late.”

He pauses to see if Zuko understands and Zuko gives the barest hint of a nod, fingers curling into a tight fist. He does understand. Maybe not entirely, maybe not every layer of weight in Uncle’s voice, but enough. Things changed for all of them when the Wall fell.

Uncle’s voice is bleak in a way that Zuko has never heard before when he finally speaks again. “I know all about impossible quests, Nephew, and how thin their rewards can be. I do not want you to know more of them than you already do.”

Zuko’s breath hitches, but he can’t make a sound and Uncle finally doesn’t push anymore. He just bends to cleaning the rest of Zuko’s wound in the early dawn quiet as Zuko sits and forces himself to be still for it, slipping into that place in his mind where physical pain feels distant and all that is left are the painful thoughts. Agni, how does anyone ever look at all the paths before them and know how to pick just one?

Sokka is feeling invigorated in a way he hasn’t in weeks, buoyed with a new idea that Ba Sing Se isn’t going to be able to take away from him or grind down against harsh reality because it has nothing to do with this damn city. There’s a noticeable bounce to his step as he strides toward the Jasmine Dragon where Zuko is already waiting for him on the veranda, leaning against one of the few sunlit columns with crossed arms. Zuko looks like a piece of artwork like this, a carving breathed with energy and life.

Sokka slows his steps to appreciate the view, then further when he realizes that Zuko is still staring into space. Zuko usually registers Sokka’s presence by this point, some instinct or fire sense or whatever alerting him to Sokka’s approach. But today Zuko is staring into the middle distance, eyes not tracking anything in particular, face set and tight. When Zuko finally does twitch and turn toward him, Sokka can practically feel the tug of Zuko’s attention in his chest. That felt rather…chi-like. Like for all his tension, Zuko is barely keeping himself in check.

“Hey there,” Sokka says, making the words come easy, head cocked in silent question.

Zuko grunts, giving Sokka a head-to-toe sweep that relaxes the set of his shoulders about half an inch.

“How’re you doing?”

“Fine.”

Sokka raises his eyebrows at Zuko’s distinctly un-fine tone. “Want to go smack some sandbags with a broom?”

Zuko barks a sound that might be a laugh, under other circumstances, head dropping back against the column. “No. Not really.”

Sokka bites his cheek, taking in the particularly dark circle under Zuko’s eye. “Do you want to just…spar, then? And play around?”

Zuko frowns, cracking an eye open to study Sokka’s face. “…Yeah. Okay. Sure.”

Sokka grins despite the cautious hesitancy of Zuko’s reply, firmly deciding to bring energy and enthusiasm to the afternoon. He grabs Zuko’s hand, tugging him around the side of the Jasmine Dragon toward their practice space and holding Zuko a half-step closer than is strictly necessary. It’s a bit of a role reversal for them, for Sokka to lead the way. It’s a tiny thing, but at the same time big enough that Sokka can’t stop sneaking glances at Zuko as they get out the swords and start warming up, trying to figure out what could be going on.

Zuko’s body language is particularly shut down today, though, and the most Sokka can work out without directly asking is that Zuko is feeling broody—which Sokka clocked in about five seconds—and is favoring his left side, which…honestly isn’t super different than usual, either, just a shade more pronounced. Zuko doesn’t seem inclined to let whatever is bothering him hold him back, though—which Sokka also didn’t exactly need close examination to determine. Zuko throws himself into katas, into strength exercises, into practicing some kind of spinning jumpy twisting-off-the-wall thingy that is so highly specific that there has to be a story behind Zuko’s sudden determined focus.

Sokka finally coaxes Zuko into sparring with him, even though he can tell Zuko isn’t in the mood to hold back enough to make it competitive. Sokka isn’t near good enough yet to beat Zuko with swords, not when Zuko isn’t confining himself just to the moves he’s already shown Sokka. But that doesn’t mean Sokka can’t make it interesting, because Sokka has a lot more than just bladework tucked into the back of his brain.

Zuko signals the start of the bout with a slap to his back thigh and Sokka immediately throws everything he can think of at him. Instead of matching Zuko’s game, he tries to be unpredictable instead, unexpected in the kind of way that only works the first time because sheer surprise rarely works twice. Sokka hauls out moves that he vaguely remembers Bato doing with a spear before the men left, his staff work from the Northern Water Tribe, the kind of wrist control needed for a boomerang or a fan, and adapts it all to the weapon in his hand.

Some of it’s a flailing mess—noted, do not try to throw a sword in a real fight without practicing first—but some of it is surprisingly successful. Kyoshi fan moves translate quite well, as it turns out. And it’s fun, trying to think on the fly of ways to trip Zuko up, knowing that there are no real consequences for failing. And best of all, Sokka can see a little brightness finally spark in Zuko’s eyes after the first two or three surprises, a little less tension around his mouth, like Zuko is excited to see what Sokka comes up with next, too.

Eventually, though, Sokka runs out of energy even with the fire of a new idea driving him. He collapses into a patch of sun, sucking in cool late fall air and watching Zuko continue to run katas. Zuko moves with swords and without, and if Sokka looks closely enough he thinks he can see the air shimmering around Zuko’s fists in a way that Sokka is pretty sure would be gouts of flame if Zuko weren’t holding himself back. It’s fascinating to watch, the way Zuko experiments and moves when he isn’t demonstrating, to see bending without the actual element as a distraction. Sokka thinks he can pick out the ways that Zuko’s bending informs his swordplay, and the traces of bladework in his firebending, which makes his mind spin with possibilities.

“Did you ever try firebending with your swords?” Sokka wonders as he braces himself into a hip stretch, tracking the quick dance of Zuko’s footwork.

Zuko hesitates, cutting Sokka a surprisingly wary look before glancing down at his swords. His voice is laced with a reluctance that Sokka doesn’t fully understand as he admits, “A few times.”

“That’s so cool,” Sokka says, half of his mind trying to figure out Zuko’s tentativeness and the other half trying to imagine what it would look like. Zuko blinks, blank for a moment before his shoulders loosen a few notches, one of those little relaxations that reveal tension Sokka never entirely understands the source of. There might be a blush beneath Zuko’s flush of exertion, which makes Sokka’s stomach flip in a rather pleasant way, and just makes him even more curious. “Can I see?”

Zuko bites his lip, spinning the hilts of his swords restlessly as he turns a slow circle, looking up, assessing the privacy of the courtyard. They’ve already used the space for plenty of private time, but there’s a difference in getting caught with your pants down and getting caught illicitly firebending. “I guess…”

Sokka nearly chokes on his surprise, coughing to try to cover his reaction in case it makes Zuko reconsider. “Should I move back?”

“No, you’re fine,” Zuko says absently, taking a few steps back and considering his space.

Sokka sits upright, eagerness pumping through him as he settles in to watch. He sucks in a delighted breath as pale flame suddenly ripples down Zuko’s swords, rolling over the blades and dripping off the tips. Sokka barely has a chance to register the liquid flow of the fire— what kind of combustion is happening for *that—*before Zuko explodes into what Sokka recognizes as one of his foundational katas.

The movements alone would be captivating—Zuko wholly focused, body and mind in sync, is something worth seeing—but his bending makes it absolutely breathtaking. Flames streak behind Zuko’s blades, extend ahead of his strikes, lick at his hands and surge and retreat over metal with his movements. Sokka can’t believe how seamlessly Zuko’s firebending seems to meld with his bladework, like the two have always been used as one. Zuko’s expression is one of total concentration, but not the tense-browed, tight, driving kind. It’s the kind of steady absorption that comes when everything is flowing and fitting, and you’re moving in perfect harmony with your intentions.

Sokka thinks that he and Zuko have very different definitions of ‘a few times.’

It ends all too soon for Sokka, with Zuko whipping the fire off his swords in a quick, hard twist of the blades. Flame crackles through the air before disappearing like it was never there in the first place, leaving nothing beyond but lingering heat and Zuko’s heavy breaths. Zuko is still a moment, head bowed, arms extended, then his eyes flick to Sokka. Their familiar gold is shy in a way that lets Sokka realize that for whatever reason, beyond the risk of discovery, it was a big deal for Zuko to show him this. And Sokka might not understand the context, but the fact that Zuko showed him anyway makes something warm and bright catch in Sokka’s throat.

“That was amazing,” Sokka breathes, letting all his awe and admiration shine through. “I’ve never seen anything like that.” Though that maybe isn’t quite right. “It kind of reminds me of the scarf dances? From the festival? The ones you said used to happen with bending?”

Zuko looks surprised, then thoughtful, his blades drawing an absent pattern through the air as he considers. “Huh. Yeah. I guess.”

Sokka thinks of Zuko’s dancing at the masquerade, his comfort with it all. “Did you ever learn that scarf dancing stuff too, with your fire?” That would be a sight to see, with real fire instead of fabric. “You said some of the aristocrats still learn it, in the Fire Nation.”

Zuko gives him a sideways look, transferring his swords to one hand and pulling his leg back into a stretch. “I think that’s enough firebending for now.” Which isn’t a no.

Sokka grins, equally delighted by the idea of Zuko knowing those graceful, intricate steps and by the newly relaxed line of Zuko’s shoulders. “What about heatbending?”

&#45;-

“You could have mentioned this before we spent the afternoon training,” Sokka mutters, watching Zuko ease himself into the tub across from him. It would normally be a sight to behold—and still is, don’t get him wrong. Sokka is just a bit more concerned right now with the swathe of bruising along Zuko’s left side.

“It’s fine,” Zuko says, voice tight.

“Oh, really?”

Zuko throws out a half-hearted glare, a telling sigh of relief escaping as he finally settles into the water. Sokka holds back his own sigh as the water temperature kicks up a few degrees. “I’ve had worse.”

Sokka is aware of that. “That probably shouldn’t be your standard for ‘fine.’”

Zuko gives a one-shouldered shrug, sliding down and dropping his head back against the edge of the tub with a little hum in the back of his throat that eases Sokka’s worries enough to let him focus on other things. The night is *not* going as planned, and Zuko blames the Jasmine Dragon’s customers, because he always does and because this time it’s actually their fault. Both Zuko and Uncle are running late due to a particularly demanding table of old men who don’t seem to appreciate the concept of a closing time while they conducted ‘their business’ and who proved woefully immune to glaring and ominous lurking as a means of driving them out.

Uncle is only just starting dinner when Sokka arrives, prep going slower than usual with Zuko still elbow-deep in sale receipts and inventory counts and order slips that he should have finished with hours ago. Sokka murmurs a quiet greeting, eyes curious on Zuko as he makes his usual offer of help that Uncle always refuses, barely lasting before the questions burst out of him.

“What are you doing?”

“The weekly sales report.” Which Zuko *hates* right now—and most days—with every fiber of his being.

“To balance the books?”

“There are three options before you, yes?”

Sokka jerks his eyes up in surprise, then winces at how revealing that was as Iroh’s eyes twinkle with a spark of wicked humor.

“Your basil mint tile is out of the question now, of course,” Iroh says, resting his teacup on his stomach. “You can of course consider your red lotus, in opposition with the cranefish, to mirror the defensive alignment if it happens, but at the risk of sacrificing the third symphony you’ve been trying to build—"

Sokka can only sit, mute, as Iroh proceeds to calmly list the pros and cons of every single option Sokka was considering, including which Sokka would take if Iroh himself were taking specific strategies, and which others to use depending on what Iroh thinks Sokka is doing, and on whether Iroh thinks that Sokka knows that he knows…

Sokka very distinctly considers whether this could be some kind of passive-aggressive revenge from Iroh, for Sokka’s blowup. He thinks it’s probably more likely that it’s Iroh’s oft-repeated advice that playing pai sho is as much about playing your opponent as it is about the board and the draw of the tiles. And Sokka is very aware that he is being played right now. But he can still feel himself second-guessing, and re-evaluating, and overthinking, and panicking over what it means that Iroh only confirms *some* of Sokka’s thoughts bout the three options, but not *all* of them.

“And of course,” Iroh continues, smiling over the rim of his teacup, “I am sure my words are confirming some of your thoughts, but not all of them, which does present a rather unique conundrum to consider—”

Sokka swallows back a strangled noise and shoots Zuko a panicked, more-than-a-little beseeching look. Zuko knows his uncle better than anyone. Zuko can tell Sokka…something. Whether Iroh is trying to talk Sokka into doing something? Or not doing something? Or whether he’s just messing with Sokka because he can? Or…anything, really, would be helpful right now.

Zuko flicks his eyes up to give him a flat look, then pauses in constructing his little tower of tiles to shove over the remaining half plate of cookies.

Sokka drops his head down onto the table, but does take a cookie when Zuko nudges the plate a bit closer, and takes a bite mostly to appease him, and it’s fucking delicious because this Upper Ring baker they’ve found is a genius, but not at *all* helpful for pai sho.

“Ah, yes,” Iroh says, amused. “A delicious suggestion, Nephew, but nevertheless one that does not help Master Sokka in his predicament.”

Sokka groans into the table at still having his mind read like this.

“I didn’t suggest anything,” Zuko says, and sounding more than a little sulky at the suggestion that he did which Sokka will laugh about later once he figures out what he’s supposed to do now.

“I would never accuse you of such, Nephew,” Iroh says. “I am of course aware of the distinct interest you show in long term multistep pai sho strategy.”

Sokka lifts his head at what feels like it could be a rather pointed comment, despite Iroh’s mild tone, to see Iroh giving Zuko a bland look and Zuko glowering back like he also isn’t sure how stung to be about it.

“I could be good at long-term strategy,” Zuko mutters.

“Hm.”

“When I want to be.”

“Ah.”

Zuko glares harder, then turns to Sokka, who freezes like an artic rabbaroo hearing a snow owl cat’s call. Sokka fully *believes* that Zuko could be good at long-term strategy if he wanted to be. He’s more than adept enough at outthinking Sokka during sparring for Sokka to have no problem with that. Zuko just categorically refuses to ever involve himself in pai sho as more than an observer, and half the time Sokka doesn’t even know if Zuko is paying attention to the game or just Sokka’s hands on the tiles, which is flattering and nice, but doesn’t help Sokka now with what he’s supposed to *say*. *Or* what he's supposed to do.

Sokka is silent just a bit too long and Zuko glowers at both of them now, transferring a rather withering glare between Sokka and Iroh while under the table, out of view, his hand suddenly lands on Sokka’s knee, Sokka nearly jumping in surprise.

“Just because I don’t want to,” Zuko says, as he drags his hand up Sokka’s inner thigh with deliberate, definitely heated intent, “Doesn’t mean I can’t.” His eyes flash molten as he gives Sokka a challenging look, firmly and quickly palming Sokka’s groin so that Sokka nearly gasps out loud before Zuko abruptly gets to his feet, moving to get more cookies and tossing over his shoulder, “And you already lost the game four moves ago.”

Sokka stares after him, dazed, before swallowing hard and trying to hide his flush and his sudden breathlessness and now triple fucking guessing himself because fuck, what if he did? Zuko watches so much pai sho, if he pays attention to any of it, he *could* know. And as he just very much demonstrated with that fucking *fondling* and the fact that Sokka is staring down another hour—*at least*—of gameplay, and that’s only if he loses quickly—Zuko knows how to plan ahead.

And Spirits, fuck, Sokka isn’t even staying the *night*, the pai sho game will probably take up most of the time he has left, which means this spark of wanting that Zuko just thoroughly lit is going to have to simmer and burn all on its own, and Sokka won’t be back until tomorrow afternoon and right now he needs to fucking *pay attention to Iroh—*

Sokka takes a deep breath, and then another to fully appreciate the extent of how thoroughly Zuko just set him up, and silently and whole-heartedly concedes that yes, when Zuko sets his mind to it, he really knows how to execute an effective long-term strategy.

&#45;-

Zuko watches Sokka disappear down the street in the darkness, lingering outside even though he can hear the faint sounds of Uncle cleaning up and closing up. Zuko can still feel Sokka’s lips against his own, his hands on his waist, can still hear the open wanting in the filthy words he whispered in Zuko’s ear in what is definitely Sokka’s own payback for earlier, not that Zuko minds it. Zuko lets the cold night air nip at his skin, trying to hold onto all the sensations of that last embrace with Sokka just a little longer, even as he knows he needs to go back inside. That he needs to shrug on a little bit of Lee, at least for a moment, and play the good nephew and help Uncle.

It’s feeling harder and harder, though, to fit back into that role every time he steps out of it.

Watching Sokka fade into shadow, feeling the bright not-fire of him becoming more and more distant, Zuko doesn’t know how much longer he can keep doing this. Zuko is aware, especially tonight, that the moments he has with Sokka—his whole life in Ba Sing Se, really —sit outside of time. And that while Zuko is waiting until Sokka comes back and staying behind as Sokka walks away again and again and again, Sokka’s life is moving forward.

Will either of them even know, when it’s the last time Sokka leaves? Or will Sokka just walk away like usual and never come back?

Zuko wants his time with Sokka to last forever, and sometimes to have never happened at all, all depending on if Sokka is there, on how painfully Zuko is feeling the strain of fitting himself into the space he’s supposed to live in.

Zuko finally drags himself back inside when he can’t feel Sokka against his fire sense anymore without stretching, the last bit of control he seems to be holding on to. He goes silently through the now-familiar motions of cleanup and shutting down the shop alongside Uncle, grateful that Uncle doesn’t press for conversation. Zuko is in no place for it, feeling stretched thin from just listening to Sokka and Uncle talk.

He feels like his three most important, grounding, anchoring things are taunting him tonight. They hang before him so his fingertips can just brush two of them, the third tantalizingly within reach if only Zuko is willing to stretch just a little further, to ignore the darkness below. He can almost feel the echo of armor around his body as he walks up to his room, weighing down his steps, a few paces behind Uncle and somehow feeling so, so alone.

## Chapter 29: What Lies Beneath

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for a bit more than canon typical violence, and a canon-ambiguous character maybe death

### Text

Someone is tailing them. Sokka registers it as he and Aang wend their way out of one of the narrow, chaotic markets that seem to crop up as needed in the Lower Ring. At first Sokka doesn’t think anything of it—the market is crowded, of course people would be leaving at the same time they are. But the shadowed, darting figure sticks with them through multiple turns, into and out of residential districts, on main streets and back-alley shortcuts.

“Are we being followed?” Aang asks, voice low as Sokka suddenly veers right when the quickest route would be straight ahead.

“I think so.” Sokka takes a quick glance behind them under the guise of inspecting a display of cabbages. The merchant seems particularly agitated. Maybe he’s in on it, too.

Aang looks around the mix of residential and commercial buildings on the street, his hesitance clear. The road is narrow, the buildings leaning and cutting across the sky. It would be tight for a fight, and there are far too many children around for both their taste.

“I know where we can go,” Sokka says, breaking away from the stall—the merchant sags in relief over his cabbage display, weird—and setting a brisk pace that isn’t remarkable but that would take work to keep up with. Around here there isn’t a lot of difference between the streets and the alleys, and this district is close enough to the Blooming Petal that Sokka knows his way around with a reasonable degree of confidence.

“Flank them?” Aang asks as Sokka ducks into a narrow side street.

“I’ll go high,” Sokka confirms as he takes an immediate sharp turn, making a point to leave a noticeable scuff in the gritty, hard-packed ground. If someone is following them, they’ll see that sign. And if not, then he and Aang can take a moment to enjoy one of the Lower Ring’s accidental courtyards born of odd zoning and haphazard city planning this far from the Upper Ring.

Sokka and Aang set up on either side of the alleyway, backs to the wall, Sokka with his boomerang at the ready, Aang gripping his staff. They both hold their breath, straining, sharing a ‘get ready’ look at the sound of almost-silent steps picking through the debris of the alley toward them.

Aang and Sokka move in perfect coordination as the figure steps cautiously into the courtyard, Aang swinging into a low sweep as Sokka brings his boomerang down from above. Sokka has a bare moment to register that the figure is shorter than he expected, and then that he’s seen that sullen expression and thick bowl cut before. With a startled yelp, Sokka diverts his blow to the shoulder, not the head, cringing as Aang still sweeps their target neatly off her feet. The girl goes down with a shout in a tangle of limbs.

“Smellerbee?” Sokka gasps, boomerang still frozen in the air as he picks out her familiar features, bizarre without the red face paint.

“I’m so sorry!” Aang cries, clutching his glider to his chest like that will somehow take the strike back. “Are you okay?”

She groans, slowly rolling to her knees, one hand rubbing the shoulder Sokka hit, the other held out as if to show that it’s empty. “Ow.”

“What are you *doing* here?” Aang asks, peeking down the alley like he’s waiting for the rest of the band to show up, too. Which would be just awful, actually.

“Why are you following us?” Sokka’s voice is laced with accusation now that his surprise is wearing off, now that he’s remembering that the last time he saw Smellerbee it ended with Sokka tied to a tree.

“Not for any reason like *that*,” she says, eyeing him like she can read his mind.

“Like what?” Aang frowns, but Sokka waves the question away and crosses his arms, waiting for Smellerbee to share why she’s here, then, if not for *that*.

“I saw you in the market, just now, and I just…” She takes a deep breath. “I need your help.”

“With what?” Aang immediately asks, the question nearly lost beneath Sokka’s loud “Excuse me?” He’s not *nearly* in the mood he needs to be in to entertain helping out Jet, or any of Jet’s Freedom Fighters. It’s been months since he has been.

“I don’t know what else to do,” Smellerbee says in a rush, both hands falling limply into her lap. “We’ve tried everything, and—”

“Who is we?” Sokka cuts in, eyes narrowing. “Who all is here?”

“Not all of us. Just me and Longshot and—Jet…” She winces, giving him another quick, guilty look. Shit. This is a complication that Sokka doesn’t need on a number of fronts.

“What do you need help with?” Aang asks again into the tense silence, glancing between Sokka and Smellerbee like he’s trying to figure out what exactly they’re talking around.

“Jet,” Smellerbee says immediately, sounding so miserable about it that Sokka is momentarily startled off the edge of his anger. “He’s…he’s getting worse.”

“Imagine that,” Sokka mutters, unable to hold back the bitter sarcasm. Smellerbee gets a look like she’s thinking about glaring, or protesting, but just ends up nodding in sullen acknowledgment. Jet might have hung the fucking moon in the sky with the way the Freedom Fighters acted toward him, but when Sokka was around Jet was doing decidedly less noble things with himself.

“Worse than what?” Aang frowns, pulling Sokka back out of his thoughts.

Smellerbee makes a frustrated noise. “Than…it’s hard to explain. He isn’t himself, anymore.”

“I don’t see how that’s a bad thing,” Sokka says, and apparently the bitterness is starting to win out over the sarcasm. Sokka hasn’t thought about Jet in a long time, and he doesn’t particularly care to be doing it now.

“It *is*,” she insists, voice plaintive. “Trust me, it’s—can I just show you?”

“We have time,” Aang shrugs, which isn’t technically false, but—

“This is like…a classic trap setup,” Sokka points out.

“It’s not. I promise, it’s not.”

“Great!” Aang says, like Smellerbee’s solemn promise was all he needed to put his faith in her. “Let’s go, then.”

Sokka thinks about protesting, digging in his heels and falling back on the schedule as an excuse to get away from whatever this is. But knowing Jet, whatever this is might end up coming back around to bite them, if they ignore it now. So Sokka just sighs and waves for Smellerbee to take the lead. He keeps himself a little bit back as they walk, though, keeping her in his line of sight and a careful eye on the roofline, making sure his boomerang is close at hand.
