He doesn’t trust any of these Freedom Fighters further than he can throw them, not after last time.

Fuck. Katara is going to lose her mind.

&#45;-

Smellerbee leads them to an apartment building that’s cramped and dingy and troublingly close to the Blooming Petal. It has the look of a place that gave up about a decade ago on trying to pretend that it was anything other than a serviceable place to sleep nominally out of the elements. Sokka mentally recalibrates how nice of an apartment Zuko and Iroh had down here.

“How long have you guys been in the city?” Sokka asks as they go up a switch-backed, narrow staircase that brings back a hint of nostalgia that has no place in this particular situation for a number of reasons.

“Since the end of the summer,” Smellerbee says, not the least bit winded as they keep going past the fourth story. “It was supposed to be a fresh start.”

Sokka grunts at the familiar words. He thinks about as much of them from her as he does when Iroh says them.

“Supposed to be?” Aang asks, because at least one of them is paying attention and isn’t caught up in memory.

“It…didn’t really go as planned,” Smellerbee admits as they finally step out onto the fifth floor. Sokka can hear barely-muffled shouting and children laughing and the clatter of cooking, the noises of too many people living too close all spilling past thin walls into the hallway.

Sokka eyes the hallway, the clear presence of so many people, a tendril of dread creeping up his spine. “Please tell me you guys aren’t trying to blow up a monorail or poison a well or some shit like that.”

“No! No, nothing like that. Just…” She sighs, opening the door to reveal Longshot braced in the doorway, just as tall and significantly more worn around the edges than Sokka remembers. Longshot glances over his shoulder as the door opens, a look of desperate relief passing over his face before he turns back toward the room, tensing and widening his stance like it’s his mission to block the door and he will not allow himself to be moved. Smellerbee slides into the room behind Longshot like this is totally normal behavior, and Aang and Sokka share a confused shrug and cautiously follow.

Sokka’s first thought is that the room is small for three people, with a low table in one corner and three pallets on the floor that barely even qualify as beds. It’s just as dingy as the rest of the building and would have the same cared-for-to-death look if it didn’t seem like a whirlwind had just hit it, clothing and blankets and dishes strewn haphazardly across the space.

In the middle of it all is Jet.

Sokka is surprised by how the sight of Jet takes him, an unexpected kick to the gut even though he’s braced for it. Jet is as tall and lean as ever, arms tightly crossed as he stares out the window with the kind of focused intent that screams ‘I’m not talking to you.’ The pose is made even more bizarre by the fact that there’s barely any window to see out of, the opening covered in wood planks. Makeshift bars, applied from the inside, like they needed to take extra measures to prevent someone from getting in. Or out.

Sokka gives Longshot’s braced stance another glance, catching Aang also eyeing the Freedom Fighter with wary caution.

“So,” Sokka says, clearing his throat and striving for a tone somewhere near vaguely disinterested. “What did you want to show us?”

He doesn’t expect Jet to explode into motion at the question, Sokka falling back an unthinking step as Jet whirls around, arms swinging wide, eyes going straight to Sokka, then Aang. He gapes for a moment, then lights up like the secret passcodes to infiltrate all Fire Nation strongholds were just placed into his hands.

“Aang!” Jet exclaims, giving Smellerbee a wide grin. “You found Aang!”

Sokka swallows back a noise of surprise as the open happiness in Jet’s words and the uncomplicated delight on his face. The pure joy in it throws Sokka off-balance so much that he barely grabs on to the fact that Smellerbee *found* Aang, like she was looking for him, and by the time he latches back onto Jet’s rapid-fire words Jet is rattling off about clues and Appa and helping, sounding entirely earnest, with none of his half-steps or lingering looks or weighty pauses or self-aggrandizing.

Sokka takes another step back, like the physical distance will help him find his mental footing. It’s like all Jet’s charisma has been replaced with nothing but pure jittering energy. *Upbeat* energy. And Sokka isn’t *upset* about that, it’s not like he *misses* how Jet was before, but… “What the fuck is wrong with him?”

Longshot grunts, and Smellerbee sighs in…relief? “You see it, then.”

“What?” Aang says, distracted, hopeful eyes never leaving Jet. “What do you mean? He— Sokka, he’s talking Appa! About clues to find him!”

“Just…hold your ostrich horses,” Sokka cautions, suspicious and confused and not wanting to crush Aang’s enthusiasm too quickly even as he knows he can’t let it grow any bigger than it already is. “He isn’t acting normally.”

“Because he wants to help?” Aang challenges, as if they don’t have plenty of reasons to distrust an offer of help from Jet. “I know you didn’t get along before, but—”

“It has nothing to do with *getting* along, it’s because he—” Sokka bites off the rest of his statement, waving a hand in annoyance, trying to wordlessly indicate the missing…sexual magnetism, or whatever, that sucked in both Water Tribe siblings in basically a day, a different version of the same the gravity that pulled an entire band of children and misfit behind him.

Smellerbee and Longshot both wince, correctly reading the gesture. Smellerbee at least has the grace to look a little regretful about it.

“This is what I was talking about,” Smellerbee jumps in, saving Sokka from needing to explain to Aang that actually he and Jet got on swimmingly, for a time. “He’s different. And we don’t know what to do about it.”

“Why do you guys keep *saying* that,” Jet complains, looking wounded, and hurt, and what is going *on*, Sokka didn’t even know Jet’s face could *make* those expressions. “You keep stopping me and trying to make me stay here! All I want to do is—”

“Help the Avatar recover his air bison companion,” Smellerbee finishes with him, Longshot mouthing the words. “We know.” She turns to Sokka and Aang, Longshot keeping both eyes on Jet like he needs watching. “It started a while ago. We aren’t exactly sure when, but…he got arrested, and…”

Sokka snorts, wholly unsurprised that Jet managed to get himself picked up by the local authorities.

“Why?” Aang asks. “What did he do?”

Smellerbee sighs, looking embarrassed beneath the curtain of her bangs. “He…accused someone of being a firebender. And then tried to attack him to make him bend.”

“Let me guess,” Sokka drawls. “He wasn’t a firebender at all?” It’s so familiar he isn’t even surprised to hear it.

“Well, he definitely didn’t firebend,” Smellerbee mutters. “So that was basically the same thing, when the police showed up.”

Sokka grunts in acknowledgment, thinking again about the apartment’s proximity to the Blooming Petal. Zuko and Iroh are lucky that Jet didn’t set his sights on them, with their Fire Nation eyes and lack of a convincing backstory.

“Maybe he just got scared after being arrested,” Aang suggests, glancing over to where Jet is *pouting*.

“We thought that too, at first. That it turned him around.”

“This is too much, though,” Sokka says, eyeing Jet and feeling desperately uncomfortable with the earnest pleading on his face as he tries to negotiate with Longshot to be allowed to show Aang some vital clue. Sokka can’t imagine any kind of simple arrest that would take away all that driving purpose and seething anger.

Aang is giving him an odd look, which Sokka chooses to ignore. He isn’t going to hash out why he’s so confident in this, at least not in front of the Freedom Fighters. If Aang hasn’t put it together by now, then Sokka certainly isn’t going to spell it out for him. Sokka needs to cling to what shreds of dignity and privacy he has left, with the way the others already insert themselves into his love life.

“At first he was just kind of…subdued. But then he suddenly started talking like this,” Smellerbee explains, all of them pausing as Jet repeats his desire to help the Avatar recover his air bison companion. “And then it was all about trying to find you guys.”

“How’d he even know we were here?”

“You guys put flyers on basically every flat surface you could find, around here.” That’s…a fair point. Sokka had killed a lot of time before and after hanging out with Zuko by putting up flyers.

“Why didn’t you let him come find us?” Aang scowls, on the verge of sliding toward anger. “If he has clues—”

“He *shouldn’t,* though,” Smellerbee cuts in, glaring through her bangs. “Where would he have gotten them?”

“Maybe he investigated or something! Maybe he wants to help!”

“Sure. Maybe,” she says, in a tone that says ‘when the North Pole melts.’

“It does seem unlikely, Aang, if they’re keeping an eye on him like this all the time,” Sokka says carefully. And they’re struggling with it, if they’ve devolved to literally trapping Jet in a room. No wonder Longshot looks dead on his feet.

“I still want to hear what he has to say,” Aang says stubbornly. “What do we have to lose?”

A lot, knowing Jet, and Smellerbee’s expression says she thinks the same about indulging him. “I don’t know if that’s a good idea,” Sokka hedges.

“Well what else do we have to work on?” Aang challenges. “More ponds?”

“…Fine.” That’s unfortunately valid. “Let’s just…bring him, then.” They’re supposed to meet up with Katara and Toph a few districts over anyway, to talk clues. It looks like Sokka and Aang will have a big one to discuss, now, one way or another.

“What? Bring him where?” Smellerbee looks a little frantic around the edges at the idea of bringing Jet anywhere.

“Yes! Bring me!” Jet shouts over Longshot’s shoulder, wiggling out of his grip in a way that is still athletic and light on his feet but just…different. Like none of his joints work quite the same as they used to. It freaks Sokka out even as he forces himself to watch Jet squirm his way free with a critical eye. How are they going to get Jet through the streets of Ba Sing Se like this without attracting the wrong kind of attention?

Spirits, why can’t anything in this city be easy…

&#45;-

It turns out Jet is surprisingly easy to get moving in a non-spastic manner, once they tell him they’re traveling with the Avatar to talk about clues for recovering his air bison companion. Those words, specifically.

Being taken seriously does wonders to calm Jet down and return a bit of driven intensity to his twitching, eager energy. It’s unsettling, more than Sokka would like to admit, the way some hard knot in Sokka’s chest loosens a little seeing that familiar glint in Jet’s eye. Sokka immediately feels weird about it. It’s not like Sokka *wants* Jet to be how he was before. But some part of Sokka can’t help but empathize with the relief that comes with finally feeling heard.

Spirits, Sokka hates how seeing Jet, even this weird mirror version of him, immediately has Sokka’s stomach churning with someone uncomfortably close to guilt, his thoughts running down the path of ‘Katara and Aang can’t know about this.’ It’s the kind of feeling, the kind of thoughts, that Sokka hasn’t had in a long time, that he thought he had moved past and now can’t seem to shake off even knowing that kind of secret probably isn’t even necessary. Enough has been said around the topic of Jet and Sokka that Katara could put the pieces together if she had a mind to. But then, maybe she hasn’t because she doesn’t. She’s never brought it up, which isn’t exactly her style.

Sokka suddenly finds that he deeply, powerfully resents Jet. For a number of reasons but specifically for putting Sokka back into this mental space where he feels like he has things to hide. And maybe also for the way Sokka can’t be upset with Jet without being upset with himself, too, because Sokka was at least an equal participant, not only in the flirting and the kissing but in the concealment.

Fuck. Sokka really hopes Katara doesn’t just murder them all on site. Aang, for wanting to bring him. Jet, for being himself. And Sokka, for going along with it all despite the loud voice in the back of his head pointing out that this can only end in disaster.

&#45;-

Toph and Katara are already waiting when Sokka rounds the corner into the little park they’ve picked out. Katara is bouncing on her toes with excitement, Toph looking positively savage in her satisfaction.

“We have a clue,” Toph grins, all bared teeth and cracking knuckles.

The words burst out of Katara like she can’t keep them contained any longer. “There’s a tunnel network beneath the city, not just the sewers! Sokka, there could be so much hiding down there!”

“We have a clue too,” Sokka says dryly, taking a pointed step to the side just as Jet turns the corner with the others.

Sokka is glad that he decided to pull ahead, because Katara reacts in an instant, waterskin cork popping and ice exploding forward to freeze Jet and his Freedom Fighters in the space of a heartbeat. Aang leaps clear in a little gust of wind like he expected it, scratching his head as he lands and shooting Sokka an uncertain look that Sokka ignores in favor of taking in the satisfying sight of Jet trapped up to his chest in ice.

Sokka might have some things he needs to work through, too.

“Who are these people?” Toph frowns, hands hovering partway toward raising pillars of stone.

Katara slowly turns to Sokka, eyes blazing. “What. Is. This.”

&#45;-

“We have to *go*, we’re wasting time!” Jet is getting agitated again, eyes starting to go a little wild. Katara is watching him like he’s a potentially rabid animal, like she’s only a few words away from locking him back in ice.

“Let’s just take a moment and relax,” Sokka says, pitching his voice to soothe, because they do not need that kind of chaotic energy right now. They’re all plenty worked up already.

“We could check it out,” Aang suggests, turning his staff restlessly in his hands. “The warehouse doesn’t sound like it’s too far from here.”

“Jet, just wait a minute,” Smellerbee says with the tones of someone repeating an oft-said phrase. “We will, okay? Let’s just take some time.”

“You always *say* that!”

“It doesn’t *sound* totally crazy…” Katara mutters, watching as Longshot and Smellerbee try to calm Jet down and simultaneously back him into a containing corner.

Sokka makes a skeptical noise in the back of his throat. “That there’s a warehouse in this part of the Lower Ring big enough to hold Appa that we don’t already know about? Because Appa was bought by some rich Earth Kingdom guy and is being shipped down south to some zoo? Which means there’s some animal dealer around that we also don’t already know about?”

“…I mean, we can’t know *everyone*,” Aang points out. “Ba Sing Se’s a big city.”

Katara shifts, uncertain. “We would have to leave the city and head back toward the South.”

“On foot,” Toph adds. “In winter.” Which Sokka is finally starting to believe is actually about to arrive, with the way the days are starting to feel.

“Guys, I don’t know about this,” Sokka sighs, tugging on his wolf tail. “It’s not impossible, but…don’t you think it’s all just a little…neat? I find it a bit hard to believe.”

“What, that you don’t know everything?”

Sokka doesn’t let himself get bothered by Aang’s tone. He knows how this affects him. There are only so many dead ends they can run into before you start getting worn down. “Aang, Zuko’s old teashop is around here. I spent a *lot* of time covering this part of the Lower Ring. I really think I would have noticed if something like that was here.”

Smellerbee pivots toward them, frowning. “Teashop?”

“Don’t worry about it,” Sokka mutters. They don’t have time for tangents right now, and he is *not* letting the Freedom Fighters find out about Zuko. “So, what now,” he asks her instead. “We follow this clue?”

“I don’t care about that,” she says bluntly. “I just want someone to help him.”

“How are we supposed to do that?” Katara asks, face set somewhere close to belligerent.

“I don’t know, otherwise I would have done it,” Smellerbee snaps. “It’s like he got arrested by the Dai Li and came back with a personality transplant.”

Toph cocks her head. “The Dai Li?” Her words are precise, with the kind of weight and sudden attention that makes Sokka abruptly remember that Katara had started this whole shindig by saying something about a secret tunnel network. They’re really going to need to circle back to that, after this whole Jet thing.

“Yeah,” Smellerbee confirms. “They showed up and grabbed him, and he came back a day later on his own being all…different.”

“Maybe he got hit in the head of something,” Aang offers tentatively, giving a sideways look to where Jet is beseeching Longshot for aid to help him reunite the Avatar with his air bison companion. What is *with* this guy, it’s like he is reading off a script…

Toph makes an uncertain noise. “What, like he got a concussion and never went back to normal?”

Katara is frowning now, engaged despite herself. “Brain injuries can do weird things. They can affect your memory, your taste, your balance. The Northern Water Tribe healers talked about cases where there were even personality changes after certain types of head injuries…”

“So we try healing him?” Sokka glances to where Jet is engaged in a vigorous appeal to a silent Longshot.

“…It can’t hurt?”

Sokka cuts Katara a sideways look, speaking under his breath just for her. “And if it does you don’t care?” Sokka isn’t judging when she shrugs and sticks her chin in the air in a way that definitely means ‘yes.’ He pretty much feels the exact same way.

&#45;-

Watching someone’s whole head disappear into glowing magic healing water is freaky, but not as much as the way that Jet squirms and keens and struggles against Longshot’s hold only to suddenly go rigid, body locked. Katara jerks away from him with a shocked noise, nearly letting the water drop.

“That is *not* a brain injury,” she says, shaky, eyeing Jet like he’s a wild, dangerous thing again. Which he is, briefly, half-lidded and calculating before the expression seeps off his face like the tide washing out, leaving only that foreign earnestness behind.

“What is it?” Aang asks, staff gripped half-ready to strike.

“I don’t know,” Katara frowns. “It felt like some kind of wall.”

“Like he doesn’t want to think about something?” Sokka does plenty of that. He’s become… probably too good at compartmentalization, since they left the South.

“No like…something got put there. It isn’t supposed to be there. It’s *him*, but like it wasn’t always part of him…” She trails off, looking frustrated by her inability to describe what is going on. There’s a moment of silence, then—

“That’s some freaky crap,” Toph says, summing it up with her usual succinctness.

“What happens if you take it out?” Smellerbee asks.

“I don’t know.” Katara scowls at her own lack of knowledge.

Longshot and Smellerbee share a glance, then, “Try,” Smellerbee orders.

“What?” Katara blinks out of her thoughts, looking alarmed as Longshot nods decisively in agreement. “I could hurt him! More!”

“Katara,” Smellerbee pleads. “He acts like he doesn’t even remember losing his family to the Fire Nation anymore.” Sokka isn’t quite sure what that means, but he sees that it has some kind of significance to Katara in the way she rocks back onto her heels at the words.

“Okay,” she says, taking a deep breath, psyching herself up. “Okay. Let me just…”

&#45;-

“Spirits—take it,” Sokka spits, struggling not to say what he really thinks—*fuck it all—*in front of the kids. Of course there would be a secret mindbending base beneath the lake all the wealthy people use as a vacation retreat. Of *course*. It’s Ba Sing fucking Se.

And fuck everything—they’ve been sending Katara and Aang to investigate the lakes. They should have been sending *Toph*. It’s not about the water. It was never about the water. Sokka was just too caught up in the lake-ness of the clue to think about could lie beneath. Stupid, stupid, stupid.

“I can take you there,” Jet growls, still breathing heavily, voice thrumming with intensity and eyes dark with rage just like Sokka remembers.

“Wow, yeah, this guy is *way* different,” Toph mutters, shifting her feet like she’s trying to read him better.

“We should go,” Aang says, eyes bright with purpose like Sokka hasn’t seen in a while. “We should go right now.”

Sokka glances around the group, seeing Jet’s tight resolve and Longshot and Smellerbee looking relieved as they stand at Jet’s back like they used to. Sokka glances toward his own people, all present, healthy, armed, and waiting for his signal.

Fuck.

Sokka is supposed to meet Zuko later today. He has the feeling that he’s not going to make it.

&#45;-

Zuko is in a nasty mood and he knows it, and Uncle knows it, and so does every fucking customer who was on the floor when the messenger came with a note from Sokka. A fucking messenger. Sokka uses *messengers.* Zuko recognized the handwriting immediately, and it took him far too long to get past the novelty of a new letter from Sokka to realize what this one *said*—that Sokka wouldn’t be able to show up for dinner and stay the night as planned.

Zuko can’t remember the last time he saw Uncle move so fast, and he is grimly amused that Uncle let the Dragon of the West peek through in order to get Zuko off the floor before he lit something on fire. As if Zuko didn’t have more control than that by this point.

The temperature of all the tea in the shop just spiked for no apparent reason, is all. Zuko knows how to wait to get to the kitchen before turning a sample basket of pastries to ash.

“Hm,” Uncle says, eyeing the mess on the table. “I didn’t care for those, either.” Zuko rounds on him and Uncle holds up a hand to cut off whatever is about to spit from Zuko’s mouth. “Maybe you should take the rest of the afternoon off.”

Zuko narrows his eyes, feeling the intensity of his glare tugging at the rigid skin of his scar. He *hates* feeling so seen. But not enough to reject the offer.

Zuko pivots away with a silent snarl, hauling off his apron and stalking up the stairs to the apartment, on the verge of literally fuming. It’s not that Zuko had specific plans for the evening that are up in smoke now. He’d just been looking forward to whatever the evening would bring all fucking *day*. And instead, it’s Zuko in his room, alone, Agni dipping toward the horizon and hours and hours and hours of night stretching out before him.

His taut, sharp-edged restlessness is reminiscent of bad nights on the *Wani*, a thought that Zuko doesn’t allow to linger. He drives it out the same way he would have dealt with it back then, channeling it all into furious, barely contained motion and feeding it into his knotted inner flame. He tears off his work uniform, ignoring the sound of straining seams, rooting through his chest of meager belongings for his cowl, and mask, and familiar dark clothes.

Zuko isn’t going to stay here and spend the night fucking waiting and *pining*. And he isn’t going to spend it enduring Uncle’s considerate, understanding, *pitying* glances either. If he suddenly has an entire night on his hands, Zuko is going to fucking do something with the time.

&#45;-

Zuko knows his own way into the tunnels by now, and he’s followed enough Dai Li agents to know he needs to travel out toward the walls, not in. It’s muscle memory at this point to jump from the ornate top of a tram car as it slows to enter the station, and from there Zuko flits from entrance to entrance until he finds one suitably private and suitably empty of heat underneath. He ignores—embraces, maybe—the risk of doing something like this so early in the evening. Zuko craves the challenge to his concentration right now, itches for the extra focus required to remain unseen with the streets still so active at the edges of the Lower Ring. Zuko only lets himself feel a tight burst of triumph when he finally makes his way off the street and into the tunnels. There’s something about slipping from the faux-normalcy of the Upper Ring into the reality of the Lower Ring and then the dark, green-lit tunnels that matches Zuko’s mood right now. This fucking city. All its perfect lines and cultivated aesthetics sitting on top of a viper rat’s warren of secrets.

Zuko lets his fire sense spill out as he drops off the ladder onto the bricked floor. His awareness sweeps wide, finding nothing beyond torches in the corridor on either side. His inner fire has a satisfied, eager rhythm as Zuko sets himself toward the heart of the city’s power, shoving his fire sense outward. He doesn’t have the patience for the cautious, studied exploration that he’s been doing up until this point, not when in his gut he knows that the Dai Li would keep their biggest treasure as close as possible to the center of their power. And all the signs, all the movement of the Dai Li, point to beyond the walls.

Zuko sets out at a ground-eating jog, one he hasn’t gotten to use in a long time. It feels good to let his stride stretch out, to let himself really *move* as he plunges through the tunnels, for once not thinking about the path back to the surface, or escape routes, or hiding places. He’s aware that he isn’t being careful like usual, that maybe he’s being goaded into recklessness, and he can’t find it in himself right now to give a single shit. His inner fire is eager for a fight and Zuko isn’t reining it back, hungry to feed things into his rage like he hasn’t been in a long time. It’s a wildness that feels at home with the swords on his back and the mask over his face and the fire simmering inside of him.

Zuko is feeling vicious and he knows it, even if he doesn’t care about it. All of his emotions are burning into his bending, lending it extra power, giving his fire sense extra reach. He warps torches as he passes to give himself shadows to work with, leaves them crackling and blazing behind him. He can barely make himself tuck away into private corners when he feels the heat of bodies moving ahead or behind him and it’s more of a struggle than he would normally want it to be to release the heat of them once his fire sense wraps around it. It’s like part of him is ravenous to grab these agents who are one more obstacle between Zuko and want he wants, who are stealing Sokka away with their fuckery—because Zuko might not know the ins and outs of Sokka’s day-to-day, but he knows it’s a short list of things that could have pulled Sokka away and that the Dai Li are at the top of it—and make them pay for it.

It’s a dangerous feeling. A dangerous mood for a firebender, and especially one trying to stay undiscovered. If only there was enough about his life here that Zuko cared to keep safe, to care about that.

He has *something*, he reminds himself, slipping into a crevice, eyes the only thing moving as two agents walk past. He takes a deep, quiet breath, trying to separate himself from his fire’s wild hunger. He has at least one thing, for now, at least one thing that is still enough, for now, and it would gut Zuko to be the reason that ‘for now’ ends sooner than it’s already going to. An end that feels so fucking *close* tonight, and Zuko’s fire twists and claws in his chest until he has to move again.

Zuko winds his way through the maze of tunnels, moving from main passages to side branches and back again, feeling coiled and on the verge of igniting. He’s so focused on speed and silence and he almost doesn’t react when his fire sense sweeps over something impossibly large, his startled brain taking a few heartbeats to register that the shape he’s feeling isn’t a mass of bodies but is all one large, warm, living thing.

Oh...shit.

Zuko…hadn’t actually planned to find something tonight. Or ever, maybe. He knew the likely places to look but he knows he isn’t the only one looking, and tonight he’d just needed to *move*. To act, to do something to make himself feel anything other than useless for a few hours.

He thinks about turning around, about making his way back to the Upper Ring and finding someone to tell. He thinks about waiting in his room, in the teashop, for Sokka to have the time to come to see him and hear it. He thinks about the possibility of nothing at all being there if Zuko leaves and comes back.

When Zuko moves again, it’s not back in the direction he came from.

Though it turns out being able to feel Appa in his heat sense—maybe, it could be…another giant creature the Dai Li are holding down here—and being able to *find* Appa are very different things. Zuko keeps that mountain of heat in the center of his awareness, but he still needs to wend his way through tunnels and rooms and passageways and dead ends, doubling back and tripling back to actually *get* there.

Zuko eventually finds his way into a wide, arched corridor. The bricks are dry, though chill, with a dampness in the air that makes Zuko think there’s water close by. He sticks close to the wall as he crosses what must be some sort of atrium. The green torches—copper, maybe, or salt. They must soak the wood in some kind of solution, though the only reason Zuko can think is for aesthetics, which….sure—come as easily to his call as any other fire, letting him create pockets of shadow and throw light ahead and pull darkness behind him.

Zuko considers the door for a moment—thick, iron-banded, heavy lock, very impressive looking, again with the aesthetics—before making quick work of it with his lockpicks. He forces himself to focus on what’s in front of him through the ringing knowledge that the giant warm thing is on the other side of this door. Now is not the time to slip.

The door swings open, green light sweeping in along its arc, and Zuko has his first sight in months of something he never thought he would ever see again.

The room is wide, endlessly tall, shadow taking over before Zuko can see a hint of ceiling. It must be getting fresh air from the surface, somehow, to not smell rancid and rank. The animal smell of it is still strong, though, musky and thick, nearly as overwhelming as the clanging of chains as Appa cringes away from the light, then surges forward with a bellow of rage. The sky bison is pulled up short, bound by each of his legs to different posts with barely enough slack to get more than a few inches off the ground if he tried to fly, rendered immobile beyond the ability to cringe and lunge.

It’s a good setup, really. Academically speaking and all. Enough space to hold the creature and walk around the perimeter, but not so much that it would be hard to pin someone in the room and trap them if that’s the direction you wanted to go in. The chains look thick, well made, and Zuko can tell even from the doorway that those shackles would be harder work than the door to crack open even if you could get Appa to hold still for it. And there are no escape routes he can see except back the way he came, where there are limited tunnels that could fit something the size of a sky bison. And being beneath water—if they are, actually, beneath water—quite effectively neutralizes any sane invading earthbender who doesn’t know the structural supports of the space already. There would be no place to go, really, not unless someone tried to go up into that darkness, and Zuko is sure that’s just as much a trap as the rest of it.

Zuko drops his gaze back to Appa. The sky bison has finally quieted, still huffing and breathing heavily but crouched low, tense. Zuko recognizes something pretending at calm when all it wants to do is fight. It looks dingy, ragged even, its coat lank and coming away in chunks that can’t be healthy with the coming winter. Appa is alive, but not being cared for. It makes Zuko’s inner fire snap, makes the torches flicker, to see something Sokka cares for treated like this.

“What am I going to do with you,” Zuko whispers. He didn’t actually expect to find Appa, not like this. He isn’t ready for it.

Appa skitters at his voice, then growls, settling down and pinning Zuko with an intense glare. Zuko didn’t know a sky bison’s face could be quite so expressive. How much do the animal companions of the Avatar really understand? Can Appa recognize him? Would Zuko be welcomed, if Appa did? Or would he remember Zuko as just another enemy?

“Is that what I am, to you?” Zuko murmurs, taking a few cautious steps forward, hands out wide and away from his weapons.

A sudden flare against his heat sense behind him—too close, how did it get so *close*—has Zuko whipping around before he can see how Appa reacts to the proximity. Zuko curses himself for letting his fire sense contract in his distraction. Not entirely, but it’s not pushed as wide as it was when his anger was riding him, when he was hunting rather than finding. Zuko’s hands dart for his swords as his fire sense rolls back out, his muscles locking when he registers not just the heat of a body but the presence of a true inner flame.

There aren’t a lot of options for firebenders in Ba Sing Se, these days. And this rhythmic, controlled inferno would never be Azula.

“What a surprise to see a familiar face here,” Uncle says, stepping into the doorway, and Zuko’s inner flame shudders at the confirmation, at the words that are hard in a way Zuko isn’t used to hearing directed toward himself.

Zuko doesn’t have a reply—he’s something far past *surprised*—but he’s sure his body language says enough as he glances away. The fact that his swords are still on his back, and not in his hands.

“You are not going to look me in the eye?”

Zuko manages to drag his gaze a fraction out of the underlit shadows. He doesn’t know why Uncle would expect that now of all times. Does Zuko ever?

“What is the end game, Nephew,” Uncle asks—demands—face tight with something that feels like anger that Zuko scrambles to understand.

Zuko flinches, his heart beating *run, hide, fight* until it’s hard to hear over the sound of it crashing in his ears. Agni, he doesn’t have an answer for that, even if he felt able to speak in the first place. He shifts, uncertain and anxious and needing to *move* before forcing himself to go motionless again. But the movement is answer enough, for someone who knows him.

“You never plan ahead, Zuko,” Uncle says, arms thrown wide in the doorway, taking up so much space in his anger that it’s all Zuko can do to cross his arms and look away and not scramble back. “And you *need* to, or else you’re going to get hurt. Or else *other people* are going to get hurt! You didn’t have a plan beyond capturing the Avatar in the North. You didn’t have a plan when you were stealing in the Earth Kingdom.” That’s…harsh. Zuko stopped doing that, mostly, once he went off on his own. But then, Uncle wasn’t there. “And you don’t have a plan with Sokka.”

Zuko can’t stop himself from rounding on Uncle for bringing Sokka into this, hands flared to cup the flames raging to burst free if his control were just a thread less strong. If it weren’t true. Because Zuko *doesn’t* have a plan when it comes to Sokka. He *can’t* have one, because whenever Zuko thinks toward the future he can never see one where he and Sokka can exist as a ‘we’, a ‘they’, an ‘us’ outside the rings of Ba Sing Se.

And whenever Zuko thinks toward the future he comes face to face with the fact that if Appa stays, then so will Sokka. And that if Appa goes, Sokka will go with him. It’s the undeniable fact beating beneath every moment they have together and apart, beneath all Zuko’s reasons for this search, unspoken even within his own mind but always lurking, a constant tension that has refused to let him settle because how can he settle when he knows there’s going to be an *end*.

When he knows there doesn’t, necessarily, have to be.

Zuko snarls around the jagged feeling in his chest of being forced to suddenly confront this thing he hasn’t wanted to admit still lives inside him, his breaths coming hard as he meets Uncle’s unimpressed stare through his mask.

“No, Zuko,” Uncle says, his hand slashing through the air like he’s rejecting Zuko’s anger and Zuko barely turns his flinch into a spin away. “When you don’t plan, things go wrong. And you can pretend it doesn’t matter but they will *keep* going wrong until you can’t brush them off anymore. This isn’t a joke!” Zuko wants to laugh, nothing like humor inside him. When has it ever been? “Look at where you are! You could *die* here. Do you even know how to get out?”

Zuko’s hands curl into fists, smoke thick on the back of his tongue. He’s been getting in and out of the Dai Li’s tunnels for long enough. He would figure it out, just like he fucking figures out everything. “Why are you here?” The question scrapes its way out of his throat. How did Uncle even find him?

“Because I cannot let you keep making these mistakes without *thinking*, for *once*, about what comes next!” Uncle shouts, the kind of shout that is for battlefields and enemies and family.

Zuko jerks away from the force of it, from the order in it. Zuko doesn’t *want* to think about what comes next. He doesn’t want to stare down the fact that none of the paths before him leave him with Sokka by his side for long, except for the ones where he loses everything else. Zuko might be living outside of time, untouched by the events of the world, but Sokka isn’t. Sokka, who was already restless with the pace of things the first time he stepped foot into that Lower Ring teashop. Every degree that passes is a degree closer to being without him and Zuko can’t *think* about that without wanting to turn everything around him to ashes.

“You cannot keep avoiding the things you don’t want to think about,” Uncle says, voice quieter but just as forceful. He knows Zuko too well. “You need to look inside yourself and find your own destiny, Zuko, not just accept the one forced on you by your father.”

Zuko whirls back toward Iroh, hissing between his teeth to hear him talk about the Fire Lord. He never brings him up unless Zuko does first, *never,* and Zuko wants to scream at him for doing it now. He nearly spikes his swords on the ground in his anger, barely managing to restrain the impulse because that would be fucking *stupid* when the Dai Li could show up at any time.

“You have a choice to make, Prince Zuko,” Iroh says, implacable, stone-faced.

Zuko goes immobile, motionless, hearing that title attached to his name again, at hearing the Dragon of the West address the Fire Prince. The people they apparently never actually left behind. It hits like chains wrapping around his chest. Like a weapon offered in the midst of battle when you’ve been disarmed. Like armor that you know will be familiar before you put it on.

“There are not many opportunities like this to reshape your fate,” Iroh warns, relentless. “This is yours. Do not waste it.” The words are bitter, as bitter to Zuko as the tea Uncle is always trying to push on him, falling from Iroh’s lips like he has no real belief anymore that Zuko will heed them but feels the need to go through the motions anyway. Said as if Zuko has before him an endless set of possible fates, with no regard for the fact that Zuko doesn’t *want* his own destiny. *Fuck* destiny. Zuko wants to feel like he actually has a choice. He wants to actually *have* a choice, any choice that doesn’t require him to tear some piece of his heart out and watch it burn.

The silence stretches out endless and all too brief as Iroh lets his words linger before pointedly, silently retreating. He disappears from Zuko’s fire sense as abruptly as he first appeared, leaving Zuko with nothing but the sky bison and the green torchlight and the farce of a choice he has left before him.

Zuko’s voice is raspier than usual when he’s finally able to speak again. “So this is my fate, apparently,” he says, turning to Appa. “Who knew.” Not any of the things he’d reached for, or tried desperately to hang on to, or to save. Just this moment with a sky bison. With the Avatar’s spirit companion, because it all comes back to the Avatar in the end. “I never thought it would end up quite so…furry.”

Appa exhales a gust that rocks Zuko back on his heels, and Zuko wonders again how much the animal understands.

“It would have been better to figure this out beforehand,” Zuko acknowledges as he turns a slow circle, taking in this trap again and testing out the theory that maybe spirit companions understand much than regular animals. “But Uncle wasn’t wrong. I’m not good at the planning stuff. I don’t like it. That’s why I need…”

No. Best not to go there.

Uncle might have been right about Zuko’s chronic inability to think past the next heartbeat, the next sunset, but the fact that he felt the need to *follow* Zuko in order to deliver that particular warning, to make sure Zuko fucking understood the gravity? Zuko might have no idea what he’s doing, but the lack of Uncle’s trust still shreds something fragile inside him. It hurts in a way that Zuko doesn’t want to acknowledge, because it feels like acknowledging it will just make it hurt even more.

“How did he get here, anyway,” Zuko mutters as he edges around Appa, both of them keeping a wary eye on the other as Zuko shifts to get a closer look at the manacles around Appa’s legs. They look heavy, stone wrapped in iron. The stone is likely a single piece, considering its earthbenders that have captured him, the iron just extra reinforcement against anyone without a key.

“Did Uncle follow me?” Has he been following Zuko this whole time? Giving the illusion of freedom and space and self-determination when really, he’s always there, watching? Zuko would like to say no, wants fiercely to reject the idea. But he can’t ignore that Uncle snuck up on him here, when Zuko didn’t think he’d pulled his fire sense in *that* much, didn’t think that he’d been *that* distracted, for Uncle to get so close before Zuko noticed.

Zuko had told Uncle, a little, about how his bending was with heat. That Zuko could feel Sokka with his fire sense. It wouldn’t be a stretch from there to assume that Zuko could feel others, too, if he wanted to. Uncle had even obliquely referenced that possibility.

Maybe Zuko said enough that the Dragon of the West, who had taught himself to redirect lightning, could come up with a way to hide himself from that kind of firebending if he needed to.

Zuko blows out a hard breath, something that wants to be a scream but isn’t allowed to be in this space shattering in his chest and ricocheting off his ribs. He crouches down against one of the iron posts, like maybe leaning against something solid might make him feel even a fraction less unsteady. For Iroh to do that, to teach himself that…it would take planning. Practice. Foresight. It would mean that when Iroh looked to the future, he saw himself in a position where he needed, at the very least, to be able hide himself from Zuko’s notice.

Zuko doesn’t want that to be how Uncle ended up here, desperately, deeply, in a way that makes him ache down to his bones. But if it wasn’t that…then that means Uncle knew where to find Appa without Zuko as his unwitting guide. That means that Uncle knew where Appa was before all this, knew that the Dai Li had him and was just…waiting for Zuko to find out, too? As a test? Agni, why keep the beast in captivity if he knew where it was held? Just for some fucking teaching moment with Zuko? Why would he *do* that?

But then, why does Uncle do anything? Why follow Zuko out of Caldera in the first place? Why play so much pai sho all around the world? Why always be there whether Zuko could admit he wanted him to be or not? Why spend months and months teaching Zuko not to be afraid of his own fire and then never let him move past the basics?

Zuko used to think he knew the answers to those things. Maybe he never did, though. Not really. It’s not like he ever asked, or particularly wanted to listen. Maybe the reasons Zuko thought were true were just cover for more secrets, like correspondents around the world and codes hidden in pai sho games and backrooms Zuko isn’t allowed to enter. A plan within a plan, always, just like the best pai sho strategies. Being Mushi and starting over and wanting Zuko to be Lee, but really…what?

“Is he trying to get me out of the way?” It’s a horrifying thought no matter what way Zuko turns it, viscerally upsetting enough that Zuko knows he should be reacting more to it than he is. He probably will react, once he stops feeling so utterly numb about it, like he can’t simultaneously contemplate this thing and occupy his own body.

Though if Iroh is trying to remove Zuko from the stage, Zuko can at least appreciate that Iroh probably thinks he’s taking a more humane approach to the task than the Fire Lord did. All depending on your perspective, of course. From where Zuko is crouching feeling his entire world for the past three years coming undone, he thinks fire might be preferable to this. At least flames don’t pretend to offer anything other than burning.

A far brush against his heat sense has Zuko sucking in a hard breath and forcing himself back into where he is. With a vicious shove he sets aside the things he doesn’t want to—can’t— think about right now, like he’s become so good at doing, the distant movement of bodies pulling his focus back to the here and the now and the metal post in front of him. Zuko is staring at the iron loop that Appa’s chains attach to, the point that holds the sky bison every time he pulls and bucks and cringes, wearing iron against iron for who knows how long.

As Zuko stares at that point, he knows that the *opportunity* in front of him isn’t about what Zuko wants, or what Uncle wants, or even what Sokka wants. It never was. It’s about what Zuko can live with under Agni’s unforgiving light. It’s about what Zuko will be able to survive having done, when he’s finally held to account for it.

The sound of steel is loud, echoing off stone as Zuko draws his swords and rises to his feet, none of his internal unsteadiness seeping into his movements because Zuko knows, when it really matters, how to lock himself down tight so the weakness never shows. Appa jerks at the noise, lowing in alarm, unable to get far, and Zuko doesn’t give himself a moment more to think. Thinking has never served him well. He just lets his inner flame slip its leash, wildness bursting into his blood as he sends fire blazing down his blade and *acts*.

&#45;-

They’re following Jet through some kind of underground fortress situation after taking the monorail to the eastern edge of the Lower Ring because of course Ba Sing Se would have efficient public transit access for its creepy secret bunker. Toph has been downright gleeful about the whole thing, despite her disappointment that Jet was able to lead them to an entrance rather than requiring her to bust her way through the ground. Aang is also vibrating with excitement, Katara full of nervous energy, and Sokka…Sokka is on edge. Mostly because it’s Jet—Sokka doesn’t think he can be anything but on edge around him—but also because he can’t not be deeply disturbed by the existence of this…mindbending.

That room full of Joo Dees all being turned into Joo Dee had been quietly, uniquely horrifying. Sokka still feels ill over his New Dee jokes, over the idea that a government could see its own citizens as so interchangeable and replaceable. It had been hard to walk away from that and leave all those women behind. But they’re here for Appa, first. Have always been here for Appa, first, as Sokka reminds himself nearly every day.

And first doesn’t mean they can’t come back.

They wind further and further underground, Sokka’s jumpy sense of suspicion latching onto every way this could be a trap. They’ve been walking forever and must be deep into the Outer Ring by now. But they don’t actually know beyond what Jet’s been able to tell them, which means if something goes wrong they don’t know exactly what they’re going to be dealing with. It’s a lot of faith to put in someone who once tried to drown a town of civilians. “I think he’ll be here,” Jet whispers, waving them to a halt before a broad, iron-banded door. “It’s a big spot.”

“Think?” Sokka scowls. “You don’t know?”

Jet shrugs, playing at unconcern as he gives Sokka a half-lidded, insolent look. “Do you know more?”

Sokka doesn’t, so he just glowers and crosses his arms as Jet glances around the group for any other sign of disagreement before throwing the door wide.

It is, in fact, a big spot. Long and wide and low, with that freaky green lighting that keeps making all of them jump at every shadow. It’s definitely big enough to hold an air bison. Though not comfortably, but maybe that would be the point. It’s certainly more than big enough to hold Long Feng and a triangle of blank-faced Dai Li.

“Of course,” Sokka mutters. The way Jet stiffens and snarls, overflowing with familiar rage as he reaches for his hooked swords, is probably the only thing that saves him from another icing by Katara.

Long Feng lets the moment stretch as he casts a theatrically slow, disappointed gaze over their group. “I had hoped that it would not come to this.”

“What have you done?” Aang demands, the words bursting out of him. “Where’s Appa?”

“I tried to be reasonable,” Long Feng continues as if Aang hadn’t spoken. “I tried to offer you the hospitality of Ba Sing Se.” It sounds magnanimous, rather rehearsed, and Sokka wonders who exactly he’s performing for. The Dai Li? It can’t be for them.

“*Where is Appa?”*

Sokka starts to sweat, then, at the pitch of Aang’s words. He exchanges a quick, strained glance with Katara. Aang cannot go blue-glowy destruction down here beneath a lake.

“Still, I must admire your persistence—”

Enough of this. “It sounds like you’ve got a great speech all ready,” Sokka cuts in. “But we’re a bit short on time, so how about you stop monologuing and answer the question.”

That earns him a stare that’s a tad too annoyed to qualify as unruffled. “You have made things difficult for me, by coming here. You don’t leave me many options.”

Great. Just great. “I’m sure if you hand over the air bison we can work it all out.”

“Oh?” Long Feng raises an eyebrow, folding his hands into his sleeves. “Would you leave Ba Sing Se, then, immediately, never to return?” They…can technically do that, even if Sokka feels like his heart is icing over at the thought. “Never to speak of what you have seen here?”

There’s a telling silence in reply apart from a tight, pained sound from Jet. None of them can forget the room of Joo Dees, or all the other doors they passed to get here, all the rooms they had no time to check to see if they were full or empty.

“I see,” Long Feng says, seeming unsurprised. “Well. Let it not be said that I did not try, until the end, to protect the King’s peace.”

“Wait, what—” This is sounding far too ritualistic and official for Sokka’s liking.

“I offered friendship, and it was refused.”

“Hold on, you didn’t offer shi—”

“You have made yourself enemies of the state,” Long Feng pronounces. “Arrest them.” The Dai Li snap as one into bending stances, and Sokka wonders frantically, uselessly, if they’re all mindbended too or just terrifyingly well-trained. “Oh, and—Jet, was it?”

Jet growls and takes a half-step forward, swords raised like he’s going to try to fight the lot of them all on his own.

“Jet, the Earth King has invited you to Lake Laogai.”

Sokka can physically *see* the impact of those words, all kinds of alarms in his brain going off as he rapidly catalogs the way Jet’s posture changes, the new set of his shoulders, the straightening of his spine, the suddenly relaxed grip on his lowering weapons.

“I am honored to accept his invitation,” Jet replies, monotone, with perfect diction, and *fuck,* apparently you can’t just erase someone’s brain fuckery with a little water magic, apparently it’s there forever. Good to know. Would have been much better to know earlier.

Long Feng sweeps another of those almost-impassive gazes over them, lips curling up at the edge in a smile that is distinctly creepy and self-satisfied. “Kill them.”

Everyone except Long Feng attacks at once. The Dai Li stomp on the earth in unison, Jet’s hooked swords flashing in the green light as he whirls on them. Jet crashes into them first by virtue of being closer, but the bombardment of rocks from the Dai Li is only seconds behind as Aang and Sokka scramble to deflect Jet’s attack with boomerang and staff.

“Toph!” Sokka shouts, throwing himself back, the edge of Jet’s blade whistling past his ear.

“On it,” she grunts, shooting her hands out and raising defensive pillars to knock the boulders from the air with pinpoint accuracy, face calm and fierce.

“Aang, help me hold him off!” An order that maybe doesn’t need to be given, but it never hurts to give Aang a specific task to focus on in battle. Aang nods, gliding sideways to force Jet’s attention to split. It’s mostly on Aang, but even a mindbended Jet can’t ignore Sokka entirely and risk giving up his back.

“Katara, we have to snap him out of it,” Sokka says as he tries to hold Jet’s creepy, blank-faced attention long enough for Aang to sweep out his legs. She nods in grim agreement, water swirling bright blue in one hand—fuck, what a target that makes her in this dim light— a handful of ice daggers in the other. Spirits, she’s going to have to heal in the midst of enemy fire unless they can take Jet down more permanently before then.

Jet’s swords catch, hooking around the curve of Sokka’s boomerang in a way he clearly didn’t expect. They struggle over their locked weapons, straining body to body for advantage, far too familiar, and Sokka doesn’t know if he’s going to be able to do anything permanent to Jet for all the animosity he holds towards the guy.

“Smellerbee, Longshot,” Sokka grunts as he manages to disengage with a heave, both him and Jet stumbling backward. “Do what feels right!”

It’s insanity, then, half-lit and dark, green torchlight flashing off blades, shadows concealing projectiles until they’re almost on top of them. Sokka grits his teeth, trying to hold off Jet’s dual swords with just his boomerang, stupidly grateful for all the time he’s spent goofing around with Zuko at things like this. It’s still hard, though, and getting harder to keep Jet’s attention and fight and defend without injuring. It should be like sparring, except that Sokka has never had to hold himself back when the other party is very much going for the kill.

Aang’s ability to airbend effectively is hampered by the low ceilings—a smart tactical selection, this room, which is…troubling—but he’s as agile as ever, adapting to throw up earthbending blocks and firing stones at the backs of Jet’s knees, disrupting his footwork.

Sokka is aware of Katara sticking near the protection of Toph, trying to find a way to jump in with healing while half of her attention stays on whipping out lashes of water. She sends them racing behind Toph’s shields and unleashes sheets of crackling black ice across the floor to disrupt stances and send strikes careening off course as feet slip.

Longshot and Smellerbee are…shouting stuff at Jet. Sokka isn’t entirely sure what, he can’t exactly concentrate on it. But in between Smellerbee grimly deflecting projectiles with her short sword and Longshot loosing arrows into the gloom—how can he even *see* right now— Smellerbee is giving everything she has to screaming. Words about The Duke and Pipsqueak, about the cause, about remembering where he came from and what the Fire Nation did to him. Which Sokka recognizes motivates Jet quite a bit, but maybe isn’t the kind of shit they want to bring him back focused on.

“Remember, Jet!” Smellerbee calls, breathless as she darts out of the way of a sudden pillar. “You’re a Freedom Fighter! You don’t fight for power, you fight for the people who can’t fight for themselves!”

Sokka tunes out everything she says next, because it turns out the Dai Li can do some freaky earthbending and *attach themselves to the walls and ceilings* like fucking *spider wasps*. Sokka is suddenly wholly occupied with attacks from above, all of them engaging in some frantic dodging, dipping, ducking, diving, and dodging as the field of battle suddenly becomes more like a box of bombardment.

“Toph!”

“On it!”

Sokka can feel the floor shivering as he scrambles to stay upright and throw himself at Jet’s back. He lets out an accompany shout as the ground *screeches* as Toph does…whatever Toph does, it’s still too fucking dark to see and half the lights have been taken out by now.

“Remember how you found me, when I was alone, and gave me a family again?” Smellerbee is still shouting, voice breaking with strain and maybe emotion. “Remember how The Duke was too afraid to even leave the trees, and you helped him be brave again?”

Jet seems to waver, to stutter, and Sokka isn’t sure if it’s from her words or from the ground shifting beneath his feet as Toph makes the floor *ripple* like a *wave,* what the *fuck,* give a guy some *warning*. Smellerbee sees the hesitation too, redoubling her volume and the speed of her words.

“Remember how you brought us here to give us a new life! You wanted to give Longshot and me a chance to be something more! Remember how you fought to give food to people who needed it, how you wanted to protect them and look out for them and help—”

Jet lets out a roar of agony, doubling over and clutching his head and stumbling as the ground heaves again. Aang and Sokka both skip back in alarm, Sokka immediately throwing himself to the floor as a pillar erupts from the wall near his head. Jet roars again, surging back to his feet, swords suddenly hooked together to extend their range. Jet swings around, arm extended as he pivots to launch a sword through the air toward Long Feng with a scream of defiance.

It is beyond cool and visually breathtaking and tactically *stupid* because now Jet is down a sword when they’re meant to be used as a pair. Spirits, how did this showy idiot ever make it so long in the forest? Long Feng raises a casual rock pillar to deflect the blade, casting them all an annoyed look before he starts kicking the top of the pillar off into razor-edged discs, layering the attack over what his agents are already unleashing. Toph is being a total champion blocker but fuck, they are so spread out.

“Guys, pull in!” Sokka shouts, pitching his voice above the sounds of battle. “Get close to Toph!”

Aang and Sokka dash toward her as Katara diverts her unneeded healing water to the offensive to cover their retreat, sending ice sheeting along the walls to dislodge the Dai Li agents perched there and unleashing showers of hail at vulnerable eyes. Sokka skids in low under a boulder, Longshot coming up behind him, scrambling to stop his momentum as he slides behind the defensive wall Toph has raised. Sokka struggles to his feet, crouched low, counting heads and good, five of them, except no, *bad*, there are *seven* of them this time, *fuck.*

“Jet!”

Sokka whips around at Smellerbee’s scream to see that Jet *isn’t retreating*. He’s snarling and acting like he’s going to fight all on his own, the stupid, emotional *fuck head.* He only has one sword left! Jet doesn’t seem to care, dodging rocks and screaming defiance and ignoring Smellerbee trying to tug him back.

“Smellerbee!” Sokka shouts. “Get over here!”

“Not without Jet!”

Longshot pops up, releasing an arrow and then dashing out to join them, *shit*. Sokka lunges to try to catch him but Katara has a hand on the collar of Sokka’s tunic and hauls him back behind Toph’s wall just before another barrage rains down. Toph grunts, hands quick and sharp, flicking faster than Sokka has ever seen her, face twisted in concentration. Aang is also bending, sheets of air to divert things off course, pillars of stone to ruin lines of sight, and it’s enough for them but Sokka already knows it won’t be enough for anyone out in the open.

“Now,” Toph orders.

Katara surges over the defensive wall like a hurricane, tentacles of water lashing from her limbs—she’s up to six now, some corner of Sokka’s mind notes, when did that happen. Aang swings low underneath her assault, leaving the water to Katara and sending sheets of air and discs of rock cutting across the room. Sokka sprints out under their cover, running for the three idiots as the one calm corner of his mind notes the sound of Toph shifting their defensive emplacement to where Jet is down, his Fighters crouched protectively over him.

“What the *fuck*,” Sokka snarls as he hauls Longshot bodily out of the way of a sudden pillar.

“He’s getting away!” Jet cries, struggling like he wants to get back to his feet as Smellerbee tries to keep him down, fingers white from the death grip he has on his remaining sword.

“What?”

“Long Feng!”

Sokka glances up to see Long Feng, face impassive as ever, casually riding a pillar of rock through the ceiling, because of course that’s a thing that you can do here. Seriously, *fuck* this city. “Who *cares*?”

“He has Appa!” Aang shouts, making like he’s going to chase Long Feng all on his own too because apparently, Jet’s brand of suicidal idiocy is *infectious*.

“No! Aang!” Sokka shoves Longshot aside and lunges, grabbing the airbender by the tail of his robe. “Appa is here! We can’t split up in a Spirits-damned underground maze, guys, what the *fuck*.” Also, that was a strategic retreat, if Sokka ever saw one, and he isn’t going to take that fucking bait if he can avoid it.

“You’re injured,” Katara says as she reaches them with Toph, effectively stalling whatever argument Aang might have tried as he pulls up to check himself for injuries.

“It’s nothing,” Jet growls, trying and failing again to rise.

“You need healing.” The water is already starting to glow in her hands, and Toph raises the barrier a little higher as cover with Aang falling in at her side and mirroring her stance, which protects Katara but also limits the visibility of everyone except Toph. Shit.

“There’s no time for that,” Jet snaps. “You need to find Appa!”

Toph and Aang let loose a shared whoop, and Sokka risks a glance around the earthen blockade to see a whole swathe of Dai Li disappearing under rubble.

“We can’t just leave you,” Katara protests, even as the coldly logical part of Sokka points out that there is no way Jet can walk without extensive healing, let alone run, not with the way he’s holding himself right now. And Jet wasn’t wrong—they don’t have time.

“Go,” Longshot rumbles, voice deep and resonant and leaving Sokka gaping because this reedy kid sounds like *that*.

“*Go*,” Smellerbee repeats, urgent as she catches Sokka’s eye. “Find Appa. It’s what you’re here for.”

“But—”

Jet’s voice is suddenly calm, emphatic, as assured and confident as Sokka has ever heard it. “Freedom Fighting is about knowing when the mission needs to come first.” Which is fucking *rich*, for him to say to Sokka, and Sokka could just punch Jet right in his fucking face right now, except—

“We have our friend back,” Smellerbee says, eyes steady through her bangs, something like calm on her face. “You still need to rescue yours.”

“…Fuck,” Sokka whispers, clenching his hands in his wolf tail. “Okay, fine. *Fuck*.” A deep breath, then louder. “Katara, Toph, Aang—we’re getting out of this room.”

Aang spins around, eyes wide as he takes in Jet. “But—”

“We need to find Appa,” Sokka says firmly, like he doesn’t share the exact same reservations. “The Freedom Fighters are going to cover for us.” Sokka waits for Aang’s hesitant nod before addressing the others. “It’s a phased retreat, okay? Katara on point. Aang, cover her. I’ll watch Toph’s back as we bring up the rear. Got it?” Heads nod all around. “Great. Do it.”

Sokka ignores the part of him shouting to stay, to wait, to give it just a few minutes more, to find another way, and focuses himself instead on the mission and what needs to be done. It’s easier than it should be, to cut that caring part of himself away and shove it into a silent corner. Sokka supposes he has a lot of practice, these days.

&#45;-

Zuko can grimly acknowledge that he does not, in fact, currently know how to get out of the tunnels as he sprints ahead of the Dai Li on his tail. It will be fine, though, no matter what Uncle would think, because Zuko has his body and his swords and his fire as a last resort. It will be fine, even if part of him feels like it’s raw and bleeding inside, even if his inner fire is dangerously eager to cut loose again, straining to burn through the feeling that Zuko is leaving—has already left—some vital part of himself behind to die. Just like Sokka always wanted, and Uncle, and the Fire Lord, and everyone else who’s ever met him. He hates how bitter it tastes to finally give in, like copper and ash.

Zuko skids around a corner, nearly slowing in surprise to find not more stone tunnels branching into this endless maze, but stone sloping down to water. Zuko is pretty sure he’s still below ground based on the weak thread of Agni’s pull, but he doesn’t have time to think about the kind of engineering and mechanics and water and air pressure that allow underground lake access without flooding the tunnels.

Sokka would know, and Zuko shoves the thought as viciously away as everything else as he dives forward, a moment of suspended weightlessness before he arrows into the water. How much time does he have before pursuit shows up? How long can he hold his breath? How far until he reaches the other side of whatever this is, if there even *is* another side?

It’s a plunge into the cold unknown, ignoring the way the water tries to leech heat from his body, the way the gloom seems to flicker between green-lit and thick blue. He holds onto Agni’s pull so he can keep oriented toward the surface, striking out like he’s done so many times before with no plan and nothing but himself and his anger and his own purpose to carry him through.

His eyes sting and strain in the water and he ignores the way his chest starts to feel tight with the need to breathe. He will make it out. There’s no other choice but to make it, to do what needs to be done because Zuko doesn’t know how to do anything else but survive. He kicks off his boots because he can’t keep the weight, sheds his swords because they restrict his movements, strips off his mask because he can’t afford the resistance, letting it all drop into the darkness below him, more pieces of himself to cut away, and that is bitter, too.

&#45;-

Sokka and the others sprint toward the door in front of them, following Toph’s instruction as she stamps on the ground and guides them toward the biggest empty space she can feel, one that’s hopefully a holding cell and not a plunge to their deaths or something. The door isn’t even locked, though, which makes sense because the space beyond is fucking *empty*, nothing but stone and high walls and six iron posts spaced around the room. Six posts. And a patch of white.

“*Appa!”* Aang shouts, diving for that patch of fur, and yes, those posts are arranged just right to restrain an air bison, aren’t they. “He was *here*.” Aang sounds like he’s on the verge of tears or rage, Sokka can’t quite tell which, but both of them are bad right now.

Sokka joins his side as Katara and Toph fan out to search for clues—they have a familiar rhythm, by now, for that task—reaching out to touch the fur cupped in Aang’s hands. Sokka’s throat tightens at the familiar softness of it and he crouches down next to Aang, trying to offer silent solace while still keeping his eyes on the door and his brain focus on what to do next.

They’re really in it deep, now. It’s not like they can just go back to the house the Dai Li gave them and try again tomorrow. And it’s not like they can leave the city, even starting in the Outer Ring, without fighting their way out. This…is not good.

Aang lets out a tight, choked noise and Sokka shifts to put a gentle hand on his shoulder, the other bracing against the stone floor so he can offer comfort but not drop his whole weight onto Aang in his sudden exhaustion. Sokka doesn’t push Aang to get back in the game, not yet at least. If Aang is going to have a little breakdown anywhere, it might as well be here. And Sokka needs the time to *think*, to figure out how they’re going to get out of this creepy as fuck, cold, subterranean—

The floor isn’t chill. The floor isn’t chill like the rest of the place.

For a disorienting moment Sokka is back in an unusually warm day for the middle of fall, the kind that Toph and Zuko said were normal but to Sokka felt like summer refusing to let the snow finally come. He’d been laying bare-chested on sun-warm cobblestones, eyes closed, mostly focused on trying to decipher the characters Zuko was idly tracing on his back as Zuko murmured something about different types of stone and heat retention and flow and boundaries and stored potential and why these cobblestones in particular were so nice for laying on. Sokka would normally have been totally interested in learning about thermodynamics from a firebender, but he’d also been totally fucked out and struggling to care about much beyond that.

But he caught enough. Enough to know that stone can store heat. To know that things don’t stay warmer than their surroundings without actual effort or energy, like what comes from bending, or the sun, or the presence of something hot to lend it warmth. And this stone is still comfortable to the touch, like something was just here, lending heat.

“Toph!”

“What?” She snaps around at the urgency in his tone, Katara raising her hands automatically into an offensive stance.

“Can you follow the tunnels back out of here? The way you found this? But only ones big enough for Appa to fit through?”

Toph stamps on the floor, head cocked, glancing up and then around as if she can actually see whatever her feet are telling her. “Yes.”

“Let’s go.”

“Where?” Aang demands, using his glider to haul himself to his feet, one hand still white-knuckled around that tuft of fur.

“Appa was just here,” Sokka says, trying to hustle him toward the door.

“I know.”

“No, like—*just* here. We can’t be more than ten, twenty minutes behind him.” Not with how cold it is down here, and how warm the stone floor still is.

Aang stares, uncomprehending, then seems to register Sokka’s words all at once like a bolt of lightning, stiffening with purpose. “They’re trying to get him out.”

“And there are only so many tunnels he’d be able to fit through.”

“Enough talking about it,” Toph orders, shoving by them. “Let’s go!”

&#45;-

Of course, the Dai Li wouldn’t let them stick to that particular plan. Toph is able to tell them that an intersection of multiple passageways has half of them seem wide enough to fit Appa, and that all the passages slope toward the surface. And then the Dai Li are coming up fast and they’re running again, with no time to deliberate or think before choosing.

Sokka knows what this is. They’re being *herded*. He’s hunted enough to recognize what it feels like to be on the other side, and he doesn’t particularly want to know what they’re being driven toward.

“We need to get out of here,” Sokka pants as they dash through another intersection. They can’t give up on Appa now, but they need to get out of the Dai Li’s territory and regroup.

“Yes,” Katara agrees, grimacing as she loses another handful of water to a slick patch of dark ice to force their pursuers to slow.

“Can you feel if there’s water above us?”

Katara glances up, and Aang slows for a second, biting his lip in concentration. “Yeah.”

“The minute we aren’t under the lake, let us know. Toph?” She grunts. “The second they give the signal? Bust us out of here.”

“With pleasure.”

&#45;-

They explode to the surface in a spray of rock and dirt, rising on a pillar—which is very convenient—into a mess of Dai Li agents—which is much less convenient. The Dai Li are oriented toward the water, but they quickly adjust, pivoting toward them as one. Long Feng is here, because of fucking course he is, maybe they *should* have just followed him out of that room in the first place.

The fight is brutal, with them trapped in so tight and so little room to maneuver. There’s only so much room to dodge, and so much time and space for fancy bending, and both sides know it. But they’re in the open air, with an airbender, next to a lake, with a waterbender, and Sokka would never want to fuck with Toph when she’s looking like that.

Bodies are flying and Sokka is trying to plot their escape out of here—a tactical retreat, because they might be marginally less fucked than they were underground, but they’re still without Appa, still an enemy of the Dai Li which is basically the state, and they still need to fight their way out.

A familiar bellow sends Sokka’s thought screeching to a halt, the noise far too loud to even consider for a moment that he could have imagined it. Still, Sokka nearly loses his footing in shock as Appa sweeps down from the dark night sky like a furious, multi-ton cloud of rage.

Aang looks like he’s just found religion. “*APPA!”*

The air bison lays waste to the battlefield with his tail and his body and his *teeth,* knocking and flinging earthbenders into the water. Katara looks only too happy to trap them in ice as she begins to back her way toward Appa, and Toph is also using the distraction to raise lightning-fast columns to toss the distracted Dai Li into the lake as she retreats toward Appa, too. And Aang is already there at his friend’s side, so it’s just Sokka bringing up the rear as Aang loses his shit with happiness, clinging to Appa, face buried in his fur, and it would be sweet and touching and sentimental except—

“Go!” Sokka urges, sprinting over the last bit of the distance. “Go! Go!”

—except more Dai Li are coming up from the tunnels, synchronized and uniform and fucking never-ending, how many does Long Feng *have*.

They pile onto Appa’s bare back, Sokka and Katara scrambling up the familiar climb. Toph raises herself on a pillar and Sokka hauls her shockingly small body onto the safety of Appa’s warm, matted fur.

“Hold on tight,” Katara says grimly, and Sokka grunts in acknowledgment. There’s no saddle. Evasive maneuvers are going to be rough. He flattens himself low, anchoring one hand in Appa’s fur and stretching the other over Toph to help pin her in place. Katara mirrors Sokka’s position, her arm crossed with Sokka’s over Toph’s back. Toph has her face buried in Appa’s fur, breathing with the kind of deliberate care that usually signals someone forcefully refusing to give in to panic. There’s a too-long unheard “yip yip,” and then Sokka is leaving his stomach behind with a familiar lurch that he didn’t even know he missed until his eyes prickle with tears to experience it again.

They take to the sky, the lake and the Dai Li quickly falling away beneath them with shockingly minimal resistance from below. Sokka risks a glance back, careful not to twist too much with only the width of Appa’s back and Sokka’s grip on his fur to anchor himself. Sokka can make out milling Dai Li on the ground below, but it’s too dark to see if anyone is fleeing, if anyone might have made it out. Sokka can only hope that they did, and press his arm a little tighter to Katara’s as she cranes to look back, too.

&#45;-

It’s starting to become true dawn as they finally land, setting down on a small island still in sight of the coast. Everyone is exhausted, worn but exhilarated and positively giddy with what feels like victory. Toph dramatically hugs the solid earth as Katara checks them over for injuries, healing scrapes and tweaks and cuts. Sokka is so relieved that they’ve finally *done it* that he isn’t even all that bothered by the fact that they’ve just walked and fought and fled through half the day and all night and he hasn’t eaten since what now officially qualifies as yesterday’s breakfast.

Sokka is leaning against Appa, enjoying the sound of everyone’s happiness and the familiar comfort of Appa’s bulk—though damn, Appa really does need a good bath—and thinking of nothing much more than whether he has what he needs to try fishing when Toph cuts through the reunion.

“So…what now?”

“Huh?” Katara says, glancing up from where she’s healing away some scrape on Toph’s knee that Toph doesn’t seem particularly concerned about.

“We found Appa. That’s what we came to Ba Sing Se for, right? So.” Toph sweeps an expectant glance around. “What do we do now?”

Everyone is silent, then, staring down a question that, clearly, none of them have bothered to think about with any specifics. Or, if they’re like Sokka, that they’ve thought about too much to be able to point to any one plan.

Katara rises to her feet, frowning as she bends her water back into her pouch. “I guess we’re back to the original mission.”

“The eclipse is still happening,” Sokka agrees.

“And I still need to master all the elements…” Aang doesn’t look particularly pleased to give fire another try.

“So…we leave, then?” Katara says, glancing around the scrubby island. “And head for Dad’s ships?”

Sokka wants to say yes. He wants to say it so, so badly. The need to see his Dad again is a nearly physical ache, and to see Bato and all the others who would be there too. But… “We can’t just leave Ba Sing Se.”

“Yes, we can.” Toph crosses her arms. “We just did.”

Sokka makes sure his voice is firm, neutral, calm. “We came to Be Sing Se for Appa, but we can still use the Earth King’s resources for the invasion.” And it suddenly feels like they have momentum behind them, finally, with Appa back. They have enough time now…it’s tighter than Sokka would like, but it will be enough if they can move fast.

Katara is frowning, though. “What, like we’re suddenly going to get an audience with him after we busted up his whole…whatever that was.”

“That’s the other thing,” Sokka says, forcing himself to stand fully upright away from Appa’s bulk. “You saw all that stuff, down there.” The rooms and the Joo Dees and the layout designed to trap.

“Yeah,” Katara says reluctantly, looking troubled.

“We can’t just leave Long Feng in charge like that and not try to do anything about it.” Sokka feels ill, thinking of those women, of Jet, of who else could be down there.

“So, what,” Toph challenges. “You want to go fight our way into the palace and see if the King is in on the plot or not?”

“I—yeah?”

Katara sighs, sounding put-upon, but Toph looks like she’s actually considering it.

“If we can get that kind of support behind the invasion—”

“Are you sure you aren’t just wanting to go back for Sparrowkeet?”

Sokka takes a slow, careful breath, because he knew it was going to go there eventually. “No.” He pauses, giving Toph a chance to call out the lie, which it isn’t. “I’m not going to try to say that that isn’t a factor. But we need all the resources and support we can get. That hasn’t changed just because we have Appa back.”

Though truthfully, Sokka doesn’t know if he would actually be able to disappear on Zuko like that if they asked him to. To just miss an afternoon, send a hasty note, and never come back. The idea is like a shard of ice in his chest, and he’s sure that Toph can hear his heart struggling to beat alongside it, wonders how long she would let him fight it before stepping in.

“We can do it without the Earth King,” Katara says, looking obstinate and shooting a venomous look back in the direction of Ba Sing Se.
