## Chapter 31: On Your Own Two Feet

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

No particular warnings in this one!

### Text

Sokka can’t stop being twitchy. He’s trying, as much as he can to not be a mess and he is keenly aware that he’s failing. He doesn’t know what to do with all his nervous energy, until finally Aang can’t take it anymore. Aang drops Appa’s reins, spinning around to face Sokka, face set in a deliberate kind of calm. “Will you just *talk* about whatever is bothering you, *please*.”

Sokka startles, stilling where he’s been unconsciously tapping out a rhythm against Appa’s saddle. “…Sorry. I’ll just—uh—” He sits on his hands. It’s not a good sign, Sokka reflects, when you wear down the patience of an airbender. But Sokka is approaching, at the speed of Appa, a meeting that he’s been simultaneously dreaming about and dreading. He doesn’t know what to do with himself now that it’s actually about to happen but isn’t happening *yet*.

Aang glances meaningfully toward Sokka’s foot, which has started bouncing. “Sokka. You want to talk.”

“I don’t—”

“You always want to talk. You always feel better when you talk.” Aang pauses, but Sokka can’t exactly contradict that considering how many heart-to-hearts Aang has sat through with him. “What’s going on? Is it Katara and Toph handling things?”

“No, they know the plan, they’ll be fine.” The two of them are scarily competent when they decide to team up. Sokka should maybe be relieved that it happens so rarely.

“Are you worried about leaving them in Ba Sing Se?”

“No, Kuei said the Kyoshi Warriors had just arrived. I’m sure it will be fine with Suki there.” Spirits, why can’t Sokka just say it?

Aang seems to have his patience back, at least, now that Sokka is talking and not fidgeting. “Is it because Zuko’s sick?”

Sokka scowls as that particular fact is tugged back to the forefront of his thoughts. “No. I mean, kind of. Maybe?” Aang makes an encouraging noise, waiting quietly, giving Sokka time to sort himself out now that they’re getting close to the heart of it. “I was maybe going to say something. And now I won’t, because he’s sick, so couldn’t tell me if he was okay with it. But that makes it feel like I’m trying to keep it a secret, which I’m *not*, I just—don’t want to say something…”

Aang scratches his head, face wrinkling in confusion. “Say something about what to who?”

Sokka braces himself and actually fully voices the idea for the first time. “About Zuko. To… my dad.”

“Oh,” Aang says, drawing out the word like suddenly it all makes sense.

“Yeah,” Sokka says, reaching out absently to rub Appa’s fur. “But I’m not going to, now. Probably. I think.”

“At all? Like—none of it?”

“I don’t know,” Sokka sighs, what little resolve he has crumbling at the faintest hint of Aang’s skepticism. “Maybe something? But maybe it’s not relevant? So it would just be kind of…weird?”

Aang is back to looking confused. “Why wouldn’t it be relevant?”

“I mean…I’m going there to talk about the eclipse plan, and explain the fleet’s role and get their support, not…talk about my love life.” Sokka can’t even picture it. He would just what —glance up in the middle of explaining the timeline and mention that oh, by the way, Sokka might also be dating someone, even though they don’t call it dating exactly, and that someone is a firebender, and his people think he’s descended from the actual sun with a degree of literalness that Sokka is still a bit unclear on.

No. Sokka should just focus on what he’s planned for, like the invasion and the request he’s making of the Southern Fleet. That’s what a Chief would expect of any warrior under his command, of anyone really on one of his ships.

&#46;..Zuko used to have a ship. For three years Zuko had a ship. The same years that the Southern Fleet has been active. Oh…fuck. What if Zuko and Hakoda have *met?*

Sokka is momentarily paralyzed with horror by the idea of not being able to chaperone the first time his dad meets his…person. Boyfriend. Whatever.

“But Sokka,” Aang is saying, and Sokka gratefully throws himself back into the conversation instead of thinking about *that*. “He’s your dad.”

Sokka eyes him. “…I know.” Hakoda’s dad-ness has kind of been the whole issue, really.

“So he’ll want to know because it’s important to you, and you’re important to him,” Aang says, like it’s obvious. “That makes it relevant.”

“I…guess?” Sokka…hadn’t been thinking of it in quite those terms: that Hakoda is his dad, which means that Sokka is his son, which should mean…things. “Maybe. It’s just been so long, you know? I don’t really know what to expect anymore.”

Aang traces the stitching of Appa’s saddle, considering. He probably knows that feeling better than anyone. “Are you worried that he’s going to be different than you remember?” Sokka groans, flopping down onto his back and throwing an arm over his eyes. “I guess. I know *I’m* different. I’ve gone ice dodging, I’ve fought in battles, I’ve traveled all over the world. I’m more than just a kid from the village, you know?” Sokka plays pai sho regularly with the Dragon of the West these days. He’s teaching a King how currency works. Spirits, what is his life.

“But he knows time has passed,” Aang points out. “I’m sure he knows all those things, too. Bato would have told him.”

“Yeah,” Sokka agrees reluctantly, swallowing back the uncomfortable awareness that knowing something and seeing something are different. “What if I’m not…”

“What?” Aang prompts, when it's clear Sokka isn’t going to finish the thought on his own.

“What if I’m not what he expects?” Sokka says all in a rush, refusing still to open his eyes. “What if he doesn’t think the plan is any good?” What if he looks at Sokka and decides that Sokka still isn’t enough, as a strategist or a warrior or fuck, as a son. What if Sokka is going to meet his Chief, not his Dad?

“The plan is good, Sokka,” Aang assures, leaning over to poke Sokka until he finally drops his arm from his eyes to glare at Aang. “You wouldn’t have all the people you do behind it if it wasn’t.”

Sokka grunts. “I guess.” Objectively, he knows it’s a good plan. He’s been working on it ever since the Spirit Library. He just…

“Do you really need your dad to tell you that it’s good?”

“Sokka hides his eyes again in the crook of his elbow, squirming. “…I *want* him to.” Spirits, he didn’t realize he was still this much of a sucker for external validation. It’s not exactly a confidence-inducing revelation.

“It’s going to be okay, Sokka,” Aang says, somehow managing to sound both soothing and chipper. “You’re the Plans Guy. This is your thing. We wouldn’t have made it this far if it weren’t for you.”

“…Thank you,” Sokka says after a moment, peeking out from beneath his arm.

Aang shrugs. “I’m not saying anything that isn’t true.”

“Still.” Sokka shoves himself back upright now that he’s no longer being crushed by his existential dread. “Thanks for saying it, buddy.”

Aang grins, turning back toward Appa’s reins and gently pulling them into a course correction. Sokka isn’t sure that they need the correction, but he thinks that Aang is still reveling in the novelty of being able to do it again. It's good, to see Aang regaining some of his balance after living so long and so uncomfortably in his state of Appa-separation-induced anger.

“Are you nervous at all?” Sokka asks, moving toward the front of the saddle to keep him company. “You’re following your literal dreams on a spirit quest or whatever, that’s got to be scary.”

“Nope!” Aang says cheerfully. “Not at all! I’m excited to learn about chakras!”

“…Right.”

“And I’m excited to master the Avatar state,” Aang adds on, like mastery of destructive power beyond imagining is less important than seeking knowledge, which…is a very Air Nomad way to think.

“Wait.” Sokka sits a little more upright. “That’s what you’re doing? Mastering the Avatar state?”

“Yup! Mastery of the chakras leads to mastery of the spiritual connection that allows access to the power of my past lives.”

Sokka…followed very little of that. But. “That sounds great. Awesome. Please…do that. That’s wonderful.” No more—or at least, only planned—scary-glowy-bendy-melty-explosions would be great. Excellent, really. Zuko isn’t the only one who has nightmares about it.

&#45;-

Zuko’s sense of rightness lingers past that first moment of truly waking from his fever. It sits somewhere in his chest, lingers low in the back of his mind, moves easily along every curve of his inner flame. It stays with Zuko through the rest of the day after waking, through the realization that he was unconscious through the last days before Sokka’s trip and that now Sokka is away, even through interacting with Uncle and customers again, which is a genuine, quietly baffling surprise.

Zuko isn’t used to feeling so…whatever this is. Content? At peace? Resolved, but not in an aggressive way? Even when he’s with Sokka and relaxed in that moment, part of Zuko is always aware that it’s a *moment*. Even Zuko isn’t so good at living in the present that he could ever truly forget the inevitability of Sokka leaving.

But for the first time in a long time, Zuko feels like he’s moving through a world that actually makes sense. That *he* finally makes sense. Like maybe this time Zuko changed in the heat of fever instead of the world changing around him. Like he’s been swept with cleansing fire and actually survived it, instead of what usually happens in the Fire Sage’s stories, leaving behind a clarity bright enough to follow. For the first time in months—years, maybe—he feels like he can actually articulate, even just to himself, what *he* wants. That he can finally see the path he needs to set himself toward.

It feels good, to have a purpose again. A reason for being. There’s an undercurrent of steadiness to his inner flame that he's been missing for months, had been trying and failing to resign himself to living without, and it feels a little more like he can live in his own skin again having it back. And Uncle seems delighted by Zuko’s contentment, or whatever it is he's feeling. His newfound levelness. He keeps sneaking not-at-all-subtle glances, as if he doesn’t quite trust the quiet on Zuko’s face to still be there.

Zuko knows he would normally resent that kind of checking in, but it doesn't bother him this time. After all, it’s an expression Zuko’s worn infrequently enough that he himself keeps being aware of the new shape his features want to relax into, the way his scar is getting gently pulled in new ways. Zuko doesn’t push back against Uncle's staring, even though he could, even though he usually would. It seems to make Uncle happy to see whatever he is seeing, and after all, indulging Uncle is the least Zuko can do, for now.

&#45;-

Sokka’s barely-settled nerves crackle back to life as he watches Aang fly away, Appa growing smaller and smaller until he’s just another fluff of white against the blue sky. Aang deserves some bonding time with Appa, just the two of them. And he seems excited to meet whatever guru is sending summons via dreams, which…Sokka can’t really muster the energy to be annoyed about, but wouldn’t a hawk be more reliable? Why does it all have to be so Spirit-y?

Five days, Sokka reminds himself as he finally loses sight of Appa entirely. Aang will be gone for five days. No time at all, really. But an eternity to be outside the walls after so long in Ba Sing Se. An eternity, if this doesn’t go well.

Sokka fixes his hair, checks his weapons, makes sure his wrist wraps are neat and straight, reties his boots, resettles his satchel, and okay, Sokka can admit that he’s just stalling now. He forces himself to move, trekking across the rocky sand toward the encampment tucked into the curve of the bay. He tries to keep his pace steady, not too hurried, not too slow. Is he swaggering too much? Or not enough? How much should a warrior swagger? Maybe he should grip his weapons? But that would be stupid, Sokka isn’t expecting a fight. But he’s so good with his boomerang, now, and shit, maybe he should have borrowed one of Zuko’s swords because he’s halfway decent at that too these days, but Sokka didn’t even think to go look for where Zuko had stashed them, and besides—

Sokka’s thoughts fizzle out—probably for the best—when he rounds the curve of rocky hillside and sees blue. The water, sure, yes, whatever, it looks great in the morning light. But the *tents*. They’re all shades of blue, Water Tribe blue, *Southern* Water Tribe blue, none of that blue-purple weirdness from the North. And it’s not just the tents, the men are in blue too —so many men, all with braids and hair beads, necklaces and earrings belts of bone and shell and leather.

For a moment Sokka doesn’t know what to do. He hasn’t seen so much of home in one place in years. He can barely process that he’s seeing it now.

“Hey.” A voice interrupts his thought as a broad-shouldered boulder of a man frowns at him from the edge of camp. “If you’re done cleaning your weapons already then pitch in with the sails.”

“Uh.” Sokka glances around, but there’s no one else the man could be talking to. “What?”

The man lets out a put-upon sigh. “Newbies. This is what happens you mix up the crews, you have to reteach everyone how to do everything.”

“Oh, no, I’m not—”

“*Sokka?”*

Sokka whirls toward the new voice, gaping at the man in front of him. “…*Panuk?”*

Panuk—because it is him, actually him, years older and with *scuff* and *scars* and *shoulders* and Sokka can barely wrap his mind around it—lets out a whoop of delight and dashes forward—*that* is familiar at least—forgoing the traditional Water Tribe greeting in favor of catching Sokka into a bone-crushing hug. Sokka wheezes, hugging back, laughing in disbelief as Panuk finally drops him back onto his feet.

“You got *tall*,” Panuk marvels, which is a ridiculous thing to say because he’s nearly a foot taller than Sokka remembers.

“You have *biceps*.” Panuk used to look like he would blow away in a strong wind.

They burst into borderline hysterical laughter. It’s absurd that this person in front of him is the friend Sokka used to know. Panuk seems to feel the same sense of giddy unreality, which is a relief. Sokka wouldn’t want to be the only one giggling in the corner.

Others wander over, curious, attracted by the sound of their laughter. Sokka doesn’t recognize them all—they must be from other villages—but the ones Sokka does know are grinning and shouting and clasping his forearm and pulling him into rough, welcome one-armed hugs like they need to touch him to believe he is there.

“Our little Sokka, all grown up!” Toklo crows, miming brushing away tears.

Sokka rolls his eyes even though part of him could actually burst into happy tears that at least some people never change. “Are you starting to stoop now, in your old age?”

As comebacks go, it isn’t particularly witty or original. But everyone shouts and whoops and laughs anyway, and Sokka can’t hold back his grin even if he wanted to. Sokka is *bantering* with them, and they aren’t just humoring it, they’re embracing it and hitting back and treating him like he’s one of the men. Not a child, or a stranger. Like he’s been here the whole time.

“You’re a sight for sore eyes, kid!”

“He’s not a kid anymore, don’t you remember?” Sokka staggers as an arm is slung around his neck. Tulok is as solid as ever. “This one went ice dodging, he’s a man now!” That sets off another round of whooping and teasing and good-natured ribbing that has Sokka blushing.

“Alright, alright!” Panuk calls, waving the other warriors back. “Let a man breathe! Besides, I’m sure he’s here for the Chief, not you idiots.”

There are boos and jeers all around, at that, but Panuk just makes a rude gesture and jerks his head for Sokka to follow. Sokka matches his stride as they move through camp toward the large tent Sokka can see sitting at the center, fisting his slightly-shaking hands at his sides when really he wants to wring them together, or fiddle with his wrist wraps. Or, honestly, reach for Panuk’s hand, which is an impulse to suppress. Sokka isn’t used to being near anyone—and *men—*his age other than Zuko. And Zuko is the only guy he’s ever walked beside like this.

Soon they’re at the tent and all thoughts evaporate right out of Sokka’s head. He blinks furiously as he ducks through the entryway, pausing at the transition from daylight to firelight. His eyes adjust just as his dad glances up from across a low table, looking lean and hard, fierce, Hakoda’s eyes lighting as a smile breaks over his face. “Sokka!”

“Dad,” Sokka breathes, blinking again against the sudden prickling behind his eyes. Hakoda stands and opens his arms like there isn’t anything else he would ever do, and Sokka stumbles forward, falling into his embrace. He wants to say something, some greeting, something impressive and man-to-man and adult, but he’s choked up with his relief. His dad is here, and Sokka is welcome, and everyone is safe and alive, and Hakoda might feel bonier than Sokka remembers but he smells just the same and hugs just as good. It feels almost like coming home.

&#45;-

Eventually, they part and Sokka belatedly realizes with a flush of embarrassment that Bato is there too, seated at the table and looking amused to finally be noticed. “It’s good to see you too, Sokka.”

“Uh, hey. You look better.” Sokka winces—Spirits, he’s just putting his foot right into his mouth already—but Dad laughs and Bato just rolls his eyes.

“It would be hard for him to look worse.”

Bato gives Hakoda a dry look. “I bet you say that every day when you look in the mirror.”

“I say that every day when I—” Hakoda cuts himself off with a glance at Sokka, who raises both hands.

“Don’t stop on my account.” Sokka hasn’t heard their teasing in too long.

Hakoda snorts, though, shaking his head and wrapping an arm around Sokka’s shoulders. “How long are you with us?”

“Five days.” Not nearly enough time, now.

Hakoda grins. “Plenty of time for business later, then. My son is here! This calls for a celebration.”

Sokka lets himself be dragged back out into the daylight, feeling like he must be visibly glowing. Even Bato’s laughter at how flustered and pleased Sokka is can’t smother the feeling. He grins in response to Dad’s happiness, chest swelling with pride, wondering if this is what it feels like to be a firebender and always be lit from the inside by an inner flame.

&#45;-

The celebration has been swirling for hours and Sokka is dizzy with laughter. It started impromptu, far too early for a proper party, but Sokka has the impression that everyone has been itching for an excuse to cut loose. Sokka knows that he’s probably just a convenient flashpoint for releasing some tension. He really only knows some of these people, and being the Chief’s son doesn’t mean as much in the South as it does in the North. But that doesn’t stop him from feeling stupidly happy at the enthusiasm that meets his presence, at the welcome, at being treated like one of the men.

Things are getting weird, this far into the night, but Sokka still throws himself with zeal at every apparently secret ritual and rite of passage to signify your manhood that gets called out from the crowd. Sokka *knows* they’re just made-up excuses to convince someone from another crew to do something ridiculous, because there’s no way anyone genuinely needs to prove they can hold a handstand for the duration of a successful tongue twister in order to be considered a man. But it sure is fun, watching everyone give it a try.

Sokka falls out of his latest attempt, breathless with laughter at the sight of Panuk red-faced and triumphant and leaning dangerously to the side as the crowd roars around him. Sokka picks himself up from the sand, stumbling out of the danger zone as Panuk begins to keel over in earnest to a chorus of good-natured disappointment. Sokka wriggles free as the men collapse on Panuk in drunken congratulation, shamelessly abandoning his friend in favor of more food.

Sokka can’t remember anything like this. Even before the men left, there were never enough people in the village for something on this scale. It’s amazing and precious and Sokka never wants it to end. This is what he’s fighting for—the sounds of raucous laughter and unencumbered revelry returning to the South.

“The men are all excited you’re here,” Bato comments from his spot by the fire, shifting to make room.

Sokka rolls his eyes, grabbing a skewer of meat and dropping down beside Bato into a little pocket of quiet. “They’re just excited for an excuse to let off some steam.” Sokka knows the sharp, uncontrollable way happiness can hit you when you finally let yourself feel it after so long keeping it subdued.

Bato smiles, unruffled. “Some excuses are better than others.”

Sokka shrugs, but he still can’t stop grinning, and he won’t argue with that.

“You seem more sure of yourself than you did a few months ago,” Bato comments after a moment, the statement nice and bland.

“I…yeah. I guess.” Which isn’t a very self-assured answer. But compared to where Sokka was when Bato last saw him, fresh from captivity and keeping Zuko-sized secrets from everyone? Sokka feels like he’s lifetimes away from who he was then. Sokka is planning a fucking *invasion* now, when back then he was barely sure he could get Katara and Aang from one point to another the next day. He can trace every mark of Zuko’s hands on his skin now, if he cares to—which he does, often—with none of the tangled confusion he might have felt back then over the fact that wearing Zuko’s touch gives him contentment and warmth.

Bato breaks through his musings, eyes thoughtful on Sokka’s face. “Are you happy?”

Sokka pauses to actually think before answering, to consider all the craziness of his life, the danger and the travel and his worries for Zuko and the stress over his plans. And to hold all that up against the fact that his little sister is thriving, his friends are well, that Sokka has a purpose and chance to make a difference in this war, that he and Zuko are…something, to each other. That maybe they could be more, if Sokka can figure out how. “Yes. I am.”

“Good.” Bato takes a sip from his wineskin, eyes fixed on the fire in a way that says his attention is fixed on Sokka. “Did you leap?”

“Yeah,” Sokka admits quietly, fiddling with his skewer. “I did.”

Bato releases a slow, careful breath that Sokka isn’t quite sure how to read. “Did you get caught?”

Sokka’s hand unconsciously moves to his wrist wrap, tracing the familiar streak of the burn underneath. “Not the first time.”

Bato considers his words. “And the next?”

“…It’s harder. To jump again.” When Sokka already knows how much it hurts to hit the ground.

“But you did.”

Sokka sighs, tipping his head back, eyes automatically finding the moon in the sky. Despite his best efforts not to, despite not even noticing it happening… “Yeah. I did.” Toph would have a field day, if she were here for Sokka finally admitting it.

“And?”

“…I think so.” It’s more intimidating than Sokka thinks it should be, to actually put words around all that's unspoken between him and Zuko.

“Good. Good.” Bato offers the wineskin to Sokka, politely pretending not to see when Sokka nearly drops it as he fumbles with the skin and his skewer and his surprise. “I’m happy for you.”

“Thanks,” Sokka says, taking a sip and immediately choking because this is *not* wine. “Did you tell Dad?”

“No.” Bato takes the skin back with a smirk for Sokka’s coughing. “This is yours to tell.”

“Right,” Sokka mutters, eyes watering and voice tight over impending Important Talks. “Thanks.”

Bato laughs as he puts the cork back in his moonshine and rises to his feet. “Don’t let fear hold you back there, either.”

“I’m not,” Sokka protests weakly, even though he totally is.

Bato just makes another amused noise, ruffling Sokka’s hair and wandering back toward the celebration. Sokka watches him go, absently fixing his wolf tail before grabbing his skewer back up and taking a moment to just…appreciate the fact that he’s here, with people who care enough to ask things like that. That they’re all here. Sokka is sure that there are faces missing that he will notice in the morning when it’s not so hectic, losses he will mourn. But for now, Sokka is content to sit with the idea that everyone is safe and whole.

A sudden cheer has him glancing back toward the circle of younger men. He’s sure Panuk is up to something again. He should join them, but Sokka wants to just…take a moment, first, to soak in all the shouting and reveling under Yue’s light, like there’s no reason for anyone not to be happy. It’s a good sight. A good sound, and he wishes that Katara and the others were here to see it. All the others.

What would Zuko think, of the stew with its heavy salt and the skewers of meat, of the moonshine, of the games and the storytelling and the teasing? Sokka wants to find out. He wants Zuko not just here but also in the South, seeing all this as it should be. He wants to experience it all himself and then all over again through Zuko’s eyes. Sokka smiles to himself as he pictures Zuko’s social awkwardness coming up against the Tribe’s aggressive sociableness, spinning out daydreams and possibilities until Panuk finally shouts out, calling Sokka back into the fold.

&#45;-

Zuko doesn’t think he’s ever seen someone in a more ridiculous outfit than the messenger pausing for dramatic effect in the doorway of the Jasmin Dragon, and he used to regularly spend time around Fire Sages. It’s…a lot. Layers of brocade and pleating and lace, which really shouldn’t all be together, chains, jewels, a hat worse than the Head Sage—Zuko makes a quick apology to Agni for thinking it—multiple layers of underrobes and tunics. None of it should work together, and none of it does, but everyone reacts with the kind of hushed stillness that says they recognize the poor man’s standard uniform.

The Earth Kingdom is truly something else.

The man takes a few stately steps into the Jasmine Dragon in a mess of rustling and clanking that would immediately irritate Zuko’s unscarred ear, if he weren’t purposefully lingering in the kitchen door instead of working the floor. Best to stay here, he decides as he takes in the man’s snooty expression, and not put himself in the path of temptation.

Uncle approaches the man with hurried steps—a messenger so important that people come to him, then—and Zuko melts further back into the doorway. He can’t hear the words being exchanged, can only read the man’s imperiousness and Uncle’s anxious eagerness turning to sudden stillness and then bow after bow after bow. The patrons murmur and smile and a few even clap, so whatever it is, it can’t be that bad. Zuko slips into the kitchen and waits. He has tea he needs to keep at the proper temperature while Uncle handles whatever this is.

Uncle is trembling when he finally comes into the kitchen, gasping in tight breaths and dabbing at his eyes. Zuko shoots upright in alarm, reaching for the stove’s fire before settling back when he realizes that the expression on Uncle’s face is one of happiness, not distress.

“Nephew, I have just received the greatest news,” Uncle says, smiling beatifically.

Zuko…is pretty sure that his idea of great news is still not Uncle’s, so he better ask. “What?”

“The Jasmine Dragon has been asked to serve tea to the Earth King!” Uncle’s joy is quiet, but he’s still more excited than Zuko has ever seen him. It’s a startling moment, one edged with chagrin, to realize that Uncle has never been this outwardly delighted before, at least not around Zuko. It probably doesn’t reflect well on Zuko to only notice how much sorrow and heaviness Uncle carries behind his quiet calm until it’s been lifted.

“I could never have hoped for this,” Uncle continues, hands clasped before him almost in prayer. “Even being invited to the Upper Ring was more than I could ever have dreamed. To serve the King my very own tea!”

Zuko hums a listening noise, hands moving without the need of conscious thought to take the sencha off the stove and slide the next order of black tea onto the burner. To serve tea to the man whose city Uncle once tried to conquer, who nominally commanded the army that killed his son. Strange, how things change.

“Nephew, there is no greater feeling than following your dreams,” Uncle says with some of his usual gravity. “And I can think of no better thing than to have this dream come true with you by my side.”

Zuko offers a hint of a smile and a little shrug, attention focused on the pot of lavender because it really does taste like wet garbage unless you get the heat point and timing just right. “When are we supposed to be there?”

“Tomorrow!”

Zuko risks a glance away from the tea, moving one hand to the pot to track the temperature with his bending. “That’s not a lot of time.” That’s actually so little time that Zuko wonders if the invitation is a genuine expression of goodwill and not some kind of trap. A politically connected rival teashop owner? There are weirder things, in the Upper Ring.

“I know, we can waste no time getting ready! Oh, I don’t even know what blends he prefers, how can I—” Uncle is off, fretting about the kitchen, and once he has the lavender ready, Zuko gently shepherds Uncle toward his blending station. Uncle can work his nerves out on new blends and Zuko can concentrate on pounding out orders. He should be able to split his attention between the shop floor and bending fresh brews in the back, as long as no one orders anything too demanding or tries to actually talk to him.

Zuko pauses, considers their usual clientele.

Well, Zuko is just going to have to do his best. He can be fine, with a day more of this. With helping Uncle realize his dream. It will make Uncle happy, and Zuko is trying to give Uncle as many little happy things to hold on to as he can, so that the memories won’t all be difficult ones.

Zuko wants to follow his own path, after all. Is planning to, even if it’s still just in small ways that Uncle hasn’t noticed yet, because Zuko wants to break it to him as gently as possible. He wants to choose his words carefully when he does it, because he thinks Uncle will have a harder time than even Zuko did with finally accepting the fact that Zuko’s way forward doesn’t lie within Ba Sing Se

The silence is deafening. Sokka can hear the crash of waves against the rocky beach, the sound of seabirds, the muffled noise of the men talking outside, the quiet rustling of the tent in the breeze. Inside the tent, though, there’s nothing except the crackling fire. Sokka might normally take comfort in that, but this one isn’t flickering to a rhythm he recognizes.

Finally, one of the second mates stirs, and like that’s permission the other captains and their seconds begin to shift, and lean, and whisper. Does that mean the man is important? Shit, Sokka can’t remember which ship he’s from. Sokka promptly forgot which ships *all* the captains and their seconds were representing, actually. Which is not good, so not good, Spirits, don’t let that be the thing that makes them distrust his ability, or not believe in the plan, or—

“There’s a reason the Fire Nation hasn’t been directly attacked in centuries,” the second points out, not antagonistic but not exactly warm either. “You need a fleet, and they know it. The Fire Nation has the best navy in the world.”

“Not better than the Water Tribe,” one of the other seconds calls out in a fine show of tribal pride that ignores quite a bit of reality, considering the state of the war.

“They’ve got more resources,” the first second—okay, this is getting hard, Sokka is just going to call him Beads in his head and hope it doesn’t slip out—sighs, like it’s a debate that’s been had too many times to be worth rehashing. “It doesn’t matter if we’re better sailors when they’ve got all that technology, and when they can control our access to lumber.”

One of the captains stirs, a particularly grizzled-looking man. “The Fire Nation fleet is diminished, though, after their attempt to take the Northern Water Tribe. It’s an opening.”

Sokka can’t hide his flinch, to hear the North—bodies washing up on the shore for days, funeral pyres so big that you could see them stretching down the beach from within Agna Qel’a’s walls, Yue choking for air—described as ‘an opening.’

Grizzled Man notices. “You were there?”

“Yes.” Sokka is impressed by how level he manages to sound.

Beads grunts. “Bad business, that.”

“Yes,” Sokka agrees, voice hollow.

Pride Guy leans forward, eager. “If you were there, does that mean you know what the Northern Water Tribe did? To defeat them?”

Sokka stares, nonplussed. “I mean…I don’t know if I would put it that way. But, I mean— technically, yeah.”

“Well? What was it?”

Sokka glances around the assembled leadership of the Southern Water Tribe, seeing nothing but shades of curiosity in the faces looking back. Do they really not know? But it was only half a year ago, he realizes with a sense of sudden unreality. And it’s not like the Northern Water Tribe leaves the North, or like the Fire Nation would share it. “The Fire Nation killed the Moon Spirit, and the Ocean Spirit possessed the Avatar in vengeance and shredded the fleet.” The silence is deafening as Sokka adds, “I wouldn’t rely on it happening a second time. Personally.”

“But the moon…” Bato glances upward, like he’s suddenly questioning whether he actually saw it last night.

Sokka stares at the fire in the center of the tent, some force of pure will keeping his voice steady. “Princess Yue sacrificed her life for the Moon Spirit’s.” Which might not be technically correct, according to Aang, but it’s how Sokka sees it. A trade that Sokka doesn’t know how to stop resenting for having to happen in the first place.

“Tui and La,” Beads mutters, looking horrified. “How did it even get to that?”

Sokka wishes he knew. He still asks himself nearly every day. “Lack of planning. Lack of imagination. Lack of resources. Take your pick.”

“But they have so much!” Pride Guy protests.

“Yeah,” Sokka says grimly, trying not to let not-all-that-old anger spark, because he’s well-aware that his particular hurt can become destructive. “I know. They got complacent, or something. They wouldn’t even let their women bend when they were being directly attacked.” Healing is useful, but twice the number of trained distance fighters wouldn’t have hurt.

“That’s half their power, gone,” someone whispers, aghast.

Hakoda speaks for the first time. “Katara…”

“Made her opinion known,” Sokka says with a humorless smile.

Hakoda frowns, looking troubled. “I’m glad that you were there to help your sister.”

Sokka eyes him sidelong. “She’s a Master bender. She didn’t need my help.” He wonders if Hakoda has registered yet that Katara has grown up, too. Does Hakoda hear ‘master’ or ‘Master’ when Sokka talks about her waterbending?

A throat clears from the back, trying to break up the tension. “It must be nice, traveling with your sister? I wish we had some people around who knew how to cook instead of these knob heads.”

It’s a joke, complete with elbowing his companions on the ribs. Sokka just stares, flat. “I can cook.” It might be a recent development, in the scheme of things, but he isn’t going to share that part of it. Not when he is too busy watching them squirm and enjoying the way Dad is glaring them down from across the fire.

Beads shakes his head in a rattle of…beads and tries to get them back on track. “So the Fire Navy is maybe less of an issue than it’s been in the past. But you said not everyone would travel by sea.”

“No,” Sokka says, happy to turn back to the plan and away from his relationship with his sister. “There are too many people. It would be too easy to scout it in advance, especially with how central Caldera is. That’s why we need small teams to infiltrate the interior separately. Then we assemble and strike. The island looks like this…”

&#45;-

Sokka feels like a puppet with its strings cut when the men finally start getting up, speaking quietly amongst themselves and beginning to depart in clumps and clusters. Sokka should probably get up too, maybe try to wiggle into a few conversations and see what way the wind is blowing. The kind of thing Toph is always telling him to do in those ‘just tea’ meetings at the palace that are never just tea. But Sokka’s pretty sure his knees won’t hold if he tries to get up right now, and he doesn’t think keeling over onto the rugs will help his case. He’s still feeling shaky from being grilled over his plan for what feels like hours, trembling through a different kind of post-adrenaline crash than the ones he’s used to following a fight.

Spirits, he’s going to have to do this again tomorrow, if all goes well. The captains and their seconds will come back with questions, and clarifications, and suggestions. Assuming that they don’t reject the plan outright, of course. Which means that doing this all again tomorrow is a *good* outcome.

Sokka wants to just crawl under a blanket and never come out again.

Hakoda is still sitting, though, and is making no move to get up even as the tent empties, so maybe it isn’t remarkable, maybe it won’t be a sign of weakness or uncertainty that Sokka isn’t standing. Bato lingers a moment, clearing out behind the last of the men with a speaking glance for Hakoda that Sokka can’t read.

“Well done, Sokka,” Hakoda says when the tent flap drops and it’s just them for the first time since Sokka landed on the shore. “I couldn’t have done it better myself.”

“Really?” Sokka feels even shakier with relief, sitting on his hands to hide the way they’re wavering.

“You did great,” Dad assures him with an understanding smile.

“They asked so many questions…” If Sokka had just managed to explain it better from the start…Maybe he should have started with the timing, instead of the map, or—

“You got them thinking,” Dad says, like that’s all that matters.

“That one guy, though…”

“Tanloq is always like that,” Dad says, rolling his eyes. “You handled him fine.”

“You didn’t exactly help.”

Hakoda raises his eyebrows, mild and unbothered by the hint of accusation in Sokka’s words. “You didn’t need my help.”

Sokka flushes. “Oh.” He ducks his head, but he can’t hide his grin as warm pleasure blooms in his chest. Spirits, when was the last time Sokka smiled this much when Zuko wasn’t around?

“Come on,” Dad says, rising to his feet. “They need some time to digest it all. There’s nothing to do but wait, now. I’ve got some work I could use your help with. Unless there’s something else you want to do?”

“No! That sounds great.” Sokka bounces to his feet, newly re-energized as they step into the late morning sunlight. And hungry, too, now that he’s calmed down enough to notice. He sneaks a peek at his dad, trailing a step or two before managing to match his stride—Sokka isn’t used to having to stretch quite so far to keep up.

And Sokka does have something he wants to talk to Hakoda about, a very large, firebender-sized something. But the idea of working next to Dad, helping him because he wants Sokka there—it’s too good to pass up.

Sokka has four more days. More than enough time for Zuko, somewhere in there.

&#45;-

Zuko watches Agni set from the back terrace railing, a cup of tea from Uncle in hand. It’s warm and Zuko is absently playing with the heat of it, pulling it away, feeding it back, making it tremble, watching the way the steam dances in the cool air. Tomorrow is the big day for Uncle. They’ve planned all they can, though Zuko can still hear Uncle in the kitchen going through their packed supplies against the list Zuko made, just one more time, just to be sure, which is what Uncle said three re-checks ago.

Zuko will finish his tea before going back inside and trying to redirect Uncle toward dinner. He can use the time it takes him to get through the cup to rebuild his patience. And to check a few items off his own list, the one Zuko started building when he woke from his fever, the one he can never commit to paper.

Earlier today Zuko had counted his share of the tips that he inexplicably managed to earn between the Lower Ring and the Jasmine Dragon—Jin would have some things to say about Zuko’s particular brand of customer service, if she saw the amount. It’s enough for one good sword, or maybe two okay ones. And boots. These city shoes Uncle found him after Lake Laogai are barely more than slippers. They would never hold up on the road. Zuko can get boots cheap, though. He might be a stickler for shopping in the Middle Ring for weapons— the Lower Ring would be too cheap, the Upper too ostentatious—but Zuko is perfectly fine scouring the Lower Ring for a pair of used boots that fit well enough. He hasn’t had a new pair in years, after all, there’s no need to start caring about that now.

And then it will be on to the part that involves significantly less planning, which means it’s the part most solidly in Zuko’s wheelhouse.

The day after tomorrow, then, it can start. Zuko will be there for Uncle on his big day, and the Jasmine Dragon is already scheduled to be closed afterward, which means Zuko has the afternoon free. Zuko would normally give the time to Sokka, if Sokka were here. Which he isn’t, which he won’t be for three more days, because he isn’t just on a trip, he's on an overnight. A visit. Or something. Which Sokka told Uncle, not Zuko. Which is fine. Zuko was sick and Sokka didn’t know the timing before, and Sokka does important things that can’t wait, and Zuko gets it. He understands. It’s fine. Sokka has his life. And that’s a good thing, because Zuko will have his own again soon, too.

&#45;-

Dinner is quieter that night, just Dad and Bato and the men that Sokka knows from home. Spirits are just as high as yesterday’s revelry, but it feels more intimate. Everyone here is genuinely celebrating, is actually happy that Sokka is here.

They swap stories, Sokka trying to relay what he can remember of home, sticking to lighthearted mischief and avoiding things like first steps missed, and toddlers who became little kids, and little kids who stopped asking for their fathers a long time ago. The crew brags in turn about brave deeds, and teases each other for their exaggerations, and soon they’re all making light of the things that terrified them at the time, trying to one-up each other.

Sokka manages to impress them—something he takes great pride in—with having survived not one but two volcanic eruptions. Hakoda looks a little green by the end of the story, which earns the Chief his own laughter. It’s good, and nice, and Sokka is happy, and keeps glancing to his right expecting Zuko to be there. Sokka didn’t realize just how much he associated this kind of feeling with his firebender. With nights spent in Iroh’s kitchen or afternoons sneaking away from the teashop for a loosely sanctioned break.

The thought doesn’t sit entirely comfortable over Sokka’s shoulders. It’s not that being with the Tribe isn’t good without Zuko, because being with the Tribe will always be good. But Sokka describes slipping out of a Dai Li ambush using a spinning jumping move, and then has to get up to demonstrate because half the men don’t believe he can do it, and Panuk is the one to ask, “Spirits, Sokka, where’d you learn something like that!” And Sokka shrugs, smiles, hitches a little over his answer, settles on, “A friend.”

And it’s not a lie—he thinks it’s a long time since it would have been one—but it feels disconcertingly close to an evasion that Sokka doesn’t want to have to make. One that he keeps edging toward, as the stories continue and it becomes clear that Sokka hasn’t quite registered how much of his life Zuko has threaded his way into until Sokka is here, trying to talk about it all without mentioning him.

&#45;-

Sokka answers questions on his proposal the next morning and somehow, it’s even worse. He’s not just explaining his ideas anymore, but needing to defend them against people he desperately wants—needs—to see him as a peer, even though they all know is that Sokka got left behind when they all went to war.

The captains and their seconds probe at the timing, at the players involved, at whether Sokka is sure of all that he is saying about the Fire Nation. Sokka has answers for all of it, even if to his own ears ‘libraries’ and ‘research’ and ‘traveling a lot’ feel inadequate as sources when it’s really more like, ‘I’m maybe doing something that could be called dating with the banished Crown Prince of the Fire Nation and he isn’t exactly a stickler for withholding if you’re willing to ask.’

Not that Sokka has ever asked anything of Zuko with the eclipse in mind. That feels like a bright line that he doesn’t want to have to force Zuko to draw. He’s just been curious about Zuko, about his life and his nation, about his thoughts, anything that would help Sokka understand him more. Sokka always has been. It’s just that once Sokka knows something, he can’t exactly unknow it when he gets back home.

And Sokka…maybe didn’t wholly realize how much he knows, until he’s discovering in this moment exactly how much of what he’s saying isn’t common knowledge. Until the guard rails around Zuko’s privacy suddenly seem alarmingly less visible, to let Sokka know what he can and can’t say.

It makes Sokka feel like a stuttering mess, tripping over his tongue, rambling, to be having this kind of revelation *now* of all times. But Hakoda is just sitting there, nodding, looking unbothered, and so is Bato, so Sokka pretends that it isn’t terrifying to feel like he’s on his own with only his ideas and his wits for backup. Spirits, even the questions going to Hakoda as Chief are being redirected to Sokka.

But Sokka can’t deny that it’s…bracing, in a way, to know that his dad thinks that he can do this. That the Chief trusts that Sokka can do it without his help. So Sokka grits his teeth and practices some of the steady breathing Zuko is always doing and plows forward, standing on his own two feet—metaphorically, they’re all sitting again, thankfully, water would be more solid than his knees right now.

And eventually it does get easier. Sokka is able to focus on just the one person asking the one question and the one topic they’re asking about, and not everyone and all their eyes and the whole fate of the entire war possibly hinging on whether Sokka can sell these men on the crazy scheme that he’s spent months stitching together.

&#45;-

“They’re going to say yes,” Bato murmurs, face neutral but eyes smiling as the others finish filing out of the tent.

“You don’t know that,” Sokka grumbles, giving Bato a half-hearted glare before dropping his forehead onto his bent knees. He feels like he needs to sleep for days after all that.

“I can tell.”

Sokka peeks one eye open. “How?”

“I’ve been doing this a long time,” Bato says as he leaves, annoyingly cryptic. “I can tell.”

“He’s right,” Hakoda laughs, lingering behind again.

“You think so?” Sokka doesn’t lift his head, hoping that will hide at least some of the neediness he’s suddenly feeling. It’s not that hearing it from Bato isn’t good. But hearing it from his dad is different.

“You’ve done a big thing here, Sokka. A brave thing.” Sokka does look up, at that. “You’ve grown up so much in so many ways.” Dad glances toward the fire before looking back. “It’s hard for a father to take, sometimes, that his boy isn’t a kid anymore. Especially knowing you did it without me. But I am so proud of the man I see in front of me.”

Sokka doesn’t know if it’s possible for any other words to be more perfect than those. He’s so many things right now he can barely breathe. Pleased and flustered and relieved so deep down to his core he didn’t even know he was tense. But he doesn’t let himself dwell in the feeling for more than a few heartbeats, because here is his opening if ever there was one. The perfect opportunity to talk about the man that Sokka has become, and all the ways that he’s grown up. They have privacy and quiet, and Sokka can work his way toward this, feel out the ground and ease his way gently into—

“I have something to tell you,” he blurts out, overly loud and voice climbing enough octaves to surprise them both.

Hakoda cocks his head, looking torn between startled amusement and seriousness. “I’m listening.”

Sokka opens his mouth, reaching for the empty place his words were just a second ago. Of course they just tumble out before he’s ready, and now when he’s on the spot they dry right up.

Hakoda is starting to look concerned when a sudden shout rings out, sharp and urgent, quickly taken up among the men outside. Hakoda surges to his feet, Sokka scrambling out of the tent after him into what Sokka quickly realizes is controlled chaos. Men run between tents, weapons in hands, faces grim, demands and commands thrown across the camp.

“Report,” Hakoda barks and Panuk pops up out of nowhere, Sokka startling so hard he nearly stumbles.

“Four Fire Nation ships, cruising formation,” Panuk says, words quick and clipped.

“Closing?”

“Yes.”

Hakoda grunts. “Have they seen us?”

“Just the ships, from their angle. Not the camp.”

“Good. The tangle mines?”

“Deployed this morning, all in place where we wanted,” Bato says, also appearing out of nowhere, and *fuck*, Sokka does stumble at that one. Is this some warrior skill he’s going to need to learn, how to sneak in plain sight?

Hakoda nods, expression relaxing a fraction even as his shoulders tense. “Prepare for battle, then.”

Bato raises a hand, signaling something, and the chaos begins to flow in a new way around them. “Pants down, punch back?”

Hakoda purses his lips, considering as he casts his eyes around the camp. “That’ll do.”

Panuk catches Sokka’s confusion and leans over to whisper, “We make it look like they caught us by surprise and lure them in by pretending to flee and then we attack them.”

Ah. They call that the ‘Blind Bait n’ Switch.’ Toph loves it. Sokka looks around the camp with new interest, trying to see how the strategy is adapted to a larger scale and the naval setting. They’d have to be much more obvious, with the distances involved, without losing believability…the margin for error, then—

“Men!” Hakoda suddenly roars. “Arm up!”

There are shouts of affirmation—weren’t they already doing that? Or was that some signal? —and Sokka sees groups starting to break off. Some send tents fluttering down in haphazard, disheveled piles while others slip out the far side of camp toward the cliff face. They can come down on the boats without being seen that way, Sokka realizes, as a small group dashes messily and noisily across the sand—a distraction.

Sokka glances at Hakoda, who’s carefully watching the diversion as he pulls on the weapons and armor that Bato hands him. Or maybe he’s watching the first feint to see if the enemy will take the bait.

“Uh…” Sokka glances down, realizing that he has nothing but his scroll case in his hands. “What about me?”

“What about you?” Hakoda spares him half an eye before looking back toward the water.

“Um.”

“You heard me.” Another half glance, this time with the hint of a smile. “The men are arming up.”

Sokka stares, blank for a moment before comprehension dawns. “I—yes—okay!” He grins, sprinting toward the tent where he stashed his travel bag. He’s already starting to feel that familiar pre-battle anxiety that he knows will turn to calm, though less of it than he’s used to. The camp mobilizing is all so organized and orchestrated that it feels almost routine. It’s hard for Sokka to believe that anything could go wrong here, with the way everyone acts like it’s so normal, even though four ships seem like a lot—

Sokka pauses in the middle of strapping another knife into his boot. Not just ships. Fire Nation ships. Full of Fire Nation soldiers acting on orders of their Fire Nation commanders. Sokka hasn’t been pitted against that in a long time. Azula, yes, but Fire Nation soldiers? The regular military grunts that Sokka knows without ever needing to explicitly ask that Zuko cares about, whose lives Zuko would want to preserve?

He’s suddenly moving a lot slower in his battle preparations.

Sokka knows that war isn’t bloodless. He’s known it his whole life, and the part of himself that wants to preserve as many lives as possible—Spirits, especially have so recently talked about the North—isn’t a small one. But this isn’t just bloodlessness in the abstract. This is Sokka, now, dealing with Fire Nation soldiers, now. People that there’s a good chance Zuko might still consider his, even if they don’t consider Zuko theirs anymore.

It’s just that Sokka doesn’t *know.* He and Zuko have never talked about this kind of stuff, but a mutual, unspoken agreement that’s suddenly feeling horribly short-sighted. Sokka never felt the need to press the matter because there wasn’t in Fire Nation in Ba Sing Se beyond Zuko and Iroh themselves. Because Sokka has never struck first, before. And sure, Sokka has been planning for months now something that's basically a first strike, but it’s all been *planning* still. Theoretical. Distant.

This is abruptly, jarringly real.

Sokka sits back on his heels, pressing the palms of his hands to his eyes like he can physically push the uncertainty out of himself. He’s suddenly staring down the exact scenario Katara posed weeks ago, and he likes it even less now than he did then, because the time has come, and Sokka isn't sure he can even see what needs to be done, let alone do it. He feels dangerously immobilized by questioning whether anything needs to be done at all, too acutely aware of all the shades of gray to see the path ahead through the fog of it.

Katara was, so, so right, like always. Sokka should have worked through this, no matter how distant or irrelevant it seemed to life in Ba Sing Se. Spirits, he should have found a way to bring up Zuko with Hakoda before Sokka suddenly needs to decide whether or not to fight the soldiers whose Crown Prince he’s sleeping with, entangled with, dating—which really doesn’t seem like a big enough concept for what he and Zuko have been doing.

Sokka should have figured all this out when he had time to *think*. He should have realized something like this was coming. Katara certainly did. But there’s no war in Ba Sing Se, especially not with Zuko, and Sokka is only now realizing how completely he took advantage of the luxury of that avoidance.

Apparently, Ba Sing Se did make him complacent. Just not in the way he was on guard for. It really would be great for Toph to be here right about now.

&#45;-

Sokka is at Hakoda’s shoulder, tense, settling and resettling his boomerang as he tries to absorb his place in the battle plan through pure proximity, wondering if he will have time to speak or if he should just interrupt sooner rather than later. Bato is in the middle of explaining the backup plan when he abruptly stops talking.

“Is that an air bison?”

Sokka whirls around, following Bato’s confused stare, to see what is definitely Appa swooping in low and fast. “They’re early.”

“Three days early.” Bato and Sokka exchange a glance. This can’t be good. Someone out there must be laughing—probably Aunt Wu—that after pitching himself into a mess of self-inflicted struggle and anguish, Sokka is watching a reprieve swoop in for a landing.

Appa comes in hard, the Tribesmen scattering to clear space as the air bison hits the beach in a gout of sand, skidding to a stop with a groan of effort. Aang doesn’t even drop the reins. “Sokka! We need to go back to Ba Sing Se!”

“What? Aang, there are Fire Nation ships out there, why—”

“Katara is in danger!”

*There* is that pre-battle calm. Sokka feels his adrenaline spike, distantly noting the physical reaction as he starts shuffling through all the contingencies that live in the back of his mind. “What’s going on? How do you know?”

“I had a vision.” Aang throws the words out like a challenge. “She is in trouble, okay? We need to get back!”

Sokka takes a deep breath, recalibrating. “You’re sure? This vision—it’s not just a dream, or open to interpretation. You’re positive?”

“*Yes!”*

“Alright. Give me three minutes to get my stuff.”

“One.”

“Two.”

“Fine, two.”

Sokka sprints across camp, weaving in between the men, unremarkable amid all the other organized madness. He grabs up his bag, stuffing in his plans. Thankfully he already has his weapons. He hesitates a moment before leaving a copy of the schedule behind. Sokka should be able to come back, but just in case…Katara in trouble could mean anything. It could mean she pissed off Toph again. It could mean she finally got fed up with the Kuei and dumped tea on his head. It could mean that she’s fighting for her life and they’ll need to flee or rescue her. Sokka should be able to come back. But better to leave the schedule, to be sure.

Sokka dashes back across camp, skidding to a stop next to Appa. Hakoda is still there, observing.

“You’re going?” Hakoda’s eyes flick up toward Aang. “With the Avatar?”

“Yeah,” Sokka pants, straightening and forcing back his uncertainty. “Katara—”

“Good,” Dad interrupts, cutting off whatever justification Sokka was going to offer up. “Keep each other safe.” Another glance up at Aang. “All of you.”

“You stay safe, too,” Sokka says, needing to *go* but also not sure how to do it. Sokka has never been the one to leave.

“I’ll do my best,” Dad smiles, clasping Sokka’s forearm man to man even though Sokka wants to throw himself into a hug. Sokka holds back, though, because he knows there are some things you can’t do before battle and still be able to fight.

“I had something I wanted to tell you,” Sokka suddenly remembers.

“When you get back.” No ‘if’, just a ‘when.’ “You can tell me then. Good luck.”

“You too,” Sokka forces out, watching as Hakoda strides away, the melee within the camp shifting to revolve around their Chief.

Sokka lets out an undignified yelp as Aang loses his patience and launches Sokka into the saddle in a burst of air. Sokka barely manages to sit upright before Appa lurches into the sky and knocks him flat again. Sokka mutters under his breath—it wasn’t *that* long over two minutes—and peers back toward the ground. The field of battle opens up below him as they climb, not yet engaged, but soon based on the distance between ships.

The plan should work, from what Sokka understands of it, especially with the tangle mines in play. It should be fine. A not insignificant part of Sokka is relieved at the chance to step back from what he was about to do, to make sure that he’s actually prepared to live with the choices he needs to make and whatever consequences will come. To maybe get the chance to have that conversation with Zuko.

But it still feels weird to fly away without knowing how the battle will go, like he’s leaving something unfinished, tools still scattered over the table. Sokka wants to stay and help and make sure everyone comes out safely on the other side, but—

“What did you see in your vision?” Sokka asks, turning to Aang and mentally shifting back into what has to be more urgent to him right now. He needs to plan.

“Not enough,” Aang says, frustrated. “Just danger. Underground, I think. Maybe now, maybe already happened, maybe about to happen.”

“Well shit,” Sokka mutters. Sidelining exploring the tunnel network beneath Ba Sing Se to plan for the eclipse is suddenly looking like a mistake. “We need to prepare for anything, then. Good thing the Kyoshi Warriors are around.” Even if Suki only brought a few of them they can use any extra competent bodies they can get their hands on.

“You have a plan?”

“No. But I will by the time we get there.”

&#45;-

Sokka didn’t factor stopping to pick Toph up into his plans. He hastily starts readjusting a number of working assumptions he’d made about what the fuck exactly they’re dealing with.

“*Toph?*”

“Hey, Twinkletoes,” Toph calls, sliding to a stop on her wave of earth. “Want to give me a lift?”

“What are you doing out of the city?” Sokka asks, urgent, leaning over to help haul her into the saddle. “Does it have to do with Katara?”

“No, I got kidnapped.”

“You got what?” Aang jerks around, Appa lowing in protest at the sudden tugging on the reins.

“It’s okay though. I got away.” She sounds distinctly satisfied about it.

“How?” Sokka asks, because he can tell she wants them to, and also because who knows what information will be relevant to the plan.

Toph’s grin is slow and shows off every single one of her teeth. “I invented metalbending.”

Aang lets out a choked yelp, nearly falling as he whips around again, and Sokka…Sokka doesn’t have time to engage with that statement, beyond noting it as a new tactical option. His mind is too busy going into freefall. If Toph is out here, that means Katara is alone in the city. Underground—already, or maybe now, or maybe about to happen, Spirits Sokka *hates* this vision shit—without an earthbender with her, or already looking for her, or ready to fight at her side.

This means whatever danger Katara is in just got much more immediate. All of Sokka’s plans had placed Toph in Be Sing Se, able to help Katara or start looking for her or fuck, able to get Zuko if things got really out of hand because Sokka knows without needing to ask that Toph has figured out where Zuko lives by now.

Zuko, who was sick, unconscious, helpless the last time Sokka saw him.

Fuck. Everyone alone, then. That’s fine. Everything is fine. Sokka can work with this. Because the three of them might be out of play for immediate action, but Katara still has the Kyoshi Warriors, and that’s not nothing. And Zuko has the Dragon of the West.

If things get really bad it doesn’t matter how sick Zuko was when Sokka left him or how sick he still might be. It doesn’t matter that anything that would be a threat to Katara, companion of the Avatar, would probably be more than happy to also take out Zuko, still very much of royal Fire Nation blood regardless of how exiled he is.

None of that matters, because Sokka is going to have a plan. And everything is going to be *fine*.

## Chapter 32: All Roads Lead To Here

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for some canon typical violence in this one

### Text

Serving tea to the Earth King goes exactly as Zuko expects beverage service for a pampered, sheltered, entitled monarch who pretends the world around him doesn’t exist to go, up until it doesn’t.

They arrive early, because Uncle is full of excited nerves and because Zuko is sure that they’re going to have to cross the whole palace complex to get to whatever room the Earth King decides to take his tea in, because that just seems like the way it would work in Ba Sing Se. The formal invitation Uncle offers is scrutinized, Uncle is scrutinized, Zuko is scrutinized, all their supplies are scrutinized, but with a little sniff—Zuko…strongly dislikes that particular noise—they’re eventually waved through the gates.

A quiet-footed, demure servant whisks them into the palace from there, moving shockingly fast despite her mincing steps. Zuko eyes her feet, reconsidering the value of Earth Kingdom-style indoor slippers. Maybe he’ll keep a pair with him. He’s going to need to do plenty of sneaking, after all, and any kind of footwear that manages to be completely quiet across pavers, wood, marble floor, *and* iron wrought stairs is nothing to turn his nose up at. Or sniff at.

The woman eventually bows them through a pair of ornate double doors, into a surprisingly modest chamber, empty except for a low table, a tall throne, and guards. A secondary, more informal receiving room, Zuko decides, as an aggravated looking chamberlain darts into the room just long enough to snap at Uncle to set up and be ready and not nearly long enough for Uncle to determine what, exactly, they need to be ready for.

“Ready to pour?” Uncle mutters, sorting through their boxes and bags. “Ready to steep? Ready to heat the water? Does he want a full formal service? Sequential tastings? This isn’t a formal throne room, but it *is* the King…”

“If he didn’t say then we can do whatever we want,” Zuko says with something approaching non-hostility, his hands calm and steady as he begins pulling out leaves to measure and place settings to set out. The comment does nothing to calm Uncle—not that Zuko particularly expected it to—but it quickly becomes clear that Zuko’s utter lack of caring about tea is suddenly and unexpectedly a distinct advantage, and one that Zuko immediately decides he will never let Uncle live down. Uncle is nervous like Zuko has rarely seen him, but to Zuko the only difference between this and the Jasmine Dragon or the Lower Ring is that Zuko only has one potential asshole to deal with instead of a whole shop full of them.

Finally, things are set up to Uncle’s satisfaction—the table set, the water boiling, the tea leaves at the ready—and then they wait. And wait. And wait. Zuko can hold a seiza as long as anyone, but this is starting to get ridiculous. There’s only so long they can believably keep this water at a gentle boil, and the room is so painfully silent that the quiet rustle of fabric as Zuko minutely adjusts his weight feels like shoving over a bookcase in a library—which wasn’t, for the record, his fault. Even if Zuko had been the one standing in the wreckage.

“It can’t be too much longer now,” Uncle murmurs, adding leaves to the pot to steep.

Zuko eyes him askance. It can be as long as the Earth King wants it to be.

“Oh, but what if the tea goes cold,” Uncle immediately frets, hands raised like he might try to fish the leaves back out of the teapot. “Or over-steeps.”

“We can brew more,” Zuko points out, wondering if it would be rude to start meditating. If they’re going to sit and do nothing, he might as well use the time for something valuable.

“But we only brought so many leaves!”

“We have plenty.” Probably it would be rude. And Zuko wouldn’t be able to relax, anyway, with all these people in the room. There are a lot of guards along the walls. More guards than Zuko first realized, when he reaches out with his fire sense and realizes there are some in the shadows to the sides of the throne, too, even though there’s no one sitting there to defend.

“It would be good to know when His Majesty will arrive so we can have everything properly ready,” Uncle sighs, shades of disapproval in his tone as he eyes the brewing tea.

Zuko grunts, trying to be casual as he gives the room a careful look. He should have gawped more, coming in. Played up the role of a refugee lifted from his humble origins. Because really, there’s a truly unnecessary number of guards given that there’s no one in the room for them to be guarding, yet. They’re all watching Zuko and Uncle quite intently. And silently. And non-responsively.

…Fuck*.* Zuko belatedly—so, so belatedly—recognizes that kind of blank focus after spending so much time slipping through the Dai Li’s tunnels. He really, really wishes he had his swords right now.

Zuko starts surveying the room again, looking for things that could be used as weapons that wouldn’t immediately come back in the form of earthbended projectiles. A *lot* of pottery, which is expected in a palace. But really, couldn’t they have some more decorative wood? Some metal sculptures? A chair other than a throne? Zuko can’t exactly hurl the table across the room, though he supposes he can always light it on fire as a very obvious and revealing distraction.

Though if he uses the portable burner Uncle brought for the tea…

Movement among the guards—a bare shifting of weight, all in sync—has Zuko tensing, and Uncle perking up and reaching to pour the tea. A slight, dark-clothed figure strides in, Dai Li robes swishing around her legs, hair neat as ever, tied up in a facsimile of a top knot with a giant green bow that bobs along with her every step. And it’s weird—jarring even—to see her in Earth Kingdom colors. They don’t suit her skin tone any more than they do his. But Zuko would recognize his little sister anywhere, no matter what she was wearing.

It takes Uncle a few more heartbeats to recognize her than the instant it takes Zuko. Maybe because Uncle never truly expected her presence in Ba Sing Se, when Zuko knew it was inescapable. And really, he should have known that Azula would find him, not the other way around. He learned that lesson when they were children, after all—the best way to make Azula seek him out was always to try to hide from her.

Uncle stills for half a heartbeat—or three of them, for Zuko—then finishes pouring and takes the cup of tea for himself. It’s the equivalent of a full-body flinch of surprise, and Zuko barely resists the urge to hiss *I told you so* as he rises slowly to his feet, settling his weight and keeping his eyes on Azula as she comes to a stop in front of the empty throne, flanked by Dai Li. She always was one for symbolism.

Zuko meets Azula’s tawny stare, his inner flame nearly-calm within his skin and in his chest in a way that feels…fragile. He can distantly feel his heart rate picking him, his adrenaline beginning to rise, but there’s no surprise in him, only readiness rather than urgency. Apparently, there’s something about the inevitable that cuts right through the possibility of panic.

*Now* the room is painfully silent, and less in a library-destroying way and more waiting-for-the-blade-to-drop. Zuko doesn’t even know where to find a grip on the taut quiet. Azula, of course, has no problems breaking the tension.

“Brother.” Her words are drawling, amused. “It is good to see you again, as always.”

Zuko takes a careful, deliberate breath. “Azula.”

“So kind of you, to accept my invitation.” Zuko’s fire shivers, for a breath. Oh, that’s going to hurt, later, when Uncle realizes that he was never invited to the palace because of his tea.

“What are you doing here?” Zuko asks, and then immediately wants to take the words back because it’s a dumb question, a completely inane question, and her single raised eyebrow says the same. She casts a disinterested glance toward Iroh pinning before Zuko with her gaze again.

“What am I doing? Cleaning up the messes that the men in this family leave behind, it seems,” she says, words nearly tart, her eyes flicking over him to see how he reacts.

Zuko wavers, uncertain. He needs more than just that, to figure out the game she’s playing. “Why did you bring us here?”

“Better question, Brother.” She makes a show of examining the lacquer on her nails. “You might say that I’m consolidating.” Zuko waits for more, refusing to ask what it is that's being consolidated and she smiles, sharp and quick, acknowledging his silence. “Maybe I wanted my family to see my moment of triumph, Zuzu. Maybe I wanted my nearest and dearest to be there when I take the Avatar.”

For a moment Zuko can’t find the breath to speak, motionless as he struggles to hold back any reaction, his inner fire biting under his skin. “You don’t have him yet,” he finally manages to say, and he isn’t supposed to care about that, not anymore, but he can hear the harsh edge to the words that makes it clear to both of them that he does.

“Astute as ever,” Azula says, brushing a speck of probably-imaginary dust off her shoulder. “But I have a Water Tribe peasant.” Her eyes flick back to him. “And that’s basically the same thing, wouldn’t you say?”

Oh, Agni. Zuko’s inner fire turns itself inside out, hard and fast enough to leave him gasping, if he were a thread less controlled right now. But not enough. She’s watching him, waiting, and there’s no way she doesn’t see the way her words hit him like a boot to the gut, the way they make his unscarred ear buzz with the sudden arrival of a panic that he can’t afford right now, even as a hysterical corner of his mind points out that Azula might be wrong about that, that having a Water Tribe peasant in Zuko's experience has never actually translated into having the Avatar.

Fuck, *fuck.* Zuko should have just given her a reaction from the start, instead of challenging her to peel back the layers over his control.

Uncle notices too, or maybe just anticipates, stepping into Zuko’s choked silence. “Do you know why they call me the Dragon of the West?”

Azula wrinkles her nose, all dismissiveness and annoyance, barely glancing at the interruption even as her eyes sharpen with interest. Over the timing of it, Zuko realizes, over the fact that she recognizes the comment as the intervention it is. Agni burn it. “I don’t have time for your stories, old man.”

Zuko, though…Zuko had nothing but time for stories, in the three years on the *Wani*, and no ability to escape then. So *he* knows how the General earned his name, and he readies himself as Iroh takes a deliberate sip of tea and finally rises to his feet.

Zuko’s fire sense is already pushing to be let loose beyond the boundaries of his skin, Zuko allowing it to creep out enough that he can *feel* the way Iroh’s heat contracts, his inner flame concentrating, growing and growing and growing, until there’s no way Iroh could possibly keep it within his skin a moment longer. Zuko lunges behind Iroh’s back, perfectly timed as Iroh’s inner flame flares up and the Dragon of the West exhales a gout of flame.

The Dai Li fall back, shouting in surprise, which honestly is just lazy, to not be prepared for sudden ignition around Imperial firebenders. Azula throws up a clean, neat block, but she clearly isn’t expecting the force behind Iroh’s attack from the bare quarter-step she takes backward under the onslaught of his flames, from the way she narrows her eyes instead of immediately snapping onto the offensive.

Zuko seizes that bare breath of almost-distraction and the cover of Iroh’s theatrics to blast a hole in the wall. It’s just wood and paper, thank anything listening because they don’t have the time or space for blasting through stone. The thin wall crumbles into debris and ash and burning as Zuko kicks out another spiral of fire to force the Dai Li back before breaking for the opening, Iroh covering their retreat.

Zuko isn’t quite sure if the expression tugging at his scar is a snarl or a smile. But Agni, it feels good to let his flames flow free again, to be done with the pretense of *Lee*.

Zuko knows that Dai Li agents won’t take long to recover from even the biggest surprises so he focuses his body on speed, trying to remember how he and Uncle came in, how to get out as they skid through hallways after hallway in the palace. Zuko can pin their direction against Agni’s above him, but the effort of finding Appa made it blindingly obvious that knowing where something is relative to himself doesn’t mean that Zuko knows how to get there. Just because he can feel where outside is, doesn’t mean he can get them outside. And he can’t rely on their route in. Zuko is sure now that they were taken on an unnecessarily long and twisted path to the throne room, one he doesn’t have time to retrace as he and Iroh dodge attacks and shoot flame and crash through paper walls and splintered wood and *fuck*, Zuko wishes he had some real boots and not these glorified house slippers.

Zuko slides under a sudden pillar of rock, nerves tight with anticipation for a roar of blue flame that never comes, that should be there but keeps being absent. He lost track of where Azula is only a few turns after the throne room, which is a terrifying thought on a number of levels. But Zuko knows she’s around somewhere, and he would very much prefer to not be forced into a fight with her.

“Enough of this,” Iroh growls as they take another turn that puts them into a corridor they definitely already ran through if the scorch marks are anything to go by. He punches a fist behind him without breaking stride, blasting a rain of debris down from the ceiling to give them a moment of cover and suddenly coming to a stop. Zuko skids, trying to stop his momentum as Iroh sets his feet into a grounded stance, the General's arms beginning to rotate, two fingers extended, through a familiar form.

Zuko scrambles toward Iroh, ducking around energy beginning to around his body, beginning to trail behind his fingers. Zuko puts a healthy distance between himself and those cold, cold spark and sets himself up to defend Iroh’s back, because the last thing they need right now is misfired lightning exploding too soon. And this hallway is narrow enough, wooden enough, blocked with debris enough, that that they should the bare moment they need for this. Especially when it’s much easier to hold off the Dai Li here in the palace than in the tunnels, in this place where Zuko can use his fire and is surrounded by flammable things. When his fire is already so eager and hungry to whip free, to fill the emptiness in his hands where he keeps expecting there to be swords.

A cold crackle over his skin has Zuko instinctively ducking for cover just before a crash of lightning lances through the room, exploding a wall in a shower of wood and marble. Fuck, that’s a lot of free ammunition to hand the earthbenders. But the agents who weren’t hit by shrapnel seem momentarily stunned by the blast—thank Agni that this must be the Dai Li’s backup squad, the way they’re surprised by everything—so Zuko scrambles to his feet, already trying to tug Iroh along, because if they’re fast enough it won’t matter what the Dai Li have to work with.

They're nearly tripping over each other, Iroh urging him forward, Zuko trying to push him faster, gaining speed as they run toward the opening, clearly intending to jump into the open air beyond. Zuko drops a step behind, covering their retreat by igniting flames around the room and giving Iroh time to clear the landing when he feels a rigid, boiling, almost too-intense fire at his back, like blasting jelly right before it explodes.

Zuko doesn’t need to count the firebenders in the city to recognize Azula’s inner flame. It’s exactly what he would have expected of her.

Zuko’s feet slow almost without his permission, *‘but I have a Water Tribe peasant’* whispering again in his ear. It could be a lie. Zuko knows it could be. He just doesn’t know how much he can gamble on that ‘could.’

For a moment Zuko teeters on the edge of the jump out of the palace, trying to find his balance in the burned-out opening where daylight meets shadows, Uncle looking up from below and Azula at his back. Agni, what a fucking metaphor. He might as well be dreaming.

“Nephew!” Uncle shouts, stumbling to his feet and looking like he’s going to try to come back up, to fight.

“Go!” Zuko’s inner fire is urgent with the knowledge that Azula is at his back, which means she’s here, *here*, with him, not wreaking havoc. “I’ll—I’ll hold her off!”

“Zuko!”

“You need to warn—” Zuko doesn’t dare say the name, not where Azula can hear, but Uncle clearly hears it anyway, his facing twisting with upset and distress and Zuko doesn’t *care*, he just needs Uncle to run. He just needs Uncle to do this one thing.

It doesn’t matter if Sokka is supposed to be out of the city, not coming back for days. He *could* be back early, could have been lured back, a ‘could’ that Zuko is equally unwilling to gamble on. And even if Sokka is away, that just means Azula’s captured Water Tribe peasant is Katara, which makes the threat in Azula’s words just as real, because there’s no world where Sokka doesn’t come for his little sister and end up crashing into Azula.

Uncle is wavering, and more than Zuko needs backup, or rescuing, or whatever Uncle thinks he can give, he needs Uncle to *run.* Uncle's already most of the way to freedom, to warning Sokka, to helping him, to keeping him safe, to giving him as much knowledge as possible so Sokka doesn’t come in blind.
